title: Difference btw fish and plant oil from PDSRG & note SuperOmega-3
content:
Hi [CUSTOMER],

Below is on page 16 or the SuperOmega-3 Fish Oils section in your Practitioner Dietary Supplement Reference Guide (PDSRG). It summarizes the basic difference, which is simply underpowered as it relates to EPA/DHA conversions but has other unique values that a marine source does not. Further, the marine/fish sources are the most studied and only ones that are clinically used for healthy lipid levels. Again, plant sources have value too.

Plant Sources of EPA and DHA

Plant sources, such as nuts and seeds including flaxseed, are rich in the essential fatty acid alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), which can be converted to EPA and DHA, though inefficiently, and therefore are not a suggested source for achieving recommended intakes.11,12,13,14,15 Studies of ALA metabolism in healthy young men indicate that approximately 8% of dietary ALA is converted to EPA and 0–4% is converted to DHA.304,17 In healthy young women, approximately 21% of dietary ALA is converted to EPA and 9% is converted to DHA.16,304 Other potential shortcomings with seed oils/ALA, such as flaxseed, as a source for achieving the daily recommendation for EPA and DHA are that they contain relatively high amounts of omega-6 fatty acids, which compete with the benefits of omega-3s (see Heart Health Section above for more on O6/O3 ratios), including hindering precursor molecule conversion to DHA.11,12,13,14,15,20 To be fair, as described in the Heart Health section, ALA and other components of specific plant oils can contribute other unique health benefits when consumed in proper amounts and especially in the presence of suggested daily intake of EPA and DHA that confirm a >8% O3I.99,100,108

Vegan/Vegetarian and Fish Allergies

From all data, it appears vegans may have to supplement to achieve daily adequate intake of EPA and DHA, with a heavier emphasis on DHA since there is very low to no plant source precursor molecule (e.g., ALA) conversion to DHA as noted above.16,17,304,305 As in fish and krill, plants in aquaculture such as seaweed and microalgae can directly provide DHA and EPA and, in fact, are the primary source of transfer to omnivores (fish consume the algae/seaweed; animals consume the fish).306,307 Additionally, microalgae sources of EPA and DHA may be a more sustainable long-term solution for supplementation as awareness of the need to meet recommendations increases.308 Therefore, supplements from microalgae are a common solution for vegans/vegetarians and persons with fish allergies to help reach recommendations305,309,310 since, as noted, seed or nut oils may not be enough and possibly counterproductive if considered the sole source. For a comprehensive review on veganism and acquiring adequate daily EPA and DHA, including dietary supplement use, readers are referred to the review by [NAME] et al. titled: Alpha-Linolenic and Linoleic Fatty Acids in the Vegan Diet: Do They Require Dietary Reference Intake/Adequate Intake Special Consideration?305 The review found that most studies show that vegans consume very low to no amounts of EPA and DHA unless they supplement. And because of inconsistent intake and conversion of ALA, along with the amount of dietary linoleic acid, vegans may need an ALA daily intake of two to four times the AI/DRI or 2.2–4.4 g/day (or 1.1 g/day per 1,000 Kcals) in the diet in order to achieve the healthier proposed omega-6 to omega-3 ratio of 4:1, and if dietary linoleic acid is higher than recommended, as it usually is, it should be reduced.305 Most of these conclusions add up to a greater need for supplementation than the omnivore, especially in athletes and active persons of all ages.305,309,310 Individuals with fish allergies should check food (claiming fortified with omega-3s) and supplement labels to ensure that the source of the omega-3s in the food is not from fish.

title: Aging speed measurement -biomarkers to measure age
content:
5. I think there's a better way to measure aging for a health/fitness program

For the type of health span/longevity program you're thinking about, I wouldn't rely on one exotic aging test. I'd build a multi-system Aging Score.

Something like:

Metabolic
- HbA1c; fasting glucose; fasting insulin/HOMA-IR; triglycerides; HDL; ApoB
- Homeostatic Model Assessment for Insulin Resistance

Inflammation
- hs-CRP

Organ health
- eGFR/creatinine; ALT/AST/GGT; albumin

Cardiovascular
- resting BP; resting HR; potentially pulse-wave velocity; coronary calcium when clinically appropriate

Body composition
- visceral fat; waist circumference; body-fat %; appendicular lean mass

Physical capacity
- VO₂max; grip strength; lower-body strength; gait speed; balance

Lifestyle/recovery
- sleep duration/quality; physical activity; cardiorespiratory fitness

And then potentially add: DunedinPACE or GrimAge as an interesting molecular layer—not as the final verdict.

That approach is also consistent with the direction aging researchers are moving: aging is multi-system, so composite biomarkers are likely more informative than one clock.

The practical takeaway

If you told me I had to choose between:

A) a $400 epigenetic test saying I'm biologically 58 instead of 65
or
B) knowing my VO₂max, strength, visceral fat, blood pressure, ApoB, HbA1c, insulin sensitivity, CRP, kidney/liver function and muscle mass,

I'd take B without hesitation.

Then I would consider adding Dunedin PACE to B if the goal were to quantify whether a comprehensive longevity intervention appears to be slowing the underlying aging trajectory.

And there is an interesting opportunity here for your Playspan/health-and-performance concept: you could establish a relatively inexpensive “Pace of Aging Score” combining routine labs + body composition + cardiovascular fitness + strength/function and track it every 6–12 months. That would arguably be more useful to a trainer/client than telling someone their theoretical biological age.

Miscellaneous information on speed of aging

Yes. “Speed of aging” can be measured to a degree, and the science is legitimate—but no current test can tell an individual with clinical precision, “you are aging at exactly 0.82× normal.” The field is much better at identifying whether someone appears to be aging faster or slower than peers and predicting future morbidity/mortality risk.

The important distinction is between biological age and pace of aging.

1. Biological age vs. speed of aging

Biological age asks:
“Compared with an average person, how old does this person's biology look?”

So a 65-year-old might have a calculated biological age of 57.

Pace of aging asks a somewhat better question:
“How rapidly is this person's physiology deteriorating right now?”

A pace score might theoretically indicate something like 0.85 biological years per chronological year, versus 1.0 being the population reference. DunedinPACE was specifically developed to estimate this type of rate rather than simply produce an “age.”

2. What biomarkers are actually used?

There are several approaches, and I would divide them into four categories.

| Category | Examples | What it reflects | My view |
|---|---|---|---|
| DNA methylation | DunedinPACE, GrimAge, PhenoAge, Horvath | Epigenetic changes associated with aging/disease/mortality | ★★★★☆ |
| Routine blood chemistry | glucose, HbA1c, CRP, albumin, creatinine, ALP, WBC/lymphocytes | Metabolic, inflammatory and organ-system aging | ★★★★☆ |
| Physical function | VO₂max, grip strength, gait speed, muscle mass, strength | Actual functional aging | ★★★★★ |
| Other molecular markers | proteomics, metabolomics, telomeres, glycan profiles | Different aspects of cellular aging | ★★★☆☆ / emerging |

One well-known clinical-style calculation is Phenotypic Age (PhenoAge). It combines chronological age with routine biomarkers such as albumin, creatinine, glucose, CRP, alkaline phosphatase and several blood-cell measures. These kinds of physiological algorithms have been associated with disease and mortality risk.

3. Epigenetic clocks are probably what you're hearing about

These measure DNA methylation, chemical modifications occurring at specific CpG sites in DNA.

There have been several generations:

First generation
Horvath Clock / Hannum Clock
→ primarily designed to predict chronological age.

Second generation
PhenoAge / GrimAge
→ designed more around health outcomes and mortality.

Third generation
DunedinPACE
→ specifically attempts to measure the rate at which someone is aging.

The newer clocks tend to be considerably more interesting for longevity research than simply asking whether DNA thinks you're 61 instead of 65. NIA reports that newer second- and third-generation measures are associated with functional limitations, cognitive impairment, chronic disease and mortality.

4. Is it legit?

At the population/research level: absolutely.
There is strong evidence that people showing accelerated biological aging on these measures tend to have worse health outcomes. Epigenetic measures can predict disease, disability and mortality beyond chronological age alone.

But there is an important caveat.

At the individual level: we're not quite there yet.
A major recent critique concluded that current epigenetic clocks do not yet meet normal standards for individual clinical decision-making. Different clocks can give different answers; results can be influenced by tissue, laboratory processing, illness, stress and other short-term factors. A change of a year or two in “biological age” after an intervention may even fall within technical/biological noise.

That's a very important distinction when companies advertise things such as:
“Your biological age was 67. After taking our supplement for six months, you're now 59.”

I would be very skeptical of that level of precision.

See #5 at top of document for best measurements

title: Weight-fat Loss Instructions
content:
Goal setting, monitoring, and adjustments

Weight/Fat Loss

Use your dotFIT programs to get your true starting calories. All will be contained in your program, including necessary weekly adjustments, but below is a summary. If measuring body fat, measurements and adjustments are bi-weekly.

Weekly goal: lose 1–2 lbs/week or approximately 1% body fat every 2 weeks. Your target daily calories are slightly lower than your daily burn. This allows you to lose at least 1 lb per week without compromising performance gains. The more overweight, the greater the allowed weekly loss, with 2 lbs loss being the maximum when performance is part of the goal.

Monitoring: weigh/measure weekly in the same dress, at the same time, and on the same scale. If necessary (see below), only adjust calories in or out every 7 days.

Adjustments: a measurable or visual reduction in body fat and/or weight should take place in a fairly consistent manner, such as a decrease in circumference inches and/or the desired average decrease in weight or body fat per week. If progress stops or slows dramatically, one or a mixture of the following adjustments is all that will be necessary to restart the process:

- Increase daily activities (e.g., daily steps or other non-athletic/exercise activities).
- Standing and pacing burns 2–3 times more calories than sitting for the same time period.
- There are approximately 2,000–2,500 steps (depending on stride) in a mile. Walking 2,000 steps will burn approximately 75–150 more calories (depending on individual size) than sitting for the same time and only takes approximately 20–30 minutes and can be done anywhere, even in the office.
- Increase workout (generally aerobic-type) time or intensity, including adding interval cardio training.
- Decrease food intake approximately 200–300 calories/day or remove a small portion of your largest meal, and repeat this reduction if after 1 week there is no change in weight/body composition.
- Repeat the process any time weight or body fat is stable for at least one week.

Always remember: if you stop losing weight/fat, you only need to eat less, move more, or a combination of the two, regardless of what you read or hear from others.

When you have achieved your body composition goals, increase your calories to maintain desired weight.

title: EAAs and older adults in exercise
content:
In the studies below, they did not factor in protein intakes. But that is the overall point. This is free living (i.e., the way people eat), and the EEA supplementation was very helpful. (Also see the Empirical data note below.) For an older person that “thinks” they are getting enough protein from food, at worst, EEA supplementation can guarantee they are (i.e., corrects any math errors). At best, it may improve overall whole-body net protein synthesis for the remainder of a hopefully long life as age-related anabolic resistance increases and overall appetite, including for protein, begins to falter.

Bottom line is that EAA supplementation integrated properly, including in what is known as “protein stacking,” in healthy competitive adults, can help maximize a person’s potential in lifelong whole-body protein synthesis (including muscle protein synthesis), helping most any adult remain active a lifetime. Whether an active adult at 95 yrs of age that has always and still is consuming 1 gm/LB/LBM/protein daily would benefit from using supplementation—who knows or even cares. This person would be an outlier, and I’m willing to guess it would still help, albeit less than the other 99.99999% of the aging population, especially in getting more protein within fewer calories. Further, it would eliminate any math issues. Overall, the preponderance of evidence favors supplementation integration in most all circumstances related to aging and anabolic resistance—there is no need to “cherry pick” data; there is far more in favor, which drives the recommendation.

Here are a few of many well-designed, human studies on essential amino acid supplementation in older adults who exercise, with the key details (who, what, dose, training, outcome), and again, most do not factor in protein intakes, but that is the point:

Randomized & controlled trials (exercise + EAAs)

[NAME] et al., 2012 (J Am Geriatrics Soc)—155 sarcopenic women (≥75 y) randomized to exercise, EAAs (leucine-rich, 3 g twice daily), both, or health education for 3 mo. Exercise + EAA improved knee extension strength (+9.3%) and increased leg muscle mass more than controls; walking speed improved across intervention groups. PubMed

[NAME] et al., 2023 (J Am Nutr Assoc)—Older adults with sarcopenia did supervised resistance training (RT) for 24 wk and were randomized to RT alone vs. post-exercise EAAs (3,000 mg) + tea catechins (540 mg). The RT + EAA (+/- catechins) group gained more skeletal muscle mass than RT alone. PubMed

[NAME] et al., 2019 (J Gerontol A)—Healthy older men & women (non-frail) in a 2×2 RCT for 24 wk: aerobic exercise (AE) ± daily EAAs. AE + EAAs increased muscle strength and EAA-stimulated MPS; lean mass unchanged. Shows function can improve even when mass doesn’t. PMC

EAA trials in older adults (no formal RT, but relevant to muscle)

4) [NAME] et al., 2009 (JCEM)—Healthy older women took EAAs twice daily between meals for 3 mo. Lean body mass increased, and basal MPS and IGF-1 expression rose. PMC

[NAME] et al., 2008 (Clin Nutr)—Glucose-intolerant elderly received EAAs + arginine between meals; lean mass, strength, and physical function improved vs. baseline. (Population was older, not specifically training.) PMC

Mechanistic/acute work in older adults (supports dosing & composition around exercise)

6) [NAME] et al., 2006 (Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab)—In the elderly, EAAs must be leucine-rich to optimally stimulate MPS; higher leucine proportion overcame anabolic resistance. PubMed

[NAME] et al., 2003 (Am J Clin Nutr)—Demonstrated EAAs are the primary driver of amino-acid-induced muscle protein anabolism in the elderly (vs. non-essential AAs). PubMed

[NAME] et al., 2020 (Nutrients)—Leucine-enriched EAA given after acute RT in older adults increased aminoacidemia and mTORC1 signaling vs. placebo, supporting peri-workout EAA use. (Proof-of-concept, signaling outcomes.) PMC

Reviews/position papers that synthesize EAA use in older exercisers

9) [NAME] et al., 2021 (Proc Nutr Soc)—Review concludes leucine-enriched EAA supplements are a practical way to augment per-meal protein and enhance training responses in older adults; often used at ~7.5 g EAA (≈40% leucine) twice daily. PubMed

title: Tryptophan info - amino Forumla
content:
This illustrates an important nutritional point:

The minimum human requirement for tryptophan is only 250–400 mg/day for most adults.

A single 6 oz serving of lean beef or chicken generally provides 1.5 to 2.5 times that requirement.

Someone consuming 100–150 g of high-quality protein per day (common among active individuals) will typically consume 1,200–2,000 mg of tryptophan daily, or about 3–6 times the amount needed to support normal protein synthesis and essential metabolic functions.

This is one reason that tryptophan deficiency is extremely uncommon in people consuming adequate amounts of complete animal proteins. The amino acids more likely to become limiting are found in lower-quality protein sources, particularly cereal grains, where lysine is usually the first limiting amino acid rather than tryptophan.

How much tryptophan does the body need daily to maintain normal protein synthesis—i.e., the daily gram or milligram requirement?

The daily requirement for tryptophan to support normal protein synthesis and general physiological needs is actually quite small compared with what is used in research for sleep or mood.

Daily Requirement

The current recommendation from the World Health Organization, Food and Agriculture Organization, and United Nations University is:

Tryptophan: 4 mg/kg body weight/day

This is the estimated requirement to maintain nitrogen balance and normal protein synthesis in healthy adults.

What this means in practical terms:

| Body Weight | Daily Requirement |
|---|---|
| 50 kg (110 lb) | 200 mg/day |
| 60 kg (132 lb) | 240 mg/day |
| 70 kg (154 lb) | 280 mg/day |
| 80 kg (176 lb) | 320 mg/day |
| 90 kg (198 lb) | 360 mg/day |
| 100 kg (220 lb) | 400 mg/day |

For most adults, the requirement is therefore only about 250–400 mg/day.

Why the requirement is so low

The 4 mg/kg recommendation is intended only to provide enough tryptophan for:

- Protein synthesis
- Production of niacin (vitamin B3)
- Synthesis of serotonin
- Synthesis of melatonin
- Other normal metabolic functions

It is not intended to maximize serotonin production, improve sleep, or enhance mood.

Typical dietary intake

Most people consuming adequate protein easily exceed this amount.

For example:

- 25 g whey protein: ~400–500 mg tryptophan
- 3 oz chicken breast: ~300–350 mg
- 2 eggs: ~160–180 mg
- 1 cup Greek yogurt: ~180–220 mg

Someone eating 100 g of high-quality protein/day typically consumes approximately 900–1,300 mg of tryptophan/day—or ~3–5 times the minimum physiological requirement.

For comparison: protein quality

Tryptophan is one of the nine indispensable (essential) amino acids. Because it is required in relatively small amounts, it is seldom the amino acid that limits protein synthesis in animal proteins. In cereal grains, however, lysine is much more commonly the limiting amino acid than tryptophan.

Summary

- Minimum adult requirement: 4 mg/kg/day
- Typical adult (80 kg): ~320 mg/day
- Typical intake from a balanced, protein-rich diet: 900–1,300 mg/day

This requirement is sufficient for normal protein synthesis and essential metabolic functions, but it is substantially lower than the 1–3 g/day of supplemental tryptophan often studied for effects on sleep, relaxation, or mood.

Given your previous work comparing amino acid quality among protein sources, this is another good illustration of why meeting the indispensable amino acid pattern—not simply total protein grams—is what determines whether a protein effectively supports human protein synthesis.

How much tryptophan is in 6 oz of animal protein such as beef and chicken?

The exact amount depends on the cut of meat and cooking method, but 6 oz (170 g) of cooked lean animal protein generally provides well over the daily requirement for tryptophan.

Approximate tryptophan content in 6 oz (170 g) cooked:

| Animal Protein | Tryptophan (mg) |
|---|---|
| Chicken breast (skinless) | 650–750 mg |
| Turkey breast | 700–800 mg |
| Lean beef (sirloin, top round) | 500–650 mg |
| Pork loin | 550–700 mg |
| Salmon | 600–700 mg |
| Tuna | 500–650 mg |

Comparison with the daily requirement

The adult requirement is:

4 mg/kg/day

| Body Weight | Daily Requirement |
|---|---|
| 70 kg (154 lb) | 280 mg |
| 80 kg (176 lb) | 320 mg |
| 90 kg (198 lb) | 360 mg |

Therefore, 6 oz of chicken breast (≈700 mg) provides approximately:

- 250% of the requirement for a 70 kg adult
- 220% for an 80 kg adult
- 195% for a 90 kg adult

Even 6 oz of lean beef (≈550–600 mg) provides roughly 150–200% of the daily physiological requirement.

Relative abundance in protein

Tryptophan represents approximately:

- Chicken: ~1.2–1.3% of total protein
- Turkey: ~1.3–1.4%
- Beef: ~1.1–1.2%
- Fish: ~1.2–1.3%

Since 6 oz of cooked lean meat contains approximately 45–50 g of protein, multiplying by these percentages yields about 500–750 mg of tryptophan, depending on the source.

Practical perspective

This illustrates an important nutritional point:

The minimum human requirement for tryptophan is only 250–400 mg/day for most adults.

A single 6 oz serving of lean beef or chicken generally provides 1.5 to 2.5 times that requirement.

Someone consuming 100–150 g of high-quality protein per day (common among active individuals) will typically consume 1,200–2,000 mg of tryptophan daily, or about 3–6 times the amount needed to support normal protein synthesis and essential metabolic functions.

This is one reason that tryptophan deficiency is extremely uncommon in people consuming adequate amounts of complete animal proteins. The amino acids more likely to become limiting are found in lower-quality protein sources, particularly cereal grains, where lysine is usually the first limiting amino acid rather than tryptophan.

title: Are there any articles or guidance to help with constipation for a client taking a GLP-1 medication?
content:
Hi [NAME],

Thanks for contacting us. As long as your client does not have a clinical issue, such as gastroparesis (stomach paralysis) and/or bowel restriction (both potential side effects in GLP drug users, in which their medical provider should be aware or confirm), then making sure they get enough fiber (work up to ~25 g/day) and micronutrients using smoothies (Alln1 SuperBlend™ and LeanMeal) as necessary and staying hydrated will certainly help. See below for more information.

Thanks again and have a great evening.

More info:

Constipation is one of the most common non-serious side effects in people using GLP-1 receptor agonists (such as semaglutide or tirzepatide). It usually occurs because these drugs slow gastric emptying and overall intestinal motility, reduce appetite (so total food volume drops), and many users unintentionally reduce fiber, fluid, and magnesium intake while dieting. If the issue is not clinical gastroparesis, the goal is simply to restore normal stool volume, hydration, and gut motility.

Practical Recommendation

For most GLP-1 users with mild constipation:
- Make sure they are taking a complete multivitamin and mineral formula (MVM) and enough protein (1 g/pound/LBM/D).
- Drink 3 L water daily.
- Add 5–10 g psyllium fiber.
- Take 200–400 mg magnesium at night.
- Ensure 20–30 g fiber/day from foods.
- Walk after meals.

This simple protocol resolves the issue for the majority of users.

Constipation is one of the most common non-serious side effects in people using GLP-1 receptor agonists (such as semaglutide or tirzepatide). It usually occurs because these drugs slow gastric emptying and overall intestinal motility, reduce appetite (so total food volume drops), and many users unintentionally reduce fiber, fluid, and magnesium intake while dieting. If the issue is not clinical gastroparesis, the goal is simply to restore normal stool volume, hydration, and gut motility.

Below is a practical evidence-based stepwise approach that trainers, clinicians, or users can follow.

1. Hydration First (Most Common Missing Piece)

Many GLP-1 users dramatically reduce food intake and forget to increase fluids.

Recommendation:
- 2.5–3.5 L fluid/day.
- Add electrolytes or a pinch of sodium to improve absorption.
- Drink 1–2 glasses of water immediately upon waking.

Adequate hydration softens stool and helps fiber work properly.

2. Add Soluble Fiber (Primary Non-Drug Strategy)

GLP-1 diets often become low-fiber because people eat less food overall.

Best evidence-based fibers:
- Psyllium husk: 5–10 g/day.
- Partially hydrolyzed guar gum (PHGG): 5–6 g/day.
- Inulin or resistant starch: 3–8 g/day.

Benefits:
- Increases stool bulk.
- Improves gut microbiome.
- Supports metabolic health.

Important: fiber must be combined with water.

3. Magnesium for Motility

Many Americans already have suboptimal magnesium intake, and magnesium can help draw water into the colon.

Common options:
- Magnesium citrate: 200–400 mg at night.
- Magnesium glycinate: 200–400 mg/day (gentler but less laxative).
- Magnesium oxide: stronger laxative effect.

Magnesium is often the simplest effective solution.

4. Maintain Adequate Food Volume

GLP-1 users sometimes eat so little that there simply isn’t enough bulk to stimulate bowel movements.

Encourage daily intake of:
- Vegetables.
- Fruit.
- Whole grains or resistant starch.
- Protein foods.

Aiming for 20–30 g fiber/day total is a good target.

5. Gut Motility Support (Optional)

Certain foods and supplements can help stimulate intestinal movement.

Helpful options:
- Kiwi fruit (2/day) – strong evidence for constipation relief.
- Prunes or prune juice.
- Coffee – stimulates colon motility.
- Light physical activity after meals.

6. Probiotics / Prebiotics

GLP-1 therapy can alter the microbiome.

Evidence-supported strains for constipation:
- Bifidobacterium lactis.
- Lactobacillus casei.

These may improve stool frequency and consistency.

7. If Needed: Gentle OTC Options

Occasional use if lifestyle measures are insufficient:
- Polyethylene glycol (Miralax).
- Docusate sodium (stool softener).

These are generally safe but should not replace diet and hydration strategies.

Warning Signs (Seek Medical Evaluation)

Constipation with GLP-1 medications should be evaluated if accompanied by:
- Severe abdominal pain.
- Persistent vomiting.
- Inability to pass stool or gas.
- Signs of gastroparesis.

✅ Practical “Trainer-Level” Recommendation

For most GLP-1 users with mild constipation:
- Drink 3 L water daily.
- Add 5–10 g psyllium fiber.
- Take 200–400 mg magnesium at night.
- Ensure 20–30 g fiber/day from foods.
- Walk after meals.

This simple protocol resolves the issue for the majority of users.

title: Low Carb intake and hormone levels
content:
What Happens to Your Hormones When You Don’t Eat Enough Carbs

Key Takeaways:

Very low carbohydrate (carb) intake can shift blood sugar hormones in ways that may make energy feel less predictable.

Carb restriction may alter thyroid, serotonin, and reproductive hormones, affecting mood, metabolism, and menstrual cycle irregularity.

Appetite might decrease as your body adapts to a lower carb intake over time, due to increased leptin sensitivity and stable or decreased ghrelin levels.

When you cut carbs too low for your body’s needs, several hormones shift in an effort to keep you going. Some of these changes can be helpful in the short term, but over time, they may disrupt energy, mood, appetite, and blood sugar control.

Key Takeaways:

Very low carbohydrate (carb) intake can shift blood sugar hormones in ways that may make energy feel less predictable.

By [NAME], MDA, RDN, CD, CDCES

Published on January 27, 2026

Low-carb eating can lead to low energy levels and disrupt your moods and menstrual cycle.

Credit: skynesher / Getty Images

Carb restriction may alter thyroid, serotonin, and reproductive hormones, affecting mood, metabolism, and menstrual cycle irregularity.

Appetite might decrease as your body adapts to a lower carb intake over time, due to increased leptin sensitivity and stable or decreased ghrelin levels.

When you cut carbs too low for your body’s needs, several hormones shift in an effort to keep you going. Some of these changes can be helpful in the short term, but over time, they may disrupt energy, mood, appetite, and blood sugar control.

1. Low Carbohydrate Intake Can Raise Cortisol Levels

Carbohydrates signal safety (feeling full and satisfied after eating) and provide fuel for energy. When intake decreases, the body often increases cortisol to release stored glucose.

This is part of a normal stress response, but chronically (long-term) elevated cortisol may leave you feeling wired, fatigued, or hungrier than usual.

If carbs are consistently low, your body may respond by producing more cortisol to support blood sugar regulation and energy needs.

These shifts can affect how you feel day to day, so it helps to understand the signs:

- Higher stress levels, even without emotional triggers.
- Midday crashes or feeling “tired but wired” at night.
- Increased food cravings, especially for sugar or quick energy.

2. Thyroid Hormones May Slow Down

Healthy glucose metabolism and carb intake are crucial for optimal conversion of T4 into its active form, T3 (thyroid hormones that regulate the body’s metabolism, energy use, growth, and development).

When carbs are very low, this conversion may slow, which can impact metabolism, temperature regulation, and overall energy.

Research has found that low-carbohydrate diets can reduce T3 levels independent of calorie intake.

For many people, this shows up as subtle but noticeable changes:

- Feeling colder than usual
- Fatigue
- Plateaus in weight loss despite consistent efforts

3. Insulin and Glucagon Rise and Fall in New Patterns

When carb intake drops very low, the glucose-regulating hormones insulin and glucagon shift quickly to keep blood sugar steady, which may make energy levels feel less predictable.

Insulin naturally decreases on lower-carb diets because there is less glucose to manage.

At the same time, glucagon rises to help maintain blood sugar by releasing stored glycogen and making new glucose in the liver.

You might notice it through symptoms such as:

- Low energy, especially during exercise
- Feeling shaky, light-headed, or irritable between meals
- Stronger hunger cues when meals are delayed

4. Leptin Sensitivity May Improve

When carbohydrate intake drops, leptin (the satiety hormone) levels often decline, but this does not always lead to increased hunger. As the body adapts to a consistent lower-carbohydrate intake over time, the hormones involved in appetite and satiety shift.

Many people on long-term low-carb or ketogenic diets experience improved leptin sensitivity, meaning the brain becomes better at recognizing fullness even with lower circulating leptin levels.

At the same time, ghrelin (the hunger hormone) is often stable or decreases, while other satiety hormones like cholecystokinin (CCK) may rise. This shift makes it easier to feel satisfied with smaller meals.

These appetite-related changes may show up in several ways:

- Feeling full sooner during meals
- Fewer cravings between meals
- A more stable, predictable appetite

5. Reproductive Hormones Can Become Disrupted

For some people with ovaries, consistently low carbohydrate intake may signal that overall caloric intake is too low for optimal reproductive function.

This can reduce the brain’s release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which in turn lowers luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone, the hormones needed for ovulation (release of a mature egg from the ovary) and regular menstrual cycles.

This pattern is common in low energy availability. It is linked to functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (when the brain’s command center stops sending signals that trigger menstruation due to stress, leading to periods stopping).

Lower leptin levels can also contribute. Leptin helps the brain determine whether the body has enough stored energy for reproduction, and research shows that a certain leptin level is important for maintaining normal menstrual cycles.

When leptin declines due to low carbohydrate or inadequate fuel intake, menstrual cycles may become irregular even when total calorie intake appears sufficient.

Signs this may be happening include:

- Irregular or absent menstrual cycles
- Increased premenstrual syndrome (PMS) symptoms.
- Lower energy during the second half (luteal phase) of the cycle.

6. Serotonin May Drop, Affecting Mood

Carbohydrates play a direct role in helping tryptophan (an amino acid) enter the brain, where it is converted to serotonin (a neurotransmitter that helps regulate several functions in the brain and body).

Research shows that carbohydrate intake influences serotonin pathways and satiety signals. When carbs are limited, serotonin production may fall, which can affect mood, appetite, sleep, and emotional regulation.

Many people notice this in day-to-day emotional patterns:

- Feeling moody, irritable, or depressed
- Trouble winding down at night
- Cravings for carbohydrate-rich comfort foods

title: What is your assessment of the safety of the acesulfame potassium used in our shakes, given the small amount present?
content:
Hey [CUSTOMER],

There are always anti-artificial sweetener people because they are constantly looking for more data to support their views, and therefore, we make all-natural products for them. But obviously the FDA-approved non-nutritional sweeteners (NNS) are completely safe within the amounts used (and actually far beyond those amounts). This is all covered in my protein lectures (see attached slides) and in the PDSRG WheySmooth, FirstString (see example below), etc., sections with the peer-reviewed references. Also, an FAQ from “ask the experts.”

Sweeteners in FirstString

Sweeteners used in FirstString appear at the end of the ingredient list as they are in minute amounts per serving and inert in human metabolism, thus having no effects within the body other than taste. For frequently asked questions (FAQs) on non-nutritive sweeteners, click here. Non-nutritive sweeteners (NNS) are those that sweeten with minimal or no carbohydrate or energy. NNS are regulated by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as food additives.229 The FDA approval process includes determination of probable intake, cumulative effect from all uses, and toxicology studies.229,230 Eight NNS—aspartame, acesulfame potassium, luo han guo [monk] fruit extract, neotame, saccharin, stevia, sucralose, and advantame (aspartame analog by Ajinomoto)—are approved for use in the United States (click here for a list, uses, and metabolism), with acesulfame K and sucralose being among the most popular,216 largely because of their unique functional properties in enhancing food products, including taste.216 As with any fitness-supporting food product, the better the taste and versatility, the greater chance of sustained use to support health and fitness goals.

Acesulfame Potassium (Ace-K)

Acesulfame potassium (chemical formula C4H4KNO4S; CAS registry number 55589-62-3) is approximately 200 times sweeter than sugar and is often combined with other sweeteners as an additional flavor enhancer in foods because it is heat stable during baking and environmentally friendly. Ace-K is typically used in frozen desserts, candies, beverages, and baked goods. More than 90 studies support its safety, and it is used in FirstString to support baking capacity and sweetness. For a complete current review on Ace-K, readers are referred to [NAME] et al.’s “A Review of the Environmental Fate and Effects of Acesulfame-Potassium.”246

Sucralose

Sucralose is also an NNS and is made from sucrose by a process that substitutes three chloride atoms for three hydroxyl groups on the sucrose molecule. Sucralose, a very versatile NNS that is 450–650 times sweeter than sucrose, possesses a pleasant sweet taste and a quality and time intensity profile that is close to that of sucrose, making it a popular NNS.216 Sucralose has been extensively studied, with more than 110 safety studies reviewed by the FDA in approving the use of sucralose as a general-purpose sweetener for food.229,230,248 A primary advantage of sucralose for consumers is its exceptional stability. It retains its sweetness over a wide range of temperature and storage conditions and in solutions over time. This stability allows manufacturers to create greater-tasting foods and beverages and maintain the fresh flavor. Like Ace-K, sucralose is heat stable, meaning that it stays sweet even when used at high temperatures during baking, making it a common sugar substitute in baked goods.250

The FDA established an acceptable daily intake (ADI) for sucralose of 5 milligrams per kilogram (Europe’s is 7 mg/kg and Canada’s is 11 mg/kg) of body weight (mg/kg) per day.*229 The amount of sucralose per serving in FirstString is ~34 mg.

*Out of safety precautions to protect all subgroups of people, the ADI represents an amount 100 times less than the quantity of sucralose found to be safe in research studies.229 For a person weighing 150 pounds (68 kg), the US ADI equates to 340 mg of sucralose—the amount found in nine cans of diet soda or more than 28 individual packets of sucralose—consumed, on average, every day over a lifetime. Therefore, you could multiply these numbers by 100 before you would cross a known safety threshold in consumption.

title: Protein-muscle full effect total-.18-.25
content:
Question #4: How Much Protein Can I Handle in a Single Meal?

This is really two questions:
How much protein do I need to maximally stimulate protein synthesis?
Is it true that anything beyond that amount is a waste?

We’ll start with the second question because [NAME] hears it from patients way more often than he’d like to.
“I tell them, no, it’s not a waste,” he said. Even if the patient has fully engaged protein synthesis, there’s a lot more going on. The total amount of daily protein in your diet and the quality of that protein matter more than how much you eat at any particular meal.

For the first question, [NAME] has three answers:
In younger adults, about 0.25 g of high-quality protein per kilogram of body weight per meal should adequately stimulate protein synthesis. That assumes the protein contains 2–3 g of leucine.
Older adults who have some resistance to leucine should aim for 0.4 g per kilogram per meal.
Maximum protein stimulation should occur with roughly 0.4–0.55 g per kilogram.

Put simply, 20 g of protein per meal should get the party started for a younger adult, 30 g should work for an older adult, and 40 g should maximally engage protein synthesis for almost anyone.

But again, higher amounts of protein at one meal aren’t “wasted.”

In fact, a 2023 study found that 100 g of protein stimulated more protein synthesis over the next 12 hours than 25 g.

Nobody is suggesting you should consume 100 g of protein in any meal. Even if we thought it was a good idea, few of us could choke down 1.2 pounds of beef, two large chicken breasts, or 16 eggs at one sitting.

The point to make to your patients is this: Consume the nutrients your body needs, and your body will figure out what to do with them.

Take one scoop approximately 10 minutes before a workout (add to NO7Rage if using this product—see below). You may continue to drink it during the workout.

Take one (1) scoop immediately following the workout.

Or use both scoops and start ingesting 10 minutes before the workout, consuming it at a pace so it is finished at the end of the activity.

Begin Creatine Supplementation at the 2nd Week of the Program

2nd Week: Start CreatineMonohydrate (CrM)*
Loading phase: Mix one (1) scoop (5 g) with 4–8 oz of a favorite fluid/shake and take four (4) times daily with a protein- and/or carbohydrate-containing meal/drink for the first five (5) days.

On training days, use one dose before the workout and one after with meals/drinks. May mix with your pre- and post-training formula.

Maintenance phase: After the five (5)-day loading phase:

On training days, take one (1) scoop daily with the post-workout shake.

On non-training days, take 1 scoop with any meal when not taking ECX (i.e., use ECX at different times so total creatine is evenly dispersed throughout the day).

Persons <175 LBS can discontinue CrM dosing when starting ECX, because ECX daily dosing will maintain CrM stores.

Add ExtremeCreatineXXXL (ECX) on the 6th day of the 2nd Week
Two (2) scoops supply 3.2 g of beta-alanine (BA), 5 g of creatine monohydrate, and 7 g of L-glutamine.

Take 2 scoops daily. Take with some protein and/or carbohydrates, but within allotted calories based on body composition goal.

Training days: Take one (1) scoop before training with the pre-workout full meal (generally 2–3 hours pre-workout). If not possible based on early training, take with the pre-workout shake. Take the remaining dose (1 scoop) anytime with a meal or shake when not taking a CreatineMonohydrate dose to help evenly spread total creatine intake throughout the day.

Non-training days: Take 1 scoop with the morning meal or shake and 1 scoop with the evening meal or shake.

Add NO7Rage at the 4th week (workout days only)
Take 1.5–2.5 scoops depending on body weight and caffeine sensitivity—start with 1.5 and increase to the recommended dose if not uncomfortably affected by caffeine—approximately 10 minutes before the workout. May mix with AF and continue to consume during the workout. See directions on the label for weight dosages.

NO7Rage contains 150 mg of caffeine per scoop. As a reference, Starbucks Grande drip coffee contains approximately 330 mg of caffeine, close to the same amount in two (2) scoops of NO7Rage.

Total daily creatine for this plan: Loading phase, 20 g/day. Thereafter until the fourth week, 10 g/day (or 5 g if <175 LBS). At the fourth week, on workout days, 12.5–15 g/day and 10 g on non-workout days (half this if <175 LBS). Total BA intake is 6.2–8.2 g/day on workout days and 3.2 g on non-workout days. To maximize uptake, creatine intake should be spread as evenly as possible throughout the day and around the workout as described, and ingested with some carbohydrates and/or protein.

title: Why don't your multivitamins contain calcium?

The reason the dotFIT Multivitamin and Mineral Formulas (MVM) do not contain calcium (no other MVM should either) is because, if you need more calcium, the amount you need would not fit into a tablet that contains the other known under-consumed vitamins and minerals (VM). From the Practitioner Dietary Supplement Reference Guide (PDSRG) regarding your question: Calcium and potassium present the exceptions to a single complete vitamin and mineral supplement (CVMS) because, if they are needed, the amounts generally would not fit in an acceptable pill size along with the other known under-consumed vitamins and minerals (VMs). title: TB 500, acc tissue repair thru actin reg - Copy
content:
TB-500 is a synthetic peptide that works primarily by regulating actin, a protein crucial for cell structure and movement, which in turn enhances cellular migration and promotes tissue regeneration, angiogenesis (new blood vessel formation), and inflammation modulation.

Key Mechanisms of Action

Actin Regulation and Cell Migration: TB-500 binds to G-actin monomers, preventing their polymerization into F-actin filaments. This process is essential for cell movement, allowing repair cells (like endothelial cells and keratinocytes) to rapidly migrate to sites of injury, thus accelerating wound closure and tissue repair.

Angiogenesis Promotion: The peptide stimulates the formation of new blood vessels by upregulating vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) expression and enhancing endothelial cell migration and proliferation. Improved blood flow ensures that damaged tissues receive essential oxygen and nutrients, which is vital for the healing process.

Anti-Inflammatory Modulation: TB-500 has significant anti-inflammatory properties, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, and suppressing the activation of NF-κB. This helps create an optimal environment for healing by calming excessive inflammatory responses that could otherwise hinder recovery.

Growth Factor and Cellular Signaling Enhancement: It influences cell growth and repair by activating pathways like Akt/PI3K and enhancing HGF (hepatocyte growth factor) expression. It also supports the mobilization and differentiation of stem cells to the site of injury, providing the cellular building blocks for new tissue.

Extracellular Matrix Remodeling: TB-500 supports the formation and organization of healthy extracellular matrix components like collagen and elastin, which is essential for strong, flexible, and functional tissue repair with reduced scar formation.

Summary

TB-500's multifaceted mechanism, centered on actin modulation, allows for a systemic approach to healing across various tissues, including muscles, tendons, ligaments, skin, and even cardiac tissue in preclinical studies. It is important to note that TB-500 is an experimental therapy and is not approved for human use by the FDA. It is sold strictly for research purposes and should be used under medical supervision.

TB-500 Overview

Thymosin Beta-4 (Tβ4) is a naturally occurring 43-amino-acid peptide found in nearly all human cells. It is produced from the TMSB4X gene and is abundant in platelets, macrophages, and epithelial tissues. In laboratory research, a synthetic version called TB-500 is often used to study Tβ4's biological activity. Neither compound is approved for systemic therapeutic use; current work focuses on understanding how this peptide regulates cell movement, tissue organization, and inflammation.

title: Lead, best answer prop65 , note and quotes
content:
California Prop 65*

NSF (and Eurofins) has certified our products to meet federal and global standards for all natural earthly metals, including lead, or you would not see the NSF on the label. Proposition 65 applies to California only*, requiring a warning on anything that might contain lead, which is found everywhere, including in your workplace. Therefore, be mindful that there is always some lead (and other natural metals found in the earth), including in the air you breathe and in natural products, but there is a set limit that you cannot exceed, and the testing confirms that. Again, all our products are far below the federal and global limits, which is verified by NSF-CS and Eurofins, our 3rd- and 4th-party testing. Again, the warning on the label is there by law for California only, including being posted in all California grocery stores, coffee shops, etc., and does NOT mean there is an unsafe level of anything. On a side note, 1 svg of natural spinach has 10 times the allowed lead in any dietary supplement. In other words, most all plant foods will always be above the allowed lead content for dietary supplements. Just make sure your supplements are 3rd-party tested like all of ours, and you will always be safe.

*The California Prop 65 lead standards are unrealistic in natural foods and disputed globally, because almost all foods contain amounts higher than allowed lead/metals (.5 mcg/svg), including 1 svg natural spinach (10Xs higher), 1 cup of coffee, etc. This is because the level is set 10–50 times lower than other global (e.g., FDA [2.2 mcg/d children; 12.5 adults], NSF, WHO, etc.) limits for lead (5–30 mcg). Based on the unrealistic levels, almost all plant foods would be prohibited.

More information

From Council of Responsible Nutrition:

“Prop 65 levels are not meant to represent a safety threshold or a cut-off for unsafe levels, but rather, a standard that triggers a label notification only in the state of California to inform consumers which products contain metals—which are naturally present in most natural sources of food and water. To put this into context, a 1/2 cup of cooked spinach would require a Prop 65 warning label, if they were required for whole foods, which they are not.”

content:
Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), or cellulose gum[1], is a cellulose derivative. CMC is used in food under the E number E466 as a viscosity modifier or thickener, and to stabilize emulsions in various products, including ice cream. CMC is used extensively in gluten-free[4] and reduced-fat food products.[5]

Use of CMC in candy preparation ensures smooth dispersion in flavor oils and improves texture and quality. It is used in chewing gums, margarines, and peanut butter as an emulsifier.[9]

[NAME], [NAME], [NAME], and [NAME]. Evaluation of the Effect of Carboxy Methyl Cellulose on Sensory Properties of Gluten-Free Cake. Research Journal of Applied Sciences, Engineering and Technology 4(19): 3819–3821, 2012. ISSN: 2040-7467. © Maxwell Scientific Organization, 2

Acesulfame potassium (Ace-K)

Acesulfame potassium is approved for use in food as a non-nutritive sweetener. It is included in the ingredient list on the food label as acesulfame K, acesulfame potassium, or Ace-K. Acesulfame potassium is sold under the brand names Sunett® and Sweet One®. It is about 200 times sweeter than sugar and is often combined with other sweeteners.

FDA approved acesulfame potassium for use in specific food and beverage categories in 1988 (53 FR 28379), and in 2003 approved it as a general-purpose sweetener and flavor enhancer in food, except in meat and poultry, under certain conditions of use. It is heat stable, meaning that it stays sweet even when used at high temperatures during baking, making it suitable as a sugar substitute in baked goods.

Acesulfame potassium is typically used in frozen desserts, candies, beverages, and baked goods. More than 90 studies support its safety.

Sucralose

Sucralose is also an NNS. It is made from sucrose by a process that substitutes 3 chloride atoms for 3 hydroxyl groups on the sucrose molecule (FDA 2006). Sucralose is 450–650 times sweeter than sucrose, has a pleasant sweet taste, and its quality and time-intensity profile is very close to that of sucrose ([NAME] et al. 2009). Sucralose has been extensively studied, and more than 110 safety studies were reviewed by FDA in approving the use of sucralose as a general-purpose sweetener for food. A primary advantage of sucralose for consumers is its exceptional stability. It retains its sweetness over a wide range of temperature and storage conditions and in solutions over time. This stability allows manufacturers to create better-tasting foods and beverages. Like Ace-K, it is heat stable, meaning that it stays sweet even when used at high temperatures during baking, making it suitable as a sugar substitute in baked goods.

[NAME], [NAME], and [NAME]. Artificial sweeteners—A review. J Food Sci Technol. 2014 Apr;51(4):611–621. Published online 2011 Oct 21. doi: 10.1007/s13197-011-0571-1. PMCID: PMC3982014

Because of its stability, food manufacturers can use sucralose to create a number of great-tasting new foods and beverages in categories such as canned fruit, low-calorie fruit drinks, baked goods, and sauces and syrups. Sucralose can also be used as a sweetener in nutritional supplements, medical foods, and vitamin/mineral supplements.

Sucralose is approved for use in food as a non-nutritive sweetener. Sucralose is sold under the brand name Splenda®. Sucralose is about 600 times sweeter than sugar.

FDA approved sucralose for use in 15 food categories in 1998 and for use as a general-purpose sweetener for foods in 1999, under certain conditions of use. Sucralose is a general-purpose sweetener that can be found in a variety of foods, including baked goods, beverages, chewing gum, gelatins, and frozen dairy desserts.

From the FDA website:
http://www.fda.gov/Food/IngredientsPackagingLabeling/FoodAdditivesIngredients/ucm397725.htm#AceK

[NAME], [NAME], [NAME], [NAME], et al. Review of the nutritional benefits and risks related to intense sweeteners. Olivier et al. Archives of Public Health (2015) 73:41. DOI: 10.1186/s13690-015-0092-x

NO risk in NNS

[NAME], [NAME]. Artificial sweeteners: safe or unsafe? J Pak Med Assoc. 2015 Feb;65(2):225–7.

Safe

[NAME] and [NAME]. Low-calorie sweeteners and body weight and composition: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials and prospective cohort studies. Am J Clin Nutr 2014;100:765–77. Printed in USA.

Conclusions: The current meta-analysis provides a rigorous evaluation of the scientific evidence on LCSs and body weight and composition.

Findings from observational studies showed no association between LCS intake and body weight or fat mass and a small positive association with BMI; however, data from RCTs, which provide the highest quality of evidence for examining the potentially causal effects of LCS intake, indicate that substituting LCS options for their regular-calorie versions results in a modest weight loss and may be a useful dietary tool to improve compliance with weight loss or weight maintenance plans.

Maltodextrin:

Maltodextrin is a polysaccharide. It is a lightly hydrolyzed starch used as an ingredient in many food products as a thickener and carbohydrate source. Maltodextrin is easily digestible, being absorbed as rapidly as glucose, but moderately sweet or sometimes bland, making it desirable in food manufacturing.

Nothing else to know except that it is a perfectly safe added ingredient that makes the product mix and taste great (and yes, it is on the FDA GRAS list).

7.3. Type of Carbohydrate

[NAME], [NAME], [NAME], and [NAME]. Acute Effects of Carbohydrate Supplementation on Intermittent Sports Performance. Nutrients 2015, 7, 5733–5763; doi:10.3390/nu7075249

117—[NAME]. Carbohydrate and exercise performance: The role of multiple transportable carbohydrates. Curr Opin Clin Nutr Metab Care 2010, 13, 452–457. ISSN 2070-6643

Carbohydrates (CHO) in sports are generally placed in 2 categories. CHO that can be oxidized, or used for energy, rapidly—up to approximately 60 g/hr—and those oxidized slower—up to approximately 40 g/hr. Maltodextrins like glucose, maltose, and sucrose fall in the rapid category. These carbohydrates are digested and absorbed at fast rates, making them readily available to working muscle and, when in small amounts, do not slow down amino acid absorption from protein. These qualities, including maltodextrins’ food-mixture compatibility, make maltodextrins ideal in a product like WS that is designed as a low-but-flexible-calorie meal protein supplement and/or pre-/post-workout protein supplement.

Exogenous carbohydrate oxidation is mainly limited by the intestinal absorption of carbohydrates. In most studies discussed in this review, the types of carbohydrate consumed before or during intermittent activity are the sugars glucose and sucrose or the glucose polymer maltodextrin. Because these carbohydrates are digested and absorbed at fast rates, they are readily available for rapid oxidation by the muscles (see [117] for review).

Xanthan Gum

Xanthan gum, a water-soluble pentasaccharide, is a water-soluble, high-molecular-weight natural polysaccharide produced by a fermentation process.

[NAME], [NAME], [NAME], [NAME], [NAME]. Xanthan gum and its derivatives as a potential bio-polymeric carrier for drug delivery system. Curr Drug Deliv. 2013 Oct;10(5):587–600.

Due to its soft texture, xanthan gum is widely used as a thickener or viscosifier in both food and non-food industries. It also works as a stabilizer for a wide variety of formulations, with applications in pharmaceuticals, DS, and food products.

J Appl Physiol (1985). 2014 Jun 1;116(11):1353–1364. Published online 2014 Apr 3. doi: 10.1152/japplphysiol.01093.2013. PMCID: PMC4044402.

We report two novel findings: 1) increased postexercise phenylalanine net balance, an indicator of overall muscle protein anabolism, across the leg was prolonged with Blend ingestion during the acute postexercise recovery phase (0–2 h postingestion) compared with Whey; and 2) dietary protein ingestion of Blend and Whey increased postexercise amino acid (phenylalanine) transport into muscle and mRNA expression of amino acid transporters associated with the regulation of mTORC1 signaling and MPS.

In summary, we found a greater and prolonged increase in MPS post-exercise with ingestion of a protein blend of whey, casein, and soy as opposed to whey protein alone. They also found that ingesting the protein blend or whey protein alone enhanced the rate of amino acid transport into muscle, increased select amino acid transporter mRNA expression, and increased post-exercise myofibrillar protein synthesis. The results provide support for consuming a protein blend to increase and prolong post-exercise muscle protein anabolism. Presumably, the greater results from the blend may be based on the varied digestibility of each source and because soy protein may help spare whey from splanchnic catabolic activity and urea synthesis ([NAME] and others 2005; [NAME] and others 2009) as well as oxidation; may have spared the whey.

High dietary protein restores overreaching-induced impairments in leukocyte trafficking and reduces the incidence of upper respiratory tract infection in elite cyclists. Brain Behav Immun. 2014 Jul;39:211–9. doi: 10.1016/j.bbi.2013.10.002. Epub 2013 Oct 10.

The present study examined whether a high-protein diet prevents the impaired leukocyte redistribution in response to acute exercise caused by a large volume of high-intensity exercise training. Eight cyclists (VO2max: 64.2 ± 6.5 mL kg−1 min−1) undertook two separate weeks of high-intensity training while consuming either a high-protein diet (3 g kg−1 protein BM−1 day−1) or an energy- and carbohydrate-matched control diet (1.5 g kg−1 protein BM−1 day−1). High-intensity training weeks were preceded by a week of normal-intensity training under the control diet.

Leukocyte and lymphocyte subpopulation responses to acute exercise were determined at the end of each training week. Self-reported symptoms of upper-respiratory-tract infections (URTI) were monitored daily by questionnaire. Undertaking high-intensity training with a high-protein diet restored leukocyte kinetics to similar levels observed during normal-intensity training: CD8(+) TL mobilization (normal-intensity: 29,319 ± 13,130 cells/μL × 165 min vs. high-intensity with protein: 26,031 ± 17,474 cells/μL × 165 min, P > 0.05), CD8(+) TL egress (normal-intensity: 624 ± 264 cells/μL vs. high-intensity with protein: 597 ± 478 cells/μL, P > 0.05). This pattern was driven by effector-memory populations mobilizing (normal-intensity: 6,145 ± 6,227 cells/μL × 165 min vs. high-intensity with protein: 6,783 ± 8,203 cells/μL × 165 min, P > 0.05) and extravasating from blood (normal-intensity: 147 ± 129 cells/μL vs. high-intensity with protein: 165 ± 192 cells/μL, P > 0.05). High-intensity training while consuming a high-protein diet was associated with fewer symptoms of URTI compared to performing high-intensity training with a normal diet (P < 0.05). To conclude, a high-protein diet might reduce the incidence of URTI in athletes, potentially mediated by preventing training-induced impairments in immune surveillance.

While resistance exercise was generally effective at stimulating MPS, W20 and W40 ingestion post-exercise increased MPS above W0 and W10 exercised values (P < 0.05), and W40 was greater than W20 (P < 0.05).

Based on the study, the following conclusions were drawn. At rest, the optimal whey protein dose for non-frail older adults to consume, to increase myofibrillar MPS above fasting rates, was 20 g. Resistance exercise increases MPS in the elderly at all protein doses, but to a greater extent with 40 g of whey ingestion. These data suggest that, in contrast to younger adults, in whom post-exercise rates of MPS are saturated with 20 g of protein, exercised muscles of older adults respond to higher protein doses.

Whey protein supplements are considered also as a cocktail of amino acids, since they contain up to 26% of BCAA, plus L-arginine, L-lysine, L-glutamine, among others. Thus, the effects of whey protein in the immune system may represent the effect of particular amino acids per se. Moreover, whey proteins are rapidly digested and absorbed, resulting in postprandial muscle protein synthesis [125,126]. Several studies observed changes in muscle growth and performance increments with the chronic ingestion of whey protein supplements [121,127,128]. In one study, triathletes subjected to exhaustive exercise exhibited a decreased mitochondrial transmembrane potential in both lymphocytes and neutrophils, which leads to apoptotic death and DNA fragmentation [8]. When whey protein enriched with L-glutamine is supplemented, this scenario is reversed, especially in lymphocytes [8], which are essential for the response against viral infections, such as URTI. On the other hand, the rapid absorption of whey products from the gut and the hyperaminoacidemia are not the only critical characteristics for maximizing muscle protein synthesis. The time that amino acids are maintained in plasma is also important for muscle protein turnover, providing gains in muscle mass. There are few studies comparing protein mixtures. [NAME], [NAME] showed that a blend of whey and soy protein prolonged the elevation in blood amino acid levels after ingestion, when compared to whey protein alone, promoting a greater total muscle protein synthesis measured by the protein fractional synthetic rate (FSR). This is in agreement with other works, which found higher nitrogen retention and less oxidation with whey blends combined with slowly digested protein, such as casein ([NAME] and others 2005; [NAME] and others 2009) as well as oxidation. Stimulating post-exercise muscle protein synthesis and amino acid concentration maintenance may also contribute to immune function; however, more studies are needed.

The amino acid profile of whey protein supplements also includes sulfur-containing amino acids, such as cysteine and taurine [121]. The high proportion of amino donors of sulfhydryl groups may attenuate the reduction of intracellular GSH concentration induced by intensive exercise [128]. Since immune cells, such as lymphocytes, can be sensitive to a range of intracellular sulfhydryl compounds, such as GSH and cysteine (Figure 2), whey supplementation may not only attenuate the oxidative stress induced by exercise but also help maintain the redox status in immune cells. Experimental evidence supports this mechanistic effect [117]. In a recent study, it was observed that the fall in GSH content in trained subjects submitted to an intense exercise program (4 weeks) occurred in parallel with a decline in lymphocyte number. However, this scenario was reversed by N-acetylcysteine supplementation [131]. Furthermore, whey protein can act as an immune modulator through other mechanisms, such as L-glutamine, which is critical for the L-glutamine-GSH axis (Figure 3). Collectively, whey proteins, via provision of an amino acid cocktail, exert per

Whey protein has been shown to stimulate MPS to a greater extent than casein and soy protein at rest and following exercise in young and older individuals (Tang and others 2009; Pennings and others 2011; Burd and others 2012; Yang and others 2012b). The differential MPS response to protein feeding is a function of the quality of the ingested protein. Proteins differ in their quality based on their amino acid (AA) content, digestibility, and bioavailability (FAO/WHO Expert Consultation 1991). Upon ingestion, whey protein is rapidly digested and, since it is acid-soluble, it exits the stomach rapidly, resulting in a pronounced rise in blood AA, which is thought to be critical to the stimulation of MPS (Katsanos and others 2006; Dreyer and others 2008; Tang and others 2009; West and others 2011). In comparison to other supplemental proteins, whey and soy proteins are considered “fast”-digested proteins, while casein is considered a “slow”-digested protein as it clots due to the acid pH of the stomach and exits slowly into the small intestine (Boirie and others 1997; Bos and others 2003). Of importance is that whey protein is a complete protein, meaning it contains all of the essential amino acids (EAAs), and has a high proportion of the branched-chain AA (BCAA) leucine, a key AA in the stimulation of MPS (Anthony and others 2001). In fact, while both soy and casein are also complete proteins, whey protein has greater EAA and leucine contents than casein, soy, and collagen proteins. In addition to having a lower leucine content, the bioavailability of amino acids from soy protein to support MPS is inferior to that of whey and casein, with a greater amount being directed toward splanchnic catabolic activity and urea synthesis (Luiking and others 2005; Fouillet and others 2009) as well as oxidation (Yang and others 2012b). In addition, the higher BCAAs, particularly leucine, found in milk, as compared with soy, are readily available to peripheral tissues and are able to support MPS (Fouillet and others 2002). The differences in protein quality characteristics between whey, casein, soy, and collagen proteins are summarized in Table 1. Together, the differences in digestibility, AA content, and AA bioavailability result in a significantly lower rise in blood leucine and blood EAA concentration following consumption of is oenergetic, isonitrogenous casein and soy (and presumably collagen) beverages, as compared with whey (Tang and others 2009; Burd and others 2012).

The importance of leucine to stimulate MPS is underscored by numerous animal and human trials showing that administration of leucine can stimulate MPS (Anthony and others 2000; Crozier and others 2005; Escobar and others 2006; Katsanos and others 2006), which has given rise to the concept of the leucine threshold (Figure 2). The leucine threshold (or leucine “trigger”) hypothesis states that in order for a robust increase in MPS to ensue following protein consumption, the muscle intracellular leucine concentration needs to reach a given level—the leucine threshold (Phillips 2014). Importantly, this threshold can be manipulated, being lowered by factors such as resistance training and being increased by factors such as aging and physical inactivity (Moore and others 2014; Witard and others 2014). Given the fluctuating nature of this threshold, the exact amount of leucine that needs to be consumed to exceed the threshold has yet to be established and will vary within a population based on age and physical activity level.

Our lab (Moore and others 2009) and others (Witard and others 2014) have found that 20 g of high-quality protein, containing 1.7 to 2.4 g of leucine, maximally stimulates MPS, a level which likely represents the absolute minimum amount of leucine needed to be consumed given that the subjects tested were resistance-trained young men. Furthermore, given the leucine threshold, whether the addition of leucine to a suboptimal dose of protein can enhance its anabolic ability has also been examined. In particular, our laboratory has previously shown that the addition of 5 g, but not 3 g, leucine to 6.25 g of whey protein isolate stimulated MPS to the same extent as an optimal (25 g) dose of whey protein isolate (Churchward-Venne and others 2014). Furthermore, the addition of leucine to a protein/carbohydrate beverage resulted in a greater increase in MPS than a protein/carbohydrate beverage alone following a bout of resistance exercise (Koopman and others 2005), indicating that leucine can enhance the anabolic effect of protein. Of importance, while leucine can independently stimulate MPS (Anthony and others 2000; Crozier and others 2005; Escobar and others 2006; Katsanos and others 2006), in the absence of EAA, MPS would be limited. As such, given the role of leucine in the stimulation of MPS and that whey protein is an excellent source of leucine, BCAAs, and EAAs and is rapidly digested, whey protein is an excellent protein source for the stimulation of MPS and thus the regulation of muscle mass across the lifespan.

Milk Proteins

The main constituents of milk are considered functional foods, with direct impact on human health. Milk has two primary “fractions” of proteins: casein and whey. Whey is the liquid portion making up approximately 20% of the total protein content of bovine milk, with casein being 80% (human milk is 60/40, respectively). Processing, such as ultrafiltration and microfiltration, creates different whey protein products. The most utilized whey proteins include concentrate (about 80–95% of protein, with or without lactose), isolate (approximately 90–95% of protein, normally without carbohydrates or cholesterol), hydrolyzed (smaller peptide fractions that are considered less allergenic but costly), and non-denatured (native protein structures).

In a wide variety of circumstances, we have found a direct linear relationship between the total rate of appearance of essential amino acids into the intracellular pool and the rate of muscle protein synthesis (Figure 2).

Thus, it is clear that the measurement of protein synthesis can only be interpreted in the context of the anabolic response when considered in relation to concurrent changes in the rate of breakdown and the total rate of appearance of amino acids intracellularly.

WHY WAS THE CONCEPT OF MAXIMAL ANABOLIC RESPONSE DEVELOPED?

The fundamental observation that has led to the concept of a maximal anabolic response to protein intake is that increases in amino acid concentrations in plasma are directly related to the stimulation of muscle protein synthesis up to a point, whereupon further increases in plasma amino acid concentrations do not translate to greater increases in protein synthesis.

When the rate of influx of amino acids from plasma into muscle is modest relative to the rate of protein synthesis, the intracellular concentrations of amino acids remain relatively constant (10).

Once the maximal rate of synthesis is achieved, the intracellular concentrations of amino acids begin to rise as a function of further increases in plasma amino acid availability (10). The concentrations of the intracellular amino acids presumably rise above the post-absorptive levels because the maximal rate of incorporation into protein has been reached. However, the point at which intracellular amino acid concentration begins to increase does not necessarily coincide with the maximal anabolic response. Rather, the anabolic response may continue to increase as protein intake increases, even without the further stimulation of protein synthesis. This response can occur if, as appears to be the case (9), further increases in intracellular amino acid concentrations provide a signal to limit the rate of protein breakdown.

The role of insulin

Insulin is an anabolic hormone that is released at an increased rate in response to ingestion of carbohydrate. Ingestion of certain proteins and amino acids can also stimulate insulin release, particularly when eaten in large quantities. In the physiological range, insulin inhibits protein breakdown and, as a result, lowers free amino acid levels in both the plasma and intracellular spaces (11). Although insulin is an anabolic hormone that activates the signals that initiate protein synthesis, an increase in insulin concentration without a concomitant increase in amino acid concentrations may not affect or even decrease the rate of protein synthesis both in muscle and at the whole-body level. This is because the decreased availability of amino acids resulting from the suppression of protein breakdown overrides any stimulatory effect of insulin on protein synthesis (11).

title: References & Protein limit info (part 3 of 3)
content:
In the setting of increased insulin and decreased endogenous amino acid concentrations, ingestion of protein will cause a significantly lower peak response of the plasma amino acid concentrations than if the same amount of protein was ingested in the absence of an insulin response. Also, insulin stimulates gut tissue net protein synthesis, which as a result causes fewer amino acids to appear in the portal vein (12). As a consequence, the rate of protein synthesis will likely increase to a smaller extent in the setting of increased insulin concentration than if there was no insulin response, even though the total anabolic response may be greater because of the simultaneous suppression of protein breakdown. Because of the reduction in the concentrations of endogenous amino acids secondary to an increase in insulin concentration, the apparent maximal synthetic response to protein intake may not reflect the true capacity for synthesis because of limitations in total amino acid availability. More importantly, the synthetic response in the setting of elevated insulin does not reflect the maximal anabolic response. The role of insulin in suppressing protein breakdown is particularly important when considering the response to protein intake in the context of a complete meal, in which the carbohydrate can result in a significant insulin response.

Is there an upper limit to the anabolic response to protein intake with a meal?

The theory described above predicts that there would be no practical limit to the anabolic response to protein intake with a meal. With greater and greater carbohydrate and protein intake, a progressively greater insulin response will result, with subsequent suppression of protein breakdown, and thus a greater anabolic response. Results from our recent studies (Figure 3) and studies of others (13–18) in which whole-body protein synthesis and breakdown have been measured suggest that in fact the theory is correct and that this relation remains even at high protein intakes. It is important to note that in all studies in which net protein synthesis has been measured, the relationship between amino acid availability and net gain is linear, with no plateau of effect at higher levels of availability.

From these data we must conclude that there is no practical upper limit to the anabolic response to protein or amino acid intake in the context of a meal.

DO THE METABOLIC STUDIES OF THE ANABOLIC RESPONSE ACCURATELY PREDICT THE TRUE ANABOLIC RESPONSE OVER DAYS AND WEEKS?

We therefore have to conclude that there is no limit to the increase in the net anabolic response to higher and higher amounts of protein intake. While on the surface this observation seems questionable, the same observation has been made repeatedly using the N-balance approach, and more modern stable isotope indicator methods also suggest continued protein accretion at intakes greater than the requirement level (13–18). A variety of studies substantiate that the tracer methods to quantify acute responses of protein synthesis and breakdown accurately predict changes over time in lean mass in tightly controlled conditions (19, 20). It is much harder to control all potentially important variables in long-term outcome studies than in acute metabolic studies, and consequently there are no prospective studies of which we are aware in which the responses of physiological outcome variables were measured in response to progressively increasing levels of protein intake.

Several studies in older individuals have documented that supplementation of the diet with amino acids or protein increases lean body mass and function. Importantly, we are aware of no studies that show that higher levels of protein intake fail to increase lean mass or muscle function over time.

CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS

The normal dinner includes more than 30 g of protein, which is generally agreed to be sufficient to elicit the maximal stimulation of muscle protein synthesis. Consequently, it has been proposed that the maximal total stimulation of muscle protein synthesis over the day will be achieved by spreading protein intake out as opposed to eating most daily protein at dinner, which is currently the most common approach (2, 21). This hypothesis assumes that the nutritional goal of protein intake is the stimulation of muscle protein FSR. However, the anabolic response is a function not only of the rate of protein synthesis, but also of the rate of protein breakdown. We believe that the total anabolic response to protein intake, particularly in the context of a complete meal that stimulates an insulin response, is therefore incorrectly characterized by exclusive reliance on the FSR measurement. Extrapolation of the FSR response to the conclusion that there is a maximal amount of protein in a meal that can stimulate net protein anabolism is not justified. In our opinion, the preponderance of evidence indicates that the more protein in a meal, the more anabolism will be observed.

This perspective is supported by a recent publication in this journal (22) in which consumption of 80% of the 1.5 gram protein/kg BW/day in a single meal was more anabolic than spreading the same amount of protein intake throughout the day. If the limit to the maximal anabolic response were 30 grams per meal, the approach of providing most protein in one meal would have been unsuccessful in achieving the optimal anabolic response. The practical implication of this conclusion is that protein nutrition can be improved by increasing the protein intake at breakfast and lunch and maintaining a high amount of protein intake with dinner, or increasing the amount of protein eaten with dinner if that is more convenient. Alternatively, replacing low-quality proteins with high-quality proteins, containing higher levels of a balanced essential amino acid mixture, will additionally stimulate protein anabolism.
