Feeding stimulates robust increases in muscle protein synthesis (MPS); however, ageing may alter the anabolic response to protein ingestion and the subsequent aminoacidaemia. With this as background, we aimed to determine in the present study the dose-response of MPS with the ingestion of isolated whey protein, with and without prior resistance exercise, in the elderly. For the purpose of this study, thirty-seven elderly men (age 71 (SD 4) years) completed a bout of unilateral leg-based resistance exercise before ingesting 0, 10, 20, or 40 g of whey protein isolate (W0–W40, respectively). Infusion of L-[1-13C]leucine and L-[ring-13C6]phenylalanine with bilateral vastus lateralis muscle biopsies were used to ascertain whole-body leucine oxidation and 4 h post-protein-consumption MPS in the fed state of non-exercised and exercised leg muscles. It was determined that whole-body leucine oxidation increased in a stepwise, dose-dependent manner. MPS increased above basal, fasting values by approximately 65% and 90% for W20 and W40, respectively (P < 0.05), but not with lower doses of whey. While resistance exercise was generally effective at stimulating MPS, W20 and W40 ingestion post-exercise increased MPS above W0 and W10 exercised values (P < 0.05), and W40 was greater than W20 (P < 0.05). Based on the study, the following conclusions were drawn. At rest, the optimal whey protein dose for non-frail older adults to consume, to increase myofibrillar MPS above fasting rates, was 20 g. Resistance exercise increases MPS in the elderly at all protein doses, but to a greater extent with 40 g of whey ingestion. These data suggest that, in contrast to younger adults, in whom post-exercise rates of MPS are saturated with 20 g of protein, exercised muscles of older adults respond to higher protein doses.

BACKGROUND & AIMS:

The requirement of leucine and essential amino acids (EAA) to stimulate muscle protein synthesis increases with age. To target muscle anabolism, it is suggested that higher postprandial blood levels of leucine and EAA are needed in older people. The aim was to evaluate the impact of oral nutritional supplements with distinct protein source and energy density, resembling mixed meals, on serum amino acid profiles and on gastrointestinal behaviour.

METHODS:

Four isonitrogenous protein (21 g) supplements were studied containing leucine-enriched whey protein with 150/320 kcal (W150/W320) or casein protein with 150/320 kcal (C150/C320); all products contained carbohydrates (10 or 32 g) and fat (3 or 12 g). Postprandial serum AA profiles were evaluated in twelve healthy, older subjects who participated in a randomized, controlled, single-blind, crossover study. Gastrointestinal behaviour was studied in vitro by looking at gastric coagulation and cumulative intestinal protein digestion over time.

RESULTS:

The peak serum leucine concentration was twofold higher for W150 vs. C150 (521 ± 15 vs. 260 ± 15 μmol/L, p < 0.001), higher for W320 vs. C320 (406 ± 15 vs. 228 ± 15 μmol/L, p < 0.001), and higher for low-caloric vs. high-caloric products (p < 0.001 for pooled analyses; p < 0.001 for interaction protein source × caloric density). Similar effects were observed for the peak concentrations of EAA and total AA (TAA). In vitro gastric coagulation was observed only for the casein protein supplements. Intestinal digestion for 90 min resulted in higher levels of free TAA, EAA, and leucine for W150 vs. C150, for W150 vs. W320, and for C150 vs. C320 (p < 0.0125).

CONCLUSIONS:

A low-calorie, leucine-enriched whey protein nutritional supplement provides a higher rise in serum levels of TAA, EAA, and leucine compared to casein protein or high-calorie products in healthy, elderly subjects. These differences appear to be mediated in part by the gastrointestinal behaviour of these products.

title: Curcumin safety and efficacy at the right dosage
content:
Please give me the scientific consensus on the daily ingestion of 200 mg of curcumin (extract of turmeric), including its safety and efficacy related to general claims such as controlling inflammation, antioxidant functions, antiviral effects, and immune support.

Pro
1 search
20 sources

Current research supports that daily ingestion of 200 mg curcumin is generally considered safe and may offer benefits for inflammation, antioxidant activity, and immune modulation, but its efficacy for antiviral effects and broad immune support is less established.

Safety

Multiple human trials, including those with much higher doses (up to 8,000 mg/day), have found curcumin to be safe with minimal adverse effects, and doses in the range of 200 mg are well below those tested for toxicity. However, curcumin’s poor bioavailability is a known limitation, and co-administration with agents like piperine can enhance absorption.

Anti-Inflammatory Effects

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials show that curcumin supplementation significantly reduces inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and interleukin-6 (IL-6). These effects are observed across a range of doses, including those as low as 120 mg, and are most pronounced in individuals with chronic inflammatory conditions. Curcumin modulates key inflammatory signaling pathways, including NF-κB and JAK/STAT, contributing to its anti-inflammatory action.

Antioxidant Functions

Curcumin supplementation has been shown to enhance antioxidant capacity by increasing total antioxidant capacity (TAC) and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, and reducing malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, indicating reduced oxidative stress. These effects are consistent across multiple clinical trials and reviews.

Immune Support

Curcumin demonstrates immunomodulatory effects, including balancing Th1/Th2 responses and modulating cytokine production, which may support immune health, particularly in conditions with immune dysregulation. However, evidence for general immune “boosting” in healthy individuals is less robust.

Antiviral Activity

While laboratory studies suggest curcumin has antiviral properties, clinical evidence in humans is limited and inconsistent. Most claims of antiviral efficacy are based on preclinical or in vitro data, not large-scale human trials.

Bioavailability Considerations

Curcumin’s low oral bioavailability limits its clinical efficacy. Formulations with piperine or as metal complexes (e.g., zinc-curcumin) can improve absorption and therapeutic effects.

Conclusion

Daily ingestion of 200 mg curcumin is safe and may help control inflammation and oxidative stress, with some evidence for immune modulation. Antiviral and broad immune support claims are not strongly supported by current clinical evidence. Enhanced formulations may improve efficacy.

Curcumin supplementation has been widely studied for its anti-inflammatory effects, particularly its ability to reduce proinflammatory cytokines. The evidence shows that curcumin can lower certain cytokines, but the effect is not uniform across all types.

Key Findings on Proinflammatory Cytokines

| Cytokine | Consistent Reduction? | Evidence & Notes | Citations |
|---|---|---|---|
| IL-1 | Yes | Significant decrease in multiple RCTs and meta-analyses | 1236+1 MORE |
| TNF-α | Yes | Significant reduction in both healthy and diseased populations | 1236+1 MORE |
| IL-6 | Mixed | Some studies show reduction, others find no significant effect | 1234+1 MORE |
| IL-8 | No | No significant reduction; some studies show no effect or even slight increase | 15 |
| MCP-1, TGF-β | Yes (in some groups) | Reductions seen in specific populations (e.g., metabolic syndrome, COVID-19) | 234 |

Mechanisms

Curcumin inhibits the NF-κB pathway, a central regulator of inflammation, which leads to decreased expression of several proinflammatory cytokines. It also modulates other signaling pathways involved in cytokine production.

Clinical Context

Chronic Inflammatory Conditions: Consistent reductions in IL-1 and TNF-α are most evident in people with underlying inflammatory conditions such as metabolic syndrome or after infection.

Acute Inflammation (e.g., COVID-19): Curcumin supplementation has been shown to reduce cytokine storm markers, including IL-1β and IL-6, in hospitalized patients.

Healthy Individuals: Effects may be less pronounced or inconsistent, especially for IL-6 and IL-8.

Summary Table: Curcumin’s Effect on Proinflammatory Cytokines

| Cytokine | Effect of Curcumin | Citations |
|---|---|---|
| IL-1 | ↓ (consistent) | 1236+1 MORE |
| TNF-α | ↓ (consistent) | 1236+1 MORE |
| IL-6 | ↓ (mixed) | 1234+1 MORE |
| IL-8 | ↔/↑ (no effect) | 15 |

Conclusion

Curcumin supplementation consistently reduces IL-1 and TNF-α, with mixed results for IL-6 and little to no effect on IL-8. The anti-inflammatory benefits are most reliable in people with existing inflammatory conditions.

title: Can the 3-low/1-high strategy be used to prepare for an evening party or social event where more calories than usual will be consumed, and is there a video or breakdown of the plan?
content:
The best carbohydrates after a workout are the ones that rapidly restore muscle glycogen, improve recovery, and support muscle protein synthesis (MPS)—especially when combined with high-quality protein. The “best” choice depends on the goal, training volume, body composition goals, and how quickly another workout is coming.

Best Post-Workout Carbohydrates for Glycogen Replenishment

Fast-Digesting / High-Glycemic Carbohydrates

These are ideal immediately after intense training because they digest quickly and raise insulin efficiently to drive glucose back into muscle.

- White rice
- Potatoes (especially white or mashed potatoes)
- Cream of rice
- Rice cakes
- Fruit (banana, pineapple, mango, raisins)
- Honey
- Sports drinks or glucose polymers
- Bagels or white bread
- Oatmeal (moderate-fast depending on type)
- Low-fat breakfast cereals

These are especially useful for:

- Athletes training multiple times per day
- High-volume bodybuilding or performance training
- Glycogen-depleting endurance or interval work
- Individuals struggling to recover or gain muscle

Best Scientific Combination

The evidence consistently shows that combining carbohydrates with protein is superior to carbs alone for recovery.

A highly effective post-workout target is approximately:

- 0.5–0.75 g carbohydrate per lb bodyweight
- Plus 25–40 g high-quality protein

Example for a 180-lb exerciser:

- Approximately 90–135 g carbs
- 30–40 g whey protein

This combination:

- Refills glycogen faster
- Enhances insulin response
- Reduces muscle breakdown
- Improves net muscle protein balance
- Accelerates recovery

Best Carb Types Based on Goals

| Goal | Best Carb Strategy |
|---|---|
| Max muscle gain/performance | Fast carbs + whey protein |
| Fat loss while preserving muscle | Moderate carbs + high protein |
| Endurance recovery | Higher total carbs + sodium/electrolytes |
| Healthy aging/longevity | Moderate clean carbs + protein blend |
| GLP-1 users | Easily digestible carbs + protein due to appetite suppression |

Real-World Practical Examples

Muscle Gain / Performance

- Whey protein + cream of rice + banana
- Chocolate milk + rice cakes
- FirstString™-style carb/protein blend

Fat Loss / Lean Recovery

- WheySmooth™ + fruit
- LeanMeal™
- Greek yogurt + berries + oats

Rapid Recovery Between Sessions

- Sports drink + whey isolate
- White rice + lean protein
- Potato + protein shake

Important Takeaway for Trainers

The best post-workout carbohydrate is not just about “sugar”—it’s about delivering glucose back into muscle efficiently while pairing it with sufficient amino acids to maximize recovery and muscle protein synthesis. Fast-digesting carbs work best when the goal is performance and recovery, while moderate, fiber-containing carbs may work better when appetite control and body composition are priorities.

Simple Trainer Rule:

“After training, feed the muscle fast: quality carbs refill glycogen, quality protein rebuilds muscle.”

title: Changing a slow metabolism
content:
Changing metabolism

Many patients with obesity blame weight gain on their metabolism. The reality is that metabolism can be blamed for weight regain after people try to lose weight! As we age, our metabolism does slow down; sometimes we think it stops working.

[NAME], MD

Metabolism, or resting energy expenditure, is directly related to how much muscle mass we have. As we age, we lose muscle, which is called sarcopenia.

What happens to our metabolism when we try to lose weight? Let's first discuss what metabolism is.

What Is Metabolism?

Metabolism refers to the chemical reactions in the body's cells that convert food into energy for sustaining life, cellular processes, and as storage for a rainy day.

Total energy expenditure (TEE) is broken down into resting energy expenditure (REE), thermic effect of food (TEF), and nonresting expenditure (NREE) or physical activity, and is made up of:

TEE = 60% REE + 10% TEF + 30% NREE

An elegant study performed by Dr [NAME] explored the effects of weight loss or weight gain on metabolism in 23 lean and 18 patients with obesity who were placed in a metabolic chamber. Weight loss of 10% or 20% body weight led to a decrease in TEE roughly equal to about 300 kcal/d, and an increase in body weight of 10% caused an increase in TEE of about 500 kcal/d. These changes led to the patient reverting to the prior weight (before weight loss or gain). In other words, Dr [NAME] postulated a feedback mechanism for the effect of fat mass decrease or increase on energy metabolism. The feedback mechanism or signal from fat was subsequently found to be leptin.

In a later study, [NAME] and colleagues investigated the effects of body fat mass change on TEE and found that a 10% reduction in weight caused a decrease of TEE by 21%, comprising a decrease in NREE of 37.5% and a decrease in REE of 11.6%.

Therefore, the biggest change in TEE comes from NREE or exercise energy expenditure. The 35% variance in NEE change was accounted for by a decrease in muscle work efficiency in generating 10 watts or low levels of work such as walking.

In other words, when persons with obesity or lean persons lose weight, the efficiency of muscle at low levels of work increases such that one burns less energy when walking than one normally would. This helps conserve energy and tends to cause the body to go back to the higher weight.

So, How Can One Change Metabolism?

Let's say one did lose weight and wants to counteract this TEE loss and increased muscle efficiency at low levels of work.

To counteract this effect, one should increase muscle work beyond low level so that more energy is expended. Another way would be to increase muscle mass so that there is more muscle that can do work.

This is exactly how metabolism can be altered or increased. What can be changed most readily, and what we have the most power over in our bodies, is the NREE.

To do this, muscles need anabolic power—the power to heal and build muscle mass. Anabolic power comes from eating healthy protein sources such as lean chicken, fish, beef, and eggs as well as dry beans, tofu, and dairy products. It seems that older adults (> 60 years) need more protein than younger adults to build muscle mass, due to the body's natural aging process which leads to sarcopenia. How much more? Studies show between 1.2 and 1.5 g/kg of body weight per day, whereas younger persons need 0.80 g/kg.

Developing sarcopenia with age involves muscle losing the ability to use protein and amino acids to rebuild injured tissue.

Let's put this in perspective for treating obesity.

Obesity is brought on by the body's defense of a higher body weight by interaction with the environment of highly processed foods that work on the reward pathway, leading to weight gain and resistance to satiety. Weight loss via diet, exercise, and medications works, but this weight loss is also accompanied by a decrease in TEE.

Weight loss is primarily fat mass loss, but depending on the degree of protein intake and muscle resistance training, 20%-50% of the total weight loss is muscle mass loss. Therefore, higher-protein diets and resistance exercise can be useful in preserving muscle mass and counteracting the decrease in TEE, maintaining energy expenditure. In older patients, an additional factor is the muscle's lack of ability to use protein as an anabolic agent to protect muscle mass and thus the need for higher protein loads to do this.

All in all, can doctors help patients boost their metabolism, especially as they lose weight and maintain that loss? Yes—through protein intake and resistance exercise training.

Here are some tips to help your patients get cardio and resistance exercise into their routine.

First find out whether your patient prefers a social exercise interaction or solo training. If social, then the gym or classes such as cycling or boot camps at those gyms may work for them, especially if they can go with a friend. If solo is better, then a gym in the home might work. Peloton bikes are expensive but the interaction is all on the website!

A personal trainer may help motivate the patient if they know someone is waiting for them.

Let's hit the gym!

Another note: There are agents in the obesity treatment pipeline that purport to change body composition while helping patients lose weight. Some of these agents are myostatin antagonists and antibodies that inhibit the activity of myostatin to break down muscle. These agents have been found to build muscle mass, but whether the quality of the muscle mass leads to an increase in muscle strength or functionality remains controversial. The next frontier in obesity treatment will be about decreasing fat mass and increasing muscle mass while making sure that increased muscle mass leads to improved functionality.

In the meantime, aside from new agents on the horizon, the best and healthiest way to keep metabolism on the up and up is to eat healthy lean proteins and exercise. How much exercise? The recommendation is 30-60 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity at least 5 days per week; plus 20 minutes of resistance exercise training 2-3 days per week for upper- and lower-extremity and core strength.

Again, let's hit the gym!

title: BPC-157 doage in syringe
content:
The BPC-157 peptide is recommended to be used at 500 micrograms/day. Using your typical insulin syringe with numbers 10–100 on it, how much would the 500 micrograms be—that is, what number would we load it to?

To answer this accurately, we need one missing piece of information:

How much liquid (mL) was used to reconstitute the BPC-157 vial, and how many total micrograms are in the vial (e.g., 5 mg)?

The number on an insulin syringe (10–100) does not represent micrograms. It represents volume (mL or “units”), so the microgram dose depends entirely on the final concentration after reconstitution.

That said, below is a clear, practical guide using the most common real-world setups, so you can see exactly how this works.

Key syringe facts (important)

A U-100 insulin syringe:
- 100 units = 1.0 mL
- 10 units = 0.10 mL
- 20 units = 0.20 mL
- etc.

Most common BPC-157 scenario

Example 1 (VERY COMMON)

Vial: 5 mg BPC-157 (5,000 mcg)
Reconstitution: 2.0 mL bacteriostatic water

Concentration
5,000 mcg ÷ 2.0 mL = 2,500 mcg per mL

Dose wanted
500 mcg per day

Volume needed
500 mcg ÷ 2,500 mcg/mL = 0.20 mL

On a U-100 insulin syringe
0.20 mL = 20 units

You would draw to the “20” mark.

Other common setups (quick reference)

Example 2
5 mg vial + 1.0 mL water
Concentration: 5,000 mcg/mL
500 mcg dose = 0.10 mL
Syringe: 10 units

Example 3
5 mg vial + 3.0 mL water
Concentration: 1,667 mcg/mL
500 mcg dose ≈ 0.30 mL
Syringe: 30 units

Simple formula you can always use

Syringe units =
(desired mcg ÷ total mcg in vial) × total mL × 100

Important safety notes

BPC-157 is not FDA-approved and is used under medical supervision.

Always confirm:
- Vial strength (mg)
- Reconstitution volume

Never assume another person’s dosing applies to your vial.

This is educational math, not medical advice.

Bottom line (most likely answer)

If you are using the most common setup (5 mg vial reconstituted with 2 mL):
500 mcg = 20 units on a standard insulin syringe.

If you want, tell me:
- Vial size (mg)
- How much liquid you used (mL)

…and I’ll give you the exact syringe number with zero guessing.

How much volume is in a typical insulin syringe?

A standard U-100 insulin syringe holds:
1.0 mL total volume

What do the numbers 10–100 mean?

The numbers do NOT represent milligrams or micrograms.
They represent insulin units, which are simply a way of marking volume.

For a U-100 syringe:
- 100 units = 1.0 mL
- 10 units = 0.10 mL
- 1 unit = 0.01 mL

Volume breakdown (most important part)

| Syringe Marking | Volume (mL) |
|---|---|
| 10 | 0.10 mL |
| 20 | 0.20 mL |
| 30 | 0.30 mL |
| 40 | 0.40 mL |
| 50 | 0.50 mL |
| 60 | 0.60 mL |
| 70 | 0.70 mL |
| 80 | 0.80 mL |
| 90 | 0.90 mL |
| 100 | 1.00 mL |

Why this matters (especially for peptides)

Insulin syringe numbers = volume only.

The actual dose (mcg or mg) depends on:
- How much powder was in the vial
- How much liquid (mL) it was mixed with

So:
The syringe never tells you the dose—only how much liquid you’re drawing.

One-sentence summary (easy to remember)

A 10–100 insulin syringe holds 1 mL total, and each “10” equals 0.1 mL (100 microliters).

- Show how this converts to micrograms for peptides
- Create a trainer-safe dosing explainer

title: Folic acid, folate, methyl-folate,5-MTHF full note new SuppBeast answers
content:
Is folic acid an okay form of folate in multivitamins? Is folic acid bad?

No, folic acid is good and a common form of folate used in fortification and multivitamin and mineral formulas (MVM). And don’t be swayed by companies or influencers pushing folate supplements. Folic acid is safe, and it’s the only form of folate that has been shown to prevent neural tube birth defects. Folic acid has been used safely and effectively for decades.

The other form common in MVM is L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate (L-methylfolate), which may be advantageous in certain circumstances because it is already in the biologically active form and bypasses the need for conversion by the MTHFR gene enzyme, which has reduced activity in some individuals. Therefore, it may be preferable for people with certain genetic variants or medical conditions affecting folate metabolism. But it's not as common as the internet would have you believe, and for most people, their body does a perfectly adequate job of converting folic acid.

Bottom line

Folic acid is absolutely a form of folate. It is a synthetic, stable, and effective form that has been used safely for decades. However, L-methylfolate is the active form that the body ultimately uses, so many premium multivitamins choose it because it eliminates the need for metabolic conversion and provides a more direct source of usable folate. For most healthy adults taking a standard multivitamin, either form is effective, although L-methylfolate is generally considered the more advanced formulation choice.

Now here's the important nuance people get wrong:

When someone says, "I want a fully methylated multivitamin"—look, I get it, I hear that phrase all the time. But here's the reality: there are only two nutrients in a multivitamin that can actually be in methylated form. That's folate (as methylfolate) and B12 (as methylcobalamin). That's it. Anyone selling you a "fully methylated multi" with a dozen methylated ingredients is either confused or marketing to your confusion. It's literally impossible, not to mention, the product would be useless.

On the B12 front, people will often ask, is there anything truly wrong with using cyanocobalamin as a form of B12 in a multi? And that’s because the same disruptive influencers are selling something using flawed science and context.

The real answer is:

Cyanocobalamin is a safe, effective, and well-researched form of vitamin B12 that has been used successfully in multivitamins for decades. Although it must be converted by the body into the active forms—methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin—healthy individuals generally perform this conversion efficiently, making it an excellent choice for preventing and correcting B12 deficiency. While premium formulations often use active forms because they require no conversion and align with a "best available ingredients" philosophy, current evidence shows little meaningful clinical advantage over cyanocobalamin for most healthy adults. The small amount of cyanide associated with cyanocobalamin is negligible, naturally detoxified by the body, and not considered a safety concern, especially considering the amount is far less than what people ingest naturally from healthy foods such as almonds, flaxseed, lima beans, and cruciferous vegetables. Overall, cyanocobalamin remains a scientifically sound, stable, and reliable source of vitamin B12, while active forms may offer theoretical or niche benefits for certain individuals or premium product positioning. This is why many premium formulas use both forms.

Takeaway:

At the end of the day, does any of this matter if your multi doesn't even have the 20 known potentially under-consumed nutrients covered first? Absolutely not—get your baseline right before splitting hairs on “methylation.”

Focus on a complete, third-party-tested multi that covers your nutritional bases. The form of folate is refinement, a good one—but it's not the hill to die on if everything else in your multi is solid.

title: Thyroid, TSH levels medication needs
content:
Does an Elevated TSH Value Always Require Therapy? (medscape.com)

Thyroxine and L-thyroxine are two of the 10 most frequently prescribed medicinal products. "One large health insurance company ranks thyroid hormone at fourth place in the list of most-sold medications in the United States. It is possibly the second most commonly prescribed preparation," said Joachim Feldkamp, MD, PhD, director of the University Clinic for General Internal Medicine, Endocrinology, Diabetology, and Infectious Diseases at Central Hospital, Bielefeld, Germany, at the online press conference for the German Society of Endocrinology's hormone week.

The preparation is prescribed when the thyroid gland produces too little thyroid hormone. The messenger substance thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is used as a screening value to assess thyroid function. An increase in TSH can indicate that too little thyroid hormone is being produced.

"But this does not mean that an underactive thyroid gland is hiding behind every elevated TSH value," said Feldkamp. Normally, the TSH value lies between 0.3 and 4.2 mU/L. "Hypothyroidism, as it's known, is formally present if the TSH value lies above the upper limit of 4.2 mU/L," said Feldkamp.

Check Again

However, not every elevated TSH value needs to be treated immediately. "From large-scale investigations, we know that TSH values are subject to fluctuations," said Feldkamp. Individual measurements must therefore be taken with a grain of salt and almost never justify a therapeutic decision. Therefore, a slightly elevated TSH value should be checked again 2-6 months later, and the patient should be asked if they are experiencing any symptoms. "In 50%-60% of cases, the TSH value normalized at the second checkup without requiring any treatment," Feldkamp explained.

The TSH value could be elevated for several reasons:

Fluctuations depending on the time of day. At night and early in the morning, the TSH value is much higher than in the afternoon. An acute lack of sleep can lead to higher TSH values in the morning.

Fluctuations depending on the time of year. In winter, TSH values are slightly higher than in the summer owing to adaptation to cooler temperatures. Researchers in the Arctic, for example, have significantly higher TSH values than people who live in warmer regions.

Age-dependent differences. Children and adolescents have higher TSH values than adults do. The TSH values of adolescents cannot be based on those of adults because this would lead to incorrect treatment. In addition, TSH values increase with age, and slightly elevated values are initially no cause for treatment in people aged 70-80 years. Caution is advised during treatment, because overtreatment can lead to cardiac arrhythmias and a decrease in bone density.

Sex-specific differences. The TSH values of women are generally a little higher than those in men.

Obesity. In obesity, TSH increases and often exceeds the normal values usually recorded in persons of normal weight. The elevated values do not reflect a state of hypofunction, but rather the body's adjustment mechanism. If these patients lose weight, the TSH values will drop spontaneously. Slightly elevated TSH values in obese people should not be treated with thyroid hormones.

The nutritional supplement biotin (vitamin H or vitamin B7), which is often taken for skin, hair, and nail growth disorders, can distort measured values. In many of the laboratory methods used, the biotin competes with the test substances used. As a result, it can lead to falsely high and falsely low TSH values. At high doses of biotin (eg, 10 mg), there should be at least a 3-day pause (and ideally a pause of 1 week) before measuring TSH.

Hasty Prescriptions

"Sometimes, because of the assumption that every high TSH value is due to sickness-related hypothyroidism, thyroid hormones can be prescribed too quickly," said Feldkamp. This is also true for patients with thyroid nodules due to iodine deficiency, who are often still treated with thyroid hormones.

"These days, because we are generally an iodine-deficient nation, iodine would potentially be given in combination with thyroid hormones, but not with thyroid hormones alone. There are lots of patients who have been taking thyroid hormones for 30 or 40 years due to thyroid nodules. That should definitely be reviewed," said Feldkamp.

When to Treat?

Feldkamp does not believe that standard determination of the TSH value is sensible and advises that clinicians examine patients with newly occurring symptoms, such as excess weight, impaired weight regulation despite reduced appetite, depression, or a high need for sleep.

If there are symptoms, the thyroid function must be clarified further. "This includes determination of free thyroid hormones T3 and T4, detection of antibodies against autologous thyroid tissue such as TPO-Ab [antibody against thyroid peroxidase], TG-Ab [antibody against thyroglobulin], and TRAb [antibody against TSH receptor], and ultrasound examination of the metabolic organ," said Feldkamp. Autoimmune-related hypothyroidism (Hashimoto thyroiditis) is the most common cause of an overly high TSH level.

Treatment should take place in the following situations:

In young patients with TSH values > 10 mU/L;
In young (< 65 years) symptomatic patients with TSH values of 4 to < 10 mU/L;
With elevated TSH values that result from thyroid surgery or radioactive iodine therapy;
In patients with a diffuse enlarged or severely nodular thyroid gland; and
In pregnant women with elevated TSH values.

This article was translated from Medscape's German Edition.

title: Collagen protein info - AA counts
content:
The amino acid composition of collagen varies slightly depending on the source (bovine, porcine, marine) and manufacturing process, but hydrolyzed bovine collagen peptides—the most common supplemental form—are remarkably consistent.

Below is the approximate amino acid profile of 1 gram (1,000 mg) of collagen protein.

| Amino Acid | Approx. mg per 1 g |
|---|---:|
| Glycine | 210–220 mg |
| Proline | 120–130 mg |
| Hydroxyproline* | 110–130 mg |
| Glutamic Acid | 95–105 mg |
| Alanine | 80–90 mg |
| Arginine | 75–85 mg |
| Aspartic Acid | 50–60 mg |
| Lysine | 35–45 mg |
| Serine | 30–40 mg |
| Leucine | 25–30 mg |
| Valine | 20–25 mg |
| Phenylalanine | 20–25 mg |
| Threonine | 15–20 mg |
| Isoleucine | 10–15 mg |
| Hydroxylysine* | 8–12 mg |
| Histidine | 6–10 mg |
| Methionine | 5–10 mg |
| Tyrosine | 3–6 mg |

### Amino acids essentially absent

Collagen contains virtually no:

- Tryptophan (0 mg)
- Cysteine
- Asparagine (reported with aspartic acid)
- Glutamine (reported with glutamic acid)

### Essential Amino Acid (EAA) content

| Essential Amino Acid | Approx. mg per 1 g |
|---|---:|
| Histidine | 8 |
| Isoleucine | 12 |
| Leucine | 28 |
| Lysine | 40 |
| Methionine | 7 |
| Phenylalanine | 22 |
| Threonine | 18 |
| Tryptophan | 0 |
| Valine | 22 |
| Total EAAs | ≈155–165 mg |

### Comparison with whey protein

| Protein Source | EAAs per 1 g Protein |
|---|---:|
| Whey Protein | ≈450–500 mg |
| Egg Protein | ≈450 mg |
| Collagen Protein | ≈160 mg |

Thus, collagen contains only about one-third of the essential amino acids found in whey or egg protein on a gram-for-gram basis.

### Why collagen is still valuable

Although collagen is a poor protein for stimulating skeletal muscle protein synthesis because it lacks tryptophan and is very low in leucine and several other EAAs, it is uniquely rich in amino acids that support connective tissue:

- Glycine: ~21–22%
- Proline: ~12–13%
- Hydroxyproline: ~11–13%

These amino acids are the primary structural building blocks of collagen in:

- Tendons
- Ligaments
- Cartilage
- Skin
- Bone matrix

This is why collagen peptides are best viewed as a specialized connective tissue support protein, not a replacement for high-quality complete proteins such as whey, milk, egg, soy, or beef when the goal is maximizing muscle protein synthesis.

Given the educational materials we've created together, I can also produce a side-by-side comparison of 1 g, 10 g, and 20 g of collagen versus whey protein, highlighting leucine, total EAAs, glycine, proline, hydroxyproline, and tryptophan. This makes a very compelling trainer education slide because it visually explains why collagen and whey are complementary rather than competing proteins.

Below is a side-by-side comparison of the essential amino acid (EAA) content in 1 gram of collagen protein versus 1 gram of whey protein. Values are approximate averages based on high-quality bovine collagen peptides and whey protein isolate/concentrate.

### Essential amino acids in 1 g of protein

Approximate essential amino acid content of collagen protein versus whey protein (mg per gram of protein).

Collagen — Whey

0 mg, 30 mg, 60 mg, 90 mg, 120 mg: Histidine, Leucine, Methionine, Threonine, Valine

Collagen contains virtually no tryptophan and substantially lower levels of branched-chain amino acids than whey.

### Summary

| Essential Amino Acid | Collagen (mg/g) | Whey (mg/g) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Histidine | 8 | 17 |
| Isoleucine | 12 | 61 |
| Leucine | 28 | 110 |
| Lysine | 40 | 95 |
| Methionine | 7 | 22 |
| Phenylalanine | 22 | 30 |
| Threonine | 18 | 69 |
| Tryptophan | 0 | 20 |
| Valine | 22 | 58 |
| Total EAAs | ~157 mg | ~482 mg |

### Key Trainer Takeaways

- Whey contains approximately three times more essential amino acids (EAAs) than collagen on a gram-for-gram basis.
- Leucine, the primary trigger for muscle protein synthesis, is nearly 4 times higher in whey (110 mg/g vs. 28 mg/g).
- Collagen contains no tryptophan, making it an incomplete protein that cannot independently support optimal whole-body protein synthesis.
- Collagen's strength lies in its exceptionally high content of glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline, making it ideal for supporting tendons, ligaments, cartilage, skin, and other connective tissues.
- For athletes and active adults, the two proteins are complementary rather than competitive: whey is the superior choice for building and maintaining muscle, while collagen provides specialized support for connective tissue health and recovery.
- This comparison makes a compelling educational slide because it clearly illustrates why collagen should not be marketed as a replacement for a complete protein, but rather as a targeted addition to an already adequate high-quality protein intake.

title: Sucralose - Europe position
content:
Sucralose Very Safe & Popular

First, you should all know that the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) is the strictest scientific food safety governing body in the world.

Just in case there was any doubt left about the safety of sucralose after that ridiculous Italian mouse study that surfaced last year suggesting that sucralose might be harmful (although results were largely dismissed by food scientists), the latest research conducted by EFSA confirmed no link between the sweetener and cancer. Published in the EFSA Journal, the findings are a direct response to allegations made by Italian researcher [NAME] of the Ramazzini Institute. EFSA, as other scientific bodies,² were critical of the Italian's study design and methodology. EFSA concluded that "the available data did not support the conclusions of the authors," agreeing with other scientists that the Italian researchers "used an unconventional design resulting in inconclusive, unreliable data."

Sucralose, being one of the 7 FDA-approved sweeteners and most popular, can be a useful tool when used in place of sugar in helping reduce overall sugar and calorie intake, as well as manage blood glucose levels. As an additional benefit, sucralose, as other low-calorie sweeteners, is non-cariogenic, meaning it does not contribute to tooth decay.²,³,⁴

FYI: EFSA set the acceptable daily intake (ADI) at 7 milligrams per pound (over 17 times more than we use in any product), and because of its safety, EFSA decided to expand the sweetener's use in foods for special medical purposes for children. As a reference for people in the US who consume products containing sucralose daily: average intake is less than 0.8 mg/d.

title: Tesamorelin and IGF-LR3 together - all info
content:
Mindful that a person is healthy, eating well, exercising, taking a complete multivitamin and getting enough protein, is taking the peptide IGF/LR3 along with Tesamorelin a good program for strength and generally considered safe. And what would be the dosages.

For a healthy adult who is already doing the fundamentals well (resistance training, adequate protein, sufficient calories, complete micronutrition, sleep, and recovery), the question becomes whether adding Tesamorelin and IGF-1 LR3 provides enough additional benefit to justify the cost, uncertainty, and potential risks.

Short Answer

Tesamorelin has the stronger clinical foundation. It is FDA-approved for reducing visceral adipose tissue in HIV-associated lipodystrophy and reliably increases endogenous growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. It may modestly improve body composition and recovery in some individuals, but it is not approved for strength enhancement.

IGF-1 LR3 is almost entirely an experimental/research peptide. There is very little high-quality human data supporting its use for muscle growth or strength in healthy adults. Most claims come from animal studies, mechanistic theory, or anecdotal reports.

From an evidence standpoint, if someone asked me which is the more defensible intervention, Tesamorelin is far ahead of IGF-1 LR3.

Potential Benefits

Tesamorelin

Mechanism:
- Stimulates the pituitary to release growth hormone.
- Raises endogenous IGF-1.
- May increase protein synthesis indirectly.
- Often reduces visceral fat.

Possible outcomes:
- Improved body composition.
- Modest lean mass increases.
- Improved recovery.
- Reduced abdominal visceral fat.

IGF-1 LR3

Mechanism:
- Directly stimulates IGF-1 receptors.
- Activates anabolic signaling pathways (AKT/mTOR).
- May increase satellite cell activity and muscle protein synthesis.

Possible outcomes reported anecdotally:
- Increased muscle fullness.
- Increased training recovery.
- Improved nutrient partitioning.
- Modest hypertrophy.

However, these outcomes remain largely unproven in controlled human studies.

Safety Considerations

Tesamorelin

Generally considered reasonably safe under physician supervision.

Common adverse effects:
- Water retention.
- Joint discomfort.
- Edema.
- Increased fasting glucose.
- Insulin resistance in susceptible individuals.

Monitoring:
- IGF-1.
- Fasting glucose.
- HbA1c.
- Lipids.

IGF-1 LR3

This is where concerns increase.

Potential risks:
- Hypoglycemia.
- Edema.
- Headaches.
- Carpal tunnel symptoms.
- Insulin resistance with chronic use.
- Theoretical concerns regarding stimulation of pre-existing cancer cells.

IGF-1 is a potent growth factor. While there is no evidence that therapeutic use causes cancer, elevated IGF-1 levels have long been associated epidemiologically with increased risk of certain cancers.

This is one reason many endocrinologists are cautious regarding long-term supraphysiologic IGF-1 exposure.

Relative Strength Benefits

If the goal is strength and muscle gain, evidence would generally rank interventions roughly like this:
- Progressive resistance training.
- Adequate calories and protein.
- Creatine monohydrate.
- Optimized sleep and recovery.
- Testosterone replacement (if clinically deficient).
- Growth hormone secretagogues (Tesamorelin, Sermorelin).
- IGF-1 LR3.

In other words, IGF-1 LR3 is often discussed as a powerful anabolic agent, but the actual human evidence is surprisingly thin.

Typical Research/Clinical Doses

Tesamorelin

Clinical dose:
- Injected subcutaneously once daily.
- Usually administered before bedtime.
- FDA-approved dosing is 2 mg/day.

IGF-1 LR3

Common research-community usage:

Some users report:
- 20–40 mcg/day conservatively.
- 40–80 mcg/day aggressively.

Cycles commonly discussed:
- 4–8 weeks.

There is no medically established dosing protocol for healthy adults because it is not an approved therapeutic drug.

My Evidence-Based Assessment

For a healthy, well-trained adult:

Tesamorelin
- Reasonable evidence for body-composition improvement.
- Generally manageable safety profile with monitoring.
- Most defensible peptide of the two.

IGF-1 LR3
- Theoretical anabolic benefits.
- Weak human evidence.
- Greater uncertainty regarding long-term safety.
- Much harder to justify from a risk/benefit perspective.

If someone already has:
- Excellent nutrition.
- Adequate protein.
- Creatine supplementation.
- Proper resistance training.
- Good sleep.

then Tesamorelin may provide modest additional body-composition benefits. IGF-1 LR3 is far less certain and is generally considered a much more experimental approach.

The biggest practical issue I see in real-world users is that expectations are often much larger than the actual measurable improvements, particularly compared with what can still be achieved through optimizing training volume, recovery, and protein intake.

Would using both simultaneously be okay in the same cycle?

From a purely pharmacologic standpoint, Tesamorelin and IGF-1 LR3 are not directly contraindicated together, because they work at different points in the growth hormone/IGF axis:

Tesamorelin → stimulates your pituitary to release more growth hormone → which then increases your body's own IGF-1 production.

IGF-1 LR3 → bypasses that pathway and directly activates IGF-1 receptors.

So, mechanistically, they can have additive effects.

However, the main concern is that both ultimately increase total IGF signaling, which is where most of the potential risks come from.

Potential Advantages of Combining

The theoretical rationale is:
- Tesamorelin raises physiologic GH pulses.
- GH may improve recovery, connective tissue support, and fat metabolism.
- IGF-1 LR3 provides more direct anabolic signaling.

Some users report:
- Better recovery.
- Improved training volume tolerance.
- Increased muscle fullness.
- Improved body composition.

But again, there is very little controlled human research evaluating the combination in healthy adults.

Potential Concerns

The biggest concerns when combining are:

1. Excessive IGF-1 Exposure

Tesamorelin already elevates circulating IGF-1.

Adding IGF-1 LR3 on top can push total IGF signaling higher than either alone.

Potential issues:
- Edema.
- Joint discomfort.
- Carpal tunnel symptoms.
- Headaches.
- Increased insulin resistance.
- Theoretical increased risk of stimulating growth of existing tumors.

2. Glucose Regulation

GH and IGF pathways interact with insulin sensitivity.

Monitoring:
- Fasting glucose.
- HbA1c.
- Fasting insulin (if available).

becomes more important when stacking compounds.

3. Diminishing Returns

Many people assume:

Tesamorelin = 10
IGF-LR3 = 10
Combined = 20

Biology rarely works that way.

Often you get:
- More cost.
- More risk.
- Smaller incremental benefit than expected.

What Would I Consider the More Rational Approach?

If the goal is:
- Better body composition.
- Recovery.
- Long-term use.

I would generally view:

Tesamorelin alone

as the more evidence-supported option.

Then evaluate:
- IGF-1 levels.
- Body composition changes.
- Recovery.
- Strength progression.

before adding another compound.

Monitoring I'd Want to See

If someone were using both under physician supervision, I'd strongly recommend periodic monitoring of:
- IGF-1.
- Fasting glucose.
- HbA1c.
- CMP (liver/kidney function).
- Lipid panel.

and stopping if IGF-1 rises substantially above the laboratory reference range.

My Overall Assessment

For a healthy, resistance-trained adult:
- Using both simultaneously is not inherently irrational from a mechanistic standpoint.
- It is commonly discussed in peptide and bodybuilding circles.
- The combination is much less studied than either alone, particularly in healthy adults.
- The largest concern is cumulative IGF exposure and metabolic side effects rather than a specific drug-drug interaction.

If the objective is maximizing long-term health, strength, and body composition, I would be considerably more comfortable with a monitored Tesamorelin protocol than with chronic combined Tesamorelin + IGF-1 LR3 use, simply because the safety and efficacy evidence is much stronger for Tesamorelin.

title: Brown fat and obestiy
content:
A major advance in understanding of brown fat and its relationship to body weight holds the potential for new treatments for obesity, according to researchers at the University of East Anglia and the University of Cambridge, in collaboration with colleagues in the US and Belgium.

The scientists explained that in mammals, brown and beige adipose tissue has a "unique ability to burn off cellular nutrients as heat in the process of non-shivering thermogenesis". This helps to protect the body against cold temperatures.

The process of burning calories as heat for thermoregulation in brown adipose tissue depends on a 33-kDa protein called mitochondrial uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1), whose molecular structure the researchers said they had now revealed for the first time in the study, published in the journal Science Advances.

When activated by fatty acids, UCP1 catalyses the leak of protons across the mitochondrial inner membrane, short-circuiting the mitochondrion to generate heat, bypassing adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthesis. In contrast, purine nucleotides bind and inhibit UCP1, regulating proton leak by a molecular mechanism that was unclear.

For the new study, the team used cryo-electron microscopy to reveal "crucial molecular details" of the structure of UCP1 when inhibited by the purine guanosine-5'-triphosphate (GTP).

Understanding of the mechanism could enable pharmacological intervention to promote brown fat and UCP1 activation, to burn off excess calories from fat and sugar as heat, without the need for physiological stimuli.

As a therapeutic strategy to combat metabolic disease, this represents "an important discovery in the race to find treatments for obesity and related diseases, such as diabetes", the researchers said.

'Brown Fat is the Good Fat'

Co-author Dr Paul Crichton, PhD, director of the Biomedical Research Centre at the University of East Anglia, explained: "As well as the conventional white fat that we are all familiar with, we can also develop brown fat. Brown fat is the good fat – it breaks down blood sugar and fat molecules to create heat and help maintain body temperature.

"Most of our fat, however, is white fat, which stores energy – and too much white fat leads to obesity. UCP1 is the key protein that allows the specialised brown fat to burn off calories as heat," he said. "We know that mammals switch on UCP1 activity in brown fat tissue to protect against the cold and to maintain body temperature – especially in new-borns, that cannot yet shiver to keep warm.

"Brown fat varies in humans, where it correlates with leanness in the population – and there has been a lot of interest in how to increase brown fat and activate UCP1 therapeutically, as a potential way to treat obesity.

"A lot of research has been focusing on finding ways to encourage brown fat and how to turn white fat into brown fat – in order to burn more calories and fight metabolic disease. But even with more brown fat, UCP1 must still be 'switched on' to gain full benefit."

More than 40 years of research had been hampered by a lack of details on the molecular makeup of UCP1, he explained. "We did not know what UCP1 looks like, to understand how it works – until now."

Lead researcher Prof [NAME], research group leader in the Medical Research Council Mitochondrial Biology Unit at the University of Cambridge, said: "Our paper reveals, for the first time, the structure of UCP1 in atomic detail, and how its activity in brown fat cells is inhibited by a key regulatory molecule."

As well as showing how a regulator binds to prevent UCP1 activity, "more importantly", understanding the structure "will allow scientists to rationalise how activating molecules bind to switch the protein on, leading to the burning of fat", he said. "The activated tissue can also remove glucose from the blood, which can help control diabetes. This is a significant breakthrough in this field."

This research was supported by the Medical Research Council, the Biological and Biotechnological Sciences Research Council, and by the National Institutes of Health/National Institute of General Medical Sciences. Nanobody discovery was funded by the Instruct-ERIC part of the European Strategy Forum on Research Infrastructures, and the Research Foundation – Flanders, and the Strategic Research Program of the Vrije Universiteit Brussel. The authors declare that they have no competing interests.

References
[NAME] SA, [NAME] P, [NAME] JJ, et al. Structural basis of purine nucleotide inhibition of human uncoupling protein 1. Science Advances. 2023:9(22):eadh4251. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adh4251.

title: Essential amino acidsEEAs & non-EAAs all info on needs&limitingFactors
content:
We know that non-essential amino acids can be made from the essential amino acids, but 2 questions: 1. Can some non-essential amino acids be made from other substrates in the body? 2. When can the ingestion of the total daily amount of non-essential amino acids become a limiting factor in growth and recovery—i.e., could a human live and grow on just the essential amino acids and enough total caloric intake?

Yes—many non-essential amino acids (NEAAs) can absolutely be synthesized from substrates other than essential amino acids (EAAs).

The body commonly makes NEAAs from:
- Glucose intermediates
- Krebs/TCA cycle intermediates
- Ammonia/nitrogen transfer
- Fatty acid metabolism indirectly
- Recycled amino groups from other amino acids

Examples:
- Pyruvate → alanine
- Oxaloacetate → aspartate
- α-ketoglutarate → glutamate
- Glutamate → glutamine, proline, arginine
- Serine can be made from glycolytic intermediates
- Glycine can be made from serine

So the body is constantly interconverting carbon skeletons and nitrogen donors to manufacture NEAAs as needed.

That is why they are termed “non-essential”—not because they are unimportant, but because the body usually has the metabolic machinery to synthesize them.

However, there is a critical nuance:

Some “non-essential” amino acids become conditionally essential during:
- Rapid growth
- Severe stress
- Illness
- Trauma
- Intense training
- Burns
- Aging
- Recovery states

This is especially true for:
- Glutamine
- Arginine
- Glycine
- Cysteine
- Tyrosine
- Sometimes proline

Yes—there absolutely comes a point where inadequate total NEAA availability can limit growth, recovery, and tissue synthesis, even if EAA intake is sufficient.

This is one of the most misunderstood concepts in protein metabolism.

EAAs are the trigger and regulatory signal for muscle protein synthesis—especially leucine.

But NEAAs still make up a huge percentage of actual tissue protein structure.

For example:
- Collagen is heavily dependent on glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline.
- Glutamine is heavily used by immune cells and gut tissue.
- Alanine and glutamate are major nitrogen carriers.
- Glycine demand may exceed endogenous production in high-growth states.

So while EAAs initiate anabolic signaling, the body still requires sufficient total nitrogen and substrate availability to complete actual tissue construction.

A useful analogy:

EAAs are like the “foremen and permits” that authorize building construction. NEAAs are still much of the “concrete, steel, drywall, and wiring.” You can’t build a skyscraper with only foremen.

Could a human live and grow on only EAAs plus calories?

Theoretically:
- A human might survive for a period if supplied all EAAs, calories, vitamins, minerals, fats, and carbohydrates.
- The body could synthesize many NEAAs.

But in reality:
- Optimal growth
- Muscle hypertrophy
- Connective tissue repair
- Immune function
- Recovery
- Long-term health

would likely become impaired because endogenous synthesis capacity is not unlimited.

Research and clinical nutrition both show:
- Nitrogen balance
- Recovery
- Wound healing
- Lean mass retention

are generally superior when adequate total intact protein or balanced amino acid mixtures are consumed versus EAAs alone.

This is why:
- Whey protein
- Milk proteins
- Meat
- Eggs
- Balanced complete proteins

consistently outperform isolated EAAs alone for long-term tissue support.

Even though EAAs are the indispensable amino acids, the body still benefits enormously from dietary NEAAs because:
- It reduces the metabolic burden of synthesizing them.
- It provides nitrogen economy.
- It supports tissues with unusually high demand for specific NEAAs.

The modern view is really:

EAAs are indispensable for initiating and permitting growth, but adequate total amino acid availability—including NEAAs—is necessary to sustain maximal growth, repair, recovery, and physiological resilience.

General rule is ≥18 years unless a younger elite athlete is properly supervised with parent consent.

The 18 years or older label cautions on creatine products have to do with manufacturers shielding themselves from liabilities and are not based on safety reasons, since science has documented CS safety in all age groups as shown and discussed above. 48, 49, 50, [i] The latest position by the International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) is the following: “If proper precautions and supervision are provided, creatine monohydrate supplementation in children and adolescent athletes is acceptable and may provide a nutritional alternative with a favorable safety profile to potentially dangerous anabolic androgenic drugs. However, we recommend that creatine supplementation only be considered for use by younger athletes who: a.) are involved in serious/competitive supervised training; b.) are consuming a well-balanced and performance-enhancing diet; c.) are knowledgeable about appropriate use of creatine; and d.) do not exceed recommended dosages”.15, 28 i

If you are further interested in youth and creatine supplementation, you are referred to the [NAME] et al. review, “Safety of CS in Active Adolescents and Youth,” Ref3.

title: Bacteriostatic water storage and more info
content:
Does bacteriostatic water need to be refrigerated if not opened yet—i.e., just stored before use?

In general, no. Unopened bacteriostatic water does not need to be refrigerated.

Here are the standard storage recommendations:

Before opening: Store at controlled room temperature, typically 20–25°C (68–77°F), with brief excursions generally allowed between 15–30°C (59–86°F) according to most manufacturers.

Keep it in its original carton or otherwise protected from direct light.

Do not freeze it.

Avoid prolonged exposure to excessive heat (e.g., leaving it in a hot car).

After opening:

Once the vial has been punctured:

It can still be stored at room temperature unless the manufacturer specifically recommends refrigeration.

Some people choose to refrigerate it because it may be more comfortable when used for reconstitution and may reduce bacterial growth slightly, but refrigeration is not generally required for bacteriostatic water containing 0.9% benzyl alcohol as the preservative.

The preservative allows the vial to be used for multiple withdrawals, but most manufacturers recommend discarding it 28 days after the first puncture, even if solution remains.

If you're using it to reconstitute peptides:

After mixing a peptide with bacteriostatic water, the peptide's storage requirements become the priority, not the water's. Most common peptide solutions (such as tesamorelin, BPC-157, TB-500, or IGF-1 LR3) are generally stored refrigerated at 2–8°C (36–46°F) after reconstitution to help maintain stability, although specific recommendations vary by product and manufacturer.

So, for your situation—an unopened vial being stored until needed—a cool, dry cabinet at room temperature is the appropriate place.

title: Vitamin D blood levels -best numbers
content:
For athletes and highly active individuals, many modern sports medicine physicians and performance nutrition specialists aim for a higher serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] concentration than the minimum needed to prevent deficiency. The goal is to optimize not only bone health but also muscle function, immune resilience, recovery, and potentially reduce injury risk.

Common target ranges

| Serum 25(OH)D | ng/mL | nmol/L | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Deficient | <20 | <50 | Increased risk of bone and muscle problems |
| Insufficient | 20–30 | 50–75 | Acceptable for many adults but not ideal for athletes |
| Good for general health | 30–50 | 75–125 | Meets most endocrine society recommendations |
| Preferred for many athletes | 40–60 | 100–150 | Frequently targeted by sports physicians and sports dietitians |
| High-normal | 60–80 | 150–200 | Sometimes used in elite athletes under physician supervision |
| Potential concern | >100 | >250 | Generally not recommended without medical indication |
| Possible toxicity | >150 | >375 | Increased risk of hypercalcemia and other adverse effects |

Why 40–60 ng/mL?

This range has become popular among sports medicine clinicians because research suggests that, compared with lower concentrations, athletes in this range may experience:

- Better muscle strength and power
- Improved muscle protein function
- Reduced incidence of stress fractures
- Better immune function, especially during heavy training
- Fewer upper respiratory infections
- Improved recovery from intense exercise
- Lower risk of muscle strains in athletes who were previously deficient

The evidence is strongest for correcting deficiency. Benefits above about 40 ng/mL are less consistent, but many experts feel there is little downside to maintaining concentrations between 40 and 60 ng/mL when achieved safely.

Research in athletes

Numerous studies in professional football, soccer, basketball, military personnel, and endurance athletes have shown that athletes with vitamin D levels below 30 ng/mL tend to have:

- Higher rates of muscle injury
- More stress fractures
- Longer recovery times
- Reduced muscle function

When deficient athletes are supplemented to reach approximately 40–50 ng/mL, many studies report improvements in muscle function and reductions in injury rates. Evidence that increasing levels from 50 to 70 ng/mL provides additional performance gains is much weaker.

What many sports physicians actually do

A common approach in elite sports programs is:

- Preseason target: 40–60 ng/mL
- In-season maintenance: Keep above 40 ng/mL
- Recheck every 3–6 months, particularly in winter or in indoor athletes

This is especially common in:

- NFL
- NBA
- NHL
- Professional soccer
- Olympic training centers

Practical supplementation

Although individual needs vary greatly:

- 1,000 IU/day typically raises serum 25(OH)D by roughly 5–10 ng/mL over several months.
- Many athletes require 2,000–4,000 IU/day to maintain levels between 40 and 60 ng/mL, especially those with darker skin, limited sun exposure, higher body fat, or who train indoors.
- Some deficient athletes require short-term higher doses under physician supervision before transitioning to a maintenance dose.

For your work with athletes

Given your focus on body composition, performance, and recovery, I would summarize the current practical consensus as:

Maintain serum 25(OH)D between approximately 40 and 60 ng/mL (100–150 nmol/L). This range is commonly targeted by sports medicine physicians because it appears to provide a favorable balance between musculoskeletal health, immune function, and recovery while avoiding unnecessarily high concentrations. There is little evidence that routinely pushing levels above 60–70 ng/mL produces additional athletic benefits in healthy individuals.

This recommendation is consistent with the practices of many sports medicine clinicians and is more aggressive than the 30 ng/mL minimum often cited for the general population, while remaining well below concentrations associated with toxicity.

title: MOTS-C,insulinSensitivityGlucoseUptakeMuscleFunct
content:
MOTS-c is a peptide that works by moving between mitochondria and the nucleus to regulate cellular metabolism. It's triggered by stress and works similarly to a hormone to improve insulin sensitivity, promote glucose uptake, and enhance muscle function. It achieves this primarily by activating the AMPK pathway, which is a key regulator of energy balance in the cell.

How MOTS-c works in the cell

Mitochondrial origin:
MOTS-c is encoded by a gene in the mitochondrial DNA.

Stress-induced release:
Under metabolic stress, it moves from the mitochondria to the cytoplasm and then can translocate to the nucleus.

AMPK activation:
In the cytoplasm, MOTS-c activates the AMPK pathway, which regulates the cell's energy balance.

Nuclear regulation:
Once in the nucleus, it regulates gene expression to promote adaptive responses to stress and metabolic dysfunction.

Exercise-mimicking effects:
MOTS-c levels increase with exercise and mimic its benefits by improving muscle function, endurance, and energy production.

How MOTS-c works in the body

Improves insulin sensitivity:
It helps muscles take up glucose more effectively, which combats insulin resistance.

Enhances glucose and fat metabolism:
It influences how the cell uses glucose and fats for energy, promoting energy production and utilization.

Modulates inflammation:
It helps regulate inflammation, which is a key factor in aging and many chronic diseases.

Supports bone health:
It promotes bone formation by stimulating osteoblasts and inhibits bone breakdown by affecting osteoclasts.

Protects against obesity:
It has been shown to reduce weight gain and fat accumulation in models of diet-induced and age-related obesity.
