title: PUO and RUO product def -research & physician use
content:
In the peptide manufacturing industry, RUO and PUO are designations used by suppliers to indicate the intended use, regulatory status, and manufacturing quality. [1, 2, 3]

RUO (Research Use Only)
RUO means the product is intended strictly for in vitro laboratory research, in vivo animal studies, or early-stage drug discovery. [1, 2]

Manufacturing & Regulation: These products are generally exempt from the Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) rigid premarket clearance and cGMP (Current Good Manufacturing Practice) requirements for human pharmaceuticals. [1, 2]

Testing & Purity: While they are synthesized for chemical purity, they are not produced under the strict safety protocols, sterility, or viral-clearance standards required for human medications. [1, 2]

Legality: RUO peptides are legal to purchase and possess for scientific purposes, but it is illegal to market, prescribe, or administer them for human consumption. [1, 2]

PUO (Physician / Provider Use Only)
PUO is a relatively newer, distributor-level label intended to market peptides exclusively to licensed medical clinics or practitioners. [1]

The Intent: Suppliers often use this label to imply a higher standard of legitimacy or oversight compared to the direct-to-consumer RUO market. [1]

The Reality: From a regulatory perspective, PUO and RUO are legally treated the same. Unless a peptide is manufactured in an FDA-registered facility as an Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) or an approved prescription drug, the PUO label does not automatically make the compound safe, legal, or compliant for human injection. [1, 2]

Key Takeaway for Safety and Sourcing
Neither RUO nor PUO signify that a peptide is a clinical-grade drug. True pharmaceutical-grade peptides must be produced under cGMP (Current Good Manufacturing Practices). You can verify legitimate drug manufacturers and FDA compliance by checking the FDA Drug Database. To understand the difference between research-grade and clinical manufacturing protocols, visit the FDA Guidance on RUO Labeling.

title: How well does the Alln1 SuperBlend powder absorb compared with pill and gummy multivitamins, and what explains the bright yellow urine shortly after taking it?

We are not sure why your urine would be discolored within 10–15 minutes after consuming the SB because it would be impossible for this condition to be caused by the SB. Bright-colored urine in healthy humans is generally from mild dehydration. The color of urine is altered by fluid intake. If this is truly happening with you, you may want to have a qualified physician, such as a gastroenterologist, check the health of your GI tract to make sure things are functioning properly.

The SB is purposely in a powdered form because the other ingredients—mushroom blend, ashwagandha, turmeric, pre- and probiotics, non-vitamin antioxidants, etc.—need to be in powdered form for proper results. This method makes the product like a controlled release; i.e., we are controlling the release by splitting the dosage. Splitting the dosage is also on the label. See below for more on absorption. And finally, gummies are simply not capable of holding and stabilizing nutrients for any length of time, so this matrix is not even in the picture until some scientist cracks the code.

Hope this all helps—have a great night.

Urine color

The natural color of urine is yellow, caused by a pigment called urochrome or urobilin. The kidneys filter urochrome out of the bloodstream, and urine contains it. The amount of fluids you drink determines the color of the pigment in your urine. The more fluids you drink, the lighter the color, and the less you drink, the stronger the color.

Urine can vary in color from pale or light yellow to deep amber or dark yellow. Urochrome breaks down hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells. In most situations, the color of your urine will depend on how diluted this pigment is by fluids. Having a lot of B vitamins in your bloodstream can also cause urine to appear neon yellow, and many foods can alter the coloring.

Proper absorption and compliance:

The ingredients in the Alln1 SuperBlendTM are in the proper clinical dosage and forms to maximize the body’s ability to utilize the ingredients at the target tissues in proper amounts to create the desired outcomes when used daily. All this peer-reviewed information is in the Practitioner Dietary Supplement Reference Guide Alln1 SuperBlend, which certified practitioners have available in their trainer consoles.

The dotFIT Multivitamin and Mineral Formula (MVM) tablets are controlled release and, when used properly twice daily, can maximize tissue saturation. However, when using the Alln1 SuperBlendTM, which contains the same basic MVM formula, people are more likely to comply and not miss a dose. In other words, one full dose at once is better than half a daily dose. The convenience and still-great absorption allow users better chances of getting a full daily dose of necessary nutrients by not missing their second dose of pills, not to mention the extra nutrition while solving for people who do not like pills.

And, of course, the other many ingredients in the Alln1 SuperBlendTM must be in a powdered form. title: SARMs diff from peptides info
content:
SARMs and peptides differ fundamentally in their chemical composition, mechanism of action, and regulatory status. Peptides are short chains of amino acids that act as natural signaling molecules, while SARMs are synthetic, non-steroidal drugs that mimic testosterone by directly binding to androgen receptors in specific tissues.

Key Differences

| Feature | SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) | Peptides |
|---|---|---|
| Composition | Synthetic, non-steroidal compounds | Naturally occurring short chains of amino acids (small proteins) |
| Mechanism | Directly bind to androgen receptors in muscle and bone to signal growth, mimicking testosterone | Act as signaling molecules, stimulating natural bodily processes like growth hormone production |
| Primary Use (Bodybuilding) | Faster muscle growth and fat loss with potentially fewer side effects than traditional steroids | Enhance natural recovery, growth, skin health, and cognitive function |
| Regulation | Investigational drugs, not approved by the FDA for any medical use, and often associated with health risks when misused | Some are FDA-approved for specific conditions; many are used under medical supervision in therapy |
| Side Effects | Potential risks include liver injury, hormone suppression, and cardiovascular issues | Generally considered safer with potential mild side effects like injection site irritation, headaches, or water retention |

Summary

SARMs offer a more targeted, synthetic approach to building muscle mass, similar to steroids but with a higher degree of tissue selectivity, though they carry significant health warnings from regulatory bodies like the FDA.

Peptides offer a more "natural" approach by encouraging the body to produce its own beneficial hormones and compounds, resulting in a broader range of benefits beyond just muscle gain, such as improved recovery, sleep, and skin health.

It is important to note that both compounds should be approached with caution and medical oversight, as their long-term effects and purity are often inconsistent when sourced from unregulated suppliers.

title: Alcohol and cortisol
content:
Yes — alcohol consumption can increase cortisol levels, especially when consumed in moderate-to-high amounts or chronically.

Alcohol acts as a physiological stressor that activates the body’s hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, leading to increased release of cortisol, the primary “stress hormone.” Acute drinking can temporarily elevate cortisol for several hours, while chronic heavy intake may keep cortisol chronically elevated and disrupt its normal daily rhythm. Elevated cortisol from alcohol is associated with impaired recovery, poorer sleep quality, increased abdominal fat storage, muscle protein breakdown, insulin resistance, and negative effects on mood and cognitive function.

For exercisers and athletes, this is one reason excessive alcohol intake can interfere with muscle recovery, body composition goals, performance adaptation, and overall recovery capacity.

Yes — alcohol consumption can increase cortisol levels, especially with higher intake, binge drinking, chronic use, or disrupted sleep caused by alcohol. Cortisol is the body’s primary stress hormone, and alcohol can activate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, leading to elevated cortisol both during intoxication and during recovery/withdrawal.

In exercisers and athletes, chronically elevated cortisol from frequent alcohol use may negatively affect recovery, sleep quality, muscle protein synthesis, body composition, mood, and performance adaptation. Even though alcohol may initially feel relaxing, physiologically it often creates a rebound stress response later in the night and into the next day.

title: Erythritol cardil issues
content:
New Study Links Sweetener to Heart Risk: What to Know
[NAME]
August 09, 2024
Add to Email Alerts
3
542
ur·i·thruh·taal

Is going sugar-free really good advice for patients with cardiometabolic risk factors?

That's the question raised by new Cleveland Clinic research, which suggests that consuming erythritol, a sweetener widely found in sugar-free and keto food products, could spur a prothrombotic response.

In the study, published in Arteriosclerosis, Thrombosis, and Vascular Biology, 10 healthy participants ate 30 grams of erythritol. Thirty minutes later, their blood showed enhanced platelet aggregation and increased markers of platelet responsiveness and activation.

Specifically, the researchers saw enhanced stimulus-dependent release of serotonin (a marker of platelet dense granules) and CXCL4 (a platelet alpha-granule marker).

"With every single person, you see a prothrombotic effect with every single test that we did," said study author Stanley Hazen, MD, PhD, chair of the Department of Cardiovascular & Metabolic Sciences at Cleveland Clinic in Ohio. By contrast, participants who ate 30 grams of glucose saw no such effect.

The erythritol itself does not activate the platelets, Hazen said; rather, it lowers the threshold for triggering a response. This could make someone more prone to clotting, raising heart attack and stroke risk over time.

Though the mechanism is unknown, Hazen has an idea.

"There appears to be a receptor on platelets that is recognizing and sensing these sugar alcohols," Hazen said, "much in the same way your tastebud for sweet is a receptor for recognizing a glucose or sugar molecule."

"We're very interested in trying to figure out what the receptor is," Hazen said, "because I think that then becomes a very interesting potential target for further investigation and study into how this is linked to causing heart disease."

The Past and Future of Erythritol Research

In 2001, the US Food and Drug Administration classified erythritol as a "generally recognized as safe" food additive. A sugar alcohol that occurs naturally in foods like melon and grapes, erythritol is also manufactured by fermenting sugars. It's about 70% as sweet as table sugar. Humans also produce small amounts of erythritol naturally: Our blood cells make it from glucose via the pentose phosphate pathway.

Previous research from Hazen's group linked erythritol to a risk for major adverse cardiovascular events and clotting.

"Based on their previous study, I think this was a really important study to do in healthy individuals," said [NAME], PhD, assistant professor in the Division of Nutritional Sciences at Cornell University, Ithaca, New York, who was not involved in the study.

The earlier paper analyzed blood samples from participants with unknown erythritol intake, including some taken before the sweetener, and it was as widespread as it is today. That made disentangling the effects of eating erythritol versus naturally producing it more difficult.

By showing that eating erythritol raises markers associated with thrombosis, the new paper reinforces the importance of thinking about and developing a deeper understanding of what we put into our bodies.

"This paper was conducted in healthy individuals—might this be particularly dangerous for individuals who are at increased risk of clotting?" said [NAME]. "There are lots of genetic polymorphisms that increase your risk for clotting disorders or your propensity to form thrombosis."

[NAME] would like to see similar analyses of xylitol and sorbitol, other sugar alcohols found in sugar-free foods. And she called for more studies on erythritol that look at lower erythritol consumption over longer time periods.

Registered dietitian nutritionist [NAME], PhD, agreed: Much more work is needed in this area, particularly in higher-risk groups, such as those with prediabetes and diabetes, said [NAME], an associate professor in the Department of Human Nutrition, Foods, and Exercise at Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, Virginia, who was not involved in the study.

"Because this study was conducted in healthy individuals, the impact of a small dose of glucose was negligible, as their body can effectively regulate blood glucose levels," she said. "Because high blood glucose concentrations have also been shown to increase platelet reactivity, and consequently increase thrombosis potential, individuals who are not able to regulate their blood glucose levels, such as those with prediabetes and diabetes, could potentially see a similar effect on the body as erythritol when consuming large amounts of sugar."

At the same time, "individuals with diabetes or prediabetes may be more inclined to consume erythritol as an alternative to sugar," [NAME] added. "It will be important to design studies that include these individuals to determine if erythritol has an additive adverse effect on cardiac event risk."

Criticism and Impact

Critics have suggested the 30-gram dose of erythritol ingested by study participants is unrealistic. Hazen said that it's not.

Erythritol is often recommended as a one-to-one sugar replacement. And you could top 30 grams with a few servings of erythritol-sweetened ice cream or soda, Hazen said.

"The dose that we used, it's on the high end, but it's well within a physiologically relevant level," he said.

Still others say the results are only relevant for people with preexisting heart trouble. But Hazen said they matter for the masses.

"I think there's a significant health concern at a population level that this work is underscoring," he said.

After all, heart disease risk factors like obesity, hypertension, diabetes, and smoking are common and quickly add up.

"If you look at middle-aged America, most people who experience a heart attack or stroke do not know that they have coronary artery disease, and the first recognition of it is that event," Hazen said.

For now, Hazen recommends eating real sugar in moderation. He hopes future research will reveal a nonnutritive sweetener that doesn't activate platelets.

The Bigger Picture

The new research adds yet another piece to the puzzle of whether nonnutritive sweeteners are better than sugar.

"I think these results are concerning," said [NAME], MD, chief of the Division of Preventive Medicine at Brigham and Women's Hospital and a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School, Cambridge, Massachusetts. They "may help explain the surprising results in some observational studies that artificial sweeteners are linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular disease."

[NAME], who was not involved in the new study, has conducted other research linking artificial sweetener use with stroke risk.

In an upcoming randomized clinical study, her team is comparing head-to-head sugar-sweetened beverages, drinks sweetened with calorie-free substitutes, and water to determine which is best for a range of cardiometabolic outcomes.

"We need more research on this question," she said, "because these artificial sweeteners are commonly used, and many people are assuming that their health outcomes will be better with the artificial sweeteners than with sugar-sweetened products."

title: KPV peptdie -skin -gut inflammation-immune system
content:
KPV is a short tripeptide made of three amino acids—lysine, proline, and valine. It is the natural C-terminal fragment of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH). KPV is studied for its potential anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial properties—aiming to soothe gut and skin inflammation without causing the skin-pigment changes linked to its parent hormone. [1, 2, 3]

How KPV Works in Research

Cellular signaling: Preclinical studies show KPV helps block NF-κB, a master protein complex that switches on inflammatory genes.

Cytokine reduction: Laboratory models demonstrate it lowers the production of pro-inflammatory chemicals like TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β.

Targeted absorption: In gut models, KPV is proposed to enter intestinal cells through the PepT1 peptide transporter, which is often more active during inflammation. [1, 2, 3]

Proposed Uses and Formulations

Gut health: Marketed or researched for conditions like inflammatory bowel disease or intestinal permeability ("leaky gut") via oral formats.

Skin conditions: Applied topically in creams or gels for local issues like eczema, psoriasis, or general redness.

Systemic inflammation: Sometimes compounded into nasal sprays or injectables. [1, 2, 3]

Safety and Regulatory Status

Lack of human trials: Almost all current data relies on cell cultures and animal models; large-scale safety and efficacy trials in humans are lacking. [1]

Regulation: KPV is not FDA-approved as a prescription medication. Products sold online or through wellness clinics often exist in a regulatory gray market as experimental research compounds, meaning purity, dosing accuracy, and sterility can vary significantly. [1, 2]

title: GHK-Cu info-Skin, etc.
content:
Have there been any clinical trials using GHK-Cu peptide, and what is the basic dosage for it to deliver on it?

Yes, there have been human clinical trials involving GHK-Cu, but they are primarily topical studies in dermatology and wound healing rather than injectable peptide trials like those for tesamorelin or GLP-1 agonists. The evidence supporting injectable GHK-Cu for systemic anti-aging, muscle recovery, or orthopedic injuries is currently much weaker and largely based on animal studies, laboratory research, and anecdotal clinical use.

Current level of evidence

Strongest evidence
- Skin rejuvenation
- Wrinkle reduction
- Collagen synthesis
- Improved skin elasticity
- Cosmetic wound healing

Moderate evidence
- Hair follicle stimulation
- Scar remodeling
- Post-procedure skin recovery

Preclinical/experimental
- Tendon and ligament repair
- Muscle recovery
- Bone healing
- Nerve regeneration
- Systemic anti-aging
- Cognitive protection

These latter applications have promising biological rationale but have not yet been confirmed in large randomized human trials.

Mechanism of action

GHK-Cu (glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine-copper) is a naturally occurring copper-binding tripeptide found in human plasma that declines with age. It appears to:
- Stimulate fibroblasts
- Increase collagen I and III synthesis
- Increase elastin and glycosaminoglycan production
- Improve angiogenesis (new blood vessel formation)
- Reduce inflammatory cytokines
- Modulate matrix metalloproteinases involved in tissue remodeling
- Influence expression of thousands of genes related to tissue repair and inflammation

Unlike BPC-157 or TB-500, GHK-Cu's strongest evidence is extracellular matrix remodeling, making it particularly attractive for skin and connective tissue repair.

Human clinical trials

Published human studies have shown improvements in:
- Fine wrinkles
- Skin elasticity
- Skin density
- Photodamaged skin
- Overall skin appearance

Most studies lasted 8–24 weeks using topical creams or serums. Improvements were generally modest but statistically significant and comparable to or better than some established cosmetic ingredients, with excellent tolerability.

A randomized clinical trial is also underway evaluating topical GHK-Cu gel for acute wound healing, reflecting the growing interest in its regenerative potential.

Injectable dosing

Because there are no standardized FDA-approved dosing protocols, injectable dosing is based on clinical practice rather than definitive trials.

The most commonly reported protocols are:
- 1–2 mg subcutaneously once daily
- Duration: 4–8 weeks

Some clinicians extend treatment to 8–12 weeks for connective tissue repair.

Many regenerative medicine clinics also use:
- 2 mg/day for 6–8 weeks
- Followed by a maintenance break before another cycle

These protocols are empirical and have not been validated in large randomized controlled trials.

Topical dosing

Most cosmetic products contain approximately:
- 0.05–0.2% GHK-Cu
- Applied once or twice daily

This is where the strongest human evidence currently exists.

Safety

Overall, GHK-Cu appears to have an excellent safety profile.

Reported issues are generally limited to:
- Mild injection-site irritation (injectable use)
- Temporary skin irritation (topical use)
- Rare allergic reactions

One theoretical concern is that because GHK-Cu promotes tissue growth and remodeling, many clinicians recommend avoiding it in individuals with active malignancy until more safety data are available. This precaution is based on theory rather than evidence of harm.

Practical takeaway

If you compare the regenerative peptides discussed so far:

BPC-157 appears strongest for tendon, ligament, gastrointestinal, and soft tissue repair (though still lacking robust human trials).

TB-500 is primarily aimed at cell migration, angiogenesis, and broad tissue healing, with human evidence remaining sparse.

GHK-Cu has the best human evidence of the three for skin regeneration and collagen remodeling, but far less evidence for injectable systemic use than is often claimed online.

For someone interested in improving skin quality, wound healing, scar remodeling, or connective tissue health, GHK-Cu is one of the more scientifically plausible peptides available. However, claims regarding whole-body rejuvenation, muscle growth, longevity, or dramatic orthopedic healing remain speculative until larger, well-controlled human studies are completed.

title: hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) and intermittent hypoxia
content:
Yes. There is science behind both hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) and intermittent hypoxia, but they should be viewed quite differently if the goal is exercise recovery.

1. HBOT — promising, but not yet a slam dunk for routine recovery
HBOT exposes someone to nearly 100% oxygen at elevated atmospheric pressure, commonly around 1.5–2.5 ATA. This dramatically increases dissolved oxygen in plasma and oxygen delivery to tissues.

The most recent evidence is more favorable than some of the older reviews. A 2026 systematic review/meta-analysis of 10 randomized studies involving 299 subjects concluded that HBOT significantly accelerated recovery from exercise-induced muscle injury, although it did not significantly improve muscle soreness overall. Benefits were seen with pressures both above and below 2.0 ATA and with 60- and 100-minute sessions.

Another 2026 systematic review/meta-analysis found that HBOT significantly reduced post-exercise blood lactate, although effects on short-term power and force production were limited.

That is noteworthy because an earlier 2021 meta-analysis had concluded that HBOT before exercise did not significantly improve performance and post-exercise HBOT did not significantly improve recovery. So the evidence is evolving, but still inconsistent.

Mechanistically, HBOT is plausible for recovery because hyperoxia can influence tissue oxygenation, edema, inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress, angiogenesis and tissue repair. But those biological effects don't necessarily translate into faster recovery from an ordinary hard workout.

My rating for routine exercise recovery: 🟡 Promising, but not established.

I would view HBOT more favorably for tissue injury/rehabilitation situations than as something every healthy gym member needs after training.

2. Intermittent hypoxia — stronger science, but primarily for adaptation/performance, not acute recovery
This one is fascinating because we're essentially doing the opposite:
HBOT → temporarily increase oxygen availability
Intermittent hypoxia → temporarily decrease oxygen availability

Intermittent hypoxia exposes someone to repeated periods of reduced oxygen—often equivalent to being at altitude—followed by periods of normal oxygen.

The resulting physiological stress can stimulate adaptations involving HIF-1α signaling, mitochondrial function, vascular adaptations, oxygen utilization and metabolic efficiency.

There is now a substantial body of evidence around hypoxic training. A recent umbrella review included 22 systematic reviews covering 487 studies and 5,333 participants. Overall, intermittent-hypoxia approaches improved aerobic and anaerobic performance and, in some circumstances, strength.

And an especially interesting 2026 network meta-analysis of 29 randomized trials involving 603 trained athletes found:
Intermittent hypoxic training significantly improved aerobic capacity
Repeated-sprint training in hypoxia improved both aerobic and anaerobic capacity
The effects depended considerably on the protocol and simulated altitude.

However, here's the important distinction for your question:
Intermittent hypoxia has much better evidence as a training/adaptation stimulus than as a post-workout recovery treatment.

So I wouldn't currently sell a 20–30 minute hypoxia session after someone's workout as a scientifically established way to "recover faster."

An interesting third option: Hypoxia + Hyperoxia
There are systems that alternate:
Hypoxia → Hyperoxia → Hypoxia → Hyperoxia
sometimes called intermittent hypoxia-hyperoxia (IHH).

A systematic review found improvements in exercise tolerance and peak oxygen uptake, among other outcomes, although there were only eight qualifying studies and the populations varied substantially.

The concept is biologically interesting because you are creating a controlled oxygen stress followed by oxygen-rich recovery periods—essentially using oxygen availability as a physiological conditioning stimulus.

But again, I'd classify this as emerging, rather than proven exercise recovery technology.

If we're comparing the recovery technologies we've been discussing

| Modality | Acute muscle recovery | Performance/adaptation | Injury/rehab | Evidence rating |
| Red/NIR PBM | ★★★★ | ★★★ | ★★★ | Good/promising |
| HBOT | ★★★ | ★★ | ★★★★ | Promising/mixed |
| Intermittent hypoxia | ★★ | ★★★★ | ★★ | Good for adaptation |
| Hypoxia/Hyperoxia | ★★ | ★★★ | ★★ | Emerging |

One caveat: those stars are my practical interpretation of the literature, not a validated scientific grading system.

For a gym Recovery Zone, I'd therefore put Red/NIR ahead of HBOT specifically for routine post-training recovery. HBOT becomes more compelling when the target moves toward tissue healing/rehabilitation, while intermittent hypoxia belongs more naturally on the conditioning/performance/longevity-adaptation side of the facility than in the pure recovery category.

There is also an interesting question here that I think is worth investigating: Red/NIR + compression/recovery chair + oxygen/hypoxia modalities and whether there is evidence for combining them or sequencing them. That could help determine which technologies actually deserve space in a gym recovery center versus which ones mainly have good marketing.

content:
http://www.dotfit.com/sucralose

Remember, 98% of sucralose passes through the body, unabsorbed. It is essentially an inert ingredient used for taste and palatability.

Sucralose Q&A

Q: Why do you use Sucralose and is it a safe artificial sweetener?

A: Yes. Sucralose is widely used as an artificial sweetener because it has been placed on the Generally Regarded as Safe (GRAS) List by the FDA, based on the results from more than 110 studies on both humans and animals. Sucralose is one of seven nonnutritive sweeteners (NNS) that the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (ADA) has listed as evidence-based (see Position Statement from the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics below) and completely safe for the general population. As such, sucralose is used to improve the taste and mixing qualities of products without adding additional calories from sugar that might otherwise lead to unwanted weight gain.

As you know, we are an evidence-based R&D company. We are bound by this scientific approach in both program and product development. In particular, our guiding principles on dietary supplement use, recommendations, formulations, and manufacturing are best summed up by stating that dotFIT products must be 100% defensible through scientific research. (See pages 7–13 of Supplement Reference Guide for specific criteria formulation and manufacturing criteria at http://www.dotfit.com/PDSRG2015Update.)

I have included more extensive information below from our R&D team regarding the current use of this ingredient, its approval by the scientific community, and a couple of common Q&As from our Fitness Vault that you may find valuable.

More Information

If someone has a non-scientific reason (i.e., not unreferenced internet or cult nutrition information that may be referenced but taken out of context of real-world usage) not to ingest minute amounts of certain ingredients, we completely understand and certainly won't try altering their emotional reasoning. We totally respect personal but individual views. For everyone else who would like to be properly enlightened on the use of NNS, please read on:

When we formulate something, we do it safely and effectively, following evidence-based rules so that the vast majority of the population can use it, afford it, and benefit. Sucralose is on the Generally Regarded as Safe (GRAS) list published by the FDA and is one of the seven nonnutritive sweeteners that are listed by the ADA as evidence-based and completely safe. Additionally, artificial flavoring and sweeteners, especially in the normal minute amounts, are often safer for the general population because of natural food allergies and can deliver the sweet taste with little to no calories, thus helping support weight control. Products taken once or twice daily and/or on workout days will cause no problems unless a person is proven to be allergic to something in the contents. Below are two related Q&As that provide additional insight. The point is, we focus on taking care of our primary users: the vast majority of athletes and exercisers. We would love to make a specialized product for everyone, but that's definitely not economically feasible for either side.

Q: I saw sucralose in one of your products and my neighbor said it was bad for you, so I hesitated to purchase.

A: I don't know your neighbor's credentials, but we can probably put this to rest by saying that because we (dotFIT) work only within an evidence-based platform, the seven sweeteners, including sucralose, approved by the FDA fall into this category and are thus acceptable for use—especially in the minute amounts in our products. There is no possibility of any kind of toxicity in normal everyday consumption. Sucralose has been shown safe at levels of over 1,300 grams or packets a day, which would be equivalent to that many nutrition bars or servings of powders daily! And by the way, 1,300 grams daily of any of the healthiest single essential nutrients in the human food supply would probably kill you very quickly, whereas sucralose wouldn't.

That said, everyone has their own beliefs on NNSs or artificial sweeteners (AS), and one of them is the neurotoxin connection, which unfortunately is heavily internet-driven. This doesn't mean there are not some potential roots of truth based on non-realistic usage, like over 1,300 packets daily. And contrary to one highly publicized but flawed study, there is no evidence that AS contribute to type 2 diabetes as high sugar and weight gain do. The ADA evidence-based guidelines include the use of NNS/artificial sweeteners for weaning people off sugar, which of course is a far greater detriment because of the calories leading to our nation's number one problem. And no, NNS/AS do not lead to weight gain, although that myth also surfaces, but the latest studies prove otherwise.

Use of NNS/AS is an argument you never win when someone has their minds made up, but we live in the current scientific thinking that is captured in evidence-based criteria, so that's what we must follow because therein lies the safest solutions for our customers that deliver desired results.

*Evidence based: fitness/weight control solutions (or clinical decisions) that represent the best available evidence.

Below is from our Fitness Vault on a related question.

Q: Is Splenda (sucralose) dangerous to consume due to the chlorine used in making it?

A: It’s true that Splenda (which is 600 times sweeter than sugar) is made using chlorine, but there is no evidence that the chlorine atoms in sucralose are any more dangerous than they are in sodium chloride (i.e., table salt). Plain sugar is transformed into sucralose by substituting three chlorine atoms for hydrogen, creating a substance that is not digested by the body and is therefore calorie-free.

Animal models (rats, average weight of 250–520 grams) have been given doses of sucralose as high as 6.2 grams per day (16 g/kg) without any toxic effects. The same amount (16 g/kg of sucralose) given to an average-size male (84.1 kg) would be 1,345 grams/day or 1,345 packets. It’s highly unlikely this amount would be consumed in one day.

The US Food and Drug Administration reviewed more than 110 human and animal studies demonstrating its safety before it approved sucralose or Splenda for human consumption.

Below is from University of California Berkeley:

Artificial & Natural

Often, artificial ingredients are used to improve a product by making it one or more of the following: better tasting, safer, less expensive but delivering the same basic nutritional value with fewer calories. Artificial sweeteners (e.g., sucralose, acesulfame potassium, etc.) are used in order to reduce total sugar content. All approved sweeteners and infinitesimal amounts of binders (as in supplements) used in many products are perfectly amenable to the human digestive system and 100% safe for the general population (see FDA, ADA, and Generally Regarded as Safe [GRAS] list for position on sweeteners, binders, etc.). Additionally, artificial substitutes (e.g., sweeteners, colorings, flavorings, binders, etc.) are often safer than the “natural” counterpart because of common natural food allergies and the ability to deliver the desired sweetness with little to no calories to potentially help control weight.

Below is from the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics

J Acad Nutr Diet. 2012 May;112(5):739–58. doi: 10.1016/j.jand.2012.03.009. Epub 2012 Apr 25.

Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: use of nutritive and nonnutritive sweeteners. [NAME], [NAME]; Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics. West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA.

Abstract

It is the position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics that consumers can safely enjoy a range of nutritive sweeteners and nonnutritive sweeteners (NNS) when consumed within an eating plan that is guided by current federal nutrition recommendations, such as the Dietary Guidelines for Americans and the Dietary Reference Intakes, as well as individual health goals and personal preference. A preference for sweet taste is innate, and sweeteners can increase the pleasure of eating. Nutritive sweeteners contain carbohydrate and provide energy. They occur naturally in foods or may be added in food processing or by consumers before consumption. Higher intake of added sugars is associated with higher energy intake and lower diet quality, which can increase the risk for obesity, prediabetes, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. On average, adults in the United States consume 14.6% of energy from added sugars. Polyols, also referred to as sugar alcohols, add sweetness with less energy and may reduce the risk for dental caries. Foods containing polyols and/or no added sugars can, within food-labeling guidelines, be labeled as sugar-free. NNS are those that sweeten with minimal or no carbohydrate or energy. They are regulated by the Food and Drug Administration as food additives or generally recognized as safe. The Food and Drug Administration approval process includes determination of probable intake, cumulative effect from all uses, and toxicology studies in animals. Seven NNS are approved for use in the United States: acesulfame K, aspartame, luo han guo fruit extract, neotame, saccharin, stevia, and sucralose. They have different functional properties that may affect perceived taste or use in different food applications. All NNS approved for use in the United States are determined to be safe.

title: Can clients rely on blood panel results showing good vitamin and mineral levels to determine whether they need additional vitamins?
content:
Hi [CUSTOMER],

Blood tests for levels of vitamins and minerals (VM) do not accurately assess insufficiency/deficiencies because they only measure the vitamin or mineral in the blood, not in the tissues where they are part of their respective enzyme systems.

Everyone falls short of the recommended RDAs of VM, as every study shows from diet alone; therefore, take a Multivitamin and Mineral Formula (MVM), regardless of what your blood test shows. Further, no blood test can test for all VMs in one or two tests. It would take about 20 different tests and still only tell you blood levels, not functional tissue/cellular activity. See below for more information.

Thanks for the question [NAME], and hope this helps.

More info

Blood tests for minerals may be flawed (plasma, serum, etc.) because those levels may not be the same in tissues, especially during a systemic inflammation response (measured by levels of C-reactive protein), which significantly lowers plasma levels but does not indicate a true deficiency*. Also, blood plasma levels are not signs of tissue saturation, especially vitamin C.

Measuring vitamin status with tissue samples or blood can be problematic because of vitamin instability (e.g., light, oxygen, heat, etc.), which is why you do not do it—it is not reliable*. 291 for ref). Also, circulating blood levels only tell you what is there, not what is in storage.

Blood mineral status is not representative of tissue or cell status. Serum and plasma differ in content. (Page 313)*

FAQ

Q: To the best of your knowledge, are there any ways to test for micronutrient deficiencies other than blood tests?

Thank you!

A: Blood tests do not do a good job. They only tell you what is in the blood (blood mineral status is not representative of tissue or cell status. Serum and plasma differ in content). You need to get related enzyme activity tested, which is impractical for all VMs, but not if you are looking for a specific deficiency or insufficiency such as iron, vitamin K, or D, etc. All this said, diet analysis (recall) will at least give you what is being ingested, but tissue measurement activity is the final call if you suspect a deficiency.

title: Peptide status and good info-LA Times
content:
http://enewspaper.latimes.com/infinity/article_share.aspx?guid=009bf5cb-fc27-4d27-b98e-b76371fbb918

Unregulated peptide use alarms researchers
Consumer demand driven by online hype and distrust of health guidance
[NAME], a USC gerontologist, is concerned about the online marketing of his peptide. (Christina House Los Angeles Times)
By [NAME]
A few months ago, [NAME] learned of a thriving online trade in MOTS-c — a peptide that, when injected into mice, seems to mimic the effects of exercise.
The dean of the USC Leonard Davis School of Gerontology was very familiar with this particular short chain of amino acids. His lab identified it years ago as one of the thousands of peptides that act as chemical messengers in the human body, one he believed might someday have therapeutic uses for humans.
But [NAME] was alarmed to learn that his discovery was being promoted by legions of longevity seekers, fitness enthusiasts and wellness influencers as “exercise in a bottle.” Though not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, it was widely available online, often in vials marked “for research use only.”
“Turns out that tens of thousands of people are injecting themselves with MOTS-c [that’s] black market, illegal, from unknown sources, unknown purity, unknown sterility, and I strongly object to that,” [NAME] said.
Driven by social media hype and a growing distrust of public health guidance, consumer demand for experimental peptides has exploded over the last decade. Now, the clamor over unregulated peptides is fueling a high-stakes policy battle within the federal government. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has described himself as a “big fan” and user of peptides and has pledged to end the government’s “aggressive suppression” of them.
Some peptides, such as insulin, human growth hormone and glucagon-like peptide-1, have delivered transformational therapeutic effects when administered to humans.
But every vial of insulin or GLP-1 medication on a pharmacist’s shelf is the product of decades of clinical trials and safety testing. There are reams of data on what these drugs do, for whom they are most effective and in what dose and form they should be administered.
For MOTS-c and a raft of other peptides widely available online, no comparable evidence exists.
Although proponents say the substances help with weight loss, energy and muscle mass, and often cite research that has been done solely on animals or on a very small number of humans, no one knows for certain how or when it should be used in humans. While many users take multiple peptides together in custom combinations, or “stacks,” there is no data on how different synthetic peptides interact with one another.
To date, most of these popular peptides have been available solely in unregulated online marketplaces. But recently, an FDA committee voted to recommend that compounding pharmacies be allowed to manufacture six different peptides already widely available online: BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, epitalon, Semax and MOTS-c. A seventh, emideltide, was voted down.
Compounding pharmacies, which mix bespoke drugs, are a loophole in the U.S. regulatory system. Though the drugs they produce aren’t FDA-approved, the pharmacies still have to follow their state’s safety and quality regulations.
[NAME] traveled to Washington, D.C., to speak before the committee, many of whose members work for the kind of telehealth, longevity and wellness companies that stand to benefit financially from the peptides’ regulation.
Given that MOTS-c already is widely used off-label and no research has shown evidence of harmful side effects, [NAME] said in his remarks that he believed “quality-controlled, prescriber-supervised” compounding was the safest way forward.
“We can’t stop the black market. So I think it’s a better choice to at least guarantee the quality, the sterility, and require that real doctors are part of the process,” he said later. “I really think this is a better choice than just letting it go on the way it is.”
Not everyone agrees with him. FDA staff who spoke at the two-day meeting advised against peptide compounding, saying there was not enough safety data to justify the move.
The vote is non-binding, and the FDA could choose to side with its own scientists.
“My impression is that the ‘lesser of two evils’ argument is a minority perspective,” said [NAME], a cell biology and human anatomy professor at the UC Davis School of Medicine who writes on peptides.
“While it’s true that most compounders can likely [produce] purer versions of these peptides than what’s in the gray market, that doesn’t address potential inherent risks of the peptides themselves,” [NAME] said. “There’s no special reason they should be allowed to bypass the standard clinical trial system just because there’s a peptide fad driven by wellness influencers and telehealth firms.”
[NAME] found MOTS-c by combing through the 97% of human DNA that doesn’t encode for genes. This biological hoard once dismissed as “junk DNA” or the “dark genome” has turned out to be full of hormones and microproteins that play important roles in directing the body’s systems and processes.
Roughly 250 papers from dozens of research labs around the world have been published on MOTS-c since [NAME]’s lab identified it. While the peptide’s risks and side effects are few, and its effects on mouse metabolism compelling, no one knows how long-term use affects humans yet, or what formula or dosage would be most effective. Influencers’ claims about the peptides’ effect on human weight loss, muscle mass, longevity and energy appear to be extrapolated from their effects on lab animals.
“Certain groups of people — for example, the fitness enthusiasts, which is the kind way to refer to gym rats — those people take one figure from one paper done on mice and take it to become gospel,” [NAME] said.
Many users have been happy to essentially volunteer themselves for further testing.
“Today I used Mots-c for the first time and I’m a believer,” a Reddit user posted this year. “I did some outdoor sports for about an hour and then came home and spent several hours doing every chore that had been piling up all week.”
The reality is more nuanced. For scientists like [NAME], these molecules are an exciting area of research that could reap significant health breakthroughs. But rigorous science takes time, and they’re up against a public that has lost patience with the traditional drug approval model — and a market that is happy to provide alternatives.
In an ideal world, [NAME] said, he would like to see MOTS-c developed into an FDA-approved drug. But in the actual world, taking a single drug from the lab to the market requires so much time (at least 10 years, usually more) and money (at least hundreds of millions of dollars, usually more) that very few candidates successfully reach that goal. His own efforts to move MOTS-c through the development pipeline stalled.
“Peptides are neither miracle cures nor snake oil. They are signaling molecules. Some have strong evidence. Some have intriguing or early data. Some are wildly overhyped, and some probably should never leave the laboratory,” Dr. Ben Gonzalez, a former emergency medicine physician at Walter Reed Army Medical Center, said at the FDA meeting. “Patients are looking for alternatives, and they are looking not at physicians. They’re looking at this gray market source.”
If compounded peptides ultimately are approved, [NAME] would like to start an online registry in which patients can anonymously record the dosage they’re taking, the reason they’re taking it and any side effects they experience, so scientists can collect data on this real-world experiment.
“The big picture is that we’re transitioning as a nation from the 20th century model [in which] all healthcare was dictated by physicians and insurance companies to a new 21st century model where consumers are demanding and receiving health and wellness services and products that they pay for in cash,” [NAME] said. “I’m not saying that’s a better model. But it’s the model we’re transitioning into.”

title: Bioengineered, definition on bars or foods
content:
When you see "Contains a Bioengineered Food Ingredient" or similar wording on a protein bar, it does not mean the protein itself was genetically engineered or that the product was created in a laboratory. In most cases, it means that one or more ingredients are derived from crops that are commonly produced using biotechnology (genetic engineering).

Common examples in protein bars include:
- Soy protein or soy lecithin (from bioengineered soybeans)
- Corn-derived ingredients (fiber syrups, maltodextrin, soluble corn fiber, etc.)
- Sugar from sugar beets
- Canola oil

In the United States, the disclosure is required under the USDA's National Bioengineered Food Disclosure Standard when certain ingredients are derived from bioengineered crops. The label is a transparency requirement, not a safety warning.

For example:
- A whey protein bar may carry a bioengineered disclosure simply because it contains soy lecithin used as an emulsifier.
- A plant-based protein bar may carry the disclosure because it contains soy protein from bioengineered soybeans.
- Two otherwise similar bars may differ, with one labeled and one not, depending on ingredient sourcing and supply-chain documentation.

From a nutrition standpoint, the presence of a bioengineered ingredient does not automatically make the bar higher or lower in protein quality, calories, sugar, or overall healthfulness. For most consumers, factors such as total protein content, essential amino acid profile, fiber, added sugar, and overall ingredient quality are much more relevant than whether the product carries a bioengineered disclosure.

A simple explanation for clients would be:
"The bioengineered label means one or more ingredients in the bar came from crops such as soy, corn, canola, or sugar beets that were produced using modern biotechnology. It's a required disclosure for transparency, not a safety warning, and it doesn't tell you anything about the protein quality or effectiveness of the bar."

Are seed oils bad for you?

The idea that seed oils are bad for you is largely a myth. But where did the idea come from?

If you are active on social media, you may have seen infographics or TikToks that call out the “eight bad seed oils,” which include:

Rice bran
Safflower
Sunflower
Corn
Canola
Cottonseed
Soybean
Grapeseed

A B C D E F G

The idea of these “8 bad seed oils” or “the hateful eight” stems from a series of scientific evidence compiled by [NAME], MD. Some of the studies referenced in her analysis do suggest a link between polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs)—which are found in seed oils—and health conditions, like heart disease. But most evidence comes from small or animal and lab-based studies and isn't strong enough to draw any conclusions.

Like anything else in your diet, seed oils are fine in moderation. They should be part of an overall balanced eating plan that includes lots of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and lean protein options.

Of course, you can get too much of a good thing. The overuse of seed oils is the most problematic, especially when they are an ingredient in ultra-processed foods. For example, if you eat a lot of deep-fried foods, pastries, crunchy fried snacks (such as chips), and donuts, you can get too much oil. These ultra-processed foods are also high in sugar, salt, and/or food additives, which are also partly to blame for the poor health outcomes.

title: How can I recover from binge eating and intense hunger after aggressively dieting to 11–12% body fat, maintain my lean physique, and enjoy favorite foods on weekends without losing control?

Hi [CUSTOMER],

Thanks for contacting us. What you are experiencing is what many people go through after dieting to reach a lower body fat. They reach it and celebrate, and then find themselves having an ongoing difficult relationship with food. The more aggressive the weight loss (continuous calorie restrictions leading to >2 lbs/week), the more common this relationship with food becomes. The primary reason for successful weight loss is the trigger event—i.e., what motivated you in the first place, such as the wedding in your case. You need to find another motivating factor for the rest of your life and then follow the weekly average calorie intake that keeps you at the goal weight/body fat. This means you can incorporate the foods you like (on weekends or whatever day) within those weekly calories. Example: if your maintenance calories are ~2,500 calories/day to maintain your desired body fat after you have reached your goal, you can consume an average of 2,200 calories/day during the week, leaving you 5 days × 300 calories = 1,500 calories extra for favorite foods on top of the normal calorie intake. And remember, you can always move more (walking, playing sports, biking, etc.) to offset the extra calorie intake, especially on the weekends.

The majority of us former athletes whose sport required regular aggressive dieting (e.g., bodybuilding, wrestling, jockeys, combat sports, etc.) have ongoing problematic relationships with food (we call it diet PTSD) that we control based on lifelong fitness goals. For me, a retired bodybuilder and now fitness/nutrition leader, I still make a living by being in shape. And you too will be able to control your overall calorie intake if you had to “support your family” by doing so.

So find your motivation, log your foods for at least 90 days, lose no more than 1 lb/week until you reach your goal, at which time your calories will be adjusted to your maintenance. Sucralose

Sucralose is also an NNS and is made from sucrose by a process that substitutes three chloride atoms for three hydroxyl groups on the sucrose molecule. Sucralose is a very versatile NNS that is 450–650 times sweeter than sucrose, possesses a pleasant sweet taste, and has a quality and time-intensity profile that is close to that of sucrose, making it a popular NNS. Sucralose has been extensively studied, with more than 110 safety studies reviewed by the FDA in approving the use of sucralose as a general-purpose sweetener for food. A primary advantage of sucralose for consumers is its exceptional stability. It retains its sweetness over a wide range of temperature and storage conditions and in solutions over time. This stability allows manufacturers to create better-tasting foods and beverages and maintain the fresh flavor. Like Ace-K, sucralose is heat stable, meaning that it stays sweet even when used at high temperatures during baking, making it a common sugar substitute in baked goods.

title: MK-677 info
content:
Hey [CUSTOMER],

Sorry for the delay, but here is an oral GH secretagogue you asked about. See below for all the information I summarized, knowing that results vary but anecdotal evidence favors some efficacy. I also included a place where you can get it if you desire, because our third-party partner deals mainly with injectables at this point.

Call me if you have any questions. And, of course, you can do your own research to see if it makes sense for you or someone in your orbit to use.

Have a great day!

Ibutamoren (MK-677): Oral, non-peptide* GH stimulant

Primary use: To increase the body’s natural growth hormone and IGF-1 levels to support muscle growth, recovery, and overall anabolic function without injections.

Mechanism: Mimics ghrelin (“hunger hormone”) to activate ghrelin receptors (GHS-R1a), which signals the hypothalamus and pituitary to increase natural GH pulse release; the liver then produces more IGF-1, leading to an increase in protein synthesis and a reduction in muscle breakdown.

Typical dosing used in research and practice is approximately 10–25 mg once daily, usually taken in the evening (or split), with many starting at approximately 10 mg to assess tolerance and adjusting based on response.

Notes: MK-677 is an oral compound that increases your body’s growth hormone by mimicking a hunger signal. That can help with recovery, muscle maintenance, and sleep—but it also makes you hungrier and can affect blood sugar, so it’s not a shortcut unless everything else is dialed in, and human results vary and are largely based on anecdotes. MK-677 is not FDA-approved and is classified as a research compound.

*1 Ibutamoren (MK-677) is a small-molecule, non-peptide compound, specifically an orally active ghrelin receptor (GHS-R1a) agonist. It’s a synthetic, drug-like molecule, not a chain of amino acids like peptides designed to bind the ghrelin receptor and stimulate GH release. Its small-molecule structure is what allows it to be taken orally and remain stable in the body. Therefore, MK-677 works like a drug, not a peptide—so you can take it orally and it still activates the GH pathway effectively.

Our peptide/GLP-1 third-party partner does not carry MK-677—so see below.

title: Incretin mimics, semaglutide info, wt loss drugs (part 1 of 3)
content:
Weighing the consequences of weight loss drugs
https://www.medpagetoday.com/opinion/second-opinions/104482?xid=nl_mpt_DHE_2023-05-12&eun=g1588485d0r&utm_source=Sailthru&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Daily%20Headlines%20Evening%202023-05-12&utm_term=NL_Daily_DHE_dual-gmail-definition

Tirzepatide (Mounjaro), perhaps with a new brand name, will likely join semaglutide (Wegovy) by year's end as an approved weight-loss treatment for people with obesity or overweight and at least one weight-related medical problem. Tirzepatide is currently only approved for diabetes but is prescribed off-label for weight loss. More potent than semaglutide, which is also approved for type 2 diabetes, tirzepatide causes an average 22.5% reduction in body weight for people without diabetes. Tirzepatide's developer Eli Lilly will reportedly use a priority review voucher purchased for $110 million to shave 4 months off the approval timeline for a weight-loss indication.

Prescriptions for these incretin mimetics for weight loss—on- or off-label—have skyrocketed. While patients may be shedding pounds, it's far from certain whether these new drugs will actually improve health outcomes, and we're concerned that the prevailing narrative hasn't given enough air time to the potential drawbacks.

Incretin mimetics were originally developed to treat type 2 diabetes by stimulating insulin production. When diabetics lost weight, these drugs were repurposed for weight loss. Both semaglutide and tirzepatide act as agonists for glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), a hormone that slows gastric emptying and signals the brain to decrease appetite and reduce energy intake. With the addition of an agonist for another incretin (gastric inhibitory polypeptide [GIP]), tirzepatide causes greater weight reduction, although the role of GIP is uncertain.

The bottom line is that patients lose interest in eating, so they eat less. But incretin mimetics must be taken over a lifetime—once the drugs are stopped, the weight returns. Given the adverse effects of weight cycling, any temporary benefit of weight loss could be offset by longer-term harms of weight regain when the drugs are stopped.

Weight Loss Doesn't Equal Better Health

These drugs may not improve health outcomes. In part, that's because for obesity they are prescribed based only on body mass index (BMI)—a measure solely defined by height and weight and developed using data only from white men. While a higher BMI may be associated with health risks in a population, BMI is a poor measure of cardiometabolic health in individuals. What's more, a little extra weight may be protective. A meta-analysis found that, compared to normal weight, grade 1 obesity (BMI 30 to <35) was not associated with higher mortality, and overweight (BMI 25 to <30) was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality.

Obesity is a risk factor for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes, but is too often used as a surrogate for these conditions. Many thin people are hypertensive or diabetic, and many higher-weight people are normotensive and don't have diabetes or hypercholesterolemia.

Health outcomes can be improved without losing weight, and research supports a weight-neutral strategy for obesity treatment. Data show that, even in the absence of weight loss, exercise training can improve most cardiometabolic risk factors associated with obesity. And increases in cardiovascular fitness and physical activity, unlike weight loss, are consistently associated with lower mortality risks.

These Drugs Come With More Than Weight Loss

GLP-1 and GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists may benefit a few highly selected patients, but given known harms—and the potential for unknown long-term harms—BMI alone should never be the deciding factor. Certainly, no one without medical problems should be using these drugs in an effort to improve health or to improve appearance. Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea can be severe enough to send patients to the hospital. These drugs also increase risks of acute pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, kidney problems, and suicidal ideation, and may increase the risk of thyroid cancer.

Media are also reporting more adverse effects, including malnutrition caused by inadequate food intake, hair loss, and unusual, vivid dreams.

There's also concern about increased adverse effects in elders and populations of color, who were inadequately represented in clinical trials for both semaglutide and tirzepatide—participants were primarily white (75%), middle-aged (45 years) women (67%). Many older adults are sarcopenic, and incretin mimetics cause loss of lean body mass as well as fat mass. Moderate obesity may be protective against cardiovascular risks after age 65. Questions also remain about the effect of these drugs on Black Americans, three quarters of whom have a BMI classifying them as overweight or obese. At best, less than 8% of trial participants were Black in the tirzepatide trial.

Consider the Messenger

Hype is common with incretin drugs, and we understand these medications can be life-changing for select patients. But there needs to be more discussion of harms, the unknown effects of lifelong use, the dearth of information on Black patients, the value of BMI as a predictor of health risks, and whether these drugs actually benefit health. Even harder to find is discussion of the robust research available that supports a weight-neutral strategy for increasing health in higher-weight patients.

Certainly, our weight-obsessed culture is one reason for this limited discourse, but omitting any unappealing facts or unknowns aligns with the interest of pharmaceutical companies. A legion of conflicted individuals and organizations funded by weight-loss drug manufacturers promote a one-sided perspective and actively advocate for broad insurance coverage, especially for Medicare recipients.

Pharmaceutical company-sponsored organizations and individuals may not believe this money influences their positions, but, if their positions didn't align with the industry view, they wouldn't be receiving that funding. Doctors paid by weight-loss drugmakers are training new residents and medical students, offering continuing medical education, providing interactive learning modules, and appearing on 60 Minutes. A slew of obesity care and advocacy organizations lobby for insurance coverage, run awareness campaigns, hold conventions, and offer advice for healthcare providers. Quotes from spokespeople to the media relay industry messages without mentioning ties with industry.

While advocates may believe they are providing unbiased evidence-based information, it's woefully incomplete and misleading. Billions of dollars are likely to be spent on these drugs. A dispassionate look at what taxpayers get for that money is the only way to assess that investment. That's not going to happen when industry is pulling the strings.

Solving Obesity: New Drugs Can't Change How Little We Know

This is the first in a three-part series from WebMD on the obesity crisis. Part two examines if new weight loss drugs will finally end the obesity crisis. Part three shows how doctors and patients can make treatment even better.

Everyone's talking about weight loss drugs.

The craze began when word leaked about Hollywood types using Ozempic and Wegovy to drop weight. Like a Southern California wildfire, news spread: These injectable drugs could help people lose 10%, 15%, or even 20% of their body weight.

Now we've blown by the tipping point. More weight loss meds are on the way, some in pill form. In the latest breakthrough, people in a phase II clinical study who took the drug retatrutide lost 24% of their body weight. That's almost on par with bariatric surgery.

Doctors (and drug companies) are thrilled, and they should be: These are the first drug treatments for obesity that work. Or, at least, the first to work well.

Yet, while these drugs may be a major win for obesity treatment, all the celebratory noise can't erase a sobering truth: There's still a lot we don't know about obesity, including what's behind an unprecedented spike in obesity rates over the past 30-plus years and, crucially, how to prevent obesity in the first place.

Heck, researchers aren't even sure how this class of drugs—GLP-1 agonists—works for weight loss. Diabetes was the original target, and weight loss effects were a surprise.

"The most effective drug we have for obesity was developed by accident," said [NAME], MD, a cardiologist and nutrition professor at Boston's Tufts School of Medicine. "That right there should be a clear sign of how little we understand about obesity."

So Much Research, So Few Answers

More than 40% of American adults live with obesity. Sixty years ago, that number was 13%.

In some ways, that's the medical failure of our time. No matter what we've done or how much science has uncovered, we've just kept gaining weight—even as rising childhood obesity rates have filled the pipeline.

Around the turn of the century—after the obesity rate soared in the '90s—scientists responded with an explosion of research. As study after study linked excessive fat to the deadliest diseases—cardiovascular disease, strokes, diabetes, cancer—the obesity fight emerged as a clear public health priority. In the last decade alone, the U.S. has invested almost $11 billion in this research. Yet there's no evidence to suggest we can halt or reverse the trend. The biggest tell: Even obesity researchers acknowledge their failures.

Time will reveal the drugs' impact, but it may be limited, given how widespread obesity has become.

The problem: The list of potential causes of obesity is so long, it's hard to pick one, much less decide how to fix it. Diet and intervention studies can tell us only so much. Few are definitive, and most leave ample room for debate.

"The underlying cause [of obesity], and therefore the issues that would guide prevention, are very difficult," said [NAME], PhD, director of the National Institutes of Health-funded Michigan Nutrition Obesity Research Center. "We've run lots of different trials to do obesity prevention, and almost all have been abject failures."

We Americans Just Eat Too Much, Right?

Overeating may be the most widely accepted explanation for rising obesity numbers. It feels intuitive: We eat too much and move too little. Which leads to the "we Americans just love our large portions and sugary foods more than our health" take.

But what if there were data to suggest that, in fact, our food intake has not changed in 20 years—even as the obesity rate has soared?

There is. Picture a chart with three lines. One line represents total food intake, and another our total food supply. A third line—the obesity rate—rises sharply, ultimately surpassing the other two, which stay flat.

"By two independent measures, calorie intake has been flat in the U.S. for 20 years while obesity has skyrocketed," says [NAME]. "That single point should call into question everything we think we know."

He revealed this plot twist in a perspective paper he wrote last year. The data is from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey on what we eat, and the Food and Agriculture Organization, which tracks the food supply.

When you consider our growing body sizes, "the data suggest that Americans have been eating relatively less," the paper notes. It says there's little evidence to suggest physical activity has changed either, undermining the idea that declining exercise could be a driver.

As often happens in this field, the argument leaves plenty of room for skepticism. Much of the data in question is based on people reporting their own behavior, and that can be unreliable—people may under-report how much they eat and over-report how much they move. Plus, while overall population data may show steady trends, this may hide differences in important subgroups, said [NAME], MD, DrPH, a professor of epidemiology and nutrition at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

That is, some groups (such as those in low-income areas) may be eating more and moving less, while others (in more privileged parts) are eating less and moving more—so overall, the line appears flat. What's more: "If you look back farther, food consumption has gone up since the 1970s," [NAME] says. That's right around the time the average body weight began to rise.

[NAME] acknowledged these limitations in his paper but said "discarding all these data because they do not fit a conventional theory of obesity would be imprudent; and other hypotheses must also be considered."

An alternate explanation: The quality of our food intake—like all those sugars and processed carbs—may have changed our bodies' response to food.

Take the microbiome. Rodent studies show that changes in the microbes that live in your gut may impact metabolism and body weight. (Some research suggests that fecal transplants may improve the metabolic health of subjects with obesity, but much more research is needed before this can be used to treat people.)

Another possibility is the impact of diet on our epigenetics, or the way our genes work. "Epigenetics is something on top of the genetic environment that allows some genes to turn on and off," said [NAME], MD, PhD, an obesity researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, who studies interactions between biology and environment. Nutrients, like fat or carbs, may do this to genes that burn or store energy, playing a role in fat storage.

These are emerging areas that scientists are still working to understand.

"I would say we're maybe 5% of the way there in what we know. And there's still 95% that's understudied," [NAME] says.

What Do We Know From 40 Years of Research?

Trying to summarize obesity research is overwhelming. So many studies, so many caveats, contradictions, and dead ends.

Arguably the biggest landmark was the discovery of leptin, a fat hormone that regulates body weight, in 1994.

"It was the discovery of leptin that changed things … that said it's not just willpower; there's biology at work," said [NAME], PhD, director of the Nutrition Obesity Research Center at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. "A lot of scientists started saying, ‘Wow, this problem of obesity is pretty interesting. I might want to look at it.'"

The studies began rolling in. In 1990, scientists published 1,900 papers on obesity, according to a search of PubMed, a website that catalogs scientific research. By 2000, that number had more than doubled, and it has risen exponentially ever since, topping 33,000 papers annually for the last 3 years. All told, that's nearly half a million studies.

Neuroscientists study rodents to see how the brain regulates food intake. Geneticists identify human genes linked to obesity. (Hundreds have been found so far.) Epidemiologists survey large populations, looking for patterns linked to weight gain, weight maintenance, or weight loss.

Nutrition researchers do diet studies, dividing people they study into groups assigned to different diets. These are notoriously hard to design. Most rely on people to follow the nutrition advice, and few last more than a year.

"‘Oh, there's a professor who has a question. I promise to change my diet and perfectly adhere to it for the next few decades!' No one is going to sign up for that study," said Christopher Gardner, PhD, director of nutrition studies at Stanford Prevention Research Center.

Most diet studies show no one diet is better for weight loss than another. Any diet can work if you reduce calories.

Still, results vary a lot. In one large diet study from Gardner in 2018, people following a low-carb or low-fat diet found a wide variety of outcomes: Some lost as much as 50 pounds, while others gained up to 20.

"A 70-pound range," Gardner said. "How can you explain that when they got the same advice?" (In fact, that was the very question Gardner had set out to answer, but he found no link between people's success and their genetics or insulin response.)

The thing is, we do know how to lose weight—the problem is keeping it off. High-quality data on long-term weight loss is sparse, but what little we have suggests most people regain lost pounds within 5 years.

"We have not, as a health professional community, been very successful with helping people lose fat and maintain that loss," Gardner said.

For Hill—who in the 1990s co-founded the National Weight Control Registry, a study tracking 10,000 people who've lost weight and kept it off—that's because people are "swimming upstream."

"Really good swimmers can do it, but most get swept down," Hill said. "We can either teach people to be better swimmers, or we can reduce the current, which is the environment."

Both of those options are easier said than done.

That Pesky Environment

The overall trend of obesity research has been a shift to understanding obesity as a disease.

Like many diseases, obesity is likely caused by a combination of genetics and our environment, said [NAME], MD, a professor of medicine and nutritional science at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis.

"Computers, cars, and cellphones keep us sitting in one place," he said. "We have food that doesn't perish. We can keep it in a can or frozen for months or years. We're never without the availability of food."

Many researchers agree, but exactly what parts of that environment are to blame, and how they interact with our bodies, is hotly debated.

Some theories:

The prevailing view focuses on the brain. Brain circuits that control food intake are responding to a changing food environment in ways that are still being revealed, resulting in overeating and obesity. (One new study found that obesity may permanently impair the brain's response to eating fats and sugars, making people less able to recognize when they're full.)

A competing hypothesis—the carbohydrate-insulin model—suggests that highly processed carbohydrates trigger hormonal responses that lead to excess fat storage.

Yet another view suggests that chemicals called obesogens (found in products like can linings, plastic bottles, clothing, and pesticides) lead to weight gain by altering hormones and metabolism in ways that promote fat.

Still other societal changes may be at play. Weight gain is a side effect of many antidepressants and other treatments for mood disorders, said [NAME], MD, director of the obesity research and treatment program at Weill Cornell Medicine, at Cornell University in New York City. "We estimated in a paper that about 15% of the obesity epidemic could be related."

Indoor temperature controls mean we burn fewer calories warming up or cooling down. Changing sleep habits can impact weight. Far fewer people smoke now, a huge health win no doubt. But when people stop smoking, they tend to gain weight.

And the list goes on. All of the above? Perhaps. But good luck getting a consensus.

"Most obesity researchers will tell you that we really don't know why obesity occurs," Hill said. "We know a lot, but I can't sit here and say, ‘Here is why we have so much obesity.'"
