content:
SOURCES:
Randy Seeley, PhD, director, Michigan Nutrition Obesity Research Center.
Dariush Mozaffarian, MD, cardiologist, nutrition professor, Tufts School of Medicine, Boston.
Walter Willett, MD, DrPH, professor of epidemiology and nutrition, T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Harvard University, Boston.
Margarita Teran-Garcia, MD, PhD, assistant dean for integrated health disparities programs, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.
James Hill, PhD, director, Nutrition Obesity Research Center, University of Alabama at Birmingham.
Christopher Gardner, PhD, director, nutrition studies, Stanford Prevention Research Center, Stanford University, Palo Alto, CA.
Samuel Klein, MD, professor of medicine and nutritional science, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis.
Louis Aronne, MD, director, obesity research and treatment program, Weill Cornell Medicine, New York City.

This is the second in a three-part series from WebMD on the obesity crisis. Part one tackles a complicated question—why does the obesity rate keep rising despite our efforts to stop it?—and can be found here. Part three shows how doctors and patients can make treatment better and can be found here.

In the mid-1980s, [NAME] strolled into a lab at Rockefeller University where a colleague was breeding mice. "I will never forget what he showed me," said [NAME], now the director of obesity research and treatment at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York City. "He had a cage with 10 mice, one severely obese and the others normal weight. He took blood from one of the thin mice and gave it to the fat mouse."

When [NAME] returned 3 days later, that obese mouse had turned thin.

It was proof of something [NAME] already suspected: Obesity had biological causes and wasn't just a failure of willpower.

Years later, in 1994, that research led to the discovery of leptin, a hormone released from fat cells that's involved in the regulation of body weight. It was a watershed moment in obesity research.

Since then, [NAME] and others have worked to build the clinical field of obesity medicine, attempting to shift the public and medical view of obesity from a purely behavioral issue to a disease worthy of medical treatment.

All the while, the U.S. obesity rate soared.

Now, another watershed moment: We finally have highly effective obesity drugs. The hype is real, and so are the weight loss results.

"I've been saying for 30 years that when we find treatments that really work, people aren't going to believe the results," [NAME] says. "It took longer than I expected, but it's gratifying now to see."

All this excitement raises a crucial question: Will the new drugs finally end the obesity crisis? Experts have their doubts.

The Big Question

The emerging class of obesity medications known as GLP-1 agonists is indeed a game changer. The weight loss drug semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) showed groundbreaking results, and studies suggest a parade of even more impressive drugs is on the way.

Yes, the drugs offer new hope to millions with obesity complications. But to truly turn the tide on our 42% obesity rate, much more work remains to be done, researchers said, including answering a big question:

How do these weight loss drugs work?

"We have new blockbuster drugs, and we don't even know why they reduce body weight," says [NAME], MD, professor of medicine and nutritional science at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. "It was by accident that this was discovered."

Oops, We Created a Weight Loss Drug

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, commonly abbreviated as GLP-1 RAs, emerged as a promising therapeutic class based on incretin therapy that regulates glucose metabolism through multiple mechanisms. (Why do incretins cause weight loss? Incretin mimetics present glucose-lowering properties, together with a reduction of appetite and food intake, resulting in weight loss. Jan 25, 2021.)

Developed to treat diabetes, the GLP-1 drugs' weight loss effects were a surprise. Now that those effects are confirmed, pharmaceutical companies and researchers are racing to figure out how these drugs work.

In the 1960s, scientists discovered the incretin effect—when you eat glucose (sugar), your body makes more insulin than it does if glucose is given intravenously. Glucose passes through the GI tract and the gut releases hormones that stimulate insulin secretion. It's "essentially a feed-forward signal to your pancreas to tell it, 'By the way, you need to be ready because there's a bunch of glucose coming,'" said [NAME], MD, director of the Michigan Nutrition Obesity Research Center, funded by the National Institutes of Health.

One of these hormones—or "incretins"—is GLP-1. In experiments, people with type 2 diabetes who were hooked up to GLP-1 saw their blood sugar go down.

"That led to the idea that if we could take this native hormone and make it last longer, we'd have a therapy for type 2 diabetes," said [NAME]. Thanks to a GLP-1-like compound in the saliva of the Gila monster, that idea became reality in the 2000s.

Along the way, a surprising side finding came to light: In early trials, diabetes patients on these drugs dropped weight.

Both Ozempic and Wegovy—brand names for semaglutide—are once-weekly injections (pill forms to treat obesity are on the way), but the latter is a higher dose.

"That dose results in about 40% of patients in the clinical trials achieving a 20% weight loss. We've just had nothing like that in terms of efficacy before," said [NAME], who has worked with some of the drug companies (including Novo Nordisk, the maker of Ozempic and Wegovy, and Eli Lilly, maker of Mounjaro) that market the GLP-1s.

By contrast, semaglutide's once-a-day predecessor liraglutide (Saxenda, also made by Novo Nordisk) can lead to about 10% weight loss.

"And one of the ironies is, we don't really know why," [NAME] says. "We don't know why semaglutide is a better molecule for weight loss than liraglutide."

Initially, scientists believed that the drugs, in addition to telling the pancreas to secrete more insulin, were also signaling the brain that you're full. "Turns out that's not really the way it works," [NAME] says. "GLP-1 made from your gut probably doesn't get into your brain very much. But you make GLP-1 in your brain as well."

For weight loss, it's the brain's GLP-1 system, not the gut's, that the drugs are thought to hijack. But exactly which parts of the brain they affect and how is unknown. "That's something lots of people are working on, including our own lab," [NAME] said. (Another surprise: The drugs may have potential as an anti-addiction treatment.)

The diabetes medication tirzepatide (Mounjaro), expected to be approved for weight loss as early as this year, is also a weekly injection, but it has a unique feature: It starts a response not just for GLP-1 but also for another incretin called GIP. Turns out, two is better than one: Trial participants on tirzepatide lost up to 22.5% of their body weight.

More of these hybrid drugs are on the way, [NAME] said. In mid-stage clinical trials, the drug retatrutide, which targets three hormones, led to 24% weight loss. "The idea is the more bullets we can load into the gun, the more we can push the biology into a place where it's easier to lose weight."

Shifting From Prevention to Damage Control

Less invasive and more scalable than surgery (only 1% of the eligible population gets bariatric surgery), the drugs offer doctors a safe, effective way to treat many patients with obesity. That's cause for excitement, but concerns remain because they are expensive, costing about $800 to $1,300 per month out of pocket. Many health insurers, including Medicare, do not cover them for weight loss.

"You have this significant advance in obesity treatment, but very few will be able to access it," said [NAME], PhD, adjunct professor of psychology in psychiatry at the University of Pennsylvania and chief scientific officer at WW (formerly Weight Watchers).

There is a push, including a proposed bill, to get Medicare to cover obesity medication. But given the expense of the drugs, the health economics do not support that move, according to an editorial in the New England Journal of Medicine. If Medicare were to cover obesity meds, the budget impact would likely be huge, potentially driving up premiums. If other payers followed suit, the impact could be felt across the U.S. health care system.

Other drawbacks include side effects—including nausea, diarrhea, stomach pain, and vomiting—that can be so bad that some patients can't tolerate them.

And critically, the drugs do not deal with the root cause of the problem, said [NAME], MD, an endocrinologist and pediatrician at the University of California, San Francisco, who has suggested that excess insulin is driving obesity. "No one has the disease that these drugs are treating. No one has GLP-1 deficiency. They're bypassing the problem. They're band-aiding the problem."

Because the drugs work by mimicking starvation—they appear to curb hunger, so you eat less—people on them lose not just fat but also healthy lean mass, [NAME] said.

Concerns about pancreatitis did not really bear out in post-marketing reports. (The drugs are still not recommended in people with pancreatitis, or a history of a type of thyroid cancer or a type of tumor called multiple endocrine neoplasia.) But predicting longer-term outcomes can be hard, notes [NAME].

Then there are philosophical questions, said [NAME], PhD, director of the Nutrition Obesity Research Center at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. "If you're continuing to not exercise and eat not healthy foods and take a medication, is that success? Have we won when people are at a lower weight but not doing a healthy behavior?"

"We Can't Treat Our Way Out of This"

The fact is, ending the obesity epidemic is a tall order, even for drugs as impressive as these.

"We can't treat our way out of this," said [NAME], MD, co-director of Wake Forest Baptist Health Weight Management Center in Winston-Salem, NC. "The treatments we have now are great, and there will be more coming. But we do need to figure out the prevention side of things."

[NAME] agrees but adds we can't diet-and-exercise our way out either.

"There's no switch to be flipped," [NAME] says. "If you told me we shouldn't spend all this money on these drugs, we should spend it on prevention—great! What would we do?"

And prevention efforts won't help the millions already living with health problems from obesity, [NAME] said.

"Getting people to stop smoking prevents lung cancer. But stopping smoking doesn't treat lung cancer," [NAME] said. "Once the physical changes occur in the lung that cause a tumor to grow, it's too late. You have to think of obesity the same way."

[NAME] points out that "fearmongering" around the drugs highlights our lingering bias that obesity is a lifestyle issue that should not be medically treated.

"People say, 'When you stop taking it, you're going to gain the weight back,'" [NAME] said. "There's truth to that, but when you stop taking your hypertension medication, your blood pressure goes up. We don't think of that as a [reason] for why you shouldn't take your blood pressure medication. But that gets trumpeted into all these conversations about whether people [with obesity] should be treated at all."

Like obesity, blood pressure was once thought to be a behavioral problem too, [NAME] said. But blood pressure meds prevent heart attacks and strokes. And it's likely obesity meds will do the same.

One 55-year-old patient on the road to kidney failure lost weight on obesity medications, including semaglutide, [NAME] said. Now, 6 years later, his kidney function is back to normal. "Normally, we think of kidney disease as irreversible," [NAME] said.

In that respect, these drugs should save money in the long run by virtue of heading off those health care costs, said [NAME], who imagines a future where obesity is not gone but better managed, like high blood pressure is now.

In the end, the drugs are another step toward what [NAME] and many others have always pushed for: Treating obesity as a disease.

How doctors and patients can do everything better—read part three here.

This is the third in a three-part series from WebMD on the obesity crisis. Part one asks a complicated question: Why has the obesity rate continued to rise despite our efforts to stop it? Part two examines whether new weight loss drugs will finally end the crisis.

After [NAME] gave birth in 2018, she retained fluid in her legs—a common occurrence after giving birth. The swelling made walking, sitting, and caring for her newborn painful and uncomfortable. She went in for a check-up, and her doctor told her it would eventually go away with regular movement and elevating her legs.

Months passed and the painful swelling wouldn't subside, so she saw a different primary care doctor. [NAME] said the second doctor didn't examine her legs, but instead implored her to focus on one thing: losing weight. She left with information on which calorie-counting apps to download.

As time went by and the swelling persisted, she went back to the second doctor and asked for a water pill to flush out the fluids—something she had seen other new parents discuss online. The doctor obliged, and within days, [NAME]'s swelling was gone. She realized she could have avoided 6 months of potential health risks and pushing through pain if only her doctor had seen her as a person, not just a bigger body.

[NAME] and her son.

Weight bias, unfortunately, is nothing new. Many studies over decades have shown that doctors sometimes look down on patients with obesity, and can have a hazy understanding of the condition overall. This makes it harder for bigger patients to receive proper care and achieve positive health outcomes, with previous negative experiences deterring some from seeing doctors at all. And so the cycle continues.

"There are a lot of things that happen in my body that I feel like I have to educate my [health care] providers on," [NAME] said. "I wish that was different."

Weight Stigma in Health Care Runs Deep

In some cases, like [NAME]'s, patients don't feel heard because they doubt their doctors can see past their obesity. At the same time, the weight loss advice that doctors tend to give—eat less, move more—often doesn't work. While some doctors do specialize in obesity treatment—obesity medicine has been growing since the field was established in 2011—most receive little training in how to talk about and treat obesity.

Then there's the fact that doctors are human and not immune to bias. Previous studies have shown weight stigma in patient-provider encounters, with a 2021 PLOS One study of nearly 14,000 people across six countries showing two-thirds of those who have experienced weight stigma also experienced it with doctors. The result: They perceived less listening and respect from doctors, more judgment due to body weight, and lower quality of health care.

There's more. The negativity of weight stigma can lead to more unhealthy behavior, including disordered eating, more weight gain, and alcohol use, and it has been linked to higher suicide risk.

All this is bad news for people and for public health, as it leaves people living with obesity reluctant to seek help for any health issue, much less for weight management. In a country with skyrocketing obesity rates, that's not good.

Obesity medicine specialist [NAME], MD, MPH, an educator and doctor at Harvard Medical School and Massachusetts General Hospital, sees patients from as young as 2 years old to upwards of 90. Among her diverse pool of patients emerges one common theme.

"Patients with obesity have been devalued and belittled," she said. "They often seek treatment under cloak of secrecy. They don't want people to know they're being treated for obesity because it must be a sign of failure or of their inadequacy of not doing things the 'hard' or the 'right' way."

When It Becomes Easier to Simply Not Go to the Doctor

For many larger-bodied patients, it's common to go years without seeing a doctor. Studies have shown that people with obesity are less likely to be screened for certain cancers and more likely to delay care, in large part due to the negative attitudes they experience in health care settings.

Research also shows that overweight patients shop for doctors 23% more often than their lower-weight counterparts. For patients with obesity, that jumps to 52%, showing just how hard it is for those patients to find a compassionate provider and stick with them.

"It's not just about hurt feelings," [NAME] said. "It's about people avoiding preventative care appointments, avoiding getting injuries treated, avoiding their health issues because they don't want to be shamed."

This rings true for [NAME], a plus-sized childbirth educator and author.

"Even though this is what I teach full-time, I didn't go to the doctor for over 2 years, and during that time I gained weight already existing in a larger body," she said. "I gained an additional 60 pounds, and it really affected my mental health."

"I spent years not going to the doctor or receiving routine health care," says [NAME], a childbirth educator and author. "I am a statistic that I teach others about."

The long hiatus began pre-pandemic, after [NAME] saw a doctor when she had a hard time breathing. A month before her appointment, she had completed a 5K and was in good health. She asked her provider for an inhaler but was told that would "hurt her heart." The doctor ordered an EKG, which showed no abnormalities, but still refused to give [NAME] a prescription for an inhaler.

As she was driving home, she nearly blacked out from lack of air. She ended up going to urgent care for an inhaler and was told she just had a restricted airway that needed help opening up after a bout with strep throat.

"I've basically had to say [to doctors]: Look at me, the human sitting in front of you that has been mistreated by the health care system," [NAME] said. "I am a person. I am not a BMI or a number on the scale. Treat me with dignity."

A New Path to Better Results

[NAME], 45, is a member of the Obesity Action Coalition and has sought treatment for obesity throughout her life. She ultimately had bariatric surgery in her mid-30s.

Before the surgery, she had given birth to twins, and her health had suffered due to polycystic ovary syndrome and thyroid issues.

"I had little kids, and I'd already tried every fad diet," [NAME] said. "My primary care physician, who has never experienced obesity herself, just kept telling me to 'just walk a little more and put down the fork and eat a little less'—that was pretty much the only advice I got from her about weight management."

Studies have shown that weight loss advice from doctors rarely includes effective methods, and typically falls into the generic "eat less, move more" variety.

This doctor was also an internal medicine specialist whose practice was said to be geared toward patients with more complicated health profiles, [NAME] said. Eventually, [NAME]'s endocrinologist recommended different treatment options, like medication and surgery.

"Even when researchers do very nice, controlled studies, only about 5% of people are able to lose 20% of their weight with lifestyle interventions alone. Forty-eight percent of people are able to lose 5% of their weight," said [NAME], MD, associate director of the Weight Center at Massachusetts General Hospital. "The biggest thing I tell people is that it's not about your character; it's about your chemistry."

Getting regular exercise and eating a balanced diet are good lifestyle choices for everyone, not just those with obesity. But according to [NAME], patients usually need another intervention for successful weight management.

At the Massachusetts General Hospital Weight Center, [NAME] says, it's about trying different therapies and seeing how patients respond. Successful treatment involves every part of a person: genetics, hormone levels, sleep patterns, food access, and mental health. And in her experience, this multidisciplinary approach works.

"A large majority of my patients—people I've been seeing for 10 or 12 years who have continued with care—probably an excess of 90% are successful in their treatment strategies," she said.

A person's weight management strategies often have to change over time. Even after [NAME] lost significant weight from bariatric surgery, her weight began to creep back up (a not uncommon experience). She started taking a prescribed GLP-1 receptor agonist—a group of drugs that includes semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy)—to help her maintain her weight.

How Doctors and Patients Can Get Better Results Together

For heavier people who don't have access to a multidisciplinary, patient-focused weight center—and doctors who don't provide those specialized services—there are still ways everyone can achieve better treatment results.

For doctors: You're seeing patients with obesity, but do those patients feel "seen"? Is your practice set up to accept and accommodate heavier patients? [NAME] suggests looking at areas you may not have thought about previously, such as gowns that fit larger bodies, larger chairs in the waiting room, and scales with higher weight limits.

Education is key, said [NAME], MD, PhD, an obesity medicine doctor at the Mayo Clinic in Jacksonville, FL. [NAME] pointed out that new therapies are being developed to manage weight loss, and some (like semaglutide) have already been used for years to treat diabetes. "While some providers are willing to start using these medications, it is not enough," she said. Remember: "We should be treating obesity as any other chronic disease, just like high blood pressure or diabetes."

For patients: Check online for lists of "weight-neutral" or "size-friendly" providers endorsed by other larger-bodied patients. Lists like these are places where patients can add the names and information of providers they've had positive experiences with.

Ask questions and advocate for yourself, [NAME] urges, even if you're not comfortable doing so. "Am I going to be given a sheet or a gown that fits my body? Are they using a blood pressure cuff with the correct size? Are they taking your blood pressure the minute you're hurried back to a room?" (According to the CDC, a patient must be seated with their back supported for at least 5 minutes with their feet flat on the ground in order to get an accurate blood pressure reading.)

But what's made the biggest difference for her is being clear with doctors and nurses about how she's feeling in the moment, and how her previous experiences in health care have contributed to that.

Since incorporating these strategies, [NAME] said she has finally been able to receive the care she deserves from a compassionate provider.

"I told [my doctor], 'I want to be healthy,'" she recalled. "And we went through my lab results together. I had done a full blood panel, and he scooted his chair toward me and looked me straight in the eye and said, 'You are healthy.'"

title: Why are the powdered product containers not filled all the way, and what response can we provide to explain the empty space?
content:
In a powdered product, there is empty space between the top of the powder and the bottom of the lid. The actual term is called “slack-fill,” and its definition is: “Slack-fill is the difference between the actual capacity of a container and the volume of product contained therein.”

Since our powdered products are being filled by machines and not by hand, they can only fill to a certain height to avoid overfill and also include a scoop. With this, there will be this space between the top of the powder and the bottom of the lid. However, powder naturally decreases in volume with time and transport.

An easier-to-understand example that most people see in real life is a box of corn flakes that has 12 ounces of corn flakes. It could have between 1–3 inches of empty space at the top of the bag, inside the box. The corn flakes have settled, and it may look like you are getting less, but you are still getting 12 ounces of corn flakes.

Seems that this would be obvious, but more people are feeling that they are getting ripped off as a result of shrinkflation, so steps are being taken to make this “difference” more clear to consumers.

To help explain this, going forward, all powdered products will have this “slack-fill” image and statement:

title: Bio-engineered food - GMO
content:
What Are Bioengineered Ingredients?

Bioengineered (BE) ingredients are ingredients in food that come from plants, animals, or microorganisms whose DNA has been altered through modern biotechnology (genetic engineering).

In simple terms:
Bioengineered ingredients = ingredients made from genetically modified organisms (GMOs).

This definition is used legally in the U.S. National Bioengineered Food Disclosure Standard (NBFDS), which requires BE foods to be labeled.

✔️ Simple Definition for Consumers
Bioengineered ingredients are GMO-derived ingredients that still contain detectable genetically modified DNA or protein and therefore must be labeled under U.S. law.

📌 Key Points
1. BE Ingredients Contain Detectable Modified Genetic Material
To be labeled “bioengineered,” the ingredient must contain detectable GMO DNA or proteins.

If the GM DNA is removed or destroyed during processing (common with oils, sugars, starches), the product may NOT be labeled BE—even if the crop was genetically modified.

2. BE = GMO (legally, same category), but not all GMOs must be labeled

Examples of GM crops used in BE ingredients:
Corn
Soybeans
Canola
Sugar beets
Cottonseed
Papaya (Hawaiian)
Certain potatoes
Certain apples
Squash

Examples of Common Bioengineered Ingredients

These come from genetically modified crops and often remain BE after processing:

From Corn
High-fructose corn syrup
Corn starch (sometimes)
Corn flour (if not extensively processed)

From Soy
Soy protein concentrate/isolate
Soy lecithin (sometimes BE, sometimes not)
Soy oil (not labeled BE because the DNA is removed)

From Canola
Canola oil (usually not BE-labeled—DNA removed)

From Sugar Beets
Table sugar (often not BE-labeled because no DNA remains)

From Cottonseed
Cottonseed oil

From Potatoes/Apples
Certain varieties engineered to resist browning or bruising

What Foods Commonly Contain BE Ingredients?
Packaged snacks
Sweetened beverages
Breakfast cereals
Baking mixes
Protein bars
Frozen meals
Condiments
Many ultra-processed foods

What Foods Are Usually Free From Bioengineered Ingredients?
Organic products (by law, organic cannot contain GMOs)
Whole, fresh animal products (meat, eggs, dairy)
Whole fruits and vegetables (except a few GM varieties)

Why Are BE Ingredients Used?
Companies use bioengineered crops because they offer:
Higher yields
Pest resistance
Herbicide tolerance
Reduced food waste (e.g., non-browning apples)
Cost savings in large-scale food production

⚖️ Labeling Rules (U.S.)
Foods must disclose BE status if:
They contain detectable modified DNA
Their ingredients are on the USDA’s BE list

Allowed forms of disclosure:
The word “bioengineered”
A symbol
Electronic/digital link (QR code)

✔️ Simple Definition for Consumers
Bioengineered ingredients are GMO-derived ingredients that still contain detectable genetically modified DNA or protein and therefore must be labeled under U.S. law.

title: Triple Agonist Retatrutide Hits New Weight-Loss Highs
content:
Triple Agonist Retatrutide Hits New Weight-Loss Highs (medscape.com)

SAN DIEGO — New designer molecules that target weight loss via multiple mechanisms continue to raise the bar for how many pounds people with overweight or obesity can lose.

Retatrutide (Eli Lilly), an investigational agent that combines agonism of three key hormones that influence eating and metabolism into a single molecule, safely produced weight loss at levels never seen before in a pair of phase 2 studies that together randomized more than 600 people with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes.

Among 338 randomized people with overweight or obesity and no type 2 diabetes, 48 weeks of treatment with retatrutide at a 12-mg dose given by weekly subcutaneous injection (the highest dose tested) safely produced an average 24% drop from baseline body weight.

Among 281 randomized people with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes, the same dose of retatrutide produced a nearly 17% cut in weight from baseline after 36 weeks of treatment.

Never Before Seen Weight Loss

Dr Ania M. Jastreboff

“I have never seen weight loss at this level” after nearly 1 year of treatment, said Ania M. Jastreboff, MD, PhD, who led the obesity study, during a press briefing here at the American Diabetes Association (ADA) 83rd Scientific Sessions.

The average weight loss by study participants taking high-dose retatrutide in the two studies “is really impressive, way beyond my wildest dreams,” commented [NAME], MBChB, PhD, an obesity and diabetes researcher at University College Dublin, Ireland, who was not involved with the retatrutide studies.

And [NAME], MD, chief scientific and medical officer of the ADA, called the results “stunning,” and added, “we are now witnessing the first triple-hormone combination being highly effective for not only weight loss but liver disease and diabetes.”

A prespecified subgroup analysis of the obesity study showed that at both 8-mg and 12-mg weekly doses, 24 weeks of retatrutide produced complete resolution of excess liver fat (hepatic steatosis) in about 80% of the people eligible for the analysis (those with at least 10% of their liver volume as fat at study entry); that figure increased to about 90% of people on these doses after 48 weeks, [NAME], MD, reported during a separate presentation at the meeting.

Adding Glucagon Agonism Ups Liver-Fat Clearance

“When you add glucagon activity,” one of the three agonist actions of retatrutide, “liver-fat clearance goes up tremendously,” said [NAME], who is director of the Obesity, Metabolism and Nutrition Institute at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston.

New Oral GLP-1 Agonist for Obesity, Type 2 Diabetes (medscape.com)

SAN DIEGO – Orforglipron, Eli Lilly’s investigational oral daily nonpeptide glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) agonist that can be taken with or without food, appears comparable with other injectable and oral agents in the class for treating obesity and type 2 diabetes, suggest two new phase 2 studies.

Currently approved GLP-1 agonists for type 2 diabetes and/or obesity are peptide-based and given by subcutaneous injection or orally. No oral GLP-1 agonists are currently approved for obesity, and only one, oral semaglutide (Rybelsus, Novo Nordisk), is approved for type 2 diabetes.

Oral semaglutide is formulated with an ingredient that helps protect it from degradation and enhances gastric absorption. To maximize absorption and efficacy, patients are advised to take it in the fasting state and not to eat or drink anything for at least 30 minutes after. Nevertheless, the bioavailability of orally ingested semaglutide is only 1% or less.

Orforglipron, in contrast, is a small molecule that isn’t a peptide, so it isn’t degraded in the gastrointestinal tract, [NAME], MD, lead author of the phase 2 trial in type 2 diabetes, told Medscape Medical News.

“It’s a chemical, a small molecule that also acts on the GLP-1 receptor, but because it’s not a protein it’s not degraded by enzymes. It’s like any other pill. Earlier pharmacokinetic studies have shown that taking it with or without food doesn’t make a difference,” said [NAME], who is principal investigator at Velocity Clinical Research, Westlake, California.

The results of the phase 2 trial of orforglipron in the treatment of adults with overweight or obesity were presented here June 23 at the American Diabetes Association (ADA) 83rd Scientific Sessions, and the findings were simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

The type 2 diabetes data were also presented, as a poster, at the ADA meeting, and simultaneously published in The Lancet.

Asked to comment, moderator of the session during which the obesity study was presented, [NAME], MD, DrPH, told Medscape Medical News: “I think the findings are exciting. It is a formulation that patients might be able to tolerate much more, in terms of not having these very strict restrictions on how to take [oral semaglutide]. It’s very cumbersome. They have to be fasting. They have to wait to eat.”

Of course, orforglipron must go through much further testing, noted [NAME], associate professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts. “The results that were shown were promising. We’ll see more as new phases are moving forward in phase 3 and so forth.”

Beyond Dosing Convenience: Possibility for Improved Access

The advantages of this novel nonpeptide GLP-1 agonist drug class — others are in earlier stages of development — could extend beyond just more convenient dosing, [NAME], MD, PharmD, lead author of the obesity study, told Medscape Medical News.

title: MK-677 (Ibutamoren) non-peptide oral to increase GH
content:
Ibutamoren (MK-677): Oral non-peptide* GH stimulant

Primary use: To increase the body's natural growth hormone and IGF-1 levels to support muscle growth, recovery, and overall anabolic function without injections.

Mechanism: Mimics ghrelin ("hunger hormone") to activate ghrelin receptors (GHS-R1a), which signals the hypothalamus and pituitary to increase natural GH pulse release; the liver then produces more IGF-1, leading to an increase in protein synthesis and a reduction in muscle breakdown.

Typical dosing used in research and practice is ~10–25 mg once daily, usually taken in the evening (or split), with many starting at ~10 mg to assess tolerance and adjusting based on response.

Notes: MK-677 is an oral compound that increases your body's growth hormone by mimicking a hunger signal. That can help with recovery, muscle maintenance, and sleep—but it also makes you hungrier and can affect blood sugar, so it's not a shortcut unless everything else is dialed in, and human results vary and are largely based on anecdotes. MK-677 is not FDA approved and is classified as a research compound.

*1 Ibutamoren (MK-677) is a small-molecule, non-peptide compound, specifically an orally active ghrelin receptor (GHS-R1a) agonist. It's a synthetic, drug-like molecule, not a chain of amino acids like peptides, designed to bind the ghrelin receptor and stimulate GH release. Its small-molecule structure is what allows it to be taken orally and remain stable in the body. Therefore, MK-677 works like a drug, not a peptide—so you can take it orally and it still activates the GH pathway effectively.

title: TB 500 info
content:
TB-500

TB-500 is a synthetic fragment of Thymosin Beta-4 (TB4), a naturally occurring protein found throughout the body. It promotes cellular migration and tissue remodeling. Because TB-500 effects appear systemic rather than localized, unlike BPC-157, injection location is generally not injury-site-specific in determining where healing occurs—that is, TB-500 is typically used as a whole-body recovery peptide rather than a site-specific peptide. If using it for acute injury support, the duration is generally 4–8 weeks. For significant tendon/ligament injuries, 8–12 weeks may be appropriate, with a tapering in the final 2–4 weeks.

Goal/primary use: support tissue repair, recovery, and reduced inflammation—commonly used for healing injuries or improving mobility, including:
• Soft tissue injury support; tendon and ligament recovery; muscle strain recovery
• Mobility and flexibility support; exercise recovery enhancement; general tissue healing

Mechanism*: enhances actin polymerization, increases angiogenesis, and promotes cell migration, accelerating wound repair and reducing fibrosis.

Dose
First 8 weeks: 2.5 mg twice weekly
Week 9–12: 2.5 mg once weekly
Week 13: off unless maintenance is warranted
2–5 mg every few weeks is often used as maintenance.

Injection site: the abdomen is typically the easiest and most commonly used, but the thigh and buttocks areas are also used. This is based on practitioner preference, since efficacy is not site-specific.

Notes
Always complete nutrition programming (including longevity-supporting supplementation), sleep, load management, and rehab first—all of which you have done.
TB-500 is not FDA-approved for human therapeutic use but is commonly used safely.
Human data are limited; most mechanistic evidence comes from animal models, but empirical (practical human experience) is strong, favoring safe results.
Because peptides mimic natural substances, when they are metabolized in the body, their constituent AAs can be recycled with little to no stress on organs or metabolism, unlike most drugs.

*Purported mechanisms: increases cellular migration to damaged tissue; promotes angiogenesis (new blood vessel formation); supports tissue remodeling and repair; regulates inflammation during healing; enhances actin regulation within cells, which is important for cell movement and repair processes.

TB-500 is a synthetic fragment of Thymosin Beta-4 (TB4), a naturally occurring protein found throughout the body. It promotes cellular migration and tissue remodeling.

Since you will be using it for a specific injury area, BPC-157 will be injected locally (site-specific) and dosed with the goal of healing the local tissue damage/irritation. It will be used for 5 weeks, followed by a 2-week tapering-off period. Injections have superior results compared to oral administration. The latter only exists because the compound is unusually stable in gastric juice.

Site-specific injections (unlike systemic injections) are normal for musculoskeletal injuries. The injection is near the injury for greater localized effects, although there is still an overall accelerated body recovery effect that also helps overcome the age-related slower exercise/activity recovery.

Goal: localized tissue repair and support and general whole-body recovery enhancement through:
  Modulating growth pathways, especially vascular endothelial growth factors, stimulating the formation of new blood vessels (angiogenesis)
  Enhancing fibroblast (cells necessary for tissue health and crucial for repair) migration and collagen synthesis to repair tissue
  Nitric oxide signaling modulation

Dose
First 5 weeks: 500 mcg per day
Week 6: 250 mcg per day
Week 7: 250 mcg 2 times evenly spread, such as Monday and Thursday
Week 8: off until further notice

Recommended injection site: near the injured area (not into it if it’s structural).

Notes
Always complete nutrition programming (including longevity-supporting supplementation), sleep, load management, and rehab first—all of which you have done.
BPC-157 is not FDA-approved for human therapeutic use but is commonly used safely.
Human data are limited; most mechanistic evidence comes from animal models, but empirical (practical human experience) is strong, favoring safe results.
Because peptides mimic natural substances, when they are metabolized in the body, their constituent AAs can be recycled with little to no stress on organs or metabolism, unlike most drugs.

How TB-500 Is Typically Used

1️⃣ Systemic (Non-Site-Specific) Use
This is the most common application.

Used For:
• Soft tissue injury support; tendon and ligament recovery; muscle strain recovery
• Mobility and flexibility support; exercise recovery enhancement; general tissue healing

Rationale:
TB-500 is a synthetic fragment of Thymosin Beta-4 (TB4), a naturally occurring protein found throughout the body. It promotes cellular migration and tissue remodeling. Because effects appear systemic rather than localized, unlike BPC-157, injection location is generally not injury-site-specific in determining where healing occurs—that is, TB-500 is typically used as a whole-body recovery peptide rather than a site-specific peptide.

Typical Injection Frequency

Loading Phase (Most Common)
• 2–2.5 mg twice weekly
or
• 4–5 mg once weekly
for approximately 4–6 weeks.

Maintenance Phase
• 2–5 mg every 1–4 weeks
Depending on goals and practitioner preference.

Because TB-500 has a relatively long half-life compared with many peptides, daily injections are generally unnecessary.

Commonly Cited Dose Ranges
These reflect commonly used clinical and performance-oriented protocols, not trainer-directed recommendations.

Loading Protocol
• 4–10 mg per week total
Typically divided into:
o 2 mg twice weekly
or
o 2.5 mg twice weekly

Maintenance Protocol
• 2–5 mg monthly
or
• 2–5 mg every few weeks
Depending on injury status and activity level.

Higher doses have been used experimentally, but human safety and efficacy data remain limited.

Typical Duration of Use

Acute Injury Support
• 4–8 weeks is most common

Significant Tendon/Ligament Injuries
• 8–12 weeks may be utilized

Long-Term Maintenance
• Some individuals use periodic maintenance dosing for several months

TB-500 is generally viewed as a medium-term recovery peptide rather than a permanent therapy.

What TB-500 Is Commonly Used For
• Tendon injury recovery
• Ligament injury support
• Muscle strain recovery
• Joint mobility support
• Exercise recovery enhancement
• Soft tissue healing support
• Post-surgical recovery support
• Reduction of movement limitations following injury

The strongest interest in TB-500 centers around connective tissue healing and tissue remodeling.

Mechanism of Action (Trainer-Appropriate Depth)
TB-500 appears to work by:
• Increasing cellular migration to damaged tissue
• Promoting angiogenesis (new blood vessel formation)
• Supporting tissue remodeling and repair
• Regulating inflammation during healing
• Enhancing actin regulation within cells, which is important for cell movement and repair processes

Unlike growth hormone peptides, TB-500 does not primarily act through:
• Growth hormone elevation
• IGF-1 elevation
• Testosterone enhancement

Its primary effects appear related to tissue repair signaling and regenerative processes.

What Practitioners Commonly Observe (Real-World Use)

| Goal | Typical Outcome |
|---|---|
| Tendon recovery | Most commonly reported benefit |
| Mobility improvement | Frequently reported |
| Muscle strain recovery | Moderate support |
| Joint comfort | Variable |
| Training recovery | Moderate support |
| Performance enhancement | Indirect |

TB-500 is generally viewed as a recovery-support peptide rather than a performance-enhancing peptide.

Safety & Regulatory Notes (Important)
• TB-500 is not FDA-approved for medical treatment.
• Human clinical data remain limited.
• Most evidence comes from animal studies, laboratory research, and practitioner experience.
• Long-term safety has not been established.

Possible Side Effects Include:
o Injection site irritation
o Headache
o Fatigue
o Temporary lethargy
o Dizziness (occasionally reported)

Not Appropriate For:
o Active malignancy
o Pregnancy
o Individuals with uncontrolled medical conditions without physician oversight

Trainers should not prescribe, source, or administer TB-500.

Trainer-Friendly One-Line Explanation
"TB-500 is a recovery-focused peptide that may help support the body's natural tissue repair processes, particularly in tendons, ligaments, and other connective tissues."

Practical Trainer / Educator Takeaway
If TB-500 is discussed at all, it should be positioned as:
• Medical-provider-managed
• Recovery-focused
• Adjunctive—not foundational

Always anchor the conversation to:
• Progressive resistance training
• Appropriate rehabilitation
• Adequate protein intake
• Essential amino acid sufficiency
• Sleep quality
• Micronutrient adequacy
• Recovery management

This keeps messaging aligned with a Playspan® / Youth-Preserving framework and avoids peptide-centric overreach.

Updated Product / Formula Summary
TB-500 is a synthetic peptide based on a naturally occurring region of Thymosin Beta-4 (TB4), a protein involved in tissue repair and cellular regeneration. It is most commonly used to support recovery from tendon, ligament, muscle, and connective tissue injuries.

The most commonly utilized loading protocol is:
• 2–2.5 mg twice weekly
for 4–6 weeks
followed by:
• 2–5 mg every few weeks for maintenance

Mechanistically, TB-500 appears to support healing through enhanced cellular migration, angiogenesis, tissue remodeling, and regulation of inflammatory processes involved in recovery.

Potential benefits reported in animal studies and real-world use include:
• improved soft tissue healing,
• enhanced tendon and ligament recovery,
• improved mobility,
• reduced recovery time following injury,
• and improved connective tissue remodeling.

The most commonly reported side effects include:
• injection site irritation,
• headache,
• fatigue,
• dizziness,
• and occasional lethargy.

Unlike Tesamorelin, TB-500 does not significantly affect growth hormone or IGF-1 levels and is primarily utilized for recovery and tissue repair rather than body composition or metabolic enhancement.

No, there is no established preferred injection site for TB-500 based on the available research or common clinical practice.

Unlike BPC-157, where some practitioners intentionally inject near the injured tissue (although evidence for site-specific superiority is limited), TB-500 is generally considered a systemic peptide. The prevailing theory is that once absorbed, it circulates throughout the body and exerts its effects wherever tissue repair signaling is occurring.

Most Common Injection Sites
For subcutaneous administration, practitioners typically use:
Abdomen (most common)
Upper thigh
Love handle/flank area
Upper buttock

These sites are chosen primarily for convenience and comfort, not because they improve efficacy.

What About Injecting Near the Injury?

For TB-500:
There is little evidence that injecting near an injured tendon, ligament, or muscle provides additional benefit.
Most peptide clinics and practitioners simply administer it subcutaneously in the abdomen.
The injection location is generally viewed as irrelevant to where the peptide ultimately acts.

For BPC-157:
Many practitioners do inject near the injury site.
This practice is based largely on anecdotal experience and theoretical mechanisms rather than strong human clinical data.

Typical Wolverine Stack Example
TB-500
2.5 mg Monday
2.5 mg Thursday
Injected subcutaneously in abdomen

BPC-157
250–500 mcg daily
Often injected near the injured area (if practical and safe)

This is probably the most common real-world approach.

Practical Takeaway
If someone is using TB-500 as part of a Wolverine Stack, the abdomen is typically the easiest and most commonly used injection site. Most practitioners focus more on consistent dosing and duration than on injection location because TB-500 is generally considered a whole-body recovery peptide rather than a site-specific therapy.

title: TB-500 Peptide Program
content:
TB-500 (often used with BPC-157 depending on injury grade)

TB-500 is a synthetic fragment of Thymosin Beta-4 (TB4), a naturally occurring protein found throughout the body. It promotes cellular migration and tissue remodeling. Because TB-500 effects appear systemic rather than localized, unlike BPC-157, injection location is generally not injury-site-specific to determine where healing occurs—i.e., TB-500 is typically used as a whole-body recovery peptide rather than a site-specific peptide. If using it for acute injury support, then the duration is generally 4–8 weeks. For significant tendon/ligament injuries, 8–12 weeks may be appropriate, with a tapering in the final 2–4 weeks.

Goal/primary use: support tissue repair, recovery, and reduced inflammation—commonly used for healing injuries or improving mobility, including:
• Soft tissue injury support; tendon and ligament recovery; muscle strain recovery
• Mobility and flexibility support; exercise recovery enhancement; general tissue healing

Mechanism*: enhances actin polymerization, increases angiogenesis, and promotes cell migration, accelerating wound repair and reducing fibrosis.

Dose (may vary in syringe volume with methods of reconstitution—follow supplier directions)
First 8 weeks: 2.5 mg twice weekly
Week 9–12: 2.5 mg once weekly
Week 13: off unless maintenance is warranted
2–5 mg every few weeks is often used as a maintenance dose.

Injection site: abdomen is typically the easiest and most used, but thigh and buttocks areas are also used based on practitioner/user preference, since efficacy is not site-specific.

Notes
Always complete nutrition programming (including longevity-supporting supplementation), sleep, load management, and rehab first—all of which you have done.

TB-500 is not FDA-approved for human therapeutic use but is commonly used safely.

Human data is limited; most mechanistic evidence comes from animal models, but empirical (practical human) experience is strong, favoring safe results.

Because peptides mimic natural substances, when they are metabolized in the body, their constituent AAs can be recycled with little to no stress on organs or metabolism, unlike most drugs.

*Purported mechanisms: increases cellular migration to damaged tissue; promotes angiogenesis (new blood vessel formation); supports tissue remodeling and repair; regulates inflammation during healing; enhances actin regulation within cells, which is important for cell movement and repair processes.

title: Workout Extreme - Energy formula dosing
content:
Dosing

Caffeine’s effects on cognitive performance (alertness, vigilance, memory, etc.) are generally experienced at relatively lower doses such as .25–2 mg/lb of body weight.

Dosages that induce improvements in exercise performance range from 1.4–3 mg/lb of body weight (not to exceed 600 mg) and are taken approximately one hour pre-activity.

Except under unique circumstances, doses greater than 4.1 gm/lb of body weight deliver no further benefit.

For exercise performance, caffeine in the anhydrous form is preferred based on the ability to accurately assess and control the dosing.

CA supplementation within recommended doses is considered safe for healthy individuals.

Competitors should experiment with dosing described here during practice sessions in order to personalize their most effective protocol, including testing abstention for two to four days.

Typical Use

Adult exercisers/athletes not bothered by stimulants seeking to delay fatigue, prolong and improve performance during events:

Five (5) capsules 40–60 minutes before activity (totaling 350 mg caffeine), unless caffeine sensitive, in which case start with two (2) capsules and adjust as necessary.

Adults not bothered by stimulants, as a pre-workout or event energy enhancement supplement or as a daily pick-me-up:

Take 1–2 servings daily (2–4 tabs/day) before the event or each serving separated as desired.

Should not be taken within four (4) hours of other products containing stimulants (especially caffeine), such as coffee, energy drinks, etc., or mixed with other stimulants. Do not use at least 5 hours before bed or with other stimulants.

Short- to long-event-duration/endurance activities (running, cycling, etc.):

Five (5) capsules 40–60 minutes before activity (totaling 350 mg caffeine), unless caffeine sensitive, in which case start with two (2) capsules and adjust as necessary; or use 1.4 to 3 mg/lb of body weight (not to exceed 600 mg) 40–60 minutes before activity.

If competing, experiment to achieve the proper dose and abstain from all caffeine, including WorkoutExtreme, two to four days before competition.

Intermittent athletes, such as football, baseball, soccer, hockey, rugby, swimming, etc.:

Five (5) capsules 40–60 minutes before activity (totaling 350 mg caffeine), unless caffeine sensitive, in which case start with two (2) capsules and adjust as necessary.

Any adult not bothered by stimulants, as a pre-workout or event energy enhancement supplement or as a daily pick-me-up: Take as directed.

If using regularly, it is recommended to cycle use three weeks on and at least one week off, or use only as needed before activities.

Should not be taken within four (4) hours of other products containing stimulants (especially caffeine), such as coffee, energy drinks, etc., or mixed with other stimulants.

title: Does dotFIT have any research on the attached 2008 New England Journal of Medicine study about alternatives to low-fat diets, such as Mediterranean diets?
content:
Hi [CUSTOMER],

The bottom line:

Calories count most in weight loss, but picking the foods that make up those calories that make you feel best is the key—pick the right ones for you personally and you will burn more calories (see attached “Calorie Is a Calorie” article).

The studies attached give the latest take on diet makeup and weight loss. Basically, it all comes out the same long term, but the goal is to do something you can sustain because, long term, weight regain is generally seen and maybe more so for very high-protein dieters (see “Macro Comp” study attached).

Faster weight loss occurs with higher protein, and protein is more satiating—at least in the short term.

The Mediterranean diet is probably one of the healthiest since it contains good fats and carbs with lean proteins—and that’s why we have one for everyone in our program.

Below are some related Q&A from our Fitness Vault (click on the links or visit the entire section of Fit-Pro Q&As):

Is the high-protein/low-carbohydrate diet best? Why?

What can we do to keep people motivated and break the weight loss and gain cycle permanently?

35. Why are so many people still so carb-cautious?

Only because they don’t know the difference between good and bad carbs, and carbs overall are not as important, from an energy supply standpoint, for the average adult as they are for athletes or active exercisers. From a health standpoint, carbs such as fruits, vegetables, and whole grains are very important and should make up 40–60% of the diet, depending on your activity levels. Unfortunately, refined grains/foods and added sugars are also carbohydrates, generally less healthy and considered contributors to weight gain when it’s actually the calories causing the weight gain—they just happen to be supplied in lousy food choices. So the message to stay away from carbs is to stay away from the bad carbs, not the good, but the average person doesn’t hear that—it’s just easier to be carb-conscious all the way around.

And finally, most people still don’t grasp the fact that total daily calories in and out are what count, NOT carbs!

Diet Monitoring & Adjustments for Body-Fat Reduction

Program Algorithms

Adjustments:

Measurable or visual reduction in body fat and/or weight proceeds in a consistent manner, e.g., a decrease in circumference inches and/or the desired average decrease in body fat per week or biweekly.

If progress stops or slows dramatically, use one or a combination of adjustments to restart the process:

- Increase daily activities (e.g., daily steps or other non-athletic/exercise activities).
- Standing and pacing burns 1.5–2 times more calories than sitting for the same period.
- There are approximately 2,000–2,500 steps (depending on stride length) in a mile. Walking 2,000 steps will burn approximately 75–150 more calories (depending on individual size) than sitting for the same time, takes approximately 20–30 minutes, and can be done anywhere, even in the office, while on the phone, or watching TV.
- Increase cardio workout time and/or intensity and include interval training if necessary.
- Example: If doing 30 minutes 5 days per week, go to 45 minutes and add interval work within the time frame.
- Decrease food intake approximately 200–300 calories per day or remove a small portion (carbohydrates/fats) of the largest meal other than the pre-workout meal (incorporate 3 days low/1 high as necessary).
- Add dietary support beyond baseline as necessary (thermogenic, energy partitioning, appetite control, etc.).

Repeat the process any time body fat is stable for one or two weeks. Always remember, if you are supplementing properly and you stop losing fat, you need to eat less, move/burn more, or use a combination of the two, regardless of what you read or hear from others. As you lower calorie intake, make sure your protein intake stays at or above 1 g per pound of body weight to protect LBM.

title: Statin side-efffects and duration
content:
What are the common side effects of statins, and do they last long or can they be overcome over time?

Statins are among the most extensively studied medications in medicine. They are very effective at lowering LDL cholesterol and reducing the risk of heart attack and stroke. Most people tolerate them well, but about 5–10% of patients in randomized clinical trials report muscle-related symptoms, while in everyday clinical practice the reported rate is higher (10–20%), partly because many aches and pains are incorrectly attributed to statins.

**Common side effects**

| Side Effect | Approximate Frequency | Usually Temporary? |
|---|---|---|
| Muscle aches, soreness, stiffness | Most common | Often yes |
| Muscle weakness | Less common | Often improves with adjustments |
| Fatigue | Uncommon | May improve |
| Mild elevation in liver enzymes | 1–3% | Usually resolves or stabilizes |
| Mild increase in blood glucose | Small increase | Persists but generally outweighed by cardiovascular benefit |
| Digestive upset (gas, nausea, constipation) | Uncommon | Often resolves within weeks |
| Headache | Uncommon | Usually temporary |

**Rare but important side effects**

Severe muscle injury (rhabdomyolysis): approximately 1–3 per 100,000 patient-years

Significant liver injury: extremely rare

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy: very rare (an autoimmune condition that usually does not improve simply by stopping the drug)

**Do muscle side effects go away?**

In many people, yes.

There are several common scenarios:

1. **The body adapts**

Many people experience mild muscle soreness during the first few weeks that gradually disappears over 2–8 weeks while continuing therapy.

2. **Changing the dose works**

Lowering the dose often eliminates symptoms while still providing meaningful LDL reduction.

3. **Switching statins works**

This is surprisingly successful.

For example:

Simvastatin → Rosuvastatin

Atorvastatin → Pravastatin

Atorvastatin → Pitavastatin

Many patients who cannot tolerate one statin tolerate another very well.

4. **Taking it less frequently**

Long-acting statins such as rosuvastatin can often be taken:

every other day

three times weekly

while still lowering LDL substantially.

**Which statins are least likely to cause muscle problems?**

These generally have the best reputation for tolerability:

Pravastatin

Rosuvastatin (despite being potent, many patients tolerate it well)

Pitavastatin

These are less likely to enter skeletal muscle than some older statins.

**Who is more likely to develop side effects?**

Risk increases with:

Age >75

Female sex

Low body weight

Kidney disease

Liver disease

Untreated hypothyroidism

Vitamin D deficiency

Heavy alcohol intake

High-dose statin therapy

Drug interactions (certain antibiotics, antifungals, calcium channel blockers, etc.)

**Can supplements help?**

Evidence is mixed.

**Coenzyme Q10**

Statins lower CoQ10 levels.

Some studies show reduced muscle symptoms.

Other studies show little benefit.

Overall, the evidence is inconsistent, but CoQ10 is generally well tolerated.

**Vitamin D**

If a person is deficient, correcting the deficiency may improve muscle symptoms.

**Creatine**

A few small studies suggest creatine may reduce statin-associated muscle symptoms because statins can impair muscle energy metabolism. However, the evidence is still preliminary, and creatine is not a standard recommendation specifically for statin intolerance.

**If side effects occur**

Current expert practice is generally:

Stop the statin temporarily to see if symptoms resolve.

Rule out other causes (exercise, thyroid disease, vitamin D deficiency, arthritis, etc.).

Restart the same statin at a lower dose or switch to another statin.

If symptoms recur, try a different statin or intermittent dosing.

If statins truly cannot be tolerated, consider alternatives such as ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, or PCSK9 inhibitors, depending on cardiovascular risk.

**Practical takeaway**

Most people (80–90%) tolerate statins without significant problems.

The most common side effect is muscle aches, which are usually mild and reversible.

Many symptoms improve within a few weeks as the body adapts or after changing the dose or switching to a different statin.

True permanent muscle injury from statins is very uncommon.

If side effects develop, it's usually possible to find an effective regimen rather than abandoning cholesterol treatment altogether.

Given the types of nutrition and supplement discussions we've had previously, I can also prepare a trainer/practitioner guide that summarizes the evidence on minimizing statin side effects through nutrition, exercise, CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D optimization, and appropriate statin selection.

title: Calories burned by body part
content:
Here’s the breakdown based on metabolic studies:

Resting Energy Expenditure per Tissue Type

| Tissue Type | Approx. Calories Burned per Pound per Day | Relative Activity |
|---|---:|---|
| Skeletal Muscle | ~6 kcal/lb/day | Moderate |
| Liver | ~90 kcal/lb/day | Very high |
| Brain | ~110 kcal/lb/day | Extremely high |
| Heart | ~200 kcal/lb/day | Extremely high |
| Kidneys | ~200 kcal/lb/day | Extremely high |
| Adipose Tissue (Fat) | ~2 kcal/lb/day | Very low |

Explanation

Adipose tissue is mostly energy storage, not an active tissue like muscle. However, it does have some metabolic cost—mostly from maintaining fat cell integrity, hormone signaling (like leptin and adiponectin), and low-level turnover of triglycerides.

So, for example:
A person with 30 lb of fat would burn roughly 60 kcal/day from that fat mass.
In contrast, 30 lb of muscle would burn around 180 kcal/day.

Key Takeaway

Fat is metabolically active, but only about one-third as much as muscle and a fraction of the activity of organs.
The main determinant of your resting metabolic rate (RMR) is your lean body mass (LBM), not fat mass.

title: Peptide strips vs injections
content:
What is the general scientific consensus on the efficacy of delivering peptides through strips that use the buccal cavity for absorption, and are there any studies that support this delivery system?

Worked for 16s

General scientific consensus

Buccal delivery of peptides is scientifically plausible, but ordinary dissolving strips should not be assumed to deliver a therapeutically meaningful or reliable dose. The buccal cavity avoids stomach acid, intestinal enzymes, and some first-pass liver metabolism. However, the cheek lining remains an effective biological barrier, particularly against molecules that are relatively large, water-soluble, and electrically charged—which describes most therapeutic peptides. Reviews consistently identify low permeability, enzymatic degradation in saliva and mucosal tissue, short contact time, swallowing of the dose, and substantial person-to-person variability as major obstacles.

Therefore, the consensus is closer to:

Buccal peptide delivery is a promising drug-delivery research platform, but it is not a generally validated substitute for injection unless the specific peptide and finished formulation have demonstrated human pharmacokinetics and clinical efficacy.

A strip can dissolve in the mouth without the peptide actually crossing the mucosa. Much of the dissolved material may simply be swallowed and then degraded.

What is needed for a strip to work?

Successful formulations generally require more than putting peptide powder into a dissolvable film. Research systems often combine several technologies:

- A mucoadhesive polymer that keeps the drug against the cheek.
- A permeation enhancer, such as a surfactant, bile salt, fatty-acid derivative, cyclodextrin, chitosan, or cell-penetrating peptide.
- Protection from enzymatic degradation.
- Precise control of peptide stability, concentration, film dissolution, pH, and contact time.
- Sometimes nanoparticles, liposomes, chemical peptide modification, or directional films that prevent drug loss into saliva.

Even with these measures, exposure is often low or variable.

Are there supporting studies?

Yes, but most support the concept rather than proving that currently marketed wellness strips work.

Insulin

Insulin is the most studied example. A small proof-of-concept human study of an oral/buccal insulin spray reported reductions in post-meal glucose, demonstrating that some biologically active insulin could be delivered through the oral cavity. However, results with buccal insulin systems have generally shown variable absorption, and no conventional insulin cheek strip has become an established replacement for injected insulin.

More recent insulin research frequently involves sophisticated carriers or cell-penetrating peptides rather than a simple dissolving strip. For example, a 2020 study found improved buccal insulin transport using a specialized cell-penetrating-peptide system, but this was preclinical formulation research—not proof that an ordinary retail strip produces equivalent systemic exposure in humans.

Calcitonin

Salmon calcitonin has also been investigated because it is a potent peptide active at comparatively small doses. Studies using penetratin-conjugated liposomes have demonstrated improved buccal permeation, but the evidence has largely been in vitro or ex vivo, rather than large clinical outcome trials.

Other peptides

Laboratory and animal research has examined buccal delivery of insulin, calcitonin, TRH, and other peptides, often showing that absorption can be increased using penetration enhancers. These findings establish biological feasibility, but they cannot automatically be extrapolated to BPC-157, CJC-1295, ipamorelin, TB-500, sermorelin, or similar wellness peptides.

Regarding BPC-157, CJC-1295, ipamorelin, and similar strips

I could not find credible published human pharmacokinetic trials demonstrating that commercially marketed buccal strips containing these peptides produce:

- Predictable blood concentrations;
- A stated percentage of absolute bioavailability;
- Comparable exposure to injection; or
- Clinically meaningful outcomes.

Claims such as “90% or 92% bioavailability” should be treated cautiously unless the seller can provide a peer-reviewed human crossover study comparing the finished strip with an intravenous or subcutaneous reference product. A company’s dissolution test, ingredient assay, testimonial, or general research on buccal technology does not establish systemic bioavailability for its product.

This concern is separate from whether the peptide itself works. For several commonly marketed compounds, including BPC-157, CJC-1295, and ipamorelin, the FDA has cited limited safety information, peptide-related impurity concerns, and potential immunogenicity issues.

Practical conclusion

The delivery route is credible in principle, but most peptide strips currently being promoted are ahead of the supporting clinical science. A properly engineered buccal pharmaceutical may deliver a particular peptide, especially a small and highly potent one. But efficacy is molecule- and formulation-specific; it cannot be inferred merely because a strip is placed against the cheek.

For evaluating a particular product, I would ask the manufacturer for:

- Human pharmacokinetic data on the finished strip, not just the raw peptide.
- Absolute or relative bioavailability with a clearly identified comparator.
- Blood concentration curves—Cmax, Tmax, and AUC.
- Independent potency, purity, and stability testing.
- Evidence that the dose remains intact through its expiration date.
- Published human clinical outcomes at the strip’s actual dose.

Without those data, the most scientifically accurate description is experimental and unproven, rather than demonstrably ineffective—but it should not be presented as comparable to injection.

For most adults seeking support for glucose control, body composition, insulin sensitivity, or cholesterol management, 500 mg of berberine HCl taken 2–3 times daily (1,000–1,500 mg/day total) is the dose most consistently used in clinical research and is generally considered the standard effective range.

title: Apolipoprotein B (ApoB) -full note
content:
Apolipoprotein B (ApoB) is the primary structural protein found on the surface of "bad" cholesterol particles, including LDL, VLDL, and triglycerides. Because there is exactly one ApoB protein on every atherogenic (plaque-building) particle, measuring it provides a highly accurate count of artery-clogging particles circulating in your bloodstream. [1, 2, 3]

Why ApoB Matters

While a standard cholesterol test estimates the amount of cholesterol, an ApoB test counts the number of damaging particles. [1]

The "Freeway" Analogy: A standard lipid panel is like counting the number of passengers on the freeway, while an ApoB test counts the actual number of cars.

Hidden Risks: Some people have normal LDL cholesterol levels but a high concentration of small, dense particles. In these cases, ApoB can reveal a high risk of heart disease that a standard test might miss. [1, 2, 3, 4]

When Is ApoB Testing Used?

Doctors often order an ApoB blood test (sometimes alongside a standard lipid panel) to further assess cardiovascular risk, especially for patients with:

- High triglycerides or metabolic syndrome
- Diabetes or insulin resistance
- A strong family history of heart disease
- Obesity or fatty liver disease [1, 2, 3]

To learn more about how ApoB is utilized to track cardiovascular health, visit the American Heart Association or the Cleveland Clinic.

Optimal ApoB Targets by Risk Category

Medical organizations like the National Lipid Association and the European Society of Cardiology recommend the following targets:

- Optimal / Low-Risk: <60–80 mg/dL
- Moderate Risk: <90 mg/dL
- High Risk (e.g., existing heart disease or diabetes): <80 mg/dL
- Very High Risk (e.g., recurrent cardiovascular events): <65 mg/dL [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

Average Ranges by Age and Sex

While "average" isn't necessarily "optimal" for heart health, comparing your score to population percentiles can put your numbers into perspective. Typical population ranges (in mg/dL) include: [1]

- Age < 40: 50–150 mg/dL
- Age 40–60: 60–160 mg/dL
- Age > 60: 70–170 mg/dL [1, 2, 3, 4]

Note: The general population average often sits around 100 mg/dL, but modern preventive cardiology considers this too high for ideal, long-term cardiovascular health. [1, 2]

Why the Number Matters

ApoB tracks all potentially harmful cholesterol particles (like LDL, VLDL, and Lp(a)) in your bloodstream. In younger adults, ApoB scores can serve as an indicator for cumulative lifetime cardiovascular risk. [1, 2, 3]

You can use an ApoB Percentile Calculator to see where you fall relative to the rest of the population, but it's important to discuss your specific target with your healthcare provider to account for other factors like blood pressure, genetics, and family history. [1, 2, 3]

title: Is the FirstString product with a “sell by 09/23” date safe and effective to consume if it has a sticker showing “Lot #61977 EXP 5/8/2025,” and can it be exchanged for a product with a current date?

The best buy date is generally within 2 years from production because that is what the potency is tested for and always guaranteed to be at if retested. If a manufacturer has surplus of a product such as FirstString, then it is sent back to NSF to be retested for full potency and a new best buy date is put on, again generally 2 years. Meaning, if that product wasn’t sold until that new date (in your case 5/8/25), the label/potency is still intact and proven at a retest. Freshness would be the only possible compromise after 2 tests, but the potency would still be correct, thus safety and efficacy. But because protein powders are mixed with fluids, you wouldn’t notice a difference in taste/freshness. As of note, it’s rare that we have anything in stock past the original expiration date as our inventories turn over quickly. See below for more information or reach out to [NAME] (cc’d here) if you have any more questions.

Thanks again and have a great day.

More Info

The “Expiration Dates” are basically a “best sold by date” with the product still potent. All dates are 2 years after production, only because you don’t need much more than that based on inventory turnover. But the product is still fine (safe and effective) for at least another 2 years after the date in case you have not used it in a while, and kept it sealed.

The definition of an expiration date for nutritional products such as ours is that the product must be within 10% of label claim of each ingredient on the last day, meaning it’s still at declared potency 2 years following production (only because they were tested at that milestone and all is still perfect, and generally no one carries more than a few months of inventory and the next lot has a new date that starts all over). Therefore, our pills and powders have a 2-year expiration, and are still safe and effective to use well after the date because the only issue might be that they are a little less potent than when manufactured, but that is something that would only happen well after the published date. Lipoprotein (a)

Their Lipoprotein (a) scoring is very deceptive. By using different measurements, it scares someone who is not looking into conversions (most would never do it). They also made up their own reference interval that is not consistent with current science (i.e., <75 nmol/L, which is 35 mg/dL). It’s clear that the goal is to be <50 mg/dL according to current science. “An assessment of five standard samples across a broad range of Lp(a) concentrations indicated that conversion to mg/dL can be approximated by dividing nmol/L values by 2.15 (r2 = 0.998 for linearity).” Therefore, your score of 101.8 nmol/L would equal 47.3 mg/dL, which is below the possible risk level of >50 mg/dL or 107.5 nmol/L. Moreover, even at >50 mg/dL (>107.5 nmol/L), you would have to have at least one more CVD risk factor (e.g., high cholesterol, triglycerides, blood pressure, etc.) for this to be a serious concern. You currently have no other risk factors.

Vitamin D

Note: 1.0 nmol/L = 0.4 ng/mL of 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration (25(OH)D); 1 mcg D3 = 40 IUs.

There is nothing to worry about here. Your free testosterone is perfect, and all results will vary based on the time of day you are tested. Don’t build on top of a weak foundation—something will give.

Is it a need, want, or sounds like good advice?

Unfollow “nutrition influencers” and withhold all purported anti-aging therapies until baseline + nutrition is whole.

“Natural” safe, effective discoveries will happen—but application needs context.
