title: 5-component skin & collagen program with topical CHK-Cu-Shel
content:
Skin health and youthful appearance goal — 5-component program

For the specific goal of maximizing collagen production, preserving existing collagen, and improving the appearance and quality of aging skin, a multiple-ingredient intervention may look like the one below. The important point is that they work through different mechanisms, so this isn't simply five versions of the same treatment. Mindful of this, the program should be approved, assembled, and monitored by a dermatologist; they will tell you tips and tricks for applying tretinoin.

5-component skin & collagen program

| Component | Practical use | Primary purpose | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Tretinoin / retinoid | Tretinoin 0.025–0.05% at night, beginning 2–3 nights/week and gradually progressing toward nightly use as tolerated | Stimulates new collagen, improves collagen organization, reduces collagen degradation, wrinkles, and photodamage | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 2. GHK-Cu topical | Apply once daily, potentially progressing to twice daily depending on formulation/tolerance | Signals fibroblasts and supports collagen/elastin production, extracellular-matrix remodeling, and repair | ⭐⭐⭐ |
| 3. Vitamin C topical | ~10–20% L-ascorbic acid in the morning | Antioxidant protection and an essential cofactor for collagen synthesis; helps with photodamage and pigmentation | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 4. BioCell Collagen peptides, oral | ~2–4 1,000 mg capsules daily | Collagen peptides, hyaluronic acid, and chondroitin sulfate to improve joint comfort, mobility, and recovery; enhancing skin elasticity and hydration and reducing wrinkles and fine lines | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 5. Sunscreen | Broad-spectrum SPF ≥30 every morning, preferably SPF 50 with significant outdoor exposure | Prevents UV-induced collagen breakdown and protects the gains from everything else | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |

Tretinoin deserves the central position. A systematic review of randomized trials found that topical tretinoin improves photoaging and induces new collagen formation, with treatment periods extending from several months to two years.

Morning

Cleanse → Vitamin C → GHK-Cu → moisturizer if needed → SPF 30–50

Vitamin C is particularly attractive because it isn't merely cosmetic. In a controlled facial study, topical vitamin C produced visible improvement after 12 weeks, and biopsies demonstrated increased collagen and increased type-I collagen gene expression. A systematic review likewise found improvement in wrinkled/photoaged skin, although the literature isn't strong enough to establish one universally optimal concentration.

Evening

Cleanse → tretinoin → moisturizer

Keep GHK-Cu primarily in the morning so you don't need to pile multiple active ingredients on the skin simultaneously.

For someone new to tretinoin, 0.025% 2–3 nights per week is a reasonable conservative starting approach under a dermatologist's guidance. Increase frequency gradually as the skin adapts. More irritation isn't synonymous with more collagen production.

If prescription tretinoin isn't appropriate, an OTC retinol/retinal product is an alternative, although tretinoin has the stronger clinical evidence.

Oral collagen: BioCell peptides have been shown in multiple clinical trials to improve joint and skin health, including reducing lines and wrinkles and improving skin hydration and circulation. Use 2 caps in the AM and 2 in the PM for the first 60 days, then reduce to 1 cap twice daily.

Note on GHK-Cu

GHK-Cu has a compelling mechanistic rationale for fibroblast activity, collagen/elastin production, tissue remodeling, and repair, but the clinical evidence ranks behind tretinoin and UV protection. Therefore, it would be considered an adjunct that potentially makes an already strong collagen program better, rather than the foundation of the program.

For now, I would avoid injectable GHK-Cu simply because the goal is maximum collagen. Currently, there is no good human evidence demonstrating that injecting 1–2 mg/day, for example, produces greater dermal collagen accumulation than topical GHK-Cu.

Strategy Summary:

Tretinoin → stimulates remodeling and new collagen
GHK-Cu → provides additional repair/remodeling signaling
Vitamin C → supports collagen synthesis + antioxidant protection
Collagen BioCell peptides (and daily protein) → supplies nutritional substrate/signaling
Sunscreen → prevents UV from destroying the collagen you're trying to build — don’t ignore the sunscreen!

Practical 12-month approach: run all five consistently, evaluate photographs and skin quality at baseline, 3 months, 6 months, and 12 months, and don't judge the program after a few weeks. Collagen remodeling is slow. Oral collagen trials generally show measurable changes after 8–12 weeks, while retinoid-driven dermal remodeling can continue for many months.

For a serious anti-aging skin program, think of it this way: tretinoin + daily UV protection are the non-negotiable foundation, with vitamin C, GHK-Cu, and collagen peptides layered on top.

title: Multiple injury sites and BPC injection scedule
content:
Yes — if someone is already using subcutaneous BPC-157 under medical supervision, there is no good human evidence that injecting it near each injured area is more effective than using a conventional subcutaneous site such as the abdomen. The rationale for BPC-157 is largely systemic, and animal studies have demonstrated effects at injured tissues even when BPC-157 was administered systemically.

So, between your two approaches, I would not see a scientific reason to rotate injections shoulder → shoulder → knee in an attempt to “target” each tissue. A standard SC site such as the abdomen, while rotating spots within that general area to reduce local irritation, is the simpler approach. In particular, I wouldn't inject directly into or immediately around a shoulder or knee joint without a clinician doing it; that's different from an ordinary SC injection and introduces additional anatomical/infection considerations.

The important caveat is that we simply don't have a human trial showing “local SC injection near an injury vs abdominal SC injection.” Human pharmacokinetic data for subcutaneous BPC-157 are also lacking. The published human experience remains extremely small; FDA's recent review identified only a handful of small clinical studies using other routes, and FDA still considers the human safety information inadequate.

Bottom line: if the purpose is to potentially support all three areas simultaneously, the available evidence provides no established advantage to chasing the injuries with the needle. A conventional SC site would make more pharmacologic sense if BPC-157 does indeed produce the systemic effects suggested by the animal literature. But we can't currently say that either approach improves shoulder or knee healing in humans with confidence.

If you'd like, I can also look specifically at whether the research supports once-daily vs twice-daily BPC-157 when you're trying to address multiple injuries at the same time.

I looked specifically for evidence comparing once-daily versus twice-daily BPC-157, including the newer literature. The answer is fairly straightforward:

There is currently no human evidence showing that twice-daily BPC-157 is superior to once-daily administration for healing an injury—or multiple injuries. A 2026 review notes that human subcutaneous pharmacokinetics have not even been characterized, so there isn't a scientifically established SC dosing interval.

For your example of both shoulders plus a knee, there's therefore no evidence-based reason to think you need three injections, or that dividing a prescribed daily amount into two injections would make it work better at three different tissues. The animal literature suggests systemic biological effects across tendon, ligament, muscle, and bone injury models, but translating that into a human dosing schedule is still speculative.

One interesting wrinkle is that the extremely limited human IV pharmacokinetic work suggests circulating BPC-157 itself has a short half-life (<30 minutes). That might sound like an argument for twice-daily dosing, but it really isn't: biological effects can substantially outlast measurable plasma concentrations, and we don't know the SC absorption curve in humans. Thus, there's no evidence that keeping blood BPC-157 concentrations elevated longer improves healing.

So I wouldn't escalate from once to twice daily solely because there are three areas bothering you. If a clinician has prescribed a particular daily dose, I'd stick with that schedule rather than increasing injection frequency or total exposure based on the number of injuries.

There's also an important update since we've discussed BPC-157 previously: FDA held a Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee meeting in July 2026 specifically addressing BPC-157. FDA continues to emphasize that human safety information is inadequate and raises concerns about immunogenicity, peptide impurities, and API characterization.

In practical terms, I'd separate the two questions:
Injection location: no convincing evidence that shoulder/knee-targeted SC injections beat ordinary abdominal SC administration.
Frequency: no convincing evidence that twice daily beats once daily, or that multiple injuries require more frequent administration.

That makes once-daily systemic administration the simpler approach rather than trying to chase three injuries with multiple injections, assuming BPC-157 is being used under a clinician's supervision in the first place. The much bigger unknown is whether BPC-157 meaningfully accelerates human musculoskeletal healing at all; the human evidence remains very limited.

Given that you mentioned the injuries are minor, rehab/loading management is considerably better supported by human evidence than manipulating BPC-157 dose frequency or injection location.

Abstract
Background:
Whether circulating sex hormones modulate mortality and cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk in aging men is controversial.
Purpose:
To clarify associations of sex hormones with these outcomes.
Data Sources:
Systematic literature review to July 2019, with bridge searches to March 2024.
Study Selection:
Prospective cohort studies of community-dwelling men with sex steroids measured using mass spectrometry and at least 5 years of follow-up.
Data Extraction:
Independent variables were testosterone, sex hormone–binding globulin (SHBG), luteinizing hormone (LH), dihydrotestosterone (DHT), and estradiol concentrations. Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality, CVD death, and incident CVD events. Covariates included age, body mass index, marital status, alcohol consumption, smoking, physical activity, hypertension, diabetes, creatinine concentration, ratio of total to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and lipid medication use.
Data Synthesis:
Nine studies provided individual participant data (IPD) (255 830 participant-years). Eleven studies provided summary estimates (n = 24 109). Two-stage random-effects IPD meta-analyses found that men with baseline testosterone concentrations below 7.4 nmol/L (<213 ng/dL), LH concentrations above 10 IU/L, or estradiol concentrations below 5.1 pmol/L had higher all-cause mortality, and those with testosterone concentrations below 5.3 nmol/L (<153 ng/dL) had higher CVD mortality risk. Lower SHBG concentration was associated with lower all-cause mortality (median for quintile 1 [Q1] vs. Q5, 20.6 vs. 68.3 nmol/L; adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 0.85 [95% CI, 0.77 to 0.95]) and lower CVD mortality (adjusted HR, 0.81 [CI, 0.65 to 1.00]). Men with lower baseline DHT concentrations had higher risk for all-cause mortality (median for Q1 vs. Q5, 0.69 vs. 2.45 nmol/L; adjusted HR, 1.19 [CI, 1.08 to 1.30]) and CVD mortality (adjusted HR, 1.29 [CI, 1.03 to 1.61]), and risk also increased with DHT concentrations above 2.45 nmol/L. Men with DHT concentrations below 0.59 nmol/L had increased risk for incident CVD events.

title: BAC Water for Reconstitution
content:
Bacteriostatic (BAC) water is sterile, non-pyrogenic water containing 0.9% benzyl alcohol (9 mg/mL) used as a solvent. Its primary purpose is to dissolve or "reconstitute" medications or powdered substances (like lyophilized peptides) so they can be injected into the body. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

How It Works

The benzyl alcohol acts as an antimicrobial preservative. Unlike plain sterile water, which must be discarded immediately after a single use, the preservative in BAC water prevents bacteria and fungi from growing. This allows the vial to be safely punctured multiple times to draw small, precise doses over a period of up to 28 days. [1, 2, 3, 4]

Common Applications

Medication Preparation: Used to dilute or dissolve concentrated drugs for intravenous, intramuscular, or subcutaneous injection.

Peptide Research: Frequently used in scientific laboratories to reconstitute freeze-dried peptides. [1, 2, 3, 4]

Important Safety Considerations

Prescription Requirement: In the United States, BAC water for injection is typically a prescription-only product and is not available over the counter. [1]

Expiration: Once a vial of BAC water is unsealed and punctured, it generally loses its effectiveness and should be discarded within 28 days. [1, 2]

Contamination: To maintain sterility, the rubber stopper on the vial must always be wiped with an alcohol swab prior to inserting a needle. [1, 2]

Not for Neonates: BAC water is contraindicated for use in newborns due to the toxicity of the benzyl alcohol preservative. [1]

Partial answer to a question from a confused consumer who said sucralose was harmful:

Of course, there is nothing harmful about sucralose in proper amounts, or we would not use it, like anything else. In fact, sucralose is one of the seven FDA-approved non-nutritional sweeteners (also no calories). That said, because of expanding media, there will always be confusion and financial bias around any ingredient/food product, and therefore, we make an unflavored/unsweetened creatine and other all-natural sweetened or unflavored alternatives, such as protein powders, Alln1 SuperBlend™, etc., for people’s personal preferences. Mindful, as you probably know, we are an evidence-based R&D company for fitness programming and products. Meaning, our products are Practitioner Products sold through professional channels, not available in the mass market. And why we are the largest provider of 3rd-party-tested nutrition programs and products in the sport and fitness channels, including collegiate and professional sports. As we always like to say here in the scientific community, “while we are bound to the evidence-based facts, everyone else is entitled to their own opinion,” and that is why we have the natural alternatives. A reminder, as you probably know, natural can be very harmful to many people (think peanuts, fruits, shellfish, gluten, etc.—see attached slide), which is why natural foods have warning labels. We have more adverse reactions to monk fruit and stevia (natural allergies), which are in our all-natural products, than any other product we sell. We have none in the other powders.

FAQ:
Q: Why artificial sweeteners? Not included in All Natural WheySmooth or BestPlantProtein
A: Better and healthier than added sugar and FDA-approved (Ref. Sweetener docs here.) 4, 2022 meta, ref4
Added sugars are a leading cause of disease, and this is why the government warns and sets limits. Ref2
Better taste = continued use to improve fitness results—no downside in “normal health” users
Higher nutrition per calorie/sweetness to support desired body composition
Sucralose tested best of sweeteners and sucrose in weight management. Ref
Supports blood sugar (approved for diabetics)
Decreases risk of adverse reactions common with “natural” sweeteners (honey, stevia, lactose, fruit sugar residues, etc.) 27, 28
Supports weight control versus contributor. 2, 2022 meta, and CV health
Approved for children. 1

*The FDA established an acceptable daily intake (ADI) for sucralose of 5 milligrams per kilogram (Europe is 7 and Canada 11 mg/kg) of body weight (mg/kg per day). The ADI represents an amount 100 times less than the quantity of sucralose found to be safe in research studies. For a person weighing 150 pounds (68 kg), the US ADI equates to 340 mg of sucralose—the amount found in nine cans of diet soda or more than 28 individual packets of sucralose—consumed, on average, every day over a lifetime.

1. Policy Statement from the American Academy of Pediatrics. The Use of Nonnutritive Sweeteners in Children. Pediatrics, Volume 144, number 5, November 2019: e20192765.
2. Higgins et al. A randomized controlled trial contrasting the effects of 4 low-calorie sweeteners and sucrose on body weight in adults with overweight or obesity. Am J Clin Nutr 2019;109:1288–1301.

FYI: Because of its safety, EFSA decided to expand the sweetener’s use in foods for special medical purposes for children.

Sucralose

Sucralose is also an NNS and is made from sucrose by a process that substitutes three chloride atoms for three hydroxyl groups on the sucrose molecule. Sucralose is a very versatile NNS that is 450–650 times sweeter than sucrose, possesses a pleasant sweet taste, and has a quality and time-intensity profile that is close to that of sucrose, making it a popular NNS. Sucralose has been extensively studied, with more than 110 safety studies reviewed by the FDA in approving the use of sucralose as a general-purpose sweetener for food. A primary advantage of sucralose for consumers is its exceptional stability. It retains its sweetness over a wide range of temperature and storage conditions and in solutions over time. This stability allows manufacturers to create better-tasting foods and beverages and maintain the fresh flavor. Like Ace-K, sucralose is heat-stable, meaning that it stays sweet even when used at high temperatures during baking, making it a common sugar substitute in baked goods.

The FDA established an acceptable daily intake (ADI) for sucralose of 5 milligrams per kilogram (Europe’s is 7 mg/kg and Canada’s is 11 mg/kg) of body weight (mg/kg per day).* The amount of sucralose per serving in WheySmooth is ~34 mg.

*Out of safety precautions to protect all subgroups of people, the ADI represents an amount 100 times less than the quantity of sucralose found to be safe in research studies. For a person weighing 150 pounds (68 kg), the US ADI equates to 340 mg of sucralose—the amount found in nine cans of diet soda or more than 28 individual packets of sucralose—consumed, on average, every day over a lifetime.

Carboxymethyl Cellulose

Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), or cellulose gum, is a popular non-toxic cellulose (fiber) derivative, an FDA-approved food additive, and on the generally recognized as safe list (GRAS). CMC is used in food as a viscosity modifier or thickener and to stabilize emulsions (emulsifier) in food products. CMC is used extensively in gluten-free and reduced-fat food products such as WheySmooth. Use of CMC also ensures smooth dispersion in flavor oils and improves texture and overall quality.

title: SARMs , Peptides and steroids
content:
Comparing SARMs, Peptides, and Steroids

Understanding the key differences between SARMs, peptides, and anabolic steroids can help you make informed decisions:

| Compound Type | Primary Function | Benefits | Risks |
|---|---|---|---|
| Steroids | Bind to androgen receptors (non-selective) | Extreme muscle growth, fat loss | Liver toxicity, hormone suppression, cardiovascular issues |
| SARMs | Selective androgen receptor modulators | Lean mass gains, minimal androgenic effects | Unknown long-term effects, mild suppression |
| Peptides | Stimulate GH release, healing | Recovery, growth, cognitive benefits | Injection site irritation, inconsistent sourcing |

SARMs vs. Peptides: Key Differences

While both SARMs and peptides offer promising benefits for muscle growth and recovery, they work through very different mechanisms and have distinct profiles in terms of safety, legality, and efficacy.

Mechanisms of Action

SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) are synthetic compounds that selectively bind to androgen receptors, primarily in muscle and bone tissue. This selectivity allows them to stimulate muscle hypertrophy and improve bone density without the widespread side effects typically associated with anabolic steroids.

“SARMs act as anabolic agents in muscle and bone, showing tissue-selective effects without the negative outcomes of full androgen receptor agonists,” [NAME] et al., Therapeutic Advances in Endocrinology and Metabolism.

Peptides are naturally occurring amino acid chains that influence hormonal signaling, promote growth hormone release, and accelerate tissue repair through various biological pathways.

“Growth hormone–releasing peptides such as GHRP-6 and Ipamorelin stimulate endogenous GH release without significantly affecting cortisol or prolactin levels,” [NAME] et al., Endocrine Reviews.

Safety Profiles and Side Effects of SARMs vs. Peptides

One of the most important differences between SARMs and peptides is their side effect profile:

SARMs, while generally safer than anabolic steroids, still carry risks. These may include:

- Testosterone suppression
- Liver toxicity
- Altered lipid profiles (reduced HDL cholesterol)

“SARM usage can suppress luteinizing hormone (LH) and reduce testosterone, impacting hormonal balance,” [NAME] et al., Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism.

Peptides, being biologically native to the body, are typically associated with fewer and milder side effects, such as:

- Injection site irritation
- Headaches
- Water retention

However, product purity and proper sourcing are essential to avoid complications.

“Low-quality peptides or improper dosing can lead to unpredictable biological responses,” [NAME] et al., Current Pharmaceutical Design.

Legal Status and Availability

SARMs are classified as research chemicals in the U.S. and are not approved for human consumption by the FDA. They are banned by WADA for use in competitive sports.

“SARMs are unapproved for human use, and their marketing as dietary supplements violates the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act,” FDA, Drug Safety Communication.

Peptides, on the other hand, have a more nuanced regulatory status. Some are:

- Available via prescription (e.g., Sermorelin, CJC-1295)
- Sold as research chemicals
- Included in anti-aging and regenerative medicine protocols

Understanding these distinctions is key to staying within legal boundaries and optimizing outcomes.

Effectiveness of SARMs for Muscle Growth and Recovery

SARMs are widely known for their muscle-building potency. Compounds like Ostarine (MK-2866) and Ligandrol (LGD-4033) have been shown to enhance lean body mass, strength, and endurance.

“In clinical trials, LGD-4033 significantly increased lean body mass without adverse androgenic effects,” [NAME] et al., Journal of the American Geriatrics Society.

Additional benefits include:

- Faster recovery
- Reduced muscle soreness
- Greater training frequency

SARMs like RAD-140 have demonstrated powerful anabolic effects, though results vary based on individual response, dosage, and compound specificity.

⚠️ Note: Long-term safety remains unknown due to a lack of extensive human studies.

Effectiveness of Peptides for Muscle Growth and Recovery

Peptides help stimulate natural growth hormone release, which supports:

- Muscle protein synthesis
- Fat oxidation
- Tissue repair

Examples:

Ipamorelin and GHRP-6 boost GH without excess cortisol or prolactin.

BPC-157 and TB-500 support tendon and ligament healing, inflammation reduction, and accelerated regeneration.

“BPC-157 enhances healing of tendons and ligaments by promoting angiogenesis and fibroblast activity,” [NAME] et al., Journal of Orthopaedic Research.

Other peptides, such as CJC-1295 and Sermorelin, can:

- Improve sleep
- Support anti-aging
- Enhance cognitive function

However, results depend on adherence, training intensity, and nutritional support.

Understanding the Side Effects and Legal Risks of SARMs and Peptides

Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators (SARMs) and therapeutic peptides have surged in popularity among fitness enthusiasts and bodybuilders for their muscle-building and recovery-enhancing potential. However, their use comes with important considerations. From hormonal suppression to legal gray areas, understanding the full scope of SARMs and peptides is essential for anyone considering their use.

Potential Side Effects and Risks of SARMs

SARMs are engineered to selectively bind to androgen receptors in muscle and bone tissue, offering a more targeted anabolic effect than traditional steroids. Despite their benefits, SARMs are not without side effects.

1. Testosterone Suppression

SARMs mimic testosterone activity in the body. As a result, natural testosterone production may downregulate in response to elevated androgen levels.

“SARMs have been shown to suppress endogenous testosterone production, which can result in fatigue, reduced libido, and other symptoms of hypogonadism”
— [NAME], Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism

Post-cycle therapy (PCT) is often necessary to help restore natural hormonal function after a SARMs cycle.

2. Liver Toxicity

Though SARMs are non-steroidal, some compounds—especially oral SARMs like Ligandrol (LGD-4033) or Ostarine (MK-2866)—can elevate liver enzymes and stress hepatic function.

“Increased liver enzyme levels were observed in clinical trials, raising concern for hepatotoxicity with long-term use of SARMs”
— [NAME] et al., Therapeutic Advances in Endocrinology and Metabolism

3. Cardiovascular Health

SARMs may unfavorably impact lipid profiles by lowering HDL (good cholesterol) and raising LDL (bad cholesterol), contributing to cardiovascular risk.

“SARMs significantly decreased HDL cholesterol, suggesting a potential for adverse cardiovascular events”
— [NAME] et al., JAMA

Potential Side Effects and Risks of Peptides

Peptides are short chains of amino acids that play regulatory roles in many physiological processes. Peptides like BPC-157 and Ipamorelin are known for tissue repair and growth hormone stimulation, respectively.

1. Injection Site Reactions and Water Retention

Since most peptides are administered subcutaneously, common side effects include redness, swelling, or discomfort at the injection site. Others like growth hormone secretagogues may cause bloating or mild edema.

“Some peptide users report water retention, headaches, or localized reactions, particularly with repeated dosing”
— [NAME], Peptides: Chemistry and Biology

2. Questionable Purity and Product Safety

The unregulated market is saturated with counterfeit peptides. Without third-party testing, users may unknowingly inject harmful or ineffective substances.

“Analysis of peptide products sold online found widespread discrepancies in content, potency, and purity”
— [NAME] et al., Drug Testing and Analysis

Legal Status and Regulation of SARMs and Peptides

Understanding the legality of these compounds is critical for avoiding penalties and health risks.

1. SARMs: Controlled Yet Available

In the U.S., SARMs are classified as research chemicals and are not approved for human consumption by the FDA. Yet, they’re easily accessible online.

“The FDA has issued warnings against SARMs being marketed as dietary supplements due to their potential for serious health risks”
— FDA, Consumer Update

Most sports organizations, including the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), have banned SARMs for athletes.

2. Peptides: A Legal Gray Area

Peptides vary in legality based on type and intended use. While peptides like Sermorelin and CJC-1295 can be prescribed legally, many others are sold online under the “research chemical” label.

“Legality often hinges on how peptides are marketed—therapeutic use may require a prescription, while others fall into a regulatory gap”
— [NAME], Regulatory Affairs Journal

Are SARMs or Peptides Better for Muscle Growth?

When it comes to hypertrophy and performance, the anabolic response of SARMs is generally more immediate and potent, though also riskier.

SARMs bind directly to androgen receptors, promoting rapid muscle growth and strength gains.

Peptides, like Ipamorelin or GHRP-6, act more indirectly by stimulating natural growth hormone release.

For long-term sustainability and safety, many athletes prefer peptides as part of a slower, hormone-supportive regimen. SARMs may be favored during short bulking phases but require meticulous post-cycle planning.

Conclusion: SARMs vs. Peptides — What Should You Choose?

Choosing between SARMs and peptides depends on your risk tolerance, goals, and access to quality products and medical oversight.

SARMs offer fast, noticeable muscle and strength gains, but carry higher risks of hormonal disruption, liver strain, and lipid imbalance.

Peptides offer a more physiological approach to recovery and growth, supporting tissue repair and hormone function with generally fewer severe side effects.

“Careful consideration of the pharmacological profile and side effects of both SARMs and peptides is essential before use”
— [NAME], Frontiers in Pharmacology

Ultimately, whichever route you choose, ensure:

- You consult a qualified healthcare provider.
- You obtain products from third-party-tested and verified suppliers.
- You follow a structured training and recovery protocol to maximize benefits and minimize harm.

title: Peptide Cheat sheet
content:
Peptide Cheat Sheet (Quick Summary + Mechanism)

1. TB-500 (Thymosin Beta-4 Fragment)
Primary Use: Supports tissue repair, recovery, and reduced inflammation—commonly used for healing injuries or improving mobility.
Mechanism: Enhances actin polymerization, increases angiogenesis, and promotes cell migration, accelerating wound repair and reducing fibrosis.

2. BPC-157
Primary Use: Promotes healing of muscles, tendons, ligaments, gut lining, and nerves.
Mechanism: Modulates growth pathways (VEGF, NO), enhances fibroblast migration, and accelerates angiogenesis and collagen synthesis to repair tissue.

3. MOTS-C
Primary Use: Improves mitochondrial efficiency, energy production, and metabolic flexibility (fat oxidation, insulin sensitivity).
Mechanism: A mitochondrial-derived peptide that activates AMPK, enhances glucose uptake, and improves metabolic homeostasis under cellular stress.

4. SS-31 (Elamipretide)
Primary Use: Protects the mitochondria, improves energy production, and reduces oxidative stress—investigated for heart, muscle, and age-related disorders.
Mechanism: Selectively binds cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane, stabilizing the ETC and reducing ROS leakage to boost ATP output.

5. AOD-9604 (Fragment of HGH 176-191)
Primary Use: Promotes fat loss without raising IGF-1 or causing GH-like systemic effects; often positioned for “stubborn fat” reduction.
Mechanism: Stimulates lipolysis and inhibits lipogenesis through the β-adrenergic and adenylate cyclase–cAMP pathways, independent of GH receptor activation.

6. Epitalon (Epithalamin / Epithalon)
Primary Use: Supports sleep, circadian rhythm, and theoretical anti-aging effects.
Mechanism: Upregulates telomerase activity, supports pineal gland signaling, and helps regulate melatonin secretion and circadian timing.

7. Kisspeptin-10 / Kisspeptin-54
Primary Use: Enhances natural reproductive hormone output—often used for improving LH/FSH production, fertility, and libido.
Mechanism: Stimulates GnRH release from the hypothalamus, which increases LH → testosterone/estrogen production along the HPG axis.

8. Sermorelin*
Primary Use: Restores the body’s ability to release GH to support recovery, body composition, and healthy aging—more subtle and long-term.*
Mechanism: Binds to GHRH receptors in the anterior pituitary to increase GH pulsatility, especially during sleep, to support anabolic signaling without suppressing natural GH production.

9. Tesamorelin
Primary Use: Increases natural growth hormone release and reduces visceral fat (FDA-approved for HIV-associated lipodystrophy). Step above Sermorelin—stronger metabolic activity, including GH signaling.*
Mechanism: Acts as a potent GHRH analog that binds GHRH receptors, increasing pulsatile GH and subsequently raising lipolysis and IGF-1 levels.

10. Ibutamoren (MK-677) Oral non-peptide GH stimulant¹
Primary Use: Increases the body’s natural growth hormone and IGF-1 levels to support muscle growth, recovery, and overall anabolic function without injections.
Mechanism: Mimics ghrelin (“hunger hormone”) to activate ghrelin receptors (GHS-R1a), which signals the hypothalamus and pituitary to increase natural GH pulse release; the liver then produces more IGF-1, leading to an increase in protein synthesis and reduction in muscle breakdown.

11. CJC-1295 (With or Without DAC)
Primary Use: Enhances natural GH/IGF-1 production for recovery, body composition improvements, and sleep quality.
Mechanism: Mimics growth hormone–releasing hormone (GHRH), amplifying GH pulse amplitude and duration—especially prolonged when DAC is included.

12. IGF-1 LR3
Primary Use: Promotes muscle growth, recovery, and nutrient partitioning through direct anabolic signaling. Often considered one of the most potent downstream mediators of growth hormone activity.
Mechanism: A modified long-acting IGF-1 analog that binds directly to IGF-1 receptors, stimulating protein synthesis, satellite cell activation, muscle tissue growth, and cellular recovery through activation of the Akt/mTOR anabolic pathway. Unlike GH secretagogues, it bypasses the pituitary and acts directly at the tissue level. (Note: Unlike Tesamorelin or Sermorelin, IGF-1 LR3 does not increase natural growth hormone production—it acts downstream of GH by directly activating IGF-1 pathways.)

* Sermorelin: A shorter-acting GHRH peptide than Tesamorelin that also stimulates GH release, but results can be less consistent and protocols vary.

¹ Ibutamoren (MK-677) is a small-molecule, non-peptide compound, specifically an orally active ghrelin receptor (GHS-R1a) agonist. It’s a synthetic, drug-like molecule, not a chain of amino acids like peptides designed to bind the ghrelin receptor and stimulate GH release. Its small-molecule structure is what allows it to be taken orally and remain stable in the body. Therefore, MK-677 works like a drug, not a peptide—so you can take it orally and it still activates the GH pathway effectively.

title: Do you recommend DIM or DHEA supplements, and can they be used together?

Thanks again, and have a great day.

More Information

Diindolylmethane (DIM), a compound commonly found in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, etc. DIM supplements are not evidence-based, meaning there is still no significant proof of their safety and effectiveness. A few clinical trials show that DIM may support healthy estrogen levels. However, DIM supplements may be harmful to some women based on individual physiology. If you are of reproductive age, estrogen is necessary to support healthy breast, bone, and endometrial tissue. If you are through menopause, DIM would have little to no benefit and, in fact, may actually lower your body's ability to keep a healthy bone density. Supplements may also interfere with certain medications, so always check with your doctor before use.

Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) is a hormone that your body naturally produces in the adrenal gland. Therefore, it is the same basic answer for DHEA, since supplemental levels can act like a drug in the body and upset the natural hormonal feedback loop.

Conclusion

The ‘expensive urine’ dismissal fails to understand that the provision of essential vitamins and minerals as well as fatty acids will be apportioned on a daily basis by the body to meet immediate needs; these will fluctuate and demands will vary. Excluding valuable micronutrients for the potential perception of useless daily excretion may yet prove to be the worst long-term health advice ever given.

Poor nutrition has been linked to an increased risk of many diseases, including cancer, heart disease, and diabetes. The human diet requires both macronutrients, which are the main source of calories, and micronutrients (≈40 essential minerals, vitamins, and other biochemicals), which are required for virtually all metabolic and developmental processes. The leading dietary sources of energy in the Western world are abundant in carbohydrates and fats[7] but deficient in micronutrients (i.e., they are energy-dense and nutrient-poor).[8]

Clinical Education holds the view that, based on this, as well as extensive additional research, consuming a high-quality multivitamin and mineral supplement as an addition to your sound dietary choices will decrease your risk of developing a nutrient-insufficiency condition which may take years off your life and life off those remaining years.

https://www.palomar.edu/anthro/biobasis/bio_2.htm

Cell Reproduction and Conception

Most human cells are frequently reproduced and replaced during the life of an individual. However, the process varies with the kind of cell. Somatic, or body cells, such as those that make up skin, hair, and muscle, are duplicated by mitosis. The sex cells, sperm and ova, are produced by meiosis in special tissues of male testes and female ovaries. Since the vast majority of our cells are somatic, mitosis is the most common form of cell replication.

Mitosis

The cell division process that produces new cells for growth, repair, and the general replacement of older cells is called mitosis. In this process, a somatic cell divides into two complete new cells that are identical to the original one. Human somatic cells go through the 6 phases of mitosis in 1/2 to 1 1/2 hours, depending on the kind of tissue being duplicated.

Six phases of mitosis

Some human somatic cells are frequently replaced by new ones and other cells are rarely duplicated. Hair, skin, fingernails, taste buds, and the stomach's protective lining are replaced constantly and at a rapid rate throughout our lives. In contrast, brain and nerve cells in the central nervous system are rarely produced after we are a few months old. Subsequently, if they are destroyed later, the loss is usually permanent, as in the case of paraplegics. Liver cells usually do not reproduce after an individual has finished growing and are not replaced except when there is an injury. Red blood cells are also somewhat of an exception. While they are being constantly produced in our bone marrow, the specialized cells from which they come do not have nuclei nor do the red blood cells themselves.

Mitosis Close Up

Before mitosis begins, cells are in the interphase stage, which is the rest period between mitotic divisions. At this time, the chromosomes are not identifiable but are an undifferentiated loose mass of stretched-out DNA molecules within the nucleus. Chromosome replication and other cell processes are occurring in preparation for mitosis. In addition, cells carry out normal metabolic activities at this time. Most mammal somatic cells, including those of humans, spend at least 90% of their time in interphase.

Interphase

At the beginning of the first mitotic stage, prophase, the thread-like doubled chromosomes contract and become visible. The two centrioles move to opposite sides of the nucleus. At the same time, the nuclear membrane begins to break down.

Prophase

During metaphase, the nuclear membrane disappears and the chromosomes become aligned halfway between the centrioles. The centromere of each doubled chromosome becomes attached by thread-like spindle fibers to the centrioles, which are at polar opposite sides of the cell.

Metaphase

During the following anaphase stage, the chromatids of each chromosome separate at their centromeres and then migrate to the opposite poles of the cell.

Anaphase

During telophase, two distinct nuclear membranes develop, encompassing the two identical sets of chromosomes. At the same time, the cytoplasm divides between the two new cells, and the cell membrane begins to pinch off the cell contents into two daughter cells.

Telophase

Finally, the new identical cells separate and once again enter interphase in preparation for a later mitotic division. While the chromosomes are no longer visible, they will be replicated just before mitosis begins.

Interphase

Meiosis

Meiosis is a somewhat similar but more complex process than mitosis. This is especially true in females. While mitosis produces 2 daughter cells from each parent cell, meiosis results in 4 sex cells, or gametes, in males and 1 in females. Unlike the cells created by mitosis, gametes are not identical to the parent cells. In males, meiosis is referred to as spermatogenesis because sperm cells are produced. In females, it is called oogenesis because ova, or eggs, are the main ultimate product. The illustration below shows the 8 phases of spermatogenesis.

Phases of spermatogenesis (i.e., meiosis in males)

Conception

Sperm carries the father's chromosomes to the mother's ovum, where they combine with her chromosomes at the time of conception. Sperm cells are microscopic, but ova may be large enough in some species to be visible with the naked eye. Human ova are about the diameter of a hair.

Human sex cells (not drawn to the same scale)

The two sequential division processes of meiosis culminate in the production of gametes with only half the number of chromosomes of somatic cells. As a result, human sperm and ova each have only 23 single-stranded chromosomes.

Summary of reduction division in meiosis

Human somatic cells, with their full set of 46 chromosomes, have what geneticists refer to as a diploid number of chromosomes. Gametes have a haploid number (23). When conception occurs, a human sperm and ovum combine their chromosomes to make a zygote (fertilized egg) with 46 chromosomes. This is the same number that the parents each had in their somatic cells. In doing this, nature is acting conservatively. Each generation inherits the same number of chromosomes. Without reducing their number by half in meiosis first, each new generation would have double the number of chromosomes in their cells as the previous one. Within only 15 generations, humans would have over 1 million chromosomes per cell and would be a radically different kind of animal. In fact, when a zygote has an extra set of chromosomes, it usually is spontaneously aborted by the mother's reproductive system—it is a lethal condition.

The complete meiosis process in human males takes about 74 hours. Spermatogenesis usually begins at 12–13 years of age and continues throughout life. Several hundred million sperm cells are produced daily by healthy young adult males. Between 200 and 600 million sperm cells are normally released in each ejaculation. Since only one sperm cell is required for conception, this huge number would seem to be an extreme overkill. However, as many as 20% of sperm cells are likely to be defective and the female reproductive tract is hostile even to healthy ones—it is acidic and contains antibodies that seek out and destroy the sperm cells. Ejaculating large numbers of sperm at the same time is nature's way of overcoming these difficulties and increasing the likelihood that conception will take place. The number of sperm cells produced can be significantly diminished by psychological and physiological stress. Sperm count also progressively declines with age after reaching a peak, usually in the early 20s. In addition, the percentage of sperm that move randomly rather than in a straight line generally increases in older men. The result is a decrease in male fertility. The genes that are responsible for sperm production are in the Y sex chromosome. Unfortunately, the mutation rate for the Y chromosome is thought to be thousands of times higher than for those in other chromosomes. This may be a major cause of male infertility. As a result, genetic testing is beginning to be used to diagnose it.

Human female reproductive system

Meiosis in human females is more complex. By the 5th month after conception, immature sex cells begin to develop in the fetal ovaries but stop at an early stage of meiosis (after prophase I). They remain in this precursor egg cell, or primary oocyte, phase until puberty, when hormones cause a resumption of meiosis for one to several cells each month. They proceed to the 1st and 2nd reduction divisions and once again stop developing. At this stage they are secondary oocytes. When a secondary oocyte is finally released from the ovaries into the fallopian tube (during ovulation), the egg still has not completed the last stage of meiosis. That happens only at conception as a result of chemical changes that occur when the main part of a sperm cell enters the ovum.

Virtually all (99.9%) sex cells in a woman's ovaries never develop beyond the primary oocyte stage and eventually are reabsorbed by her body. By 20 weeks after conception, there are approximately 7,000,000 primary oocytes. All but about 1,200,000 are lost by birth. At puberty, there are only around 400,000 of them remaining. Throughout life, there is a constant decline in the number of potential eggs. Each time one is successfully ovulated, as many as 2,000 are lost. Normally, women have on average 11–14 ovulations per year for 33–36 years. This means that less than 500 secondary oocytes usually are produced out of the store of hundreds of thousands of primary oocytes. The actual number of ovulations is highly variable and often much lower since the process is governed by hormones and ultimately other factors, including psychological stress, nutrition, physical activity, and pathological conditions. The fact that women rarely have more than a few children is evidence that only a small fraction of the successfully ovulated eggs are fertilized and become viable zygotes. Beginning about age 27, a woman's fertility progressively declines. Around 35–37 years old, the decline becomes much steeper and the chances of conception significantly lower. By the early 50s, most women begin the transition to menopause, when they stop ovulating altogether. The temporary cessation of ovulation and subsequent infertility can occur much earlier in life as a result of reduced blood estrogen levels caused by excessive physical activity. This is very likely the reason that roughly a quarter of American women athletes in high school and college cease having menstrual periods. It also results in a significant decrease in their bone density.

NOTE: Humans may be the only animal species in which females now normally live for many years following menopause. Freed from having more children themselves, human grandmothers are in a position to assist their own daughters and sons in rearing their offspring. This potentially increases the chances that grandchildren will survive, thereby giving our species an advantage over other animals in the competition for survival. However, people rarely lived beyond menopause until a little over a century ago, when modern medicine and other technological advances made it possible. Prior to that time, we were more often like other animals in that most of us succumbed to disease, accidents, or predators before middle age and menopause.

NOTE: Ongoing research suggests that it may be possible within a few years to return fertility to postmenopausal women by stimulating stem cells in their ovaries to produce new eggs.

Study Suggests Way To Create New Eggs in Women—National Public Radio audio report on February 27, 2012.
To return here, you must click the “back” button on your browser program. (4 mins, 3 secs)

When human sexual intercourse occurs, it takes about 5 minutes for sperm to reach the upper end of the fallopian tubes, where conception usually takes place. Of the several hundred million sperm cells that enter a vagina, rarely do more than a few hundred successfully pass through the cervix and uterus. Only about 100 reach the upper end of the fallopian tubes. Sperm cells are guided over this path mostly by heat sensing. The upper ends of the fallopian tubes are about two degrees warmer than the lower ends. Secondary oocytes secrete chemicals that also may guide sperm cells to them when they are in close proximity. Usually, only the most viable sperm cells reach the secondary oocytes and play their part in conception. Those sperm that fail in this competition are often genetically abnormal. The endurance test that they must go through in the female reproductive tract is nature's way of eliminating these poorer specimens.

Among humans, fertilization usually occurs within a day after ovulation. It takes about 4 days for secondary oocytes to pass through the fallopian tube in their journey to the uterus. Conception must occur early in this process. Sperm usually can remain viable for up to 48 hours in the female reproductive tract, but secondary oocytes remain viable for only about 24 hours after they have left the ovaries. This means that sexual intercourse must occur from a few days before to one day after ovulation if conception is desired. In most non-human mammals, birds, reptiles, fish, and insects, fertilization is made more likely by the fact that females are sexually receptive only around the time of ovulation. This period of female sexual receptivity is called estrus. In most species, it is common for all females to have their ovulations around the same time of year. This reproductive synchronization results in a common mating season. In humans and some other primates, sexuality is far less related to the timing of ovulation. Among these species, there is no mating season. More precisely, the entire year is a mating season since they have a more or less chronic interest in sex. This is another way in which nature has chosen to increase the likelihood of conception.

Half of the sperm cells produced normally carry the X chromosome and half have the Y chromosome. Subsequently, we would expect that 50% of human babies would be males and 50% females, but this usually is not the case. The ratio of male to female newborns in the U.S. and most of the world is 105–110 males to 100 females. The ratio of males to females at conception is generally even higher than it is at birth. This is fortunate in the long run for society because male spontaneous abortions and infant mortality rates are higher. In addition, males are more likely to die from accidents and combat as teenagers and young men. Males in developed nations who survive to adulthood also can expect to die at a younger age than women.

Male-Female Ratios in the United States

Males | Females
at conception | 130–150 | 100
at birth | 105–110 | 100
at age 20 | 98 | 100
at age 65+ | 68 | 100

Current cultural practices in China and India result in even higher rates of male births. Since 1979, China has had a national policy of allowing parents to have only one child in order to reduce population growth. A traditional preference for male children and the ready availability of ultrasound technology has led to large numbers of abortions of female fetuses. This occurs despite the fact that abortions for the purpose of preventing the birth of female children is illegal. There are now 119 boys born for every 100 girls in China, and in some regions the ratio is as high as 144 to 100. A consequence of this practice is the growing scarcity of marriageable women. As of the 2005 census, there were 32 million more young men than women in China. While India does not have a one-child policy, it is facing a similar problem because of the selective abortion of female fetuses, especially in the more prosperous states of North India. This is driven by the economic difficulty of raising large families and the preference for male children. The huge excess of marriageable men in China and India could be socially and politically explosive in the near future.

In societies that encourage a form of marriage in which one man has more than one wife at the same time (polygyny), higher numbers of female children are usually born than in the predominantly monogamous nations. Why this reverse birth ratio pattern occurs is not entirely understood. However, it is very likely connected with the fact that each wife has less frequent sexual intercourse. Girls are more likely to be conceived when conception is close to the time of ovulation. When there is intercourse at other times as well, the sperm cells are more likely to be waiting for ovulation at the upper end of the fallopian tubes. They do not have as far to go to reach the egg.

Life's Greatest Miracle—PBS Nova series video on conception, gestation, and birth
This link takes you to an external website. To return here, you must click the “back” button on your browser program. (8 parts of 4–10 mins each)

Why Twins?

Multiple births at the same time are rare for humans and most other primate species. Having fraternal, but not identical, twins apparently runs in family lines, and is also somewhat more likely for women over age 30.

Fraternal twins may look similar but are not genetically identical. In fact, they are no more identical than any brother or sister. They share their mother's uterus during gestation but come from two different eggs fertilized with different sperm. Subsequently, they are called dizygotic twins. In contrast, identical twins are mostly identical genetically because they result from one zygote splitting into two or more separate ones within a few days after conception. As a consequence, they are called monozygotic twins. If the division of the original zygote does not occur until the 9th to the 12th day after conception, the monozygotic twins are likely to be mirror twins. That is, they will have small mirror-image differences internally and externally. For instance, one may be left-handed and the other right-handed. Likewise, the cowlick in their hair at the back of the head will be on opposite sides. If the division of the zygote occurs after day 13, the monozygotic twins are likely to be born conjoined.

Any differences between monozygotic twins later in life are mostly the result of environmental influences rather than genetic inheritance. However, monozygotic twins may not share all of the same sequences of mitochondrial DNA. This is due to the fact that the mitochondria in a cell may have somewhat different versions of DNA, and the mitochondria can be dispersed unequally when a zygote fissions. Female monozygotic twins can also differ because of differences between them in X-chromosome inactivation. Subsequently, one female twin can have an X-linked condition such as muscular dystrophy and the other twin can be free of it.

NOTE: X-chromosome inactivation in females was described at the end of the first topic section of this tutorial ("Basic Cell Structures"), and mitochondrial DNA is described in the last topic section ("Molecular Level of Genetics").

There has been at least one recorded instance of twins who are identical on their mother's side but share only half of their father's genes. These “semi-identical” twins result from two sperm cells fertilizing the same egg. This double fertilization of an egg apparently occurs in about 1% of human conceptions. In most cases, the embryo is not viable and dies.

title: Cell reproduction info (part 2 of 2)
content:
Dizygotic twins can also be produced when a woman has sexual intercourse with more than one man around the time she is ovulating. If multiple viable eggs are released from her ovaries, each can be fertilized by sperm from a different man. This is referred to as heteropaternity.

Why Intersex?

Normally in humans, one sperm cell combines its chromosomes with those of one ovum at conception, and that in turn develops into a single embryo that will become a fetus. Very rarely, however, two zygotes fuse and become a single embryo. If it survives gestation, a baby will be born who is a true chimera—it is genetically two “people” in one body. If those two “people” are not the same gender, the baby will likely be an intersex individual (also known as hermaphrodite)—it will have both male and female sex organs and other body tissues. Some researchers believe that the frequency of chimeras being born will be increasing as in vitro fertilization becomes more common since two or more embryos are usually placed in the uterus with this procedure.

She was implanted with a fertilized egg from a healthy younger woman. The baby was 6 weeks premature and weighed only 1.4 kilograms (3.1 pounds), which is less than half the normal newborn weight. Two other fetuses died during the pregnancy (News at Nature.com, January 17, 2005).

She noted that there is a skewing of sex ratios that corresponds to latitude. In temperate and subarctic latitudes, there are slightly more boys born compared to tropical latitudes. NUTRI-CHART 5 lists the Nutrients Involved in ENERGY METABOLISM

Often times the B vitamins are marketed as giving us energy (you can find them in many energy drinks). But remember, since we don't have the enzymes to break down these vitamins, we don't get energy from them directly, but indirectly they are involved in energy metabolism (generating energy from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins). There are 8 B vitamins involved in energy metabolism. These are thiamin, riboflavin, vitamin B6, niacin, folate, vitamin B12, pantothenic acid, and biotin. These B vitamins function as part of coenzymes for cellular respiration. This means that they activate the enzymes that bring about the reactions that release the energy from the macronutrients. The below chart illustrates many of the coenzymes essential for various metabolic functions, and this is just a small sample of the thousands of roles that B vitamins serve the body. Return to the below document that was posted in an earlier week in Moodle, where by now you should have filled in most of the blank lines.

On the bottom of this illustration it asks, “What are NAD and TPP?” NAD and TPP are coenzymes containing B vitamins. NAD stands for niacin adenine dinucleotide, so the B vitamin that coenzyme contains is niacin. TPP stands for thiamin pyrophosphate, so the B vitamin it contains is thiamin.

Without any of those B vitamins, cellular respiration couldn't happen in the body. Fatigue, and eventually death, would be the result. It would be like having no way to strike a match for (or otherwise start) a fire. You could have a large woodpile, but you couldn't get heat from that wood. PLEASE USE YOUR TEXT TO FILL IN FOOD SOURCES, TOO MUCH, TOO LITTLE, AND JUST RIGHT COLUMNS IN YOUR NUTRI-CHARTS FOR THE B VITAMINS.

In addition to those B vitamins, there are other vitamins and minerals involved with energy metabolism as well. Vitamin C and iodine are both necessary for the synthesis of thyroid hormones. Vitamin C helps produce thyroxin, a hormone that helps regulate the basal metabolic rate. Someone with a low BMR would be sort of like a really wimpy fire that burned slowly.

Iodine (I), chromium (Ch), manganese (Mn), choline, and sulfur (S) are minerals that are important for the reactions of cellular respiration to happen. Please look at Nutri-Charts and text for more information on these nutrients. They will not be discussed in the lecture here.

NUTRI-CHART 5 lists the Nutrients Involved in BLOOD HEALTH

Above we discussed some of the nutrients involved in energy metabolism. Without the blood to transport nutrients and oxygen, energy metabolism would never happen, and we would not survive. Healthy blood is vital to maintaining life as it transports virtually everything in our body, including wastes to be excreted. Some of the MINERALS involved in blood health include iron (Fe—that stands for ferrous), zinc (Zn), and copper (Cu—that stands for cupric).

Iron (Fe)

There are 2 major dietary forms of iron: heme iron and non-heme iron. Heme iron is only found in foods of animal origin, within hemoglobin and myoglobin. The structure of heme iron is shown below.

Approximately 40% of iron in meat, fish, and poultry is heme iron, and the other 60% is non-heme iron. Non-heme iron is the mineral alone. See food sources below.

It is estimated that 25% of heme iron and 17% of non-heme iron are absorbed; however, vitamin C and a special meat factor in meat, fish, and poultry enhance the absorption of non-heme iron. Approximately 85–90% of the iron we consume is non-heme iron. In addition to getting iron from food sources, if food is cooked in cast-iron cookware, a small amount of iron can be transferred to the food. The story below is an iron fish that is being used in Cambodia to increase iron intake in an area with prevalent iron deficiency.

Canadian’s lucky iron fish saves lives in Cambodia

Many breakfast cereals are also fortified with iron, as the following video shows.

Here is a link to the above video: https://youtu.be/pRK15XSqtAw

Iron is a component of numerous proteins in the body, including hemoglobin, myoglobin, and enzymes. Hemoglobin contains heme that is responsible for red blood cells’ red color. Hemoglobin carries oxygen to tissues. Myoglobin is similar to hemoglobin in that it can bind oxygen. However, instead of being found in blood, it is found in muscle. There are also a number of enzymes that use iron as a cofactor. Iron deficiency is the most common deficiency worldwide, estimated to affect 1.6 billion people. In the U.S., it is less common, but an estimated 10% of toddlers and women of childbearing age are deficient. Iron deficiency often results in a microcytic (small cell), hypochromic (low color) anemia that is a result of decreased hemoglobin production. With decreased hemoglobin, the red blood cells cannot carry as much oxygen, and without decreased oxygen, energy metabolism slows. A person with this anemia feels fatigued, weak, apathetic, and can experience headaches and delayed cognitive development in children.

Those who are particularly at risk are:

Women of childbearing age—because of losses due to menstruation
Pregnant women—because of increased blood volume
Vegetarians—because they do not consume heme iron sources
Infants—because they have low iron stores that can quickly be depleted

To give you a better understanding of these risks, it is helpful to look at how much higher the RDAs are for women of reproductive age and pregnant women compared to men.

Women of reproductive age: 18 mg/day
Pregnancy: 27 mg/day
Men: 8 mg/day

As most things go with nutrition, more is not necessarily better. One of the most common causes of childhood poisoning is from the ingestion of way-too-many multivitamin/mineral supplements at one time. Parents may be tempted to encourage children to “take their vitamins” by comparing them to candy. Children then may have the idea that they are as safe as candy, which they are not.

A child who swallows too many of them may need to have their stomach pumped because they can damage their heart.

Too much iron from supplements can also decrease the body's ability to absorb copper.

Zinc (Zn)

Zinc is required for more than 100 different enzymes in the body. An example of an enzyme that it is needed for is the synthesis of hemoglobin, which is why zinc is important for blood health. Zinc also plays roles in maintaining the structure of proteins in the body and helps regulate gene expression. Zinc can be found in red meats, some seafood, whole grains, and enriched cereals and grains. Non-heme iron and phytates and fiber found in whole grains and beans inhibit absorption, and animal protein can enhance absorption. See food sources below.

TOO MUCH dietary zinc does not appear to lead to toxicity, but too much zinc from supplements can decrease the absorption of copper, has been shown to decrease immune function, and can decrease HDLs. TOO LITTLE zinc is uncommon in the United States, but can be a problem in countries that consume predominantly grain-based foods.

Copper. I won't say anything else besides what's in the NUTRI-CHART. Some of the VITAMINS involved in blood health include folate, vitamins B12 and B6, and also vitamins C and K. These vitamins were discussed elsewhere, so they won't be discussed here.

title: Tesamorelin info
content:
Tesamorelin is FDA-approved for only one indication:
Reduction of excess abdominal visceral adipose tissue (VAT) in adults with HIV-associated lipodystrophy. It was approved under the brand name Egrifta.

What it is
Tesamorelin is a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH). It stimulates the pituitary gland to increase natural growth hormone (GH) secretion, which subsequently raises IGF-1 levels and promotes lipolysis (fat breakdown).

What it is NOT FDA-approved for
Tesamorelin is not FDA-approved for:
- General weight loss
- Obesity treatment
- Athletic performance enhancement
- Muscle building in healthy individuals
- Anti-aging therapy
- Body recomposition in the general population

Why people use it off-label
Outside its approved indication, clinicians sometimes prescribe tesamorelin off-label for:
- Reduction of visceral fat in non-HIV individuals
- Improvement of body composition
- Support during age-related declines in GH secretion
- Potential preservation of lean mass during fat-loss phases

However, these uses are based on emerging research and clinical experience rather than FDA-approved indications.

Trainer-level takeaway
Primary Use: Increases natural growth hormone release and reduces visceral abdominal fat. FDA-approved specifically for reducing excess visceral fat in adults with HIV-associated lipodystrophy.

Mechanism: Acts as a potent GHRH analog that binds pituitary GHRH receptors, increasing pulsatile GH secretion, which elevates IGF-1 and promotes preferential mobilization of visceral fat stores.

How Tesamorelin Is Typically Used

1. Systemic (Non-Site-Specific) Use
This is the standard and intended application.

Used for:
- Growth hormone axis stimulation
- Reduction of visceral adipose tissue
- Support of lean body mass retention
- Metabolic and lipolytic signaling
- Sleep-related GH pulse enhancement

Rationale:
- Tesamorelin stimulates the pituitary gland to release GH.
- Effects are systemic, not localized.
- Mimics physiological GH pulsatility more closely than exogenous GH.
- Injection is never site-specific for tissue repair, unlike BPC-157.

Typical Injection Frequency
Once daily is standard.
Usually administered in the evening to align with natural GH rhythms.
Consistency (same time daily) is emphasized over higher dosing.

Commonly Cited Dose Ranges (may vary in syringe volume with methods of reconstitution—follow supplier directions)
These reflect approved clinical use and common off-label protocols, not trainer-directed recommendations.

2 mg once daily is the FDA-approved dose (for HIV-associated lipodystrophy).

Off-label longevity/body composition protocols often range:
- 1–2 mg per day

Lower doses (<1 mg/day) generally show less reliable GH elevation.
Unlike many peptides, Tesamorelin dosing is not usually split.

Typical Duration of Use
12–26 weeks is common in clinical and applied settings.
Some protocols extend to 6–12 months under medical supervision.
Effects on visceral fat and IGF-1 are gradual, not immediate.
Tesamorelin is not a short-cycle peptide like BPC-157.

What Tesamorelin Is Commonly Used For
- Visceral fat reduction (strongest evidence)
- GH/IGF-1 axis support
- Lean mass preservation during fat loss
- Metabolic health support
- Sleep-related recovery signaling

Mechanism of Action (Trainer-Appropriate Depth)
Tesamorelin works by:
- Stimulating endogenous GH release from the pituitary
- Increasing IGF-1 downstream signaling
- Enhancing lipolysis, particularly in visceral fat
- Preserving natural feedback loops (unlike exogenous GH)

This preserves:
- Pulsatile GH secretion
- Lower risk of GH suppression
- Reduced likelihood of insulin resistance compared to GH injections

What Practitioners Commonly Observe (Real-World Use)

| Goal | Typical Outcome |
|---|---|
| Visceral fat reduction | Most consistent benefit |
| Lean mass retention | Moderate support |
| Strength gains | Indirect |
| Recovery | Subtle, cumulative |
| Sleep quality | Often improved |

Tesamorelin is not an acute performance enhancer.

Safety & Regulatory Notes (Important)
Tesamorelin is FDA-approved, but only for HIV-associated lipodystrophy.
Off-label use requires medical oversight.

Possible side effects include:
- Water retention
- Joint stiffness
- Increased IGF-1

Not appropriate for:
- Active malignancy
- Uncontrolled diabetes

Trainers should not prescribe, source, or administer.

Trainer-Friendly One-Line Explanation
“Tesamorelin helps the body release its own growth hormone more effectively, supporting fat loss and recovery without shutting down natural GH production.”

Practical Trainer/Educator Takeaway
If Tesamorelin is discussed at all, it should be positioned as:
- Medical-provider-managed
- Long-term and systemic
- Adjunctive—not foundational

Always anchor the conversation to:
- Resistance training
- Sleep optimization
- Protein and EAA sufficiency
- Micronutrient adequacy
- Load management and recovery

This keeps messaging aligned with a Playspan®/Youth-Preserving framework and avoids peptide-centric overreach.

Update product/formula
Tesamorelin is a synthetic Growth Hormone Releasing Hormone (GHRH) analog primarily used to stimulate the body’s natural pulsatile growth hormone release, which subsequently raises IGF-1 levels. Its best-studied and FDA-approved use is the reduction of excess visceral abdominal fat in HIV-associated lipodystrophy.

The standard clinically studied and FDA-approved dosage is:
- 2 mg subcutaneous injection once daily

The newer Egrifta WR formulation is dosed at:
- 1.28 mg once daily due to formulation differences and bioequivalence improvements.

Mechanistically, tesamorelin works upstream at the pituitary to increase endogenous GH secretion, which then elevates IGF-1 and promotes lipolysis, especially in visceral adipose tissue.

Clinical trials using the 2 mg/day dose demonstrated:
- ~14–18% reductions in visceral abdominal fat
- Improvements in triglycerides and liver fat
- Preservation or modest increases in lean body mass
- Minimal effect on overall body weight

In off-label performance/anti-aging settings, many clinics still use dosing near the original 2 mg nightly range because that is where most human efficacy data exist. Some protocols use lower doses (e.g., 0.5–1 mg/day) to reduce side effects or cost, but these lower-dose approaches are far less validated in published human research.

The most common side effects reported include:
- Edema/water retention
- Joint pain
- Tingling or numbness
- Injection site reactions
- Possible insulin sensitivity changes.

title: Women vs men IGF- blood levels -why
content:
Women’s IGF-1 blood reference ranges are often listed slightly higher than men’s because of normal sex-specific physiology, not because women have “more GH” overall. The key drivers are below.

The Main Reasons Women’s IGF-1 Ranges Run Higher

1. Estrogen Enhances Hepatic IGF-1 Signaling (Context-Dependent)

IGF-1 is produced primarily in the liver in response to growth hormone (GH).

Estrogen modulates GH receptor sensitivity and downstream IGF-1 signaling.

In premenopausal women, physiologic estrogen levels:
- Support efficient GH → IGF-1 coupling
- Increase circulating IGF-1 binding dynamics

This can shift the population normal range slightly upward.

Important nuance: oral estrogen lowers IGF-1, while endogenous estrogen does not. Reference ranges assume typical physiology, not hormone therapy.

2. Women Secrete GH More Frequently (Pulsatility)

Women have:
- More frequent GH pulses
- Lower amplitude per pulse, but greater total daily GH exposure
- IGF-1 reflects integrated GH exposure over time, not peak GH

Men tend to have fewer, higher GH spikes → less total daily exposure.

This pulsatility difference alone explains much of the range shift.

3. Body Composition Differences

IGF-1 correlates with:
- Lean mass quality
- Insulin sensitivity
- Metabolic efficiency

Women, especially premenopausal women:
- Maintain higher insulin sensitivity at equivalent BMI
- Have different fat distribution (less visceral fat pre-menopause)

These factors support higher baseline IGF-1 at rest.

4. Age- and Sex-Stratified Reference Data

IGF-1 ranges are statistical, not ideal targets.

Labs stratify by:
- Age
- Sex
- Population norms

Because healthy women cluster slightly higher, the upper and lower bounds shift upward.

This does not imply advantage or disadvantage—just different baselines.

What This Does NOT Mean

- Women do not have “more anabolic hormone” than men
- Higher IGF-1 does not automatically mean better muscle gain
- Men with IGF-1 in the female range are not abnormal

Muscle hypertrophy is still driven primarily by:
- Androgens
- Mechanical tension
- Nutrition
- Recovery

Trainer / Client-Friendly One-Liner

“Women often have slightly higher normal IGF-1 ranges because estrogen and growth hormone work together differently—it’s a normal, healthy sex difference, not a problem or advantage.”

Practical Interpretation Tip

Always interpret IGF-1 relative to age and sex, not across genders.

More important than the absolute number:
- Trends over time
- Symptoms
- Context (sleep, nutrition, training load, hormone status)

Diet Monitoring & Adjustments for Body Fat Reduction

Program Algorithms

Adjustments:

Measurable or visual reduction in body fat and/or weight proceeds in a consistent manner, e.g., a decrease in circumference inches, and/or the desired average decrease in body fat per week.

If progress stops or slows dramatically, use one or a combination of adjustments to restart the process:

- Increase cardio workout time and/or intensity and include interval training if necessary.

- Decrease food intake approximately 200 to 300 calories per day or remove a small portion (carbs/fats) of the largest meal other than the pre-workout meal (incorporate 3-days low/1-high as necessary).

Repeat the process any time body fat is stable for at least one week. title: Beetroot juice and salts in exercise
content:
Beetroot Review

Beetroot juice (BRJ) and nitrate salts (NIT) are compared in terms of their effects on exercise performance and physiological function.

BRJ may have additional advantages compared to NIT, such as reducing oxygen consumption during high-intensity exercise, enhancing performance improvements with training, and improving recovery post-exercise.

The potential benefits of BRJ beyond nitrate may be due to its rich spectrum of phytonutrients, including polyphenols, which could have antioxidant and/or anti-inflammatory properties.

Studies comparing BRJ and NIT have shown mixed results, with some studies indicating greater benefits with BRJ and others showing no significant differences.

Further research is needed to directly compare the effects of BRJ and NIT on exercise-related outcomes, taking into account factors such as the amount of nitrate in the supplements, blinding of participants, and the use of reproducible physiological outcomes.

Dietary nitrate supplementation, including beetroot juice, has various beneficial effects on exercise performance and physiological adaptations.

Nitrate from beetroot juice is converted to nitrite and then to nitric oxide in the body, which plays a role in vasodilation and improving blood flow.

The effects of dietary nitrate supplementation can vary depending on factors such as dosage, duration of supplementation, and individual response.

Other nitrate-rich vegetables and fruits can also provide similar benefits to beetroot juice.
