title: Mitochondria derived proteins-peptides
content:
What is the process of mitochondria-derived proteins, formerly called mitochondria-derived peptides?

Mitochondria-derived proteins (MDPs), formerly called mitochondria-derived peptides, are a relatively newly recognized group of small signaling proteins that are actually encoded within the mitochondrial genome itself. For decades, scientists believed mitochondria only encoded 13 proteins involved in energy production. We now know mitochondria also produce several small bioactive proteins that function almost like hormones or cellular “stress messengers.”

The process works roughly like this:

Mitochondrial DNA transcription

Mitochondria contain their own small circular DNA separate from nuclear DNA. Within regions once thought to be “non-coding,” small open reading frames (sORFs) are transcribed into RNA.

Translation into small proteins

These RNAs are translated by mitochondrial or sometimes cytoplasmic ribosomes into tiny proteins—usually under ~100 amino acids long. Examples include:

- Humanin
- MOTS-c
- SHLPs (Small Humanin-Like Peptides)

Stress sensing and signaling

Production often increases during:

- Exercise
- Caloric restriction
- Oxidative stress
- Fasting
- Mitochondrial dysfunction

The mitochondria essentially “report” cellular energy status to the rest of the cell and body.

Cellular and systemic actions

These proteins can leave the mitochondria and sometimes even circulate in blood, acting on distant tissues. Their actions include:

- Improving insulin sensitivity
- Enhancing glucose uptake
- Supporting mitochondrial biogenesis
- Reducing oxidative stress
- Protecting neurons
- Reducing inflammation
- Supporting muscle metabolism and exercise adaptation

Communication with the nucleus

One of the most interesting features is “retrograde signaling,” where mitochondria communicate back to the nucleus to influence gene expression related to:

- Longevity
- Stress resistance
- Metabolism
- Cellular repair

One of the most studied examples is MOTS-c:

MOTS-c appears to activate metabolic pathways similar to exercise and energy stress, particularly the AMPK pathway, helping cells shift toward better glucose utilization and fat oxidation.

Another is Humanin, which has attracted major attention for:

- Neuroprotection
- Anti-apoptotic effects
- Potential roles in healthy aging and diseases like Alzheimer’s

The reason the terminology shifted from “peptides” to “proteins” is largely scientific refinement. Initially, these molecules were discovered as very short amino acid chains and called peptides. - Neurodegeneration

One of the major emerging concepts is that exercise, proper nutrition, sleep, and metabolic health may partly exert their anti-aging and performance effects by improving mitochondrial signaling and increasing beneficial MDP activity.

title: Age Experience intersect note
content:
Hi [CUSTOMER],

I will put something together this weekend regarding building your supplement program around training intensity that will give you the best chance of still being able to build muscle naturally.

At some point you will have to come to grips with aging and building muscle. Once you have approached the "age experience" intersection* of training, the only thing you can do is slow the inevitable decline by doing all the right things (e.g., diet, supplements, training, etc.). To continue to add muscle at this intersection, you would have to add hormones, which is not something you want to do because of the future health ramifications. And all you will get is a few more years of building and a very good chance of injury.

*Age experience intersection is a place where the body will naturally plateau in progress and varies for all sports depending on the primary needed function/skill. In other words, physical performance (or size) will no longer improve. As an example: a person competing in tennis (a game of reflexes combined with quickness) most of their lives will reach this intersection in the late 20s or early 30s. A person just starting tennis at age 30 can get better for the next 10 years (so maybe reach the point at age 40–45) but, of course, will never be as good as the professional player who came to their plateau at the other person's starting age.

In the case of weightlifting, if you were a bodybuilder and trained intensely from ages 15 through 40, you will definitely not put on more muscle naturally. But if you started lifting at age 40, you could add muscle for the next few years and then maintain it for many more—but you would never be as big as if you had started in your youth. However, you could be bigger at age 60 than the shrinking bodybuilder by age 60 because of overuse in the latter.

Anyway, that's the "age experience intersection" explanation. Hey, just think, competitive gymnasts come to this point in their teens!

On a personal note, you'll never know the pain I went through after retiring. Watching yourself shrink is tough, but tougher was losing the strength. I just channeled all my passion and thoughts into the businesses, and that took the sting out.

I will send you something soon, my friend.

title: Bempedoic Acid, non-statinLowerChol
content:
Bempedoic acid 180 mg lowers cholesterol by inhibiting the enzyme ATP citrate lyase (ACL) in the liver, which is a key enzyme in cholesterol synthesis. This inhibition reduces the availability of acetyl-CoA, a building block for cholesterol and fatty acids. As a result, cholesterol production decreases, and the liver upregulates LDL receptors, increasing the removal of LDL cholesterol from the blood.

Detailed mechanism of action

Prodrug activation: Bempedoic acid is a prodrug that requires activation into its active form in the liver via the enzyme very-long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase 1 (ACSVL1).

Inhibition of ACL: The active form inhibits ATP citrate lyase (ACL). ACL is located upstream of HMG-CoA reductase (the target of statins) in the cholesterol synthesis pathway.

Reduced cholesterol synthesis: By blocking ACL, bempedoic acid reduces the conversion of citrate to acetyl-CoA in the cytoplasm. This directly decreases the supply of acetyl-CoA, a crucial precursor for the synthesis of both cholesterol and fatty acids in the liver.

Upregulation of LDL receptors: The reduction in liver cholesterol synthesis leads to an increase in LDL receptors on the surface of liver cells (hepatocytes).

Lowered LDL-C: The increased number of LDL receptors allows more LDL particles to be taken up from the blood, resulting in lower circulating LDL cholesterol levels.

AMPK activation: Bempedoic acid also activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), which further downregulates key enzymes in cholesterol and fatty acid synthesis.

Oral BPC-157 → commonly used for gut healing
Injectable BPC-157 → preferred for muscle, tendon, and ligament injuries

Despite being a peptide, BPC-157 is unusually stable in gastric juice, which is why oral use exists—but local tissue concentrations are much lower than with injections.

What Practitioners Generally Observe (Real-World Use)

| Goal | Preferred Method |
|---|---|
| Single tendon/ligament injury | Local injection |
| Chronic joint pain | Local or regional |
| Multiple injuries | Systemic |
| Gut issues | Oral or systemic injection |
| Whole-body recovery | Systemic |

Key Safety & Scope Notes (Important)

BPC-157 is not FDA-approved for human therapeutic use.
Human data are limited; most mechanistic evidence comes from animal models.
Trainers should not prescribe or inject—this is medical-provider territory.
Always position nutrition, sleep, load management, and rehab first.

Trainer-Friendly One-Line Explanation

“BPC-157 is often injected near an injury for faster local effects, but it also works systemically, which is why some protocols don’t inject directly at the injury site.”

Here’s the commonly reported clinical-research–based guidance you’ll see discussed for injectable BPC-157, with important context and cautions.

Typical Injection Frequency

Once daily is most common.
Twice daily (split dose) is sometimes used for more severe or acute injuries.
Courses typically last 2–4 weeks, occasionally up to 6 weeks in stubborn cases.
Many protocols favor daily consistency rather than large, infrequent doses.

Commonly Cited Dose Ranges

These are not FDA-approved dosing guidelines—only ranges reported in research settings and practitioner discussions.

200–500 mcg per day is the most frequently cited range.

Some protocols use:
- 250 mcg once daily, or
- 250 mcg twice daily (AM / PM)

Higher doses (e.g., 750–1000 mcg/day) are sometimes mentioned but do not appear clearly superior and may increase uncertainty around safety.

Injection Location (High-Level)

Often described as localized near the injury site (muscle, tendon, joint region).
Systemic use (e.g., abdominal subcutaneous injection) is also discussed in GI or multi-tissue recovery contexts.
Current evidence suggests BPC-157 acts systemically, even when injected locally.

(Deliberately avoiding step-by-step injection instructions.)

What It’s Commonly Used For

- Tendon and ligament injuries
- Muscle tears
- Joint pain
- Gut lining support (in non-injectable forms more often)

Mechanistically, BPC-157 is studied for:
- Angiogenesis support
- Fibroblast migration
- Collagen organization
- Nitric oxide signaling modulation

Safety & Regulatory Notes (Important)

BPC-157 is not FDA-approved for human use.
Long-term safety data in humans is lacking.
Quality control varies widely between sources.
Should not replace rehab, nutrition, sleep, or medical evaluation.

Practical Trainer / Educator Takeaway

If BPC-157 is discussed at all, it should be framed as experimental, adjunctive, and secondary to:
- Progressive loading & rehab
- Adequate protein & essential amino acids
- Micronutrient sufficiency
- Sleep and recovery hygiene

This positioning aligns well with a “basics first, advanced tools last” philosophy—especially important in trainer-led environments.

content:

title: Science peptide sheet -all
content:
Here’s what I’ll do for you in one pass:
Science-heavy expanded guide – with mechanism, what we actually know from data, typical study / “street” ranges (framed carefully), and risks.
Trainer-friendly version – simple language and coaching cues you can use with clients.
Important safety framing (for you + any trainers reading this):
With the exception of tesamorelin (for a very specific HIV-related indication) and elamipretide in narrow rare-disease contexts, these peptides are not FDA-approved for general use, quality control is highly variable, human data are sparse, and most “protocols” are based on uncontrolled experience. Nothing below is medical advice or a recommendation to use—only a map of what’s out there so trainers can have informed conversations and know when to refer out.
A. Science-Heavy Expanded Guide
1. TB-500 (Thymosin Beta-4 Fragment)
What it is / status
Synthetic fragment of the endogenous peptide thymosin beta-4, involved in tissue repair and cell migration. PMC
Used experimentally for soft-tissue healing; not FDA-approved for any indication.
Mechanisms (proposed)
Binds to G-actin, promoting actin polymerization, cell migration, and cytoskeletal remodeling in fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and myocytes. PMC
Upregulates angiogenesis (VEGF, endothelial cell migration), decreases inflammatory cytokines, and may reduce fibrosis. PMC+1
Evidence snapshot
Animal data: improved healing in cardiac injury, corneal wounds, dermal wounds, and some musculoskeletal models. PMC
Human data remain limited and mostly small/uncontrolled.
Dosing in literature / practice (informational only)
Formal dose-finding in humans is sparse; clinical monographs and compounding protocols often describe systemic doses in the low mg per week range, divided into several subcutaneous injections. A4M
True evidence-based “optimal” dosing is unknown.
Risks / concerns
Short-term: injection-site reactions, edema, fatigue, headache; overall tolerability in small series appears reasonable. Swolverine+1
Theoretical risks: pro-angiogenic and pro-migration effects raise concern about tumor promotion or unwanted angiogenesis in susceptible individuals (cancer history, proliferative retinopathies, etc.), though this has not been definitively shown in humans. PMC
Long-term human safety is essentially unknown.
2. BPC-157 (Body Protection Compound-157)
What it is / status
15-aa peptide derived from a gastric protein thought to protect and repair gut mucosa. PMC
No FDA approval; banned by WADA and many sport bodies. PMC+1
Mechanisms (proposed)
Potent pro-angiogenic actions (VEGF signaling), enhances fibroblast migration, collagen deposition, and tendon/ligament repair in preclinical models. Physiology Journals+1
Modulates NO signaling, exerts anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, and supports gut barrier integrity. PMC+2 PMC+2
Evidence snapshot
Robust rodent data: improved healing of tendons, ligaments, muscles, bone, and GI tract; some neuroprotective signals. Physiology Journals+1
Human evidence is minimal and largely anecdotal; a recent narrative review emphasizes high promise but very low-quality human data. PMC
Dosing in literature / practice (informational only)
Most data are in animals (e.g., microgram/kg injections). Physiology Journals
Compounded “clinic” protocols commonly cite ~250–500 mcg once or twice daily, oral or SC, but this is not evidence-based and often extrapolated from preclinical work.
Risks / concerns
The new 2025 review highlights that while preclinical safety seems acceptable, the lack of regulated manufacturing, dosing standards, or long-term human follow-up is a major concern. PMC+1
Potential issues: injection-site reactions, unknown effects on aberrant angiogenesis (e.g., tumors, diabetic retinopathy), possible drug–drug interactions through endothelial/NO pathways.
3. MOTS-c
What it is / status
16-aa mitochondria-derived peptide encoded by mtDNA, secreted in response to metabolic stress. Cell
Investigational only; no current broad FDA indication.
Mechanisms
Activates AMPK, increases glucose uptake, and shifts muscle toward fatty acid oxidation and improved insulin sensitivity. PMC+2 Cell+2
Modulates expression of nuclear genes related to metabolism and proteostasis (exercise-like transcriptional signature). BioMed Central+1
Evidence snapshot
Animal studies: improved exercise capacity, metabolic flexibility, and healthspan with intermittent dosing in aged mice. Nature+1
Early human data: small studies/observations linking MOTS-c to exercise response and metabolic health; interventional human trials remain very limited.
Dosing in literature / practice (informational only)
Mouse work commonly uses intermittent injections several times per week; dose scaled in mg/kg. Nature+1
Compounding-clinic “protocols” often describe 5–15 mg SC, 2–3x/week, extrapolated from animal scaling—this is experimental and not validated.
Risks / concerns
Human safety data are sparse; theoretical concerns involve over-activation of AMPK, unintended weight loss, hypoglycemia in susceptible patients, or interactions with other metabolic drugs.
Unknown effects in cancer, given metabolic reprogramming roles.
4. SS-31 / Elamipretide
What it is / status
Synthetic mitochondria-targeted tetrapeptide that binds cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane. ScienceDirect+1
Investigated in cardiomyopathy, Barth syndrome, and other mitochondrial disorders; regulatory status is evolving and indication-specific (recent FDA decisions have been mixed). The Hub+1
Mechanisms
Binds cardiolipin, stabilizing inner mitochondrial membrane structure and respiratory chain complexes, reducing ROS production and improving ATP generation. ScienceDirect+1
Has antioxidant and anti-apoptotic effects in high-stress tissues like heart and skeletal muscle.
Evidence snapshot
In Barth syndrome, longer-term elamipretide improved functional capacity and cardiac stroke volume in a phase 2/3 trial, though regulatory endpoints have been contentious. PMC+2 Nature+2
Multiple mitochondrial disease and heart failure trials show mixed but encouraging signals on exercise tolerance and mitochondrial biomarkers. ScienceDirect
Dosing (from trials, not a protocol)
Trials often use daily SC or IV dosing at fixed mg amounts (e.g., ~40 mg/day SC in some human studies), but regimens are disease- and protocol-specific. PMC+1
Risks / concerns
Reported adverse effects: injection-site reactions, transient headache, nausea, and some GI symptoms; overall tolerability moderate in trials. PMC+1
As a drug under active regulatory scrutiny, use belongs inside clinical trials / specialist care, not fitness settings.
5. AOD-9604 (hGH Fragment 176–191)
What it is / status
Synthetic fragment of the C-terminus of human GH, designed to retain lipolytic but not growth-promoting properties. PMC+1
Failed to demonstrate consistent weight-loss efficacy in human obesity trials; development as an anti-obesity drug was discontinued, though some clinics still market it off-label. PMC+2 paragonsportsmedicine.com+2
Mechanisms
Activates lipolysis and inhibits lipogenesis in adipose tissue, likely via cAMP-mediated signaling, without robust GH-like effects on IGF-1 or glucose. PMC+1
Evidence snapshot
Animal studies: meaningful reductions in body fat in obese mice. OUP Academic
Human trials: relatively benign safety profile across several hundred participants, but inconsistent or modest efficacy on fat loss → program was largely abandoned. PMC+2 jofem.org+2
Dosing (research)
Obesity trials used oral or injectable daily dosing at various mg ranges; exact regimen depends on protocol. PMC+1
Commercial peptide clinics often use daily SC injections, but there is no evidence-based standard.
Risks / concerns
Trials suggest good short-term safety—GI symptoms, headache, mild joint issues most common. jofem.org+1
Biggest concern is overpromising fat-loss efficacy and using it as a crutch instead of foundational lifestyle changes.
6. Epitalon / Epithalamin
What it is / status
Synthetic version of a tetrapeptide originally isolated from the pineal gland; studied as a “geroprotective” peptide. PMC+1
Not FDA-approved; research is mostly from Eastern European/Russian groups plus newer mechanistic work.
Mechanisms
Induces telomerase expression and telomere elongation in human somatic cells in vitro. PMC+1
Appears to modulate clock genes, melatonin secretion, antioxidant defenses, and immune balance, potentially affecting circadian rhythm, redox homeostasis, and inflammation. PMC+2 Healthspan+2
Evidence snapshot
Some long-term clinical observations suggest reduced mortality and improved markers of aging in elderly cohorts receiving pineal peptides, but methodology is often limited and not widely replicated. Alzheimer’s Drug Discovery Foundation+1
High-quality, modern placebo-controlled human trials are still lacking.
Dosing (reported in research)
Protocols from Russian trials often used short courses (10–20 days) of low-mg daily injections, repeated annually or semi-annually, but details vary widely. Alzheimer’s Drug Discovery Foundation+1
Risks / concerns
Available data suggest good tolerability in older adults over years, but much of this is from a single research ecosystem. Alzheimer’s Drug Discovery Foundation
Theoretical risk: telomerase activation could promote survival of pre-malignant cells; cancer risk needs much better characterization.
7. Kisspeptin (Kisspeptin-10, -54)
What it is / status
Endogenous peptide family critical for activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis. PMC+1
Studied as a diagnostic and therapeutic tool in reproductive medicine (e.g., infertility, IVF triggers). Frontiers+1
Mechanisms
Binds KISS1R (GPR54) on GnRH neurons → stimulates GnRH release, which increases pituitary LH/FSH, leading to increased gonadal steroid production. PMC+1
Integrates steroid feedback and environmental cues (e.g., energy availability) into reproductive hormone output.
Evidence snapshot
Human work: bolus IV kisspeptin robustly increases LH/FSH in both men and women; kisspeptin is being trialed as a safer oocyte maturation trigger in IVF. PMC+1
Dosing (research)
IVF and endocrine research uses carefully titrated IV or SC boluses/infusions under specialist supervision; mg ranges are protocol-specific and not appropriate for “recreational” copying. Frontiers+1
Risks / concerns
Acute flushing, nausea, headache; risk of ovarian hyperstimulation if misused in IVF contexts. Frontiers
Not appropriate for gym-level optimization; belongs entirely in reproductive endocrinology settings.
8. Tesamorelin
What it is / status
Synthetic GHRH analog, FDA-approved as EGRIFTA® / EGRIFTA SV / EGRIFTA WR for HIV-associated lipodystrophy with excess visceral fat. FDA Access Data+1
Mechanisms
Binds pituitary GHRH receptors, increasing pulsatile GH secretion and thereby raising IGF-1 and promoting lipolysis, especially in visceral depots. FDA Access Data
Evidence snapshot
Multiple RCTs show reductions in visceral adipose tissue and modest metabolic effects in HIV patients; GH/IGF-1 axis clearly stimulated. FDA Access Data+1
Label dosing (for its approved indication, not a gym protocol)
Labeled regimen is 1.4 mg SC once daily in the abdomen for HIV-associated lipodystrophy, with detailed monitoring recommendations. FDA Access Data+1
Risks / concerns
Hypersensitivity reactions (rash, urticaria, even anaphylaxis), injection-site reactions, arthralgia, edema, carpal tunnel–like symptoms, increased IGF-1, and potential glucose intolerance / diabetes risk. FDA Access Data+2 Mayo Clinic+2
Contraindicated in active malignancy and used cautiously in anyone with a cancer history because of GH/IGF-1 axis activation.
9. CJC-1295 (with/without DAC)
What it is / status
Synthetic GHRH analog; “with DAC” version is conjugated to increase half-life to days.
Not FDA-approved; used off-label in anti-aging / performance circles.
Mechanisms
Binds GHRH receptors → increases amplitude and duration of endogenous GH pulses, especially in response to natural stimuli (sleep, exercise).
With DAC, maintains elevated baseline GHRH signaling over several days, yielding a sustained rise in GH and IGF-1.
Evidence snapshot
Early clinical work showed dose-dependent increases in GH and IGF-1 over weeks; long-term outcome data on body composition, CV risk, or cancer are lacking.
Dosing in literature / practice (informational)
Trials used single or weekly injections at fixed mcg/kg doses; “clinic” protocols often mention ~1–2 mg once or twice weekly with DAC, or smaller, more frequent dosing without DAC—none of this is outcome-validated.
Risks / concerns
Similar to other GH axis stimulators: edema, arthralgia, paresthesias, carpal tunnel–type symptoms, potential worsening of sleep apnea, and theoretical tumor-promotion risk.
Additive risks when stacked with other GHRPs or GH itself.
Trainer-Friendly Version (Talking Points & Guardrails)
You can treat this as your coach-facing crib sheet when clients ask about peptides.
Quick Legend
Status: ✅ FDA-approved for narrow indication | 🔬 Experimental | 🚫 Not approved / banned in sport
Trainer rule of thumb: You can explain mechanisms & risks, but you do not recommend, source, or help dose these. Always refer to a qualified medical provider.
1. TB-500 (Thymosin Beta-4 fragment) – 🔬 Experimental
What clients think it does: “Heals injuries faster, helps joints and tendons.”
Plain-English mechanism: Signals cells involved in repair to move in, build new blood vessels, and remodel tissue.
Key risks to mention: Long-term safety unknown; in theory anything that boosts blood vessel growth and cell migration could be a problem in people with cancer or eye disease.
Trainer line: “Interesting early data in animals, but human safety’s not nailed down—this is something to discuss with a sports med or regenerative-medicine MD, not something we handle on the gym floor.”
2. BPC-157 – 🚫 Not approved, banned in sport
What clients think it does: “Fixes everything—gut, tendon, ligament, shoulder, you name it.”
Plain-English mechanism: Acts like a repair signal that can boost blood flow and collagen formation in injured tissues and may protect the gut lining.
Key risks: Human trials are almost non-existent; quality is all over the place; potential concern for abnormal blood vessel growth and unknown long-term effects. It is prohibited by many sports organizations. PMC+1
Trainer line: “Because it’s banned in sport and not well-studied in humans, I’d want your physician fully in the loop before you even consider it.”
3. MOTS-c – 🔬 Experimental “exercise-mimetic” signal
What clients think it does: “Gives you better energy, fat burning, and endurance.”
Plain-English mechanism: A natural mitochondrial signal that makes muscles handle fuel more like a trained athlete—better glucose handling and more fat use. BioMed Central+1
Key risks: Very new; we don’t know long-term effects on blood sugar, weight, or cancer risk.
Trainer line: “Lifestyle, training, and nutrition already drive the same AMPK pathways that MOTS-c targets—and those are proven and safe.”
4. SS-31 / Elamipretide – 🔬 Rare-disease drug candidate
What clients think it does: “Repairs mitochondria and boosts energy/heart function.”
Plain-English mechanism: Sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane and helps your powerplants make energy with less oxidative damage. ScienceDirect+1
Key risks: Still being sorted out in clinical trials; absolutely not a general performance peptide.
Trainer line: “Right now this is a specialist drug for rare mitochondrial issues, not a mainstream recovery tool.”
5. AOD-9604 – 🔬 Safe-ish, but weak evidence for fat loss
What clients think it does: “GH-like fat burner without side effects.”
Plain-English mechanism: A small piece of GH that was engineered to tilt fat cells toward breaking down fat instead of storing it, without much impact on growth. PMC+1
Key risks: Human trials show it’s well-tolerated but not very impressive for weight loss; the big risk is people using it instead of fixing food, steps, and training. PMC+1
Trainer line: “Even in clinical trials AOD didn’t move the needle much—your calories, protein, steps, and sleep still do 99% of the work.”
6. Epitalon – 🔬 Longevity / anti-aging peptide
What clients think it does: “Reverses aging, lengthens telomeres, fixes sleep.”
Plain-English mechanism: May turn on telomerase, help keep telomeres from shortening, and tune circadian and antioxidant systems. PMC+1
Key risks: Aging and cancer are tightly linked—boosting telomerase in the wrong person is a theoretical issue; long-term, high-quality studies are thin. Alzheimer’s Drug Discovery Foundation
Trainer line: “Even if the longevity angle pans out, this is something that belongs in a medical anti-aging clinic, not a casual stack.”
7. Kisspeptin – ✅/🔬 Medical reproductive tool, not a “test booster”
What clients think it does: “Boosts testosterone, helps fertility, fixes libido.”
Plain-English mechanism: It’s basically the on-switch for the brain’s reproductive hormone cascade (GnRH → LH/FSH → testosterone/estrogen). PMC+1
Key risks: Can strongly affect fertility hormones; in IVF settings, misuse can cause ovarian hyperstimulation and other serious issues. Frontiers
Trainer line: “Any hormone-level work like this is strictly for an endocrinologist or fertility specialist.”
8. Tesamorelin – ✅ FDA-approved (very specific use)
What clients think it does: “Lean-out peptide that burns belly fat by boosting GH.”
Plain-English mechanism: Mimics the brain’s GHRH signal, which makes the pituitary release more GH in pulses, raising IGF-1 and helping reduce visceral fat. FDA Access Data
Key risks: Can raise blood sugar, IGF-1, and cause edema, joint pain, numbness, and allergic reactions; contraindicated in active cancer. FDA Access Data+1
Trainer line: “It’s a real, prescription-only drug for a specific HIV-related condition—if someone’s using it outside that, they absolutely need a physician supervising.”
9. CJC-1295 (with or without DAC) – 🔬 GH-axis stimulator
What clients think it does: “Long-acting GH booster for recovery, lean mass, and sleep.”
Plain-English mechanism: Acts like a long-lasting GHRH, making the body release more of its own GH and IGF-1 over time.
Key risks: Same issues you’d worry about with elevated GH/IGF-1: edema, carpal-tunnel-type symptoms, possible blood sugar and cancer-promotion concerns, plus no long-term outcome data.
Trainer line: “If someone’s trying to get GH-like effects, they also inherit the GH-like risks—this is doctor territory, not coaching territory.”
How Trainers Can Use This in Practice
1. Normalize curiosity, but anchor in basics.
“It makes sense you’re hearing a lot about peptides; they’re a hot topic. The things we know extend healthspan and performance are still: training, protein, sleep, weight control, and smart supplementation we can fully vet.”
2. Draw the “scope of practice” line clearly.
“I can explain what these compounds try to do and what the risks are, but I don’t prescribe, source, or advise doses. If you’re serious about them, we pull a qualified physician into the conversation.”
3. Use peptides as a door to better fundamentals.
If a client wants BPC-157 for tendon pain → talk load management, movement quality, protein, collagen + vitamin C, and sleep, and suggest an ortho/sports-med consult

title: Autophagy and mTOR1 & 2
content:
Are there different pathways for mTOR and what are they. Are they named different such as mTOR1 and mTOR2? It seems like one is involved in regulating autophagy along with AMPK, and one is involved in initiating muscle protein synthesis. We want to maintain muscle as we age, so why would shutting down mTOR help that situation unless it is different pathway.

Yes — you are exactly on the right track. There are two main mTOR signaling complexes, and understanding the difference resolves the apparent contradiction between autophagy/AMPK signaling and muscle protein synthesis.

The two pathways are:
1. mTORC1 (mTOR Complex 1)
2. mTORC2 (mTOR Complex 2)

They share the same core protein (mTOR = mechanistic Target of Rapamycin) but interact with different partner proteins and control different biological processes.

The Two mTOR Pathways Explained

1. mTORC1 – The “Growth / Protein Synthesis” Pathway

mTORC1 is the pathway most associated with:
• Muscle protein synthesis
• Cell growth
• Nutrient sensing
• Anabolism
• Inhibition of autophagy

Activated by:
Resistance exercise
Leucine / essential amino acids
Insulin
IGF-1
Energy sufficiency

Main outputs:
Activates p70S6K
Activates 4E-BP1
Initiates translation of new muscle proteins

What it does in muscle

mTORC1 essentially tells the cell:
“We have enough nutrients and energy — build tissue.”

This is the pathway responsible for muscle hypertrophy after training.

2. mTORC2 – The “Metabolic Regulation / Survival” Pathway

mTORC2 has very different roles.

Major functions:
• Regulates AKT signaling
• Controls cell survival
• Regulates cytoskeleton structure
• Helps regulate glucose metabolism
• Influences insulin sensitivity

Activated by:
Growth factors
Insulin signaling

Key difference

mTORC2 does not directly drive muscle protein synthesis the way mTORC1 does.

Instead, it regulates metabolic signaling upstream of mTORC1.

Where AMPK and Autophagy Fit

AMPK is essentially the energy stress sensor of the cell.

When energy is low:
AMPK → inhibits mTORC1

This causes:
• Autophagy activation
• Cell repair and recycling
• Mitochondrial renewal

Autophagy removes:
damaged mitochondria
misfolded proteins
cellular waste

Think of it as cellular housekeeping.

Why Shutting Down mTOR Can Actually Help Maintain Muscle

This is where the timing concept becomes important.

Cells benefit from oscillating between two states:

| State | Signal | Result |
| Growth state | mTORC1 high | Build tissue |
| Repair state | AMPK high / mTORC1 low | Clean & repair |

If mTORC1 stays constantly high, problems occur:
• damaged proteins accumulate
• mitochondria become dysfunctional
• metabolic disease risk rises

This phenomenon is sometimes called:
“chronic anabolic signaling”

It accelerates aging and degeneration.

The Ideal Physiology (Especially for Aging Athletes)

Healthy physiology cycles between:
Repair → Build → Repair → Build

Example:
Morning (fasted / exercise)
AMPK ↑
Autophagy ↑

After eating + training
mTORC1 ↑
Protein synthesis ↑

This pattern allows both:
• cell renewal
• muscle growth

Why This Matters for Aging and Muscle

As we age:
Basal mTOR activity increases
Autophagy decreases
Damaged proteins accumulate
Mitochondrial function declines

So occasional mTOR suppression (fasting, exercise, caloric restriction) allows cells to clean house.

Then feeding + protein + resistance training activates mTORC1 to rebuild.

Trainer-Friendly Analogy

You can explain it like this:
AMPK / Autophagy = Cleaning the factory
mTORC1 = Building new machines

If you only build and never clean → the factory breaks.
If you only clean and never build → nothing grows.

Healthy aging requires both cycles.

Practical Application for Muscle & Longevity

Best evidence-based pattern:
Resistance training
→ stimulates mTORC1

Protein intake (especially leucine/EAA)
→ activates muscle protein synthesis

Periods of energy deficit or fasting
→ stimulate AMPK & autophagy

This cycle maintains:
• muscle mass
• metabolic health
• mitochondrial quality

One Sentence Trainer Takeaway

“Longevity physiology alternates between AMPK-driven repair and mTOR-driven rebuilding — the key is cycling between them, not chronically activating either one.”

If you'd like, I can also show you something extremely useful for your trainer curriculum:
The 4-Switch Longevity Model
1️⃣ AMPK
2️⃣ mTOR
3️⃣ Sirtuins
4️⃣ IGF-1

Understanding how these interact makes the Playspan® longevity concept very easy for trainers to teach.

If this is true about fasting helping athletic performance or to build maximum muscle including in aging, why are competitive athletes or serious exercisers trying to maintain muscle hypertrophy, told to eat every 4-hours whenever possible because we know the body goes into a catabolic state ~4 hours after a meal and we want to stimulate the muscle protein synthesis as soon as possible.

This is an excellent question, and it gets to the difference between two goals that are often confused:
Maximizing muscle hypertrophy in the short term (competitive athletes)
Optimizing long-term health, recovery, and muscle preservation with aging

Both use the same physiology (mTOR, AMPK, protein synthesis, autophagy), but they emphasize different priorities and time horizons.

Why Athletes Eat Every ~3–4 Hours

The recommendation for athletes trying to maximize hypertrophy or recovery comes from how muscle protein synthesis (MPS) behaves after eating protein.

After a protein meal:
Amino acids rise in blood
Leucine activates mTORC1
Muscle protein synthesis increases

This response typically lasts ~3–4 hours.

After that:
Amino acid levels fall
mTORC1 activity drops
MPS returns to baseline

So athletes eat again to re-stimulate MPS.

Typical hypertrophy pattern:

| Time | Effect |
| Breakfast protein | MPS ↑ |
| 3–4 hours later | MPS returns to baseline |
| Next protein feeding | MPS ↑ again |

Thus the classic recommendation:
Protein feedings every 3–5 hours.

The “Muscle Full” Effect

There is also an important phenomenon called the muscle full effect.

After a protein feeding:
MPS increases for ~2–3 hours
Then the muscle becomes temporarily resistant to further stimulation
Even if amino acids remain high.

So the body needs time between meals before it can respond again.

This is why spacing protein meals matters.

Where the “Catabolic State” Idea Comes From

The idea that the body becomes catabolic after ~4 hours is partly simplified language.

What actually happens:
After several hours without food:
Muscle protein synthesis declines
Muscle protein breakdown slightly increases

However, in healthy people:
Net muscle loss over a few hours is very small.

Even overnight fasting does not cause meaningful muscle loss if daily protein intake is sufficient.

Why Fasting Is Sometimes Recommended for Longevity

Longer fasting periods trigger:
• AMPK activation
• autophagy
• mitochondrial repair

These processes improve:
metabolic health
insulin sensitivity
cellular repair

But they temporarily suppress mTORC1, meaning muscle growth signaling is reduced during the fast.

So fasting is not optimal for maximizing hypertrophy, but it may help long-term cellular health.

The Key Difference: Performance vs Longevity Priorities

| Goal | Strategy |
| Maximize muscle growth | Frequent protein feedings |
| Maximize longevity/metabolic repair | Periods of fasting |
| Balance muscle + health | Cycles of feeding and fasting |

Competitive athletes prioritize maximal anabolic signaling.

Longevity strategies emphasize periodic repair signaling.

What Actually Preserves Muscle Best (Evidence-Based)

For maintaining or building muscle, especially with aging, the most important factors are:
Total daily protein intake
Resistance training
Adequate leucine per meal

Meal frequency matters far less than once believed.

Current evidence suggests:
3–4 protein meals per day
is generally sufficient.

Example:
Breakfast
Lunch
Post-workout / Dinner
Optional pre-sleep protein

For Aging Muscle (Sarcopenia Prevention)

Older adults often benefit from larger protein doses per meal because of anabolic resistance.

Typical recommendation:
0.4–0.5 g protein/kg per meal

Example:
80 kg adult
~35–40 g protein per meal
3–4 meals/day

What the Best Athletes Actually Do

Interestingly, many elite athletes now combine both concepts:

Feeding periods
protein every ~4 hours
mTOR stimulation

Recovery windows
overnight fasting
AMPK/autophagy activation

Example daily rhythm:
Morning training (fasted or light meal)
Post-training protein
Lunch protein
Dinner protein
Overnight fast (10–12 hours)

Trainer-Friendly Explanation

You could explain it like this:
“Muscle grows when mTOR is activated by protein and training, but long-term health requires occasional periods where AMPK and autophagy clean and repair cells. The goal isn’t constant growth signaling — it’s cycling between repair and rebuilding.”

But it appears that the 10–12 hour fast is enough for extra time, since meals are 4–5 hours apart, there is enough time and rest to restart MPS.

Simple Takeaway

For maximum hypertrophy:
• 3–5 protein meals per day
• 0.4 g/kg per meal
• resistance training

For muscle + longevity balance:
• same protein intake
• allow 10–12 hr overnight fast – agrees with me

If you'd like, I can also show you something extremely interesting for your trainer curriculum:
Why constant mTOR activation may actually accelerate aging in muscle — yet resistance training still increases lifespan.

That paradox is one of the most fascinating discoveries in exercise physiology.

This is one of the most interesting paradoxes in exercise physiology and aging research, and it actually fits very well with the Playspan® concept you often teach — balancing repair and performance.

The key idea is that mTOR itself is not harmful.
The problem is chronic, unopposed mTOR activation without periods of cellular repair.

The mTOR Paradox: Growth vs Aging

mTOR is fundamentally a growth signal. It tells cells:
“We have nutrients and energy — build tissue.”

This is extremely beneficial in the right context:
• muscle growth
• tissue repair
• immune function
• recovery from exercise

However, if mTOR is constantly elevated, several aging processes accelerate.

Why Constant mTOR Activation Can Accelerate Aging

When mTORC1 stays chronically high:

1. Autophagy is Suppressed

Autophagy is the cell’s recycling and cleanup system.

It removes:
• damaged mitochondria
• misfolded proteins
• cellular debris
• dysfunctional organelles

But mTORC1 directly inhibits autophagy.

If autophagy stays suppressed too long, cells accumulate damage.

2. Damaged Mitochondria Accumulate

Mitochondria constantly generate oxidative stress.

Normally, old mitochondria are removed through mitophagy.

Without this process:
• ROS increases
• energy production declines
• metabolic disease risk rises

This is a hallmark of aging tissue.

3. Cellular Resources Shift Toward Growth Instead of Repair

Cells only have so much energy.

Constant mTOR signaling prioritizes:
• protein synthesis
• cell growth
• proliferation

Instead of:
• DNA repair
• mitochondrial renewal
• protein quality control

Over decades this leads to cellular dysfunction.

This Is Why Caloric Restriction Extends Lifespan

Caloric restriction activates:
• AMPK
• Sirtuins
• Autophagy

These pathways suppress mTOR periodically and allow cellular repair.

In nearly every animal model studied:
Lower chronic mTOR signaling → longer lifespan.

But Resistance Training Activates mTOR — Yet Extends Life

Here is the key difference.

Exercise causes transient mTOR activation, not chronic activation.

The pattern looks like this:

| Phase | Pathway | Effect |
| Training | AMPK ↑ | Energy stress |
| Recovery + protein | mTORC1 ↑ | Muscle repair |
| Between sessions | Autophagy ↑ | Cellular cleanup |

This cycling produces a repair → rebuild → repair → rebuild rhythm.

Exercise Actually Activates Both Longevity Pathways

During exercise:
AMPK increases dramatically.

This triggers:
• mitochondrial biogenesis
• glucose uptake
• fat oxidation
• autophagy

After exercise, when protein is consumed:
mTOR activates to rebuild muscle.

This sequence is sometimes called metabolic flexibility signaling.

Why Sedentary Overnutrition Is the Problem

Chronic mTOR activation happens most often with:
• constant calorie surplus
• high insulin levels
• lack of exercise
• obesity

This produces permanently elevated mTOR signaling.

In that situation:
• autophagy remains suppressed
• metabolic dysfunction increases
• aging accelerates

Exercise Restores the Natural Cycle

Resistance training and physical activity restore the normal biological rhythm.

Exercise phase
AMPK ↑
Autophagy ↑
Energy stress

Recovery phase
mTOR ↑
Protein synthesis ↑

This oscillation appears to be optimal for longevity.

Evidence From Human Longevity Studies

People with the highest lifespan consistently show:
• regular physical activity
• strong muscle mass
• metabolic flexibility

Muscle mass itself is one of the strongest predictors of longevity.

Low muscle mass increases risk for:
• frailty
• metabolic disease
• mortality

Why Muscle Is a Longevity Organ

Skeletal muscle functions as a metabolic control center.

It regulates:
• glucose disposal
• insulin sensitivity
• inflammation
• mitochondrial function

Maintaining muscle through life dramatically reduces disease risk.

The Real Longevity Strategy

The goal is not suppressing mTOR.
The goal is cycling mTOR appropriately. (exactly what we recommend)

Healthy physiology alternates between:
Repair state
(AMPK, autophagy)
and
Growth state
(mTOR, protein synthesis)

Trainer-Friendly Analogy

You might describe it like this:
AMPK and autophagy clean the gym.
mTOR builds new equipment.

If you only build and never clean → the gym becomes dysfunctional.
If you only clean and never build → the gym never improves.

Health requires both processes cycling together.

A Simple Summary for Your Trainers to maximize muscle health for both strength and longevity (muscle and overall cellular health).

When you add resistance training and timed meals to properly control mTOR: although constant mTOR activation accelerates aging because it suppresses cellular repair—resistance training improves longevity because it activates mTOR only temporarily, while exercise itself activates AMPK and autophagy. This cycle of repair and rebuilding keeps tissues younger and stronger over time.

So 10–12 hr overnight fast is the longest you would want to fast (typical overnight). From there, spacing meals with the 1st soon after rising and then divide remaining meals into 3–5 feedings depending on the goal and age is the perfect strategy for both goals.

Younger hypertrophy/strength athletes can be more aggressive in maximizing mTOR1 activation through more frequent protein/amino acid feedings to help maximize performance, taking advantage of when hormone levels are higher.

If you'd like, I can also show you something extremely useful for teaching trainers:
A simple “Longevity Signaling Map” showing the interaction of the four master pathways:
mTOR
AMPK
Sirtuins
IGF-1

Once trainers see that diagram, the entire nutrition + training + supplement strategy suddenly makes

title: TB-500 and BPC-157 woverine stack usage
content:
In what is commonly referred to as the "Wolverine Stack," BPC-157 and TB-500 are not dosed on the same schedule, even though they are often started at the same time and used synergistically.

The rationale is that they appear to work through somewhat different mechanisms:

BPC-157 = more localized tissue repair signaling, angiogenesis, tendon-to-bone healing, gut repair, and cellular protection.

TB-500 = more systemic tissue remodeling, cell migration, connective tissue recovery, and mobility support.

Typical Wolverine Stack Protocol

BPC-157
250–500 mcg daily

Often split:
250 mcg AM
250 mcg PM

Or 500 mcg once daily

Usually continued for 4–8 weeks

TB-500
2–2.5 mg twice weekly

Example:
Monday = 2.5 mg
Thursday = 2.5 mg
Total = 5 mg/week

Usually continued for 4–6 weeks loading

Followed by:
2–5 mg every 2–4 weeks maintenance if desired

Example 6-Week Wolverine Stack

Weeks 1–6

Daily
BPC-157: 500 mcg/day

Twice Weekly
TB-500: 2.5 mg Monday
TB-500: 2.5 mg Thursday

This is probably the most commonly discussed protocol among sports medicine clinics and peptide practitioners.

Site-Specific vs. Systemic

One common approach is:

BPC-157

Injected:
Near injured tendon
Near ligament
Near joint
Near muscle injury

Examples:
Patellar tendon
Rotator cuff region
Achilles tendon
Elbow tendon

TB-500

Injected:
Abdomen
Thigh
Anywhere subcutaneously

Because TB-500 is generally considered systemic, practitioners usually do not attempt site-specific administration.

Why They Are Combined

The theory is:

BPC-157

Provides:
Local repair signaling
Angiogenesis
Tendon-to-bone healing support
Cytoprotection

TB-500

Provides:
Cellular migration
Tissue remodeling
New blood vessel formation
Connective tissue recovery

Together they potentially cover multiple phases of tissue healing.

Practical Duration

For an athlete with a tendon or soft tissue injury:

| Compound | Typical Duration |
| BPC-157 | 4–8 weeks |
| TB-500 | 4–6 week loading phase |
| Combined Stack | 4–8 weeks |

Many practitioners discontinue both once symptoms resolve rather than cycling indefinitely.

Trainer/Educator Takeaway

If discussing the Wolverine Stack in an educational setting, the key point is that BPC-157 is typically administered daily because of its shorter activity profile and localized healing focus, while TB-500 is generally administered only once or twice weekly because of its longer systemic activity. They are started together, but they are not usually injected at the same frequency.

One additional note: despite widespread use in athletic and recovery communities, both compounds remain investigational, human clinical data are limited, and neither is FDA-approved for injury treatment. Therefore, they should be viewed as adjuncts to the fundamentals that drive recovery—appropriate rehabilitation, progressive loading, adequate protein intake, sleep, and overall nutrition.

title: Calories&WtLossQ&A (part 1 of 2)
content:
Is Weight Loss Really All About Calories In and Out?

Below are 2 articles from the Fitness Vault that put the issue in perspective and answer many related questions:

We know that you have always been a strict believer in weight loss being a simple calories-in-versus-calories-out equation. Is this still true?

A Calorie Is a Calorie—or Is It?

Although all experts agree that calorie balance is the root of weight changes, below is a quote from one of the world's leading experts on weight control:

We asked Dr. Jules Hirsch, emeritus professor and emeritus physician in chief at Rockefeller University, who has been researching obesity for nearly 60 years, about the state of any research that "appears" to contradict calorie balance facts and weight control. Dr. Hirsch, who receives no money from pharmaceutical companies or the diet industry, wrote some of the classic papers describing why it is so hard to lose weight and why it usually comes back.

"Perhaps the most important illusion is the belief that a calorie is not a calorie but depends on how much carbohydrates a person eats. There is an inflexible law of physics—energy taken in must exactly equal the number of calories leaving the system when fat storage is unchanged. Calories leave the system when food is used to fuel the body. To lower fat content—to reduce obesity—one must reduce calories taken in, or increase the output by increasing activity, or both. This is true whether calories come from pumpkins or peanuts or pâté de foie gras. To believe otherwise is to believe we can find a really good perpetual motion machine to solve our energy problems. It won’t work, and neither will changing the source of calories permit us to disobey the laws of science."

Below is the complete set of Q&A based on the calorie balance/weight control questions.

We know that dotFIT has always been a strict believer in weight loss being a simple calories-in-versus-calories-out equation.

The laws of energy are facts that form our entire world. The moment you think weight control/mass changes are not about the laws of energy, you have no basis to work with and you forever fall into the diet abyss. Once you make peace with the facts, you are free to choose how to accomplish the goal.

I think we have all had a client who swears to consuming an extreme calorie deficit and still does not see weight loss. This simply means their food-recording method is flawed, not the laws of energy.

If we truly believe that the client is honest in their logging (they may be honest, but then the math is flawed on either one or both sides of the equation—mass changes don't lie), what is the best way to approach this situation? Get them an armband, put them on the program, enter their weight each week, and follow directions. The feedback NEVER tells you how much you truly ate, ONLY what you need to do to hit your goal. You can't argue with the energy expenditure numbers from the armband, and you can't argue with weekly average mass change from the same scale/body-fat measurement, so the feedback is ALWAYS correct—this is where you start. Now, for the next steps, see similar Q&A below.

Most people that you describe here will forever be lost in their denial or complete lack of understanding, making their recording accuracy impossible. Therefore, in their minds, they are right. If the latter is the problem, you can start by giving them this article from the dotFIT Fitness Vault: "How You May Be Sabotaging Your Weight" http://www.dotfit.com/content-1453.html, followed by using our Plateau Solution Q&As.

If denial is the problem, it's beyond your expertise other than education of the facts and hoping they have a life-changing moment that will make them stick to the proper eating/calorie plan. Trust me, if they have to, they will eat exactly as told and lose the weight.

What can we do to keep people motivated and break the weight loss and gain cycle permanently?
http://www.dotfit.com/content-35967.html

There is no such thing as "permanently" for everybody, but there are people that have successfully lost weight and kept it off for long periods of time. These people's plights have been chronicled in a database housed at the University of Pittsburgh and Colorado Denver. It's called The National Weight Control Registry (NWCR). The "trigger event," or reason for losing weight, was the primary factor in sticking with a lifestyle/diet that allowed the weight loss and maintaining it—i.e., highly motivated. The second part to the equation is becoming "addicted" to that lifestyle, which these people have now accomplished. The information that has been captured from these successful maintainers was a list of common denominators—i.e., common aspects of their new daily routines. Listed below are the salient like-factors that created success. Also keep in mind, because it's evidence-based, these factors are built into and shape the dotFIT program.

Common denominators to successful weight loss and maintenance (data from NWCR), all contained in the dotFIT program—current evidence-based criteria:

- Low-fat (including proteins), restricted-calorie diet (portion control)
- Regular physical activity (~1 hour/day, including walking)
- Maintain eating patterns (structured, recording, meal replacements)
- Breakfast (begins the structure)
- Self-monitoring of weight
- Correcting rebounds before they become large gains
- Meal replacements as appropriate

The dotFIT program's agnostic nature (they can participate on their terms) reduces the need for compliance, and the use of the armband and coaching can guarantee success.

#1 most popular question: How do you get through weight loss/fat plateaus?
http://www.dotfit.com/content-35872.html

We can make anyone look different every day if they follow their program. Just like we do for bodybuilders, actors, or other athletes and celebrities that must control body fat to look a certain way in order to win or collect a paycheck. You only come to a weight or body-fat plateau for one reason: diet compared to activity. And to correct it there is only one answer, albeit many ways to accomplish the answer, and that's to burn more and/or consume less. What, including how much, you put back into your body post-exercise and throughout the day is what makes your exercise-induced body-composition changes. Nothing happens if you don’t eat except shrinking until death. Nothing happens to body fat if you consume the same amount of calories you burn. So, obviously, it is a simple matter of adjusting food and/or movement. Below is the complete answer:

There are 2 series of solutions to the plateau problem: 1) if you are complying with the proper program, then the solution is an adjustment to the program because your body has gone through an adaptation to the workload and calorie intake. The good news is that the dotFIT (dF) program always correctly makes that adjustment for you when you enter your weekly/biweekly measurements by giving you the option to create a new program based on results (or lack of results) and goal date. 2) You are unable to comply with weekly program instructions based on motivation and/or the program doesn’t fit your desired lifestyle.

Complying with the program:

- Change the workout and/or intensity, including mode of cardio.
- Increase daily activities any way you can (read below).
- Reduce calories at each meal or consume half of your largest meal.
- Add weight-control supplements to help burn more and/or eat fewer calories.
- Incorporate the armband for accuracy and daily visibility to help increase all activities.

When it comes to weight/fat loss, when you come to a plateau, you must burn more, consume less, or a combination of the two—period! So first let's understand why the body eventually plateaus even when you are doing exactly what you were doing when you were losing weight, which, of course, is the problem. The main reason the body comes to plateaus during dieting or exercise (besides consciously or unconsciously not properly following the plan) is that when weight is lost and as you become more fit, your body uses fewer calories to perform the same work, which forces you to have to perform more (or significantly different) work and/or eat less in order to continue to progress. A second common reason is an overall reduction in daily activities away from the gym. A person may, through a change in employment or other lifestyle alterations, simply start to move less throughout the day, and now exercise cannot offset the decrease in daily calorie burn. And finally, this: during dieting or at any time following significant weight loss, one will often tend to binge-eat as the body attempts to recover lost pounds. And it only takes one “binge” to wipe out a week’s worth of accurate dieting. Most people can’t believe this because they worked hard to consume the proper amounts for 7 or 10 straight days, so the one binge is either underestimated, forgotten, or they never grasped the fact that every calorie counts no matter when it’s eaten and all figures into one’s daily average. All this said, our general recommendation for plateaus for people who eat well and exercise regularly (and are “tapped out” as far as time or cutting calories) is to increase your daily movements at home or at the office. Never sit when you can stand or pace, such as when using the phone. Standing and/or pacing can burn more than 2 times the calories as sitting! Click here for our article with more tips: http://www.dotfit.com/content-1484.html. Additionally, changing the workout (including interval training, intensity, and type of cardio you perform) can help burn a few more calories in the same timeframe. And finally, you can add supplements like CarbRepel, FatRelease, and/or ThermAccel that can help you burn more daily calories by bumping your metabolism and/or inducing more daily movements, partially block incoming calories, and help control appetite.

Summary for compliers:

Monitoring: Weigh/measure in the same clothing, at the same time, and on the same scale. Take care to also use the same method or device for body-fat measurements. If necessary (see below), only adjust calories in or out every seven days.

Adjustments: A measurable or visual reduction in body fat and/or weight should take place in a fairly consistent manner, such as a decrease in circumference inches and/or the desired average decrease in weight or body fat per week. If progress stops or slows dramatically, one or a mixture of the following adjustments will be necessary to restart the process:

- Increase daily activities (e.g., daily steps or other non-athletic/exercise activities).
- Standing and pacing burn 2–3 times more calories than sitting for the same time period.
- There are approximately 2,000–2,500 steps (depending on stride length) in a mile. Walking 2,000 steps will burn ~75–150 more calories (depending on individual size) than sitting for the same time and only takes ~20–30 minutes and can be done anywhere, even in the office, while on the phone, or watching TV.
- Increase workout time or intensity.
- Decrease food intake approximately 200 to 300 calories per day or remove a small portion of your largest meal.

Repeat the process any time weight or body fat is stable for at least one week. Always remember: if you stop losing weight/fat, you need to eat less, move more, or a combination of the two, regardless of what you read or hear from others. Once you have achieved your body-composition goals, increase your calorie intake, decrease activities, or use a combination of the two in order to maintain the desired weight.

Not or unable to comply:

The inability to comply with a program designed to accomplish a fitness goal is almost always due to lack of motivation. Therefore, the first thing we need to do for our clients that fall into this category is to lower the motivation threshold for success. Make it easy to follow the plan by making it their plan and not forcing them to change their life in order to succeed. Instead, start with minor adjustments to their current lifestyle, including eating habits. Example: don’t tell them what to eat; just tell them how much by knowing how many calories they burn. Make the exercise program fit into their current lifestyle, even if it’s only walking to start. Just make sure they burn more calories than they consume if losing fat is a goal. Show them immediate results and instant gratification by teaching them how to watch their fat/weight come off by the minute or hour using the dotFIT program with or without the armband. Motivation comes with constant visibility to results. Seeing is believing and constant reinforcement that what you’re doing is working.

You must be the creator of your program or you won’t be the master.

The only way you will own a behavioral change is if you create it. Start the client any way you can, sticking to this simple rule: burn more calories than you consume, on average, until you reach your goal. Just follow the number. The good news is that “one good turn deserves another,” meaning, as the body changes and the client starts to look and feel better, they will also do things better. BUT the first turn has to come easily and on their terms, or they are set to fail or eventually give up. Square pegs don’t fit in round holes—they need to own their program because it fits the life they choose, not a life someone else chooses for them. Everyone wants to be lean, but they must arrive their way. Your guidance and using the dotFIT program allows total flexibility, thus dramatically lowering the need for motivation. NO one can stick to a program they can’t or won’t want to do forever. Show them that the world is the gym: keep moving any way you can; and their food is their diet: they can eat ANYTHING they want, just not EVERYTHING they want. Knowing your numbers and seeing immediate feedback makes motivation far less necessary to succeed. All that said, there are some proven motivational tips listed below, and remember that creating new habits is a continual process but has the best chance of leading to lasting change.

- Create a vision of your ideal self.
- Set 90-day goals.
- Set weekly SMART goals.
- Track success rate weekly.
- Adjust along the way.
- Use setbacks to learn and grow.

Outline of Steps:

1. Create a vision

Write down the answers to these questions:

- What do you value most?
- How does your health and fitness relate to what’s important to you?
- Envision your ideal self. What do you look like?
- What do you feel like?
- What are you doing?
- What are you NOT doing?
- What are the benefits to realizing your vision?
- What are your strengths that will help you?
- When have you been successful in the past? How did that feel?
- What accomplishments are you proud of?
- Who can provide support?
- What resources can you use along the way?
- What would life be like if you reached your vision?
- What would life be like if you didn’t?

2. Commit to your vision

Write it down in the present, sign your name, and share it with someone.

- Post cues to remind you of your vision.
- Sticky note on mirror.
- Schedule a daily appointment to review.
- Find a photo or paint an image.

3. Set 90-day goals

- What do you want to accomplish in the next 90 days?
- What behaviors will help you reach your vision?
- Write down 3–5 in order of importance.

4. Set weekly SMART goals—specific actions needed to reach 90-day goals and vision.

- Identify 1–5 things you’d like to work on.
- S—specific—what, when.
- M—measurable—how much.
- A—action-based.
- R—relevant—to the 90-day goal.
- T—time-bound.

Vague vs. SMART goals:

- I will drink more water VS. I will drink 1 glass of water with lunch and dinner 5 days a week.
- I will work out regularly VS. I will do an aerobic class after work, 3 days a week.
- I will eat 5 servings of fruits and vegetables a day VS. I will eat a piece of fruit at breakfast and snack 4 days a week.

5. Review what went well on a weekly basis and make adjustments.

Recall your best experiences over the past week.

For your weekly SMART goals, calculate your percent success rate. Example:

Goal: Drink 1 glass of water at lunch and dinner 5 days/week.
Result: 3 days = 60% success.

Questions to answer:

- What contributed to your success?
- What could have made it higher?
- What challenges did you face?
- Is this goal too ambitious or too easy?
- What are you getting out of this goal?
- On a scale of 1 to 10, how confident are you that you can maintain this behavior in the next few weeks? If you’re not at least a 7, consider revising the goal.

6. Turn setbacks into learning experiences. Trial and correction, not trial and error, leads to success.

- Evaluate setback.
- Identify triggers that put you at risk—people, places, environments, situations.
- Make a list of ways to modify or eliminate triggers and do it now or set a SMART goal.

#2 most popular Q&A: How do I avoid the starvation mode when dieting? http://www.dotfit.com/content-35585.html

The good news is that the “starvation mode” does not exist for any human being. Unfortunately, even some well-known health professionals have contributed to this myth, but it is simply not true. The so-called “starvation mode” is the point where the body supposedly decides not to lose more weight, even when you eat “hardly anything,” by slowing down the metabolism because the body is afraid you will starve to death. To put your entire issue into perspective, first realize that the people around the world who truly die of starvation do not pass away overweight.

This myth was born from a combination of facts: 1) we physically move very little in the modern world, thus burn few daily calories compared to our ancestors; and 2) most people unconsciously or consciously tend to underreport their TRUE calorie intake by 20–45% (the more overweight, the more they underreport). Therefore, we are actually eating more and moving less than we think.

The main reason the body comes to plateaus during dieting or exercise (besides consciously or unconsciously not properly following the plan) is that when weight is lost and you become more fit, your body uses fewer calories to perform the same workload. Your muscles are more efficient, making work easier, and you are moving less body weight during all activities, forcing you to add work or eat less in order to continue to progress. Also, dieting often makes people become less energetic, forcing a reduction in their daily activities and therefore burning fewer calories overall. My general recommendation for plateaus for people who eat well and exercise regularly (therefore are “tapped out” as far as time or cutting calories) is to simply increase your daily movements at home or at the office. Stand or pace anytime you can instead of sitting: pace the room while on the phone or thinking, take stairs instead of elevators or escalators, park farther away from your final destination, take a walk at lunch, walk to a colleague’s office to talk rather than use email or the intercom, etc. Additionally, you can try changing your workout, including the intensity and type of cardio you perform, which can help you burn a few more calories in the same workout timeframe. And never sit down or stop moving in the gym.

What's the largest calorie deficit I can be in and still avoid the starvation mode?

title: Calories&WtLossQ&A (part 2 of 2)
content:
What you mean is: What is the biggest deficit you can be in and not lose muscle/lean body mass (LBM)? We say this because there is no starvation mode, only the myth and a bad excuse for not losing weight when supposedly dieting. First of all, any time you lose weight you lose both muscle and fat (1/4 muscle, 3/4 fat) unless you supplement and weight-train. BUT even with weight training, you can't lose any more than .7% of weight/week without losing muscle. For example, a person weighing 200 lbs can lose 1.4 lb/week (~750 cal/day deficit)—BUT they must supplement at least a daily multivitamin and mineral (MVM).

The greater the deficit, the more you need to supplement, meaning ideally, to preserve or increase LBM, you need to consume a diet consisting of ~500–1000 fewer calories than you burn, an MVM, and a pre/post workout formula. This is what all dieters should do because the goal is to increase LBM during weight loss to help burn more calories, not less. This can help offset the fitness/weight loss paradox: "The more fit and lighter we get, the fewer calories we burn when all things are equal and thus end up at plateaus, which forces us to make an unwanted adjustment."

I only eat 1000 calories daily but can't lose weight. Do I have a slow metabolism? What should I do?
http://www.dotfit.com/content-35588.html

With all due respect, only a 90-lb bedridden person would burn so few calories daily. Therefore, unless that describes you, you need to improve the accuracy of your food-intake records. So that's the good news; only the math is flawed, not your metabolism. Currently, it's very clear that metabolisms between like-people (same weight, gender, etc.) don't significantly vary, so metabolism is definitely not your problem.

Regardless of your food or exercise recording, first remember: anytime you are attempting weight loss, come to a weight-loss plateau, or are gaining unwanted weight, you need to move more, eat less, or a combination of the two if you want to proceed to the weight-loss goal—PERIOD. The evidence-based (scientific) formula for weight loss is contained within the dotFIT program. Set your goal to lose 1–2 lbs/week, follow the directions each time you enter a new weight, and you will reach your goal. If you follow the program, a measurable or visual reduction in body fat and/or weight should take place in a fairly consistent manner, such as a decrease in circumference inches and/or the desired average decrease in weight or body fat per week. If progress stops or slows dramatically, one or a mixture of the following adjustments will be necessary to restart the process:

- Increase daily activities (e.g., daily steps or other non-athletic/exercise activities).
- Standing and pacing burn 2–3 times more calories than sitting for the same time period.
- There are approximately 2,000–2,500 steps (depending on stride length) in a mile. Walking 2,000 steps will burn ~75–150 more calories (depending on individual size) than sitting for the same time and only takes ~20–30 minutes and can be done anywhere, even in the office, while on the phone, or watching TV.
- Increase workout time or intensity.
- Decrease food intake approximately 200 to 300 calories per day or remove a small portion of your largest meal.

Repeat the process any time weight or body fat is stable for at least one week. Always remember: if you stop losing weight/fat, you need to eat less, move more, or a combination of the two, regardless of what you read or hear from others.

Why should I have to "count calories" to reach my goal?
http://www.dotfit.com/content-35968.html

You don't have to if you are trending as desired to your goal and validating this through measurements/weight/appearance, etc., and feeling your best. In other words, you can tell without counting calories that you are moving in the right direction based on measurements or appearance. If you come to a plateau, you simply need to eat less and/or move more than whatever you were doing that kept your mass stable (plateau), and this can simply be a reduction in portion sizes.

Counting calories is a good place to start for most people. Once you know how much you burn, you now know how much to eat to get started losing (or gaining) weight. Keep in mind that, according to the data housed at the National Weight Control Registry (NWCR) on successful weight maintainers—people who lose weight and keep it off—people record foods regularly.

The moral of the story is: if you can do it without counting calories, go for it, but percentages tell us more people will be successful if they pay attention to calories.

And Finally

When food logging does not match estimated, thus perceived, deficit:
http://www.dotfit.com/content-35969.html

It is basically impossible for anyone to accurately record foods, even if they weigh all foods and use label counts. Here’s why:

- Labels are rarely accurate (can be up to 300% off).
- Same-food calorie counts often vary between sources.
- It is impossible to accurately guess restaurant meals.
- Incomplete recall (missing items, including sauces, dressings, etc.).
- Generally, people underreport 20–40%.
- You cannot account for LBM gains as the program can (only a measurement in body mass can determine this), and therefore part of a human-calculated deficit may have been deposited in LBM, lowering the perceived deficit (i.e., client records a 500 average-calorie deficit but gained 1 lb of muscle and therefore the deficit was ~200)*.
- Water—occasionally, due to uncontrollable circumstances, you may have gained some temporary water weight, and therefore at this point in time the scale may not represent your body-mass change, thus the deficit accurately.

If you believe you have lost fat or weight and your scale does not confirm it, wait another week until your next weigh-in. Weight gain due to water retention will quickly subside or stabilize, and within a 2-week timeframe you will receive a more accurate accounting of your combined food intake, deficit, and body weight. Additionally, our body-fat or circumference measurements (biweekly) will capture the true progress trend and match it to the weekly loss goal.

*LBM—you may have gained LBM since your last weigh-in, offsetting a weight reduction from loss of BF—this is a desirable situation, but fat loss will soon surpass the LBM increase when weight reduction is the primary goal. Therefore, simply use the body-fat reading as the current trend indicator.

Bottom line: all program short-term discrepancy issues go away over time—the true trend will emerge generally by the end of the 2nd week, but certainly by the 3rd, and no more excuses by the end of the 4th (after 2 follow-up BF & WT measurements), meaning the program numbers are correct and you must adjust accordingly.
