title: Hormone home-tests accuracy, testosterone levels, adrenals,etc.
content:
At-Home Hormone Tests: Are They Accurate?
A proliferation of at-home tests are available to check thyroid function and other hormones, offering patients the comfort of testing these levels remotely. This availability is expected to grow to a $4.79 billion market by 2030, according to Research and Markets analysis.
The growing demand can be attributed partly to a rise in comfort with testing at home due to the COVID-19 pandemic, which increased people's confidence in remote healthcare.
But are these tests reliable? And should people be taking them at home?
Medscape asked [NAME], PhD, professor of medicine, physiology, and surgery at the Medical College of Wisconsin, Milwaukee, and [NAME], MD, MBA, chief of endocrinology, diabetes, and metabolism at Suburban Hospital, Johns Hopkins Medicine, Bethesda, Maryland, for their opinions on these tests, based on their backgrounds in research and clinical practice, respectively.
"I really believe that if it's done for the right reasons by educated people who are not just out to make a profit — I hate to say that, but — if it is really in the best interest of the patient, they can be wonderful," said [NAME] when asked about the reliability of these tests.
However, it's important that patients work with their healthcare providers to ensure the appropriate use and interpretation of the results, noted [NAME], who has developed salivary cortisol tests with at-home sampling.
What are the most common reasons for patients taking at-home tests? Are they bringing the results to their visits?
[NAME]: Personally, I do not encourage my patients to use those at-home hormonal tests, but more and more they are ordering them online. Just recently one of my patients told me she ordered a hormonal test online. She was wondering if I could interpret [the results]. I think this is how it should be. I'm glad that the patient wanted me to interpret the test, but ultimately, I have to be very careful to know why she even ordered it.
Although I've never asked my patients why they are getting them, I'll speculate. Obviously, those companies have done a great job at advertising them. You type "at-home hormonal test kits" [into a search engine and] there are dozens, if not hundreds, of companies that offer them. I think people are having a hard time finding endocrinologists. There are only 5000 endocrinologists in the United States, and obviously there aren't enough to see these patients or reliably evaluate … hormone tests, so patients are [saying], "I'm just going to test it. It's not too much money. It's about $100 to $200. I'm going to test it and figure out what is going on."
There are some hormonal test kits that have been around for a long time, such as ovulation prediction kits. The test uses a urine sample to measure luteinizing hormone levels. It can predict ovulation, when women can more easily become pregnant.
What are the main reasons you see for patients using these tests?
[NAME]: I'm not a clinician; I'm a lab guy. Doctors send me the results often and ask me to explain them.
I've had many doctors send me the adrenal stress indexes and adrenal fatigue indexes, and I'm very skeptical of those. The assays are probably fine, but … the interpretation is dubious, so it's like any blood test. I had a great mentor who said, "Don't order a test if you don't know what to do with the results, because if you order enough tests, something is always going to be abnormal."
What are some of the pros and cons of these tests?
[NAME]: Convenience is the biggest pro. Some companies, for example, aim [their tests] at treating hyperthyroid, a very common hormonal problem. People just have to prick their fingers [rather than] go to the lab to have their blood drawn, which can sometimes be painful. They send the test kit back through the mail. The results will [be sent] in a few days and … can be seen by a physician and a patient at the same time. So the convenience factor is such that the patient can mail everything in and jump on a quick televisit to discuss the results.
The challenge is that they are not very reliable. Some of the hormones fluctuate very little, but some can fluctuate a lot—for example, testosterone in males. If you measure it in the morning, you are going to get a more reliable [result] compared to measuring in the afternoon or in the evening. There are certain standards, so obviously, when I talk to my colleagues and see students and fellows and residents, I tell them to make sure that these patients know to make sure this hormone kit is made by a Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA)-certified lab.
CLIA checks laboratories to ensure that they are delivering quality results. Whatever the results coming back, it's not just "jump and interpret the results as high, low, or normal." As physicians, we [need to ask ourselves] why we would even get this test in the first place. What is the history? Before we even start testing hormone levels, [the patient] needs to have symptoms. Does this patient have fatigue, weight gain, or leg swelling? These are the symptoms of hyperthyroidism, and then you check the hormone levels.
It's okay for the patient to bring the results, and I tell everyone, "Do not dismiss your patients," but it is important that physicians are the ones that interpret those results.
Are the tests accurate? Do they provide appropriate information for patients?
[NAME]: That's an interesting question because there are two answers. One is that if it is done under the guidance of a bona fide doctor—in this case, an endocrinologist—and the patient is taught how to do it properly, and it is being ordered for the right reason, then it is great. If it's done because you see it in some magazine that says, "Assess your stress levels. Send us 142 samples"—I'm exaggerating; it's usually 10 or 20—"and we will figure out what's wrong with you" without ever seeing the patient or talking to the patient, that becomes very suspect.
[NAME]: It depends on the test. Let's start with some very commonly used and basic tests, like hormonal pregnancy tests. Many people use pregnancy tests at home [which measure human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) hormone]. If positive, then odds are you are probably pregnant, so [this is] super-helpful. Even if you get one positive result, you probably want to double-check with a more certified lab.
It is more challenging to see that some people are googling their conditions, like, "I'm tired, I'm fatigued, I'm gaining weight, [therefore] I must have hypothyroidism. I talked to my neighbor; it's probably thyroid, so I am going to go and get a kit." Is this a good thing?
I think it is also important to note that even though a test is CLIA-certified, it doesn't mean the test results are accurate. There are multiple ways of testing different hormones … but how will a patient [know this]? As a consumer, you would never know the exact methodology behind the test.
How and when should these results guide clinical practice?
[NAME]: I would use this test not to diagnose the problem but to provide follow-up. Let's say someone is diagnosed with hypothyroidism with a blood test in a doctor's office. You start a female patient on a thyroid replacement therapy. As a physician, we know the thyroid medicine, but sometimes it takes months or even a year to titrate to the appropriate dose the patient needs. Do you always need to come do the bloodwork in person? Probably not. If you already have a diagnosis and you want to titrate to the appropriate dose, then I think it's a reasonable idea to use those [at-home] kits to help titrate the dose of your medication.
What advice do you have for other clinicians who may encounter this with their patients?
[NAME]: One is, listen to the patient. Physicians should not be ignorant of these tests because they are widely available online, and some of them are even covered by flexible spending accounts. Physicians should be extremely cautious of certain assays looking for so-called adrenal fatigue. You must educate yourself about what's available in the market. I did some extra research myself today by looking up what is available.
I realized, when I dove deeper, for the male hormone testing, for example, the total testosterone is not measured in the outpatient setting a lot; we would also have to take additional measurements.
If things don't sound right in the hormone testing, I would advise the patient to go to a specific lab and test the results before assigning a big diagnosis. I would like to always confirm it with a CLIA-certified lab, which is reputable.
[NAME] is an award-winning medical journalist. She is a graduate of New York University's Science, Health, and Environmental Reporting Program. Previously, she studied professional writing at Michigan State University, where she also took premedical classes. Her work has taken her to Honduras, Cambodia, France, and Ghana and has appeared in outlets like The New York Times Daily 360, PBS NewsHour, The Huffington Post, Undark, The Root, Psychology Today, Insider, and Tonic (Health by Vice), among other publications.

title: Client Peptide cheat sheet
content:
✅ Client-Facing Handout (Simple, No Jargon)
A clean, friendly one-pager you can give to clients who ask about peptides.

Peptides: What They Are, What They’re Not, and What You Should Know

What Are Peptides?
Peptides are small chains of amino acids. Some are natural signals your body uses for healing, energy, hormones, or metabolism.

A number of synthetic versions are being marketed for recovery, fat loss, and anti-aging.

Most of them are NOT FDA-approved and have NOT been studied long-term in healthy people.

What These Peptides Claim to Do
People use popular peptides because they believe they will help with:
• Faster injury healing
• Better recovery
• More energy
• Fat loss
• Improved hormones
• Anti-aging

Some of these ideas come from animal studies or small human experiments. Most claims are not proven.

The Big Risks You Should Know
Even if peptides sound “natural,” they come with real concerns:

1. Quality and purity vary a lot
Most peptides are made by compounders or online labs. Purity can be inconsistent.

2. Long-term safety is unknown
We don’t yet know how most peptides affect long-term health, hormones, or cancer risk.

3. Some peptides are banned in sports
For example, BPC-157 is prohibited for athletes.

4. Hormone-related peptides affect your body strongly
Peptides that raise growth hormone or sex hormones can affect blood sugar, swelling, nerves, or fertility.

5. Many require medical supervision
Some peptides are actually prescription drugs for specific medical conditions—not general fitness tools.

The Most Important Thing
Whether you use peptides or not, the biggest improvements in health, fat loss, energy, and performance STILL come from:
• Eating the right amount of calories
• Getting enough protein
• Training consistently
• Sleeping well
• Managing stress
• Moving more throughout the day

Peptides cannot replace these essentials.

And they often work less than people expect unless the basics are already dialed in.

If You’re Considering Peptides
Here’s the safest path:

Talk to a qualified medical professional
Don’t buy peptides online or from unregulated sources.

Get baseline labs (hormones, glucose, IGF-1, lipids)
A doctor needs to know where you’re starting.

Fix the basics first
Diet + training + sleep will give you 80–90% of the results.

Use peptides—if at all—only as add-ons, not substitutes

title: Overtraining; over-reaching definitions & solutions
content:
Overreaching vs. Overtraining — What They Really Mean

Athletes and serious exercisers often use the terms interchangeably, but in exercise physiology they are very different conditions.

Functional Overreaching (FOR)

This is the planned, short-term increase in training stress designed to temporarily reduce performance so the body can later rebound stronger.

Definition

A short-term accumulation of training stress that causes:
- Temporary fatigue
- Reduced performance
- Increased soreness
- Lower recovery capacity

…but resolves with adequate recovery and often results in:
- Improved performance
- Greater fitness adaptations
- Supercompensation

Typical Timeframe

Days to ~2 weeks

Example

A bodybuilder during a high-volume training block or an endurance athlete during an intensified training camp.

Key Point

Functional overreaching is often intentional and beneficial.

Non-Functional Overreaching (NFOR)

This is where training stress exceeds recovery capacity long enough that performance declines persist without positive adaptation.

Definition

Excessive training stress with inadequate recovery leading to:
- Prolonged fatigue
- Stalled or declining performance
- Mood disturbances
- Poor recovery

…but not yet full overtraining syndrome.

Typical Timeframe

Weeks to months

Recovery Time

Several weeks

Warning Signs

- Workouts feel harder than normal
- Loss of motivation
- Elevated resting heart rate
- Sleep disturbances
- Persistent soreness
- Appetite disruption
- Irritability

Overtraining Syndrome (OTS)

This is a true clinical/performance condition.

Definition

A chronic maladaptive state where excessive training stress and insufficient recovery cause long-term physiological, neurological, hormonal, and psychological dysfunction.

Hallmark Feature

Persistent performance decline despite rest.

Recovery Time

Months

Sometimes a year or more

Symptoms

- Severe fatigue
- Reduced performance
- Sleep disruption
- Depression/anxiety
- Increased illness frequency
- Loss of libido
- Appetite changes
- Elevated or suppressed cortisol patterns
- Reduced HRV
- Hormonal disturbances
- Increased injury rate

The Most Important Truth:
Performance Decline Is the Primary Diagnostic Marker

Not soreness.
Not fatigue.
Not “feeling tired.”

The key indicator is:
“The athlete cannot produce their normal output despite continued effort.”

How to Truly Identify Overtraining or Overreaching

No single blood test or questionnaire definitively diagnoses it.

Real identification requires:
- Performance tracking
- Recovery monitoring
- Symptom patterns
- Exclusion of other causes

The Best Real-World Markers

1. Performance Metrics (Most Important)

If performance repeatedly declines:
- Strength drops
- Power output decreases
- Sprint speed worsens
- VO₂ max markers decline
- Pace slows
- Recovery between sets worsens

…despite continued effort and nutrition, that is the strongest indicator.

2. Resting Heart Rate (RHR)

A sustained elevation:
+5–10 bpm above baseline

may indicate excessive sympathetic stress.

However:
- Some athletes instead show unusually low HR
- So trends matter more than single values

3. Heart Rate Variability (HRV)

HRV reflects autonomic nervous system balance.

Generally:
Lower HRV = higher stress/reduced recovery

But:
- HRV alone cannot diagnose overtraining
- Best used alongside performance metrics

4. Mood & Motivation Changes

One of the earliest indicators.

Common signs:
- Irritability
- Anxiety
- Reduced drive to train
- Emotional flatness
- “Heavy body” sensation

Many sports physiologists consider mood disturbance one of the most sensitive markers.

5. Sleep Disruption

Especially:
- Waking during the night
- Early awakening
- Feeling “wired but tired”

This often reflects autonomic dysregulation.

6. Illness Frequency

Repeated:
- Colds
- Respiratory infections
- Slow wound healing

can indicate chronic stress-related immune suppression.

7. Hormonal & Blood Markers

These can support diagnosis but are not definitive alone.

Possible findings:
- Elevated cortisol
- Reduced testosterone:testosterone ratio
- Low free testosterone
- Altered thyroid hormones
- Elevated CK (creatine kinase)
- Increased inflammatory markers

But:
Many highly trained athletes show these transiently without true OTS.

The Simplest Practical Distinction

| Condition | Recovery Needed | Performance Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Functional Overreaching | Days–2 weeks | Performance rebounds higher |
| Non-Functional Overreaching | Weeks | Performance stagnates or declines |
| Overtraining Syndrome | Months+ | Persistent decline despite rest |

Why It Happens

Overtraining is rarely caused by training alone.

Usually it’s the combination of:
- High training load
- Caloric deficit
- Poor sleep
- Psychological stress
- Travel
- Dehydration
- Micronutrient deficiencies
- Inadequate protein/carbohydrate intake

This is why nutrition support becomes critical during heavy training.

Important Trainer Takeaway

Many athletes think they are “overtrained” when they are actually:
- Under-recovered
- Underfed
- Under-slept
- Or simply acutely fatigued

True overtraining syndrome is relatively rare.

Most cases in gyms are:
- Functional overreaching
- Non-functional overreaching
- Or low energy availability masquerading as overtraining

Practical Monitoring System for Trainers

The best real-world approach is tracking:
- Performance output
- Sleep quality
- Mood
- Motivation
- Appetite
- HRV/RHR trends
- Recovery capacity

If:
- Performance drops for >2 weeks,
- Motivation crashes,
- Recovery worsens,
- And sleep/mood deteriorate,

…you should reduce training stress and increase recovery support immediately.

One-Line Summary

Overreaching is temporary fatigue from hard training that can improve performance after recovery; overtraining is a chronic maladaptive state where performance continues to decline despite rest and recovery.

title: KissPeptin,StimGnRH,secretionByGnRH neuron
content:
Kisspeptin works by binding to its receptor on neurons in the hypothalamus, which stimulates the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). This begins a cascade: GnRH then signals the pituitary gland to release luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which in turn stimulate the gonads (ovaries or testes) to produce sex hormones like estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone. This process is crucial for reproduction, puberty, and the menstrual cycle.

The chain of command

Kisspeptin starts the signal: Kisspeptin is a peptide hormone that acts on neurons in the hypothalamus.

GnRH is released: When kisspeptin binds to the KISS1R receptor on these neurons, it triggers the release of GnRH.

LH and FSH are released: GnRH travels to the pituitary gland, which then releases LH and FSH.

Sex hormones are produced: LH and FSH travel to the ovaries or testes, stimulating them to produce and release sex hormones such as estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone.

Key roles in reproduction

Puberty:
Kisspeptin signaling is essential for the onset of puberty.

Menstrual cycle:
It helps regulate the release of eggs from the ovary and is involved in the normal control of ovulation.

Fertility:
It is a key regulator of the reproductive axis and is essential for fertility.

Other functions:
Kisspeptin is also involved in a variety of other processes, including the integration of reproductive hormones with brain activity related to emotions and mood.

title: Cardio after weight training best -
content:
https://studyfinds.org/cardio-before-or-after-weights/?utm_source=studyfinds.beehiiv.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=studyfinds-newsletter-6-15-25

But the real differences emerged when it came to fat loss and muscle performance. Participants who lifted weights first experienced significantly greater reductions in overall body fat and visceral fat—the type of fat most strongly linked to cardiovascular disease risk.

Resistance training depletes muscle glycogen stores—the sugar that’s stored in the muscles, which acts as your body’s quick-access fuel. Imagine glycogen as petrol in your car’s fuel tank. When you lift weights first, you effectively drain this fuel tank, forcing your body to switch energy sources.

With glycogen stores already low, when you transition to cardio, your body must rely more heavily on fat reserves for energy. It’s akin to a hybrid car switching to battery power once the petrol runs low. This metabolic shift helps explain the greater fat loss seen in the weights-first group.

This recent study’s findings align with broader research. A comprehensive systematic review published in 2022 found resistance training alone can significantly reduce body fat and visceral fat, the type linked to chronic diseases. Muscles are metabolically active tissues, continuously burning calories even at rest, which amplifies these effects.

Conversely, performing cardio first might compromise your strength training effectiveness. Cardio uses up glycogen stores, leaving muscles partially depleted before you even lift a weight. It also induces fatigue and may reduce your muscles’ ability to produce explosive power and strength.

A recent systematic review on concurrent training (the practice of combining both resistance and aerobic exercise within the same program) supports this—highlighting that explosive strength gains might diminish if aerobic and strength training occur in the same session, especially if cardio is performed first.

These findings align with other research on concurrent training. A systematic review and meta-analysis examining exercise sequence effects found that resistance-first protocols produced significantly superior strength improvements compared to endurance-first training.

The American Heart Association’s 2023 statement on resistance training confirmed resistance exercise significantly improves lean body mass and reduces fat, especially when combined with other exercise types. However, resistance training alone was found less effective in improving cardiovascular health. This underscores the importance of including cardio in your exercise routine.

title: Turkesterone
content:
Turkesterone:

Takeaway:
Our trainers sell creatine alone or combined in our Performance Bundles, which either way far outperform any potential muscle protein synthesis (MPS) benefit of Turkesterone.

More Info
Recent studies on Turkesterone, a phytoecdysteroid (500 mg/d), show mixed results, with limited, often conflicting evidence in human trials regarding muscle growth and performance improvements. The proposed mechanism is an increase in muscle protein synthesis. While some studies suggest it may aid in recovery or provide subtle ergogenic effects, recent 2024–2025 research indicates no significant increases in lean muscle mass, muscle strength, or metabolic rate compared to placebos. Almost all Turkesterone studies are animal and cell studies, with only three small human trials. Science consensus: across the board, creatine supplementation alone far outperforms Turkesterone for performance and muscle gain.

Your business solution: All else equal, the three different performance/muscle gain bundles we sell, which all include creatine, far surpass the potential gains (if any) compared to Turkesterone supplementation. Further, long-term effects of Turkesterone use are virtually non-existent, leaving its long-term safety profile unknown. Long-term safety and efficacy use of creatine and other bundled evidence-based products is well established.

Key Findings on Turkesterone Studies:
Muscle Growth/Performance: A 2025 study found no significant changes in body composition, strength, or power in participants over four weeks. Earlier studies suggested potential, but more robust human research is needed.

Safety & Side Effects:
Studies show doses up to 2,000 mg are generally well-tolerated with no significant adverse impacts on blood pressure, heart rate, or liver function. Minor issues like nausea or stomach discomfort may occur.

Mechanism: As a phytoecdysteroid, it is thought to act on muscle cells through pathways different from traditional steroids, focusing on protein synthesis stimulation rather than androgen receptor binding.

Long-Term Effects: Data on the long-term effects of Turkesterone use is virtually non-existent, leaving its long-term safety profile unknown.

Legality in Sports: It is currently not banned in sports, though similar ecdysteroids are on the WADA monitoring list.

YouTube +1

Conclusion of Current Research
The majority of studies supporting high efficacy are in animals (rodents) or cell cultures, with human data still in its infancy. Although safe, studies to date fail to definitively support its effectiveness as a potent, natural anabolic agent for muscle growth.

3.5. Turkesterone and Ajuga turkestanica
Turkesterone is a PE, with 27 carbon atoms and seven OH-groups; it is considered that the OH groups at C-20 and C-11 are responsible for the anabolic effects [28,215]. Turkesterone is considered to possess an anabolic effect, and it is used as DS by athletes, instead of anabolic steroids [28,30]. It is found in some endemic plants, such as A. turkestanica, R. carthamoides, Triticum aestivum L., Vitex scabra, etc. [13,69,216,217,218]. The highest content of turkesterone is considered to be in Ajuga turkestanica [19]. Moreover, in DSs, turkesterone is derived from A. turkestanica [28].

Ecdysteroid-enriched preparations of A. turkestanica (or pure turkesterone) exhibit anabolic effects [216,219].

Ajuga turkestanica, a plant species of the Lamiaceae family, grows wild in the Boysun mountainous region of Central Asia, Uzbekistan. It is a perennial plant that normally grows on clay, petrous, and rubbly slopes and rocks, with a height of 40–60 cm [14]. Both the aerial parts and root sections are utilized in folk medicine to prevent obesity, hair loss, and gastrointestinal diseases [14,216].

The phytochemical profile of A. turkestanica has indicated the existence of several biologically active secondary metabolites, such as carbohydrates, iridoids, diterpenes, phytoecdysteroids, flavonoids, sterol glycosides, and phenylethanoid glycosides [14,53,216]. The A. turkestanica extract contained 2.1% (w/w) turkesterone and 0.9% (w/w) 20HE [19]. Other isolated PEs are cyasterone, ajugasterone B, α-ecdysone, ecdysone 2,3-monoacetonide, and 22-acetylcyasterone [59,221,222].

Extracts from A. turkestanica are associated with wound-healing effects [223], as well as antiproliferative, anti-stress and immunostimulating, antimicrobial, and antioxidant effects [12,59]. Most of these effects are likely due to the presence of PEs [224]. Table 9 presents studies about the biological effects of turkesterone. Ajuga turkestanica and turkesterone products are commercially available not only online but also in bodybuilding centers [12]. The studies presented in the tables reported the various effects of turkesterone and A. turkestanica. Turkesterone is associated with a reduction in lipid accumulation in human adipocytes [69]. In a stress-induced mouse model, ecdysterone and turkesterone were found to prevent stress-related consequences and restore immunological activity [138]. Additionally, turkesterone exhibited beneficial effects on the endocrine and exocrine function in alloxan-induced diabetic rats, suggesting its potential therapeutic application in diabetes management [225]. Furthermore, PEs from A. turkestanica demonstrate hypoglycemic activity in models of hyperglycemia and diabetes, suggesting their potential therapeutic use in managing blood glucose levels [227]. Turkesterone presents a safer option to conventional anabolic steroids, displaying significant anabolic effects without inducing androgenic side effects in in vivo animal studies [19,219]. Moreover, A. turkestanica also enhances muscle regeneration and maintenance [29,226]. These results suggest that turkesterone extracted from A. turkestanica possesses diverse physiological effects, including potential performance enhancement and antiadipogenic, immunomodulatory, and hypoglycemic activities, making it a promising candidate for sports nutrition. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms of action and therapeutic potential of turkesterone and A. turkestanica [19,29,59,69,77,138,219,220,225,226,227].

4. Conclusions
Phytoecdysteroids, widely distributed across various plant species, have been valued for their adaptogenic properties and potential to enhance muscle strength and performance. 20-hydroxyecdysone and turkesterone are two of the most noteworthy PEs, which are found in plants such as R. carthamoides, S. oleracea, C. quinoa, and A. turkestanica. Nowadays, these plants are used not just in plant-based diets for their high nutritional value but also as major components of DSs. Since 2020, ecdysterone has garnered attention and has been included in the WADA’s monitoring program due to its ability to enhance physical endurance. Studies on the benefits of 20HE, turkesterone, and extracts from these plants are limited. The preparations from these plants show promise not only as nutritional supplements but also as therapeutic agents for treating medicinal disorders, such as chronic tiredness, heart disorders, and neurodegenerative diseases. Future double-blind randomized multicenter trials are critical for fully assessing the effectiveness and safety of these preparations for cardiovascular disease, chronic tiredness, obesity, and osteoporosis. These studies will provide valuable insights into the therapeutic potential of phytoecdysteroid-rich extracts.

What is turkesterone?
Turkesterone is a type of ecdysteroid, a steroid-like compound found in certain plants and insects. The supplement form is commonly sourced from Ajuga turkestanica. Unlike anabolic-androgenic steroids, turkesterone is not thought to work by binding to the androgen receptor the way testosterone or Dianabol would.

In plain English: it’s often marketed as “anabolic without the steroid side effects,” but that claim depends on whether it actually produces meaningful muscle/strength outcomes in humans.

Does turkesterone work? What the best human studies show
Here’s the key point: the most relevant evidence is human trials measuring body composition and performance. And the most direct turkesterone supplementation studies we have right now are short (four weeks) and generally show no meaningful advantage vs placebo.

Human study #1: 500 mg/day turkesterone for four weeks (DXA body comp)
A 2024 study randomized active men and women to 500 mg/day turkesterone or placebo for four weeks and measured changes via DXA. Result: no significant differences in body mass, lean mass, fat mass, or body fat percentage compared to placebo.

Human study #2: “turkesterone-containing product” (Turk Builder®) for four weeks
A 2025 randomized, double-blind trial tested a turkesterone-containing product for four weeks and tracked body composition, handgrip strength, mood, and sleep. Result: no significant differences between treatment and placebo groups across those measures.

Acute study: multiple doses and short-term markers
A 2024 preliminary study looked at acute dosing and markers like IGF-1 and resting metabolic rate over a short window. It did not find statistically significant effects, though it notes the work is “foundational” for future research.

Bottom line from human trials so far:
If you’re expecting obvious hypertrophy or strength jumps in a month, current human studies suggest you’ll likely be disappointed.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| [NAME] et al. (2024) | Randomized, placebo-controlled | 500 mg/day, four weeks | DXA body composition | No significant change vs placebo |
| [NAME] et al. (2025) | Double-blind, placebo-controlled | Turk Builder® 1 cap/day, four weeks | Body comp, handgrip, mood, sleep | No significant differences vs placebo |
| [NAME] et al. (2024) | Acute dosing study | Multiple doses, short time window | IGF-1, RMR, metabolic markers | No significant effects; exploratory |
| [NAME] et al. (2019) (ecdysterone) | Training intervention (ecdysterone) | 10 weeks (varied dosing) | Performance / training outcomes | Suggestive effects, but different compound & context |

How might turkesterone work? (Mechanism)
Ecdysteroids are hypothesized to influence pathways related to muscle protein synthesis, energy metabolism, and recovery. A 2024 review summarizes proposed mechanisms (protein synthesis support, ATP-related effects, and other metabolic influences), but also makes clear that mechanisms are still being clarified and don’t guarantee real-world hypertrophy.

Key takeaway: A plausible mechanism can be interesting, but users ultimately care about outcomes, and current human outcomes are not impressive.

Turkesterone benefits: what’s realistic?
Muscle gain: Not convincingly supported by current short-term human trials.

Strength/performance: No clear improvements in the direct turkesterone trials; ecdysterone research is a different bucket.

Recovery/“feel” effects: Mostly anecdotal—hard to separate from placebo without longer, larger trials.

Turkesterone dosage (what people use vs what studies used)
Many supplement brands recommend around 500 mg/day, commonly split into 1–2 doses. That’s also the dose used in one of the most direct four-week trials.

If you insist on trying it:
Use a consistent dose daily for 6–8 weeks (longer than most studies),
Track body weight, waist, lifts, sleep, and training volume,
Don’t change 10 variables at once (diet + training + 6 new supplements),
Stop if you experience side effects.

Turkesterone side effects & safety
Direct long-term safety data in humans is limited. However, broader ecdysteroid literature often describes a favorable safety profile in mammals and summarizes toxicology background.

That said, athletes should also understand regulatory context: ecdysteroids are not currently prohibited, but are on WADA’s monitoring list (meaning it’s being tracked and could change in the future).

Commonly reported issues are usually mild (e.g., GI discomfort), but high-quality data is sparse. If you’re pregnant/nursing, have a medical condition, or take medications, talk to a qualified healthcare professional first.

FDA disclaimer: These statements have not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration. This content is for educational purposes and is not medical advice.

Turkesterone vs creatine (and what you should take instead)
If your goal is to build muscle and get stronger, creatine monohydrate is still the king because it has a much larger, higher-quality evidence base than turkesterone. If you’re choosing where to spend money, creatine + protein + total calories + training progression will almost always beat “hype” supplements.

title: Tesamorelin (Often Referred to as Sermorelin) info incl updated dosage
content:
Using the same format in this document you did for BPC-157. Please create the content for the peptide Tesamorelin (often referred to as sermorelin), especially best dosing protocols and duration of use.

Below is the Tesamorelin (often confused with sermorelin) peptide profile, written to match the same structure, tone, and trainer-safe format used for the BPC-157 document, with clear separation between evidence-based use, real-world protocols, and safety boundaries.

(Referenced and formatted consistently with your uploaded BPC-157 document: 17c93b7f-88ea-462c-8447-9954aaf…)

Ordering peptides: https://nexgenmdscientific.com/ — NextGen site to order

About the Product:
Promotes fat loss, especially in the abdominal area, while increasing IGF-1 levels and supporting lean muscle growth.

Key Benefits:
- Powerful GH-releasing peptide
- Clinically shown to reduce visceral (belly) fat
- Improves metabolism and cognition

What to Expect:
Noticeable abdominal fat reduction and improved energy within 6–8 weeks.

Total: 10 mg, $160.00

Tesamorelin (Often Referred to as Sermorelin)
Purpose: Growth Hormone Axis Optimization

Important clarification:
Tesamorelin and sermorelin are different peptides.
Tesamorelin is a long-acting GHRH analog, while sermorelin is a shorter GHRH fragment. They are often grouped together in conversation because they stimulate endogenous growth hormone (GH) rather than replacing GH directly.

How Tesamorelin Is Typically Used

1. Systemic (Non-Site-Specific) Use
This is the standard and intended application.

Used for:
- Growth hormone axis stimulation
- Reduction of visceral adipose tissue
- Support of lean body mass retention
- Metabolic and lipolytic signaling
- Sleep-related GH pulse enhancement

Rationale:
- Tesamorelin stimulates the pituitary gland to release GH.
- Effects are systemic, not localized.
- It mimics physiological GH pulsatility more closely than exogenous GH.
- Injection is never site-specific for tissue repair, unlike BPC-157.

What Makes Tesamorelin Different From Sermorelin

| Feature | Tesamorelin | Sermorelin |
|---|---|---|
| Peptide length | Full GHRH analog | GHRH (1-29) fragment |
| Half-life | Longer | Short |
| Dosing frequency | Once daily | Often 1–2× daily |
| FDA status | Approved for HIV-associated lipodystrophy | Not FDA-approved |
| GH stimulation | Stronger, sustained | Milder, shorter pulse |

Typical Injection Frequency
Once daily is standard.
Usually administered in the evening to align with natural GH rhythms.
Consistency (same time daily) is emphasized over higher dosing.

Commonly Cited Dose Ranges
These reflect approved clinical use and common off-label protocols, not trainer-directed recommendations.

2 mg once daily is the FDA-approved dose for HIV-associated lipodystrophy.

Off-label longevity/body composition protocols often range from 1–2 mg per day.
Lower doses (<1 mg/day) generally show less reliable GH elevation.
Unlike many peptides, Tesamorelin dosing is not usually split.

Typical Duration of Use
12–26 weeks is common in clinical and applied settings.
Some protocols extend to 6–12 months under medical supervision.
Effects on visceral fat and IGF-1 are gradual, not immediate.
Tesamorelin is not a short-cycle peptide like BPC-157.

What Tesamorelin Is Commonly Used For
- Visceral fat reduction (strongest evidence)
- GH/IGF-1 axis support
- Lean mass preservation during fat loss
- Metabolic health support
- Sleep-related recovery signaling

Mechanism of Action (Trainer-Appropriate Depth)
Tesamorelin works by:
- Stimulating endogenous GH release from the pituitary
- Increasing IGF-1 downstream signaling
- Enhancing lipolysis, particularly in visceral fat
- Preserving natural feedback loops, unlike exogenous GH

This preserves:
- Pulsatile GH secretion
- Lower risk of GH suppression
- Reduced likelihood of insulin resistance compared to GH injections

What Practitioners Commonly Observe (Real-World Use)

| Goal | Typical Outcome |
|---|---|
| Visceral fat reduction | Most consistent benefit |
| Lean mass retention | Moderate support |
| Strength gains | Indirect |
| Recovery | Subtle, cumulative |
| Sleep quality | Often improved |

Tesamorelin is not an acute performance enhancer.

Safety & Regulatory Notes (Important)
Tesamorelin is FDA-approved, but only for HIV-associated lipodystrophy.
Off-label use requires medical oversight.

Possible side effects include:
- Water retention
- Joint stiffness
- Increased IGF-1

Not appropriate for:
- Active malignancy
- Uncontrolled diabetes

Trainers should not prescribe, source, or administer.

Trainer-Friendly One-Line Explanation
“Tesamorelin helps the body release its own growth hormone more effectively, supporting fat loss and recovery without shutting down natural GH production.”

Practical Trainer/Educator Takeaway
If Tesamorelin is discussed at all, it should be positioned as:
- Medical-provider-managed
- Long-term and systemic
- Adjunctive—not foundational

Always anchor the conversation to:
- Resistance training
- Sleep optimization
- Protein and EAA sufficiency
- Micronutrient adequacy
- Load management and recovery

This keeps messaging aligned with a Playspan®/Youth-Preserving framework and avoids peptide-centric overreach.

If you want next:
- A side-by-side: Tesamorelin vs. Sermorelin vs. GH
- A trainer-safe peptide “do not recommend/client may ask” table
- A client-facing stripped-down version that removes dosing entirely

Just tell me how you want to deploy it (trainer cert, laminated card, PDF, slide, or policy doc).

Update product/formula

Tesamorelin is a synthetic Growth Hormone Releasing Hormone (GHRH) analog primarily used to stimulate the body’s natural pulsatile growth hormone release, which subsequently raises IGF-1 levels. Its best-studied and FDA-approved use is the reduction of excess visceral abdominal fat in HIV-associated lipodystrophy.

The standard clinically studied and FDA-approved dosage is:
2 mg subcutaneous injection once daily.

The newer Egrifta WR formulation is dosed at:
1.28 mg once daily due to formulation differences and bioequivalence improvements.

Mechanistically, tesamorelin works upstream at the pituitary to increase endogenous GH secretion, which then elevates IGF-1 and promotes lipolysis, especially in visceral adipose tissue.

Clinical trials using the 2 mg/day dose demonstrated:
- ~14–18% reductions in visceral abdominal fat
- Improvements in triglycerides and liver fat
- Preservation or modest increases in lean body mass
- Minimal effect on overall body weight

In off-label performance/anti-aging settings, many clinics still use dosing near the original 2 mg nightly range because that is where most human efficacy data exist. Some protocols use lower doses (e.g., 0.5–1 mg/day) to reduce side effects or cost, but these lower-dose approaches are far less validated in published human research.

The most common side effects reported include:
- Edema/water retention
- Joint pain
- Tingling or numbness
- Injection site reactions
- Possible insulin sensitivity changes

Is a 1 mg daily dose 6 times a week of Tesamorelin considered effective?

Yes, a 1 mg daily dose of Tesamorelin taken 6 days per week (6 mg/week total) would generally be considered biologically active and likely effective, but it is below the dose that has been most extensively studied clinically.

Typical Dosing Comparison

FDA-approved dose (HIV-associated visceral fat):
- 2 mg daily
- 7 days/week
- Total = 14 mg/week

Your example:
- 1 mg daily
- 6 days/week
- Total = 6 mg/week

This is approximately 43% of the FDA-approved weekly exposure.

What Might You Expect at 1 mg, 6×/week?
Because Tesamorelin stimulates the body's own pulsatile GH release rather than supplying GH directly, there is generally a dose-response relationship.

Potential benefits still likely:
- Mild increase in GH secretion
- Moderate increase in IGF-1
- Some support for recovery and body composition
- Potential reduction in visceral fat over time
- Lower risk of excessive IGF-1 elevation

Benefits likely reduced compared with 2 mg/day:
- Magnitude of visceral fat reduction
- Speed of body composition changes
- Total IGF-1 increase
- Potential anabolic effect

In Practice
Among anti-aging, longevity, and physique-focused physicians, it is not uncommon to see:
- 1 mg/day
- 1–2 mg/day
- 2 mg/day

depending on:
- Age
- Baseline IGF-1
- Goals (longevity vs. fat loss vs. body composition)
- Cost considerations

Many practitioners will start at 1 mg/day, check:
- IGF-1
- Fasting glucose
- HbA1c
- Body composition changes

They then decide whether increasing to 2 mg/day is warranted.

Takeaway
A 1 mg daily dose taken 6 days per week is generally considered an effective “entry-level” Tesamorelin protocol, especially for improving GH signaling and modestly raising IGF-1. However, it is roughly half of the clinically studied dose, so the effects on visceral fat reduction and body composition would typically be expected to be more modest than those observed with the standard 2 mg/day regimen.

For a healthy adult focused on strength, recovery, and body composition rather than treatment of HIV-associated visceral adiposity, many clinicians would consider 1 mg/day a reasonable starting dose, provided IGF-1 and metabolic markers are monitored periodically.

title: MK-677 AKA Ibutamoren-Ipamorelin
content:
MK-677

Takeaway
Our PTs have referral access to the better version of the compound through a third-party provider, so there are no liabilities.

More Info
MK-677, popular in the bodybuilding and biohacking communities, is an oral compound (25 mg/day) with more side effects than the injectable Ipamorelin. Both are ghrelin receptor agonists that increase GH. The latter does not increase appetite or water retention like MK-677. Ipamorelin is considered a safer, more targeted, and precise option for long-term health and, when combined with GHRH (like CJC-1295), is considered a “classic” combination for anti-aging and body composition.

Legal and Safety Status (why you want a third-party seller)
Not FDA Approved: MK-677 is classified as an investigational new drug.
Illegally Sold: It is often illegally marketed as a “dietary supplement” or “research chemical.”
Prohibited in sports: It is banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and the Department of Defense (DoD).
Your business solution: The better version (Ipamorelin) and other peptides are available through a third-party doctor group partner; therefore, there is no club potential liability. Ordering, screening, and payment go directly through the partner with significant referral revenue share.
Critically, MK-677 is not approved for human consumption by the FDA, is not a legal dietary supplement, and is banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA).
Operation Supplement Safety | OPSS +1

Primary Benefits and Effects
Studies have shown that MK-677 mimics the hunger hormone ghrelin, which boosts GH, leading to several potential, albeit mostly experimental, benefits:
Muscle Growth & Recovery: It is used to enhance body composition, increasing lean body mass and improving recovery times after workouts.
Improved Sleep Quality: It has been shown to increase REM sleep duration and overall sleep quality.
Bone Density: Studies indicate it may increase bone turnover and mineral density.
Anti-Aging & Fat Loss: By raising IGF-1 levels, it may help counteract age-related decline in hormone levels, potentially reducing body fat.
Wikipedia +2

Side Effects and Risks
Because MK-677 is not approved for human use and its long-term safety is not established, users may experience significant risks:
Operation Supplement Safety | OPSS +1
Increased Appetite & Weight Gain: A very common effect due to ghrelin receptor stimulation.
Water Retention & Swelling: Fluid retention is frequently reported.
Insulin Resistance & Hyperglycemia: It can increase fasting blood glucose levels and reduce insulin sensitivity, increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes.
Cardiovascular Concerns: Some clinical trials raised concerns regarding heart failure risk, leading to warnings about its safety in certain patients.
Other Side Effects: Joint pain, numbness, and fatigue.
Operation Supplement Safety | OPSS +1

Legal and Safety Status
Not FDA Approved: MK-677 is classified as an investigational new drug.
Illegally Sold: It is often illegally marketed as a “dietary supplement” or “research chemical.”
Prohibited in Sports: It is banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and the Department of Defense (DoD).
Operation Supplement Safety | OPSS +2

Dosage
While not approved, anecdotal reports often cite dosages of 10–25 mg per day, taken orally. Consulting a healthcare professional before using such substances is highly recommended.

Hormonal Agents
Performance Enhancing Substance: MK-677 (Ibutamoren)

ARTICLE OVERVIEW
What are the safety concerns?
Can MK-677 negatively affect a Service Member’s career?
Related readings
MK-677, also known as Ibutamoren, is a “growth hormone secretagogue,” a substance that stimulates the production of growth hormone. It is not approved for human use, which makes it an unapproved drug. It is also not legal for use as an ingredient in dietary supplements or any other consumer or commercial products. It can only be used for research purposes.
MK-677 is on the DoD Prohibited Dietary Supplement Ingredients List and the World Anti-Doping Agency Prohibited List. It is not legal for use.
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has posted warning letters to companies illegally selling products containing MK-677. These types of products are sometimes labeled as dietary supplements with a “Supplement Facts” label, as a research chemical with a “Research Facts” label, or even labeled as “For Research Use Only.”
Even though it is illegal, MK-677 is currently marketed with claims to help build muscle or increase muscle mass, decrease body fat, and increase energy. In addition, products that contain MK-677 are often combined with SARMs (or even indicate MK-677 as a SARM). SARMs are also illegal and prohibited for use.

What are the safety concerns?
A number of health risks have been associated with the use of MK-677 (Ibutamoren).
FDA lists Ibutamoren as an ingredient that “...poses significant safety risks due to the potential for congestive heart failure in certain patients.” A clinical trial was stopped early due to concerns that Ibutamoren may increase the rate of heart failure.
Ibutamoren is listed in the Australian Poisons Standard. The long-term safety is not established, and the potential adverse effects “...may include those associated with the administration of growth hormones and the potential for downstream health effects such as cardiovascular and hormonal effects.”
MK-677 has also been reported to negatively impact bone and bone mineral density, increase fasting blood glucose levels, heighten the risk of hyperglycemia, and affect insulin sensitivity.
Other side effects include anxiety, diarrhea, increased fluid retention and swelling, increased hunger, muscle or joint pain, numbness, and nausea.
When combined with SARMs, MK-677 could negatively impact serum lipids, liver enzymes, testosterone levels, or worse. Beyond the Hype: Potential Health Risks of MK-677
Last Updated: Tuesday July 8, 2025
([NAME] Foundation) MK-677 (also known as Ibutamoren) is getting a lot of attention online. More and more often, we are getting asked about this substance during our ALL ME® Assemblies. Claims of muscle development, recovery, performance, and more have caused usage to rise, but here is what you need to know about MK-677 and your health.
MK-677 is a growth hormone secretagogue, meaning it increases your body’s production of human growth hormone (HGH) and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). It first showed up as an investigational drug when looking at child growth hormone disorders and frailty in older adults. This drug is still in investigational status, meaning it has not been approved for human consumption.
Despite not being approved for human consumption, this compound is still being found online and popping up in dietary supplements. Its use comes with serious risks, especially when taken without medical supervision. The most common side effects include insulin resistance, increased appetite, weight gain, and swelling due to water retention. Long-term use may increase the risk of developing type 2 diabetes and contribute to the growth of cancerous tumors due to elevated IGF-1 levels. Users have also reported side effects such as joint pain, numbness, and fatigue. Because MK-677 is not approved by the FDA for over-the-counter use and has not been thoroughly studied in healthy individuals, its long-term safety profile remains uncertain. One of the main reasons it has not moved beyond investigatory status is due to an observed increased risk of cardiovascular damage during one of the research studies.
Above all else, it is important to know that any use of MK-677 is currently illegal and banned in all legitimate forms of competition. While the claims may sound promising online, they are not worth the potential risk to your health. Nutrition, sleep, and hard work remain your best tools to achieving your goals the right way!

title: BPC-157 % TB 500 use before surgery or in damaged meniscus
content:
Would using BPC-157 and TB-500 do any good for a torn meniscus if you have not had the surgery yet?

Possibly, but with an important caveat: BPC-157 and TB-500 are unlikely to "heal" a torn meniscus, especially if the tear is large, displaced, or located in the poorly vascularized inner portion of the meniscus.

The rationale for using them before surgery is that they may help:
- Reduce pain and inflammation.
- Improve healing of surrounding soft tissues (capsule, ligaments, tendon attachments).
- Potentially enhance healing in the outer ("red zone") portion of the meniscus where blood supply exists.
- Improve function and allow better participation in physical therapy.
- Potentially reduce the need for surgery in some minor tears.

However, the challenge is that the meniscus has limited blood supply, particularly in the inner two-thirds. A mechanical tear that causes:
- Locking.
- Catching.
- Joint instability.
- A displaced flap or bucket-handle tear.

typically will not be corrected by peptides because the tissue remains mechanically torn regardless of inflammation status.

If I were looking at this clinically:

Small degenerative tear or minor traumatic tear:
- Physical therapy.
- Strengthening around the knee.
- Weight management if needed.
- Activity modification.
- Possible BPC-157/TB-500 trial.

In this situation, some individuals report meaningful improvement and may avoid surgery.

Large tear with mechanical symptoms:
- Peptides may reduce symptoms and improve recovery capacity.
- They are unlikely to replace a necessary surgical repair or meniscectomy.

Why some surgeons don't object:

Even if surgery is ultimately required, entering surgery with:
- Less inflammation.
- Better quadriceps strength.
- Better range of motion.
- Less pain.

often leads to a better postoperative outcome. Therefore, using BPC-157/TB-500 during the prehabilitation phase is not an unreasonable strategy, although evidence in humans remains limited.

What the evidence actually says:

The strongest support for BPC-157 and TB-500 comes from:
- Animal studies.
- Mechanistic data.
- Anecdotal clinical reports.

High-quality human trials specifically showing healing of torn menisci are essentially lacking. So any recommendation is based more on biological plausibility and clinical experience than definitive evidence.

Practical takeaway:

For a torn meniscus that has not yet undergone surgery, BPC-157 and TB-500 may help reduce pain, inflammation, and improve the healing environment around the knee, particularly when combined with a good rehabilitation program. They are most likely to help with symptom improvement and recovery capacity, but they should not be expected to reliably repair a significant meniscal tear that would otherwise require surgical intervention.

title: ApoB test & results
content:
What is an Apo B blood test?

An Apo B or Apolipoprotein B-100 test is a blood test that can tell you about your risk for cardiovascular (heart and blood vessel) disease. To do this, it measures the amount of Apo B, which carries substances in your blood that help make plaque, a waxy fat that can block your arteries.

Apolipoprotein B takes lipids where they’re going. But it only gives rides to the kind of lipids that have a bad reputation: low-density lipoprotein (LDL), very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), and others. You won’t find the good cholesterol, high-density lipoproteins (HDL), hanging around with Apo B. When you see Apo B, you can be sure LDL is there, too.

Some healthcare providers believe an Apo B test is more accurate than a lipid panel (which measures all those cholesterol types) to estimate cardiovascular disease risk.

Optimal ApoB Targets by Risk Category

Medical organizations recommend the following targets:

Optimal / Low-Risk: <60 - 80 mg/dL
Moderate Risk: <90 mg/dL
High Risk (e.g., existing heart disease or diabetes): <80 mg/dL
Very High Risk (e.g., recurrent cardiovascular events): <65 mg/dL

Average Ranges by Age and Sex

While "average" isn't necessarily "optimal" for heart health, comparing your score to population percentiles can put your numbers into perspective. Typical population ranges (in mg/dL) include: [1]

Age < 40: 50 - 150 mg/dL
Age 40 - 60: 60 - 160 mg/dL
Age > 60: 70 - 170 mg/dL [1, 2, 3, 4]

Note: The general population average often sits around 100 mg/dL, but modern preventive cardiology considers this too high for ideal, long-term cardiovascular health. [1, 2]

What type of results do you get and what do the results mean?

Your Apolipoprotein B-100 test results can range from 20 to 400 milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL).

If your Apo B is higher than 130 mg/dL, you’re at a higher risk of heart and blood vessel disease.

Some cardiology guidelines recommend a target of less than 65 or 80 mg/dL of Apo B. They suggest these goals for people between ages 40 and 75 who take statins.

What is a normal Apo B level?

A normal Apo B level is:
66 to 133 mg/dL for males
60 to 117 mg/dL for females

Conditions that can make your Apo B test results higher

Your Apo B test results may be higher if you have:
A pregnancy.
High cholesterol.
Nephrotic syndrome, a kidney issue.

Apo B testing

An ApoB (Apolipoprotein B-100) blood test measures the number of particles in your blood that carry "bad" cholesterol (LDL). It is considered a more accurate marker for cardiovascular disease risk than a standard LDL-C test, as it directly counts atherogenic particles. High levels indicate increased risk for plaque buildup and cardiovascular disease, often used to monitor treatment.

Key Aspects of the ApoB Test:

Purpose: Measures the main protein found in LDL and other fat-carrying particles.
Significance: Because each LDL particle contains one ApoB molecule, this test directly measures the total count of dangerous particles, better identifying risk when LDL cholesterol seems normal.
When it is used: Recommended for people with diabetes, obesity, high triglycerides, or a family history of heart disease, as well as for monitoring the effectiveness of statin therapy.

title: Expired drugs - good for long time, expiration dates
content:
More on using expired drugs
Douglas S. Paauw, MD

DISCLOSURES
October 02, 2023
68
950
Add to Email Alerts

A patient inquires about whether he or she can use an EpiPen after the expiration date. What should you advise?

The EpiPen is unlikely to be effective after the expiration date.
The EpiPen may be dangerous to use after the expiration date.
The EpiPen is likely to be okay up to 2 years past the expiration date.

Douglas S. Paauw, MD

I think that choice C is the most accurate and will get to all the evidence shortly. The expiration date is not the date that the drug stops being effective or potentially becomes toxic. It is a date, required by law, that the manufacturer can guarantee greater than 90% original potency of the medication.

Epinephrine is a costly drug and is usually replaced when the EpiPen expires. [NAME] and colleagues studied six epinephrine syringes 30 months past their expiration date.[1] Three of the syringes and one control, nonexpired syringe were analyzed using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry and nuclear magnetic resonance to determine epinephrine content. The contents of the other three syringes of epinephrine were cultured for bacteria and fungus, which yielded no microbial growth. The study showed that the content of epinephrine present in the original sample remained unchanged, compared with the control.

[NAME] et al. looked at 35 EpiPens 3-36 months past their expiration dates.[2] The percentage of epinephrine found remained 84%-101%, with all EpiPens less than 24 months past expiration having > 90% of the labeled epinephrine dose. [NAME] and colleagues evaluated a combination of 40 EpiPens and EpiPen Jrs that were 1-50 months past expiration.[3] These pens had not been kept in ideal conditions, as some had been in cars, outdoor cabins, and other environments without temperature control. Sixty-one percent of the EpiPens and 56% of the EpiPen Juniors had > 90% of the labeled epinephrine content. I think expired EpiPens can be used as a back-up option—that is, they are safe to use if there is not an EpiPen available that is not expired.

Shelf life extension program

[NAME] and colleagues reported data from the Shelf Life Extension Program (SLEP).[4] A total of 122 drugs were studied, representing 3,005 lots. Based on testing and stability assessment, 88% of the lots were extended at least 1 year beyond their original expiration date for an average extension of 66 months, but the additional stability period was highly variable. Several antibiotics were studied, including ciprofloxacin (mean extension, 55 months), amoxicillin (mean extension, 23 months), and doxycycline (mean extension, 50 months).

What about other drugs not in pill form?

I am frequently asked about the longevity of medication formulations that are not in pill form. For example, I have been asked about using expired eye drops. There are few data on this. [NAME] et al. studied whether travoprost that was past the expiration date still lowered intraocular pressures.[5] Intraocular pressures in glaucoma patients treated with travoprost 6 weeks after the seal was broken were compared with pressures when drops were used immediately after the container seal was broken. There was no significant difference in intraocular pressure between the two treatment groups during the study.

I found one case report of harm from using expired eye medications. Use of expired eye drops was associated with a case of bilateral toxic epithelial keratopathy.[6] Eye drops can be contaminated and cause irritation from the breakdown products of preservatives.

Many people use inhalers for many years. This is especially true for albuterol, which is often used for very intermittent symptoms. I found one recent study on the stability of albuterol. [NAME] et al. studied expired albuterol inhalers and solutions up to 20 years past expiration.[7] Almost all lots of albuterol maintained > 90% of product (73%-103%), many years past their expiration date. Even at 73% retained activity, the dose would likely be effective.

Pearl: Expired epinephrine and albuterol appear to retain activity several years past expiration.

Dr. Paauw is professor of medicine in the division of general internal medicine at the University of Washington, Seattle, and he serves as third-year medical student clerkship director at the University of Washington. He has no conflicts of interest. Contact Dr. Paauw at [EMAIL]

title: Magtein magnisium supp
content:
In 2 grams (2000 mg) of Magtein (Magnesium L-Threonate), you'll find approximately 144 to 145 mg of elemental magnesium, as Magtein is about 7.2% elemental magnesium by weight, with most brands providing around 144–145 mg per 2 g dose for brain health support.

Here's the breakdown:
Magtein (Magnesium L-Threonate): A specific compound designed to cross the blood-brain barrier.
Elemental Magnesium: The actual magnesium mineral content.
Calculation: A 2000 mg serving of Magtein typically yields about 144–145 mg of elemental magnesium (2000 mg × ~0.072 = ~144 mg).

Always check your supplement's label for the exact elemental magnesium amount, as it's the crucial figure for your daily intake.

A 2-gram (2000 mg) serving of a Magtein (magnesium L-threonate) supplement generally provides 144 mg to 147 mg of elemental magnesium. This amount accounts for about 7% to 8% of the total weight of the magnesium L-threonate compound.

The remaining weight in the 2 grams of magnesium L-threonate is primarily the L-threonate molecule, a water-soluble substance derived from the metabolic breakdown of vitamin C.

If the product is in capsule or powder form, other inactive ingredients are also present, which vary by manufacturer. Common "other ingredients" found in Magtein supplements include:
- Hypromellose (cellulose capsule)
- Rice flour
- Stearic acid (vegetable source)
- Silicon dioxide
- Cellulose
- Magnesium stearate

These ingredients function as fillers, anti-caking agents, or make up the capsule itself, ensuring the product can be manufactured and consumed easily.

title: Methylated vitamins - full answer, forms
content:
[NAME]/[NAME],

[NAME], I know you answered this question in detail as an “experts” question previously, and I received a question as well on it this weekend, so I thought I would dig into it deeper with [NAME].

From [NAME], our chemist/pharmacist for complex formulas.

Are your multivitamins methylated?

Only B9 and B12 are available in the market in their methylated forms.

“Methylated forms are better absorbed by the body. Non-methylated forms need to get activated and converted into a methylated form by the body to be effective.” – [NAME]’s definition.

ActiveMV and Over50MV both use 2 forms of B12 (cyanocobalamin and methylcobalamin).

WomensMV uses methylcobalamin as form of B12.

Alln1 SuperBlend uses both B9/Folate (calcium L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate) and B12 (methylcobalamin) in the methylated forms.

The guy that emailed me thought that every vitamin could be methylated, so that was a big part of his confusion/question. Anyway, use as you see fit.

Are all your vitamins methylated vitamins? How would I be able to tell?

Hi [NAME],

Thanks for contacting us. Your question is vague, in the fact that not all vitamins should contain a methyl donor to be effective (actually, it is a problem for some). What you want in any vitamin is an absorbable form (i.e., a form that is already prepared as the body would prepare it once extracted from a food source). All our vitamins (and minerals) are in a pre-formed structure to allow the body proper “functional absorption” (active at the target tissue), which is better than bioavailable absorption. All our labels have the form listed. Do not be fooled that all vitamins need a methyl group to be effective. In all our products, if it needs a methyl group, it will be part of it and listed on the label, such as B12 or Folate in our Alln1 SuperBlendTM. If you would like to talk to a chemist further, [NAME] (VP of Product Development) is cc’d here to help.

Thanks again and have a great night.

What is a ‘Methylated’ Nutrient?

A methylated nutrient is a compound attached to a molecule made up of one carbon and three hydrogens, known as a “methyl group” (CH3).

Common methylated nutrients include:

S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe)
L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate, or L-5-MTHF (an “active” form of folate, also known as just L-methylfolate)
Methylcobalamin (an “active” form of vitamin B12)
Trimethylglycine (TMG or Betaine)
Inositol
Choline
Phosphatidylcholine

You can see the word “methyl” within the name of some of these nutrients. In these cases, methylated nutrients are easy to identify. But in other cases, like choline or inositol, you may not realize they are methylated!

title: Why is glucuronolactone included in the NO7RAGE pre-workout formula, given the limited evidence for its effects by itself?

Thanks for contacting us. You are correct: there is no solid evidence that glucuronolactone has any value in energy drinks, and yet it is a common ingredient in many. If you have ever attended one of our Practitioner lectures on NO7RAGE, you would have heard us discuss this. It has always been in the formula, and there is no downside, including no extra cost, as it comes with the raw materials. title: Calories in and calories out document
content:
The laws of thermodynamics are not to be disputed on planet Earth (specifically the 1st law). Every true scientist knows how this works.

The First Law of Thermodynamics states that energy can be converted from one form to another with the interaction of heat, work, and internal energy, but it cannot be created nor destroyed, under any circumstances (i.e., energy can just be converted from one form to another).

Therefore, any change in body composition is the average difference between calories in and calories out regardless of the makeup of the calories because we are measuring a result, not the foods that led to it. That said, proper foods will increase the calories burned, but at the end of the day, energy cannot be created or destroyed, meaning that the difference between calories/energy in and out is transformed and measurable.

Human body composition (including body weight) example
(Numbers used are to make the math easier—but equations are true)

If you were 200 LBS and 20% body fat and consumed 2,000 calories/day of mostly French fries, and 2 weeks later you were 21% body fat and 201 LBS (~2 LBS body fat gain and 1 LBS LBM loss), this means you consumed ~7K more calories than you burned (~500 calories/day more intake). This is presumably from the inability to burn many calories because of poor diet, no protein synthesis, loss of LBM (reduces calories burned), energy, etc.

Taking the same person eating 2,000 calories of 1 gram/lb. protein/day, some good carbs (e.g., fruits, vegetables, grains), and fats, and 2 weeks later (after consuming 28K calories) being at 18% body fat and weighing 195 LBS (gained ~1 LBS muscle) would mean that the average deficit would look like this: 4 LBS fat loss = ~14K calorie burn above 28K (14 days of 2,000-calorie intake) = 42K usage; 1 LBS muscle gain = ~1,700 calorie deposition into muscle; therefore, 42K minus 1,700 = 40,300 calories burned. Total 2-week calorie deficit = 12,300 ÷ 14 days = ~878 calories a day average.

And of course, the reason for the extra burn from the same number of calorie diet is because the diet was healthy/energetic and designed to build muscle (when paired with exercise). Basically, a healthier diet creates the desire and allows you to move more, and the deficit or surplus doesn’t lie.

Moral of the story is that body composition change will always be a product of energy in versus energy out because energy cannot be destroyed or created, only transformed/transferred—but the makeup of the calories consumed is responsible for the performance, or total calories burned. But the mass change can always be quantified by the difference between the two when measuring body composition.

In other words, the same number of calories in, but a completely different outcome because of the calorie makeup. However, after the fact, the result is 100% defined by the difference between calories/energy in and calories/energy out. Moreover, knowing your calories in and out tied to your body composition goal is necessary so that you can continue to adjust these amounts/numbers (or foods/supplements that may move the numbers) to make your desired progress and overcome plateaus. The right calories consumed will help you voluntarily increase your calories burned, and the difference between the two at any point is quantifiable based on body composition and weight changes.

title: PCOS what it is
content:
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common, often inherited, hormonal disorder affecting 5-13% of women of reproductive age. It is characterized by high levels of androgens (male hormones), irregular periods, and/or small, harmless fluid-filled sacs (follicles) on the ovaries. It is a leading cause of infertility and can lead to long-term issues like Type 2 diabetes if untreated.

Key Aspects of PCOS

Hormonal Imbalance: The core issue is an overproduction of androgens (such as testosterone) and a lack of progesterone.

Ovulation Issues: Due to the imbalance, eggs may not release properly, leading to missed or irregular periods and fertility struggles.

"Polycystic" Misnomer: Despite the name, you do not need to have cysts on your ovaries to have PCOS. The "cysts" are actually follicles containing immature eggs that failed to release.

Insulin Resistance: Many people with PCOS are resistant to insulin, causing the body to produce more, which further increases androgen levels.

Common Symptoms

Irregular Periods: Infrequent, very long, or missed periods.

Excessive Hair Growth (Hirsutism): Often on the face, chest, or abdomen.

Skin/Hair Changes: Severe acne, dandruff, or male-pattern hair loss (thinning).

Weight Gain: Specifically difficulty losing weight or increased abdominal fat.

Diagnosis and Management

PCOS is diagnosed using the "Rotterdam criteria," which includes assessing irregular ovulation, high androgen levels, and/or polycystic ovaries via ultrasound. While there is no cure, it is manageable through:

Lifestyle Changes: Weight loss, a healthy diet, and exercise to manage insulin resistance.

Medication: Birth control pills to regulate periods, metformin for insulin, and anti-androgen medicines for hair/acne.

Potential Long-Term Health Risks

If left unmanaged, PCOS increases the risk for diabetes, high blood pressure, cholesterol issues, and uterine cancer.

title: Micronized creatine  -no evidence
content:
Hi [CUSTOMER],

The quick answer is:

There is no scientific evidence that micronized creatine is more effective than standard creatine monohydrate. It’s the same molecule but smaller, meaning it may be less gritty when you mix it, but there is absolutely no safety or efficacy benefit. Here are some simple notes:

Regular creatine monohydrate remains the gold standard. It has been used in thousands of studies over more than 30 years and consistently improves strength, power, muscle mass, recovery, and high-intensity exercise performance.

Micronized creatine is still creatine monohydrate. The only difference is that the particles have been milled into much smaller sizes, so it mixes easily in fluids and may be less gritty when ingesting.

What it does NOT do:

- Increase absorption into muscle
- Increase muscle creatine stores
- Produce greater gains in strength or muscle
- Require a lower dose

Water-soluble or micronized creatine

Takeaway:

Our professionals deliver the only proven, science-backed creatine monohydrate and would not offer an alternative source because of the lack of evidence to date that any form is better, including solubility. Creatine does not have to totally dissolve in water (or fluid mix) before you ingest it. Your digestive tract takes care of preparing any creatine (from your food or supplements) for proper absorption once it enters the body, regardless of its solubility or size.

More info

The sales numbers or marketing claims for “water-soluble creatine” or micronized creatine, although the form means nothing related to efficacy, are simply a product of the hype around creatine and influencer money to separate a brand from the norm—nothing to do with results, just marketing spin.

Creatine supplementation does not have to be “water-soluble” or micronized to be safe and effective. In fact, all powdered creatine products are water-dispersible, but they are not all highly water-soluble or need to be. Most powdered creatine monohydrate (CrM) products are considered moderately soluble in water but proven superior to all other creatine forms, including the advertised “water-soluble” or micronized creatine products. Creatine supplementation does not need to be “water-soluble” or micronized for the body to use it. The body (GI tract) dissolves the ingested creatine and puts it into solution to absorb it.

The evidence-based scientific position, including The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) position stand on creatine, states:

Creatine Monohydrate is the most extensively studied and clinically effective form. Claims that other forms deliver greater uptake or are superior are currently unfounded—basically a marketing spin to help justify their increased costs. In other words, the other forms (“water-soluble”/micronized) are more expensive with no efficacy advantage.

Bottom line

If both products are pure creatine monohydrate like dotFIT’s NSF CS product, 5 g/day of either product will produce essentially the same physiological results.

That remains the consensus among organizations such as the International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) and the vast majority of creatine researchers. If new evidence emerges showing a true performance advantage, it would represent a significant change from the current scientific consensus.

Matthew F. Watto, MD: Welcome back to The Curbsiders. I'm Dr. Matthew Watto, here with America's primary care physician, Dr. Paul Nelson Williams. Paul, are you ready to talk about some adrenal insufficiency? We had a great conversation with Dr. Kargi, and I'd like you to start us off.
