But if you have someone with chronic malaise and poor appetite and maybe unexplained weight loss, and your GI workup is not really leading you anywhere, it's probably worth thinking about adrenal insufficiency. Even though primary adrenal insufficiency is pretty rare—we're talking cases per millions—secondary adrenal insufficiency is actually fairly common. It's probably worth thinking about and testing for more often than I have in the past. So for me, it's having a lower threshold to start looking for it.

Watto: When it's adrenal crisis, you probably think about it, but then it's too late. Ideally, you would think about it before that happens. But the symptoms can be quite vague. The mineralocorticoid symptoms, like salt cravings, dizziness, near syncope, and muscle cramps, might make me think of it because they sound more like something endocrine is going on. But if it's just a little weight loss, a little fatigue, or a little nausea, that's everybody.

Williams: Right. If a patient came to me saying, "I'm craving salt," that might hasten the workup a little bit, but that's not the typical presentation.

Watto: If you are going to check a cortisol level, you should really check it in the morning, between 7 AM and 9 AM. If you check it too early, it might not have peaked yet, so you might get a level that looks low. But if you had checked an hour or two later, it might have been above a threshold, and then you would know you could rule out the diagnosis. The cutoffs depend on your source: < 3–5 µg/dL that early in the morning is pretty much diagnostic of adrenal insufficiency. If it's > 15 µg/dL, that's a pretty robust cortisol and the patient probably doesn't have adrenal insufficiency. But if the level is between 5 µg/dL and 15 µg/dL, you're in a gray zone, and that's where you might think about doing a stimulation (stim) test.

Dr. Kargi gave us a quick and dirty version of the stim test. Paul, have you had a chance to try this yet?

Williams: I have not. Have you? I'm sure you've been just waiting for the chance.

Watto: I would love to do this. I don't know whether I'm set up to do it in the office right now. But this is an aspirational goal for my practice, and I'm sure some physicians are set up in their office already to do it. You can give either intramuscular or subcutaneous cosyntropin 250 µg. You don't even have to get a baseline cortisol level right before the injection. Let's say the patient's previous cortisol level was between 5 µg/dL and 15 µg/dL, so you weren't sure about the diagnosis. You bring them back to the office one day, give them a shot of cosyntropin, and then 30–60 minutes later, have a random cortisol drawn. If it's > 19 µg/dL, you've ruled out adrenal insufficiency. If it's anything else, send them to an endocrinologist to sort it out. You might be able to make the diagnosis yourself doing that.

Any treatment pearls to leave the audience with?

Williams: I hope endocrinologists don't take issue with this. I say this with respect and admiration, but it feels kind of vibe-based to me. Without a lab value to guide treatment, you are dependent on the patient telling you how they feel much of the time. You have to let their symptoms guide you. It is probably worth noting that because hydrocortisone has a relatively short half-life, within hours, in fact, you typically have to do twice-daily dosing, sometimes even three times daily dosing to get patients to where they feel okay. It sounds like there's a fair amount of trial and error and some adjustments that you have to make depending on what's going on with the patient at any given time. You land somewhere between a dose of 15–30 mg per day, but there will be some variability, even within an individual patient, depending on what's going on with them from a physiologic standpoint.

Watto: They are going to take one dose in the morning and then a second dose in the afternoon, but they don't want them to take it too late in the evening because it could cause insomnia, and you want to try to mimic physiologic levels as much as you can. Two-thirds of the daily dose is given early in the morning and then another third of the daily dose later in the day if you are prescribing two-times-daily dosing.

And Dr. Kargi had a low threshold for doubling the dose. If the patient has a cold, double the dose for 2 or 3 days. With a high fever, triple the dose for a few days. If they are going for surgery, they are probably going to be getting some intravenous hydrocortisone while they're in the hospital.

We really turned over every stone we could possibly think of on this podcast. There were so many great pearls that we don't have time to go through them all here. But we talked about steroid tapers and a lot more. You can check it out here.

title: Juan 150lbs Suppbesast
content:
[NAME], before we get started on your answer:

Caveat to all numbers is the accuracy of your numbers (e.g., calorie count, body fat, etc.), but it doesn’t matter; they are just numbers you have assigned to where you are today—or placeholders for a starting place. Because you have found your maintenance, that is the spot we work from. The ongoing body fat directional changes and actual overall body composition numbers will capture the true results regardless of your numbers. We are looking at actual changes to measure progress so we can add, subtract, etc., to move in the right direction until we reach the goal.

Let Me Break This Down For You

First off—respect. Seriously. Losing 30 pounds since November, building substantial muscle, running a restaurant 4 days a week on 10–12-hour shifts, AND maintaining a structured morning routine with training? That's not a guy who lacks discipline. That's a guy who's hitting a very specific, very solvable problem.

Here's the thing—what you're experiencing is textbook metabolic adaptation, and the good news is we know exactly what's happening and what to do about it.

What's Actually Going On

At 150 lbs and 5'6", you're not a big guy. You've lost 30 lbs, built muscle, and your body has fully adapted to “1,400 calories” (or whatever your weekly average caloric intake has been in the past weeks). That IS now your maintenance level. Your metabolism has slightly downregulated to match your intake, including adapting to a lower body weight, so you naturally burn fewer calories doing the same activities than when you were at a higher body weight. It's not broken—it's actually doing exactly what it's designed to do. It protected you. Now we have to outsmart it.

The "stay the course" advice from your current coach? Look, I'm not here to throw anyone under the bus, but when the data is telling you something isn't working anymore, you don't just stay the course. You adjust. That's the whole game.

Your Numbers First

Let me give you some context here. At 150 lbs and roughly 20–25% body fat, you're carrying approximately:

- 112–120 lbs of lean body mass (LBM)
- 30–37 lbs of body fat

To get to 10% body fat, assuming you maintain or even add a little muscle, you're looking at getting down to roughly 125–130 lbs total weight—or building enough muscle that 10% body fat sits at a higher scale weight. Either way, you've got real work ahead, but it's absolutely achievable.

---

Here's My Breakdown—Step by Step

1. Stop Thinking About the Scale and Start Measuring Body Fat Every Two Weeks

The scale is lying to you right now. You said it yourself—you've gained substantial muscle. That muscle is probably masking some fat loss on the scale. Get a reliable body fat measurement method (DEXA if you can access it, or a good caliper protocol) and track that every two weeks. That's your real progress marker. Weight is almost meaningless at your stage.

2. You Need a Calorie Recalculation—But Probably NOT Another Cut

Here's where I'm going to push back on both camps—the "cut more" crowd AND the "just eat more" crowd. At 1,400 calories, you're already very low for a 50-year-old active male running a restaurant. Cutting further risks:

- Accelerated muscle loss
- Further metabolic suppression
- Hormonal disruption (especially important given your peptide protocol and DHEA use)
- Feeling like garbage, which tanks your performance and adherence

The bottom line is— you've established “1,400” as your new maintenance. The move isn't necessarily to drop to 1,100–1,200. That's a dangerous road at your size and activity level.

3. Strategic Calorie Cycling Is Your Next Move

This is what I'd look at seriously. Instead of a flat 1,400 every day, consider:

- Training days (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat): Bump to 1,600–1,700 calories, with the added calories coming from targeted carbohydrates around your workout window.
- Non-training/restaurant work days (Wed, Fri, Sun): Keep at 1,300–1,400, staying lower-carb/carnivore-leaning (lean proteins—but get some very low-calorie vegetables in).

This does two things—it gives your metabolism a signal that starvation isn't happening (preventing further adaptation), AND it puts fuel exactly where it needs to go: into your training. You're on a low-carb carnivore base, which can be fine, but on training days your muscles want glucose. Even a targeted 50–100 g of quality carbs around your workout can meaningfully change your body composition trajectory and help your peptides work better.

4. Your Protein Needs to Be Non-Negotiable

At your LBM, you need at minimum 112–120 grams of protein daily, but ideally closer to 130–150 grams. On a carnivore-leaning 1,400-calorie diet, this is achievable, but you need to be hitting it consistently. Protein is the most important macro for preserving and building muscle while in a deficit. It also has the highest thermic effect—your body burns more calories just digesting it.

Your dotFIT Aminos in the morning is a great start. Make sure you're counting that toward your total (2 scoops can be counted as ~30 g in your case toward your daily total—but no more regardless of how much you use). Get protein in at every meal or feeding opportunity.

5. Address the Metabolic Reset With a Short Diet Break

This is something the research supports strongly. After an extended period of caloric restriction (and you've been at this since November), your leptin drops, your thyroid slows, and your metabolism adapts. A 1–2-week diet break at true maintenance—which for you might actually be 1,800–2,000 calories based on your activity—can partially restore metabolic rate before you re-enter a deficit. This isn't quitting. This is strategy.

6. Add NEAT—Your Restaurant Days Are Actually An Asset

Here's something people miss. You're on your feet 10–12 hours in a restaurant 4 days a week. That's significant non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT). Make sure you're not unconsciously compensating by sitting more on your off days. On your off days, prioritize walking. Even 30–45 minutes of easy walking adds meaningful caloric expenditure without touching your recovery or muscle mass. Your rowing machine baseline is great for movement—keep that. But add deliberate walking on off days (use a Fit-Bit/phone or any step counter).

7. Your Training Needs a Progressive Overload Check

X3 bands to failure is solid. But here's my question—are you actually progressing? Meaning, is each session getting harder in some measurable way? More reps, longer time under tension, shorter rest periods, thicker bands? If you've been doing the same exercises at the same resistance for weeks, your body has adapted to that stimulus too. The muscle-building signal has to keep coming. Talk to your coach about how you're tracking progression in those movements.

8. Build a Proper Foundation With Your Supplement Stack

You've got some solid pieces in place—DHEA, D3+K, MTHF, creatine (excellent for body composition and strength at your age), and the peptides. But I want to make sure you've got a complete multivitamin/mineral formula locked in as your foundation. When you're in a caloric deficit, micronutrient gaps are real and they affect everything—energy, recovery, hormonal function, sleep.

I'd strongly recommend the dotFIT All-in-1 SuperBlend as your comprehensive multi base. At 50, in a deficit, training hard, running a restaurant—your micronutrient demands are high and your food variety may not be covering all the gaps, especially on a carnivore-leaning approach. The All-in-1 SuperBlend is designed for active people with serious goals and covers those bases properly alongside everything else you're doing. Take 1 scoop in the AM and one in the PM.

9. Consider Adding the dotFIT Weight Loss & Liver Support Stack

Here's something directly relevant to your situation. At your stage—pushing past a plateau toward a lean body composition goal—adding a liver support and fat metabolism product like dotFIT Weight Loss & Liver Support can be genuinely useful. Your liver is central to fat metabolism, and supporting it matters especially when you're coming off an extended deficit and working long restaurant days. Pair that with LeanMeal as a structured meal replacement to nail one or two of your daily feedings with precision—protein, fiber, controlled calories. It removes the guesswork on those busy restaurant days when you might grab whatever's available. Take 2 shakes daily, added to 2 traditional food meals, to help with calorie accuracy and daily energy levels.

10. Get Real Data With Consistent Tracking for the Next 30 Days

Before you make any big changes, spend the next 2–3 weeks doing one thing: tracking everything with precision. I mean everything. Use an app, weigh your food if you need to on days off, and log honestly. You might think you're at 1,400, but restaurant environments are notorious for untracked bites, tastes, and samples. Once you have clean data, you'll know for certain what you're working with and can make a truly informed adjustment.

---

The Bottom Line for [NAME]

You've done the hard part—you've built a foundation of muscle that most guys your age haven't got. Now we're talking about precision, not punishment. The answer isn't just "eat less" or blindly. And finally, when we achieve the goal, the calories will go up to a new maintenance and the workload can be lessened so our calories out and in are stable.

title: Chromosomes info
content:
Chromosomes are tiny packages of DNA inside your cells that store your body's genetic instructions. They keep your DNA neat and safe, make sure it copies correctly when cells divide, and pass traits from parents to children. You can learn more about these structures from the National Human Genome Research Institute. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

Core Jobs of Chromosomes

Store DNA: They wrap long DNA strands tightly around proteins so they fit inside tiny cell nuclei.

Guide Cell Division: They help split DNA evenly when old cells make new cells.

Control Traits: They carry genes that tell your body how to grow, look, and work.

Pass on Heredity: They ensure children get a balanced mix of traits from both parents.

title: Calcium L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate folate forms best for supps
content:
No, they are not exactly the same; Calcium L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate is a form of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate that is stabilized by being a calcium salt. 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-MTHF) is the biologically active form of folate (Vitamin B9) that the body can use directly, while Calcium L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate is the common, stable, and commercially available form of that active nutrient used in supplements.

Here's a breakdown:

5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-MTHF):

This is the naturally occurring, metabolically active form of folate found in the human circulation and in food. It's the form the body uses to convert homocysteine to methionine, among other vital functions.

Calcium L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate:

This is a synthetic, stable salt form of the active 5-MTHF. Adding calcium makes the naturally occurring 5-MTHF more stable and suitable for use in dietary supplements and food fortification.

In summary:

When you see "5-MTHF," "L-5-MTHF," or "Calcium L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate" on a supplement label, it refers to the same biologically active nutrient. The "calcium" part simply indicates the form it's formulated in for stability and availability in a supplement.

title: Lead testing uncovers ‘deeply concerning issue' in spirulina
content:
https://www.nutraingredients.com/Article/2026/04/06/lead-testing-uncovers-deeply-concerning-issue-in-spirulina-supply-chain/?utm_source=newsletter_daily&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=06-Apr-2026&cid=DM1269247&bid=956316591

Global demand for spirulina is booming, with the market for this superfood projected to reach $1.3 billion by 2032. But new testing revealed some cracks in quality and safety that suggest some top-selling products may expose consumers to elevated lead levels.

Cyanotech conducted an initial screening of 37 top-selling spirulina and greens products, which were selected based on their “top-selling” status based on data from SPINS, Amazon sales and review volume, market visibility on Google, and social listening. Subsequent third-party testing by Eurofins confirmed the presence of lead in nearly half of the samples. The company then expanded the analysis to a second phase, in which Alkemist Labs tested 19 products across multiple lots, with a greater focus on organic-labeled products.

Because spirulina is a bio-accumulator, it absorbs not only nutrients but also any contaminants present in the water where it is cultivated. Since it is grown in aquatic systems, the quality of that environment directly determines the ingredient’s purity.

“What makes this especially important is how spirulina is consumed. It is harvested, dried, and delivered in a highly concentrated form,” [NAME] explained. “A single serving of powder represents a large amount of original biomass, so everything in it is concentrated as well, including all the beneficial nutrients—but also any contaminants present.”

title: Why do the products contain sucralose and artificial flavoring?
content:
Hi [NAME],

Thanks for contacting us. Congrats on taking the NASM Nutrition course! NASM is our favorite partner. We use sucralose in a few food products, such as protein powder mixes, because it is an evidence-based non-nutritional sweetener (NNS) approved by the FDA and the most popular of all NNS because of its taste and safety profile. The tiny amounts needed for sweetening make protein mixes taste better without the calories of added sugars. Further, we have NNS in some of our powder formulas because most people prefer the benefits over natural added sugar (see below). We also have all-natural sweeteners in products for people who prefer all-natural. Therefore, if you have a preference for all-natural, pick those dotFIT powders such as BestPlantProtein, All Natural WheySmooth, Alln1 SuperBlendTM, Vegan AminoFormula, etc.

In case you are interested, see below for peer-reviewed facts on non-nutritive sweeteners from the Practitioner Dietary Supplement Reference Guide (PDSRG). Moreover, remember to be careful how you interpret internet data and studies related to NNS, especially when they are in the minority of conclusions, use dosages that are not in moderation as normal, study populations including reverse causality, or use supraphysiological amounts in small animals. Also below is an FAQ.

Co-factors Including Sweeteners Used in Food Products Such as Nutrition Bars and Powders

Co-factors in a protein/CHO powder are combined to deliver better taste with low/no calories, texture, mixing ability, uniform nutrient distribution, ingredient flow and stability, including during cooking or baking, and a practical product shelf life.

Sweeteners Background

Health outcomes or adverse reactions to natural and/or added caloric sweeteners (CS), such as refined sugars, honey, syrups, fruit sugars, sucrose and their constituent molecules, include, but are not limited to, obesity, blood sugar spikes, tooth decay and allergic responses from the residues from their sources of origin. This has spawned the need and growing use of non-nutritive sweeteners (NNS). Further, these issues related to CS have led to prevention policies such as sugar-sweetened beverage taxes and front-of-package labels, and may also be incentivizing companies to utilize NNS as a way of reducing CS. (New FDA label format can be viewed here.)

Recognizing there are industry and cult biases towards the use of NNS, none have been validated or accepted. The major scientific bodies around the world have firmly established their safety, including for use with children, thus requiring no label warnings as added CS and other natural ingredients (e.g., peanuts, shellfish, wheat, dairy, etc.).

In summary, FDA-approved NNS advantages over CS include:

- Higher nutrition per calorie/sweetness to support desired body composition, especially when used to replace CS.
- Sucralose tested best of NNS and sucrose in weight management236.
- Supports blood sugar (approved for diabetics)224,229,235.
- Lower risk of adverse reactions common with “natural” sweeteners (honey, stevia, lactose, fruit sugar residues, etc.)216,217.
- Supports weight control versus being a contributing factor in weight gain230,235.
- Approved for children230,231,232.

Finally, the [NAME] et al. review titled “Low-/No-Calorie Sweeteners: A Review of Global Intakes” concluded that “Overall, the studies conducted since 2008 raised no concerns with respect to exceedance of individual sweetener acceptable daily intakes (ADIs) among the general population globally. Additionally, the data identified do not suggest a shift in exposure over time, with several studies indicating a reduction in intake.”

Q: Why artificial sweeteners? Not included in All Natural WheySmooth, Unflavored, BestPlantProtein and Vegan AX
A: Better and healthier than added sugar and FDA approved (Ref. Sweetener docs here.) 4,2022meta, ref4.
Added sugars are a leading cause of disease and why the government warns and sets limits. Ref2.
Better taste = continued use to improve fitness results.
Higher nutrition per calorie/sweetness to support desired body composition.
Sucralose tested best of sweeteners and sucrose in weight management. Ref.
Supports blood sugar (approved for diabetics).
Decrease risk of adverse reactions common with “natural” sweeteners (honey, stevia, lactose, fruit sugar residues, etc.)27,28.
Supports weight control versus contributor2, 2022meta, and CV health.
Approved for children1.

*The FDA established an acceptable daily intake (ADI) for sucralose of 5 milligrams per kilogram (Europe is 7 and Canada 11 mg/kg) of body weight per day. The ADI represents an amount 100 times less than the quantity of sucralose found to be safe in research studies. For a person weighing 150 pounds (68 kg), the US ADI equates to 340 mg of sucralose—the amount found in nine cans of diet soda or more than 28 individual packets of sucralose—consumed, on average, every day over a lifetime.

title: IGF-1 LR3 peptide info
content:
IGF-1 LR3 (Long R3 Insulin-Like Growth Factor-1) is a synthetic analog of IGF-1 designed to have a much longer half-life and greater biological activity than natural IGF-1. It has an added 13-amino acid extension and a modification at the 3rd amino acid position, which reduces binding to IGF-binding proteins and allows it to remain active in circulation far longer.

Its primary mechanism of action is direct activation of the IGF-1 receptor on muscle and other tissues, stimulating anabolic signaling pathways such as PI3K/Akt/mTOR and MAPK. These pathways increase protein synthesis, satellite cell activation, muscle cell proliferation, glucose uptake, tissue repair, and recovery while also reducing protein breakdown.

The primary uses of IGF-1 LR3 are typically related to:
- Supporting lean muscle growth and recovery
- Enhancing tissue repair after intense training or injury
- Improving nutrient partitioning and body composition
- Research into muscle regeneration, metabolism, and anabolic signaling

Because IGF-1 signaling also influences cellular growth broadly throughout the body, there are important safety considerations, including potential effects on blood glucose regulation and theoretical concerns regarding abnormal cell proliferation. Most legitimate clinical discussions emphasize medical supervision and careful monitoring.

Dosage

There is no medically established or FDA-approved dosing protocol for IGF-1 LR3 in healthy individuals for muscle growth or performance enhancement. Most dosing information comes from experimental use, peptide clinics, and bodybuilding communities rather than large controlled human trials.

That said, the most commonly referenced “performance-support” dosing ranges are:
- 20–50 mcg daily as a conservative/common range
- 50–100 mcg daily in more aggressive experimental protocols

Typical cycle lengths discussed are 4–6 weeks, followed by time off to reduce receptor desensitization risk.

The rationale behind these doses is to activate IGF-1 receptors enough to increase:
- muscle protein synthesis
- satellite cell activation
- recovery
- nutrient uptake

without excessively increasing side effects such as hypoglycemia, edema, nerve compression symptoms, or unwanted tissue growth.

NEXGEN dosing

After 6 weeks we will assess progress (subjective) and decide if an IGF-1 LR3 peptide add is warranted.

IGF-1 LR3 (5/6 weeks, 50–100µ daily; 1mg=20 50µ shots/vial [25 units/shot]) 1 vial=1mg (1000µ)

Primary Use: Promotes muscle growth, recovery, and nutrient partitioning through direct anabolic signaling. Often considered one of the most potent downstream mediators of growth hormone activity.

Mechanism: A modified long-acting IGF-1 analog that binds directly to IGF-1 receptors, stimulating protein synthesis, satellite cell activation, muscle tissue growth, and cellular recovery through activation of the Akt/mTOR anabolic pathway. Unlike GH secretagogues, it bypasses the pituitary and acts directly at the tissue level. (Note: Unlike Tesamorelin or Sermorelin, IGF-1 LR3 does not increase natural growth hormone production—it acts downstream of GH by directly activating IGF-1 pathways.)

Mechanistically, IGF-1 LR3 primarily works through the Akt/mTOR anabolic signaling pathway:

A major concern with higher or prolonged dosing is that IGF-1 signaling is not muscle-specific—it can stimulate growth pathways in many tissues. Because of that, most medically oriented sources recommend conservative exposure, short durations, and monitoring of:
- fasting glucose
- insulin sensitivity
- IGF-1 blood levels
- general metabolic markers.

title: Sweeteners OK by ADA and all else
content:
Statement from American Heart Association and American Diabetes Association Supports Low-Calorie Sweeteners as Useful Substitutes for Sugar

ATLANTA (July 10, 2012) – Using low-calorie sweeteners in beverages and other foods has the potential to help people reach and maintain a healthy body weight and is helpful for glucose control for people with diabetes, according to a scientific statement from the American Heart Association and the American Diabetes Association. The statement is published in the American Heart Association journal Circulation and the American Diabetes Association journal Diabetes Care, and confirms previous support statements from these two major health organizations.

According to scientific statement lead author, Christopher Gardner, Ph.D., associate professor of medicine at Stanford University in California, “While they are not magic bullets, smart use of non-nutritive sweeteners could help you reduce added sugars in your diet, therefore lowering the number of calories you eat. Reducing calories could help you attain and maintain a healthy body weight, and thereby lower your risk of heart disease and diabetes. But there are caveats.”

“For example, if you choose a beverage sweetened with non-nutritive sweeteners instead of a 150-calorie soft drink, but then reward yourself with a 300-calorie slice of cake or cookies later in the day, non-nutritive sweeteners are not going to help you control your weight because you added more calories to your day than you subtracted,” said Dr. Gardner. “However, if you substitute the beverage with non-nutritive sweeteners for a 150-calorie sugar-sweetened soft drink, and don’t compensate with additional calories, that substitution could help you manage your weight because you would be eating fewer calories.”

Non-nutritive (low-calorie) sweeteners covered in the statement include acesulfame potassium, aspartame, neotame, saccharin, stevia, and sucralose. The safety of these non-nutritive sweeteners is supported by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

The American Heart Association recommends that most women eat no more than 100 calories per day and men no more than 150 calories per day of added sugars. This recommendation is based on research that showed diets high in added sugars contribute to obesity and cardiovascular heart disease. Limiting intake of added sugars can help reduce calorie intake and can help people achieve or maintain a healthy body weight.

Beyond calories, and focusing more specifically on added sugars, non-nutritive sweeteners have their place for people with diabetes.

“For example, soft drinks sweetened with non-nutritive sweeteners do not increase blood glucose levels, and thus can provide a sweet option for those with diabetes,” said [NAME], R.D., CDE, one of the statement authors speaking on behalf of the American Diabetes Association.

“The use of non-nutritive sweeteners may be used in a carbohydrate-controlled food plan, to potentially reduce carbohydrate intake which may aid in weight management and diabetes control,” said [NAME].

“We are pleased to learn of this new position statement,” noted [NAME], Ph.D., president of the Calorie Control Council. “With the increasing rates of overweight and obesity, low and reduced calorie sweeteners and the products that use them offer consumers great taste with fewer calories – and controlling calories can aid in weight control and diabetes management.”

“For anyone trying to monitor or reduce their intake of calories or added sugars, the potential impact of choosing ‘diet products’ with non-nutritive sweeteners needs to be considered within the context of the overall diet. Strategies for reducing calories and added sugars also involve choosing foods which have no added sugars or non-nutritive sweeteners – such as vegetables, fruits, high-fiber whole grains, and non- or low-fat dairy,” Dr. Gardner said.

A full PDF of the statement can be found on the American Heart Association’s website.

Ibutamoren (MK-677): oral, non-peptide GH stimulant

Primary use: To increase the body's natural growth hormone and IGF-1 levels to support muscle growth, recovery, and overall anabolic function without injections.

Mechanism: Mimics ghrelin ("hunger hormone") to activate ghrelin receptors (GHS-R1a), which signals the hypothalamus and pituitary to increase natural GH pulse release; the liver then produces more IGF-1, leading to an increase in protein synthesis and reduction in muscle breakdown.

Typical dosing used in research and practice is approximately 10–25 mg once daily, usually taken in the evening or split, with many starting at approximately 10 mg to assess tolerance and adjusting based on response.

Notes: MK-677 is an oral compound that increases your body's growth hormone by mimicking a hunger signal. That can help with recovery, muscle maintenance, and sleep—but it also makes you hungrier and can affect blood sugar, so it's not a shortcut unless everything else is dialed in. Human results vary and are largely based on anecdotes. MK-677 is not FDA approved and is classified as a research compound.

title: Caffeine vasodialator notes
content:
Coffee Effects

The alkaloid caffeine contained in coffee has positive inotropic and chronotropic effects on the heart via catecholamine release and raises systolic blood pressure; for instance, 250 mg raises systolic pressure by 10 mm Hg after 15 minutes. Caffeine causes mild cerebral vasoconstriction, relaxes bronchial smooth muscles, increases gastric acid secretion via gastrin release, and transiently increases diuresis. Theobromine and theophylline alkaloids in caffeine act as vasodilators, cough suppressants, and bronchodilators. The habituation effect occurs over time.

Four to five cups of coffee daily can reduce gout attacks in men by up to 40% through increased uric acid excretion, while more than six cups may reduce attacks by 59%, although decaffeinated coffee is preferable as a supportive measure.

Coffee enriched with chlorogenic acid–rich green coffee bean extracts showed increased DNA protection against oxidative damage and increased plasma-reduced glutathione via glutathione reductase activation. Roasting lowers chlorogenic acid, trigonelline, cafestol, and kahweol levels while increasing melanoidin and nicotinic acid levels.

Coffee and healthy aging

The researchers found a correlation between how much caffeine the women typically drank (which was mostly from coffee) when they were between 45 and 60 years old and their likelihood of healthy aging. After adjusting for other factors that could affect aging, such as their overall diet, how much they exercised and whether they smoked, those who consumed the most caffeine (equivalent to nearly seven eight-ounce cups of coffee per day) had odds of healthy aging that were 13 percent higher than those who consumed the least caffeine (equivalent to less than one cup per day).

Drinking tea or decaffeinated coffee was not associated with healthy aging, the researchers found. That may be because the study participants generally consumed less tea and decaffeinated coffee overall, so perhaps there were fewer chances for the researchers to find benefits linked to them, said [NAME], an adjunct professor of nutritional sciences at the University of Toronto who led the study. Tea and decaf coffee also have less caffeine, and tea has different plant compounds from regular coffee, so that may explain the results, too, she added.

Despite the benefits shown for food intake, satiety and body composition, the mechanism by which CFE exerts its benefits largely remains unknown. It was therefore an aim of this study to investigate possible biochemical mechanisms of CFE. Following 16-weeks of supplementation and despite the reduction in calorie intake in the CFE group, there were no associated changes in satiety hormone markers (namely leptin and ghrelin) from baseline in the CFE group. The placebo group however showed significantly elevated levels of leptin, cortisol and NPY from baseline. Typically, when leptin levels increase, satiety would improve, and weight loss or maintenance occur. However, as leptin is produced in adipose tissue25, as fat mass increases, leptin production increases26,27. Weight gain is also associated with a decreased sensitivity to leptin27, reducing the ability to achieve satiety. Leptin acts to reduce the desire to eat28, while cortisol29 and NPY28 increases the desire to eat. Therefore, at times of hunger, leptin levels are typically low and NPY levels high, initiating a feeding desire and increasing cortisol levels. The elevated cortisol leads to eating, which in turn increases leptin levels, reducing NPY activation and subsequent cortisol levels30,31.

Cortisol can induce a dose-dependent increase in leptin32, and this may be why leptin and cortisol have been shown to have inverse circadian rhythms, indicating a possible satiety regulatory relationship33,34.

This theory is partially supported by the correlation data (Table 3), where it is shown that in the placebo group, as leptin values increase so does the fat mass, while cortisol levels decrease (inverse relationship with leptin). An effect not seen in the CFE group. This is also supported by a study where CFE was shown to reduce anxiety and stress as well as act on cortisol regulation35.

title: Methylated vitimins
content:
Methylated vitamins

Takeaway:
All the vitamins our PTs deliver, including those in the SB, are properly prepared for maximum absorption/cellular function and contain the 2 methylated vitamins that can be methylated (folate and B12).

More Info
Methylated vitamin statements are very misleading and wholly untrue. They are based on 2 vitamins that are methylated or can be methylated, not that they necessarily should be. Generally, due to the spreading influencer misinformation, many supplement marketers misuse the term “methylated multivitamin.” What they actually mean:

- Contains 5-MTHF instead of folic acid
- Contains methylcobalamin instead of cyanocobalamin

It does NOT mean all B vitamins (or A, D, E, K) are methylated—because chemically that is impossible.

I beat the shit out of the influencer’s comments about this topic. Folic acid (synthetic folate) is actually the only form approved for claims of prevention, especially during pregnancy. Although we play the marketing game and use the only 2 methylated forms of vitamins (folate and B12) available that can be methylated (folate as calcium L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate and B12 as methyl cobalamin). If the others could be methylated, they would be basically worthless*. Just influencers taking a science topic analogous to what they have done with seed oils, and unknowingly (or not) twisting or misrepresenting the science so it generates revenues. (See Q&As.) You cannot methylate most vitamins—period!

Your business solution: All complete MVM formulas and Alln1 SuperBlend™ have the VMs prepared in forms the body can use. They all are in a pre-formed structure to allow the body to not just absorb them (optimal bioavailability) but also allow proper “functional absorption” (active at the target tissue*), which is better than just bioavailable absorption. All our labels have the forms listed.

*Example: Vitamin B6 does not undergo methylation to become active, unlike folate and B12. Instead, it is converted into its active coenzyme form, pyridoxal-5-phosphate (P5P or PLP).

Q: Is the SuperBlend methylated? Thank you in advance! Respectfully, [NAME]

A: Thanks for contacting us. There is a lot of junk science regarding methylated vitamin forms, so we seem to be getting this question often. See below for your answer and be mindful that only B9 (folate) and B12 are available in the market in their methylated forms, and the body will convert forms as needed depending on the destination regardless of origin as long as you have enough. The Alln1 SuperBlend (and dotFIT MVMs) uses both B9/folate (calcium L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate) and B12 (methyl cobalamin) in the methylated forms, as do our multivitamin and mineral formulas (MVM).

Q: Are all your vitamins methylated vitamins? How would I be able to tell?

A: Your question is vague, in the fact that not all vitamins should contain a methyl group to be effective (actually, it is a problem for some). What you want in any vitamin is an absorbable form (i.e., a form that is already prepared as the body would prepare it once extracted from a food source). All our vitamins (and minerals) are in a pre-formed structure to allow the body proper “functional absorption” (active at the target tissue*), which is better than bioavailable absorption. All our labels have the form listed. Do not be fooled that all vitamins need a methyl group to be effective. In all our products, if it needs a methyl group, it will be part of it and listed on the label, such as B12 or folate in our Alln1 SuperBlend™ and MVMs. If you would like to talk to a chemist further, we will connect you with our pharmacist/chemist for the facts here.

Many supplement marketers misuse the term “methylated multivitamin,” generally due to the influencer misinformation.

What they usually mean is:

- Contains 5-MTHF instead of folic acid
- Contains methylcobalamin instead of cyanocobalamin

It does NOT mean all B vitamins (or A, D, E, K) are methylated—because chemically that is impossible.

Vitamin B6 does not typically undergo methylation to become active, unlike folate and B12. Instead, it is converted into its active coenzyme form, pyridoxal-5-phosphate (P5P or PLP). However, B6 is a critical cofactor that supports the methylation cycle and is necessary for producing the methyl donor SAMe.

Key Details on Vitamin B6 and Methylation:

Active Form: While not “methylated” (e.g., methyl-cobalamin), the active, bioavailable form of Vitamin B6 is pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (P5P), often found in high-quality methylated B-complex supplements.

Role in Methylation: Vitamin B6 (as P5P) is essential for the conversion of homocysteine into cysteine via the cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) enzyme.

Supports Methylation Cycle: It is required for the proper functioning of the entire one-carbon metabolism (methylation) pathway.

While you cannot typically buy “methyl-B6,” ensuring you consume the active form, P5P, helps bypass enzymatic conversion issues.

https://www.cspi.org/article/folic-acid-best-choice-healthy-pregnancy. You would think I wrote this 😊—it scientifically supports everything I said and rails on the nutrition influencers saying formulating with 5-MTHF is better than folic acid—as it is not true.

Conclusion from the review: Ignore the hype. Don’t worry about MTHFR gene variants. There is no reason to spend more money on a prenatal MVM (or any MVM) with 5-MTHF. And don’t be swayed by companies or influencers pushing folate supplements. Folic acid is safe, and it’s the only form of folate that has been shown to prevent neural tube birth defects.

Some prenatal vitamins claim that people with an MTHFR variant need to take a vitamin that contains a version of folate called L-methylfolate, or 5-MTHF. Why? Folic acid has to undergo conversion before becoming the active form that the body can use, whereas 5-MTHF doesn’t require conversion. Sounds important. But it doesn’t matter. People with the variant can still process folic acid without any problems. “When getting the same amount of folic acid, people with the [variant] have an average amount of folate in their blood that is only slightly lower” than people without the variant, says the CDC.

But that doesn’t stop influencers and supplement companies from pushing supplements with folate instead of folic acid.

What supplemental vitamins can actually be methylated and put into a multivitamin and mineral formula? Our pharmacist says only 2 are available, and they are B9 (folate) and B12.

Great question—and this is highly relevant if you're formulating a practitioner-grade MVM where form matters.

Your pharmacist is partially correct in the strict chemical sense, but incomplete in the functional sense.

If we define “methylated” literally (meaning the molecule already contains a methyl group—CH₃ attached as part of its active structure), then only a few vitamins are commercially available in true methylated forms.

Let’s break this down precisely.

✅ Vitamins That Exist in TRUE Methylated Forms

1. Vitamin B9—Folate
5-Methyltetrahydrofolate
Also called L-5-MTHF
Branded forms: Quatrefolic®, Metafolin®
This is the biologically active, methyl-donor form.
Bypasses MTHFR conversion.
Highly stable for use in multivitamins.
✔ Fully methylated.
✔ Very common in high-quality MVMs.

2. Vitamin B12
Methylcobalamin
One of the active coenzyme forms of B12.
Direct methyl donor.
Used in the methylation cycle (methionine synthase reaction).
Other B12 forms:
Adenosylcobalamin (mitochondrial form)
Hydroxocobalamin
Cyanocobalamin
✔ Methylcobalamin is truly methylated.
✔ Stable in properly formulated MVMs.

⚠️ Vitamins That Are NOT “Methylated” (But Often Confused As Such)
These do NOT exist as methylated vitamins:

- Vitamin B6 (exists as P5P—pyridoxal-5-phosphate, not methylated)
- Riboflavin (B2)—exists as riboflavin-5-phosphate, not methylated
- Thiamin (B1)—no methyl form
- Niacin (B3)—no methyl form
- Pantothenic acid (B5)—no methyl form
- Biotin—no methyl form
- Vitamins A, D, E, K—no methylated forms

There are activated or coenzyme forms, but not methylated versions.

🧬 Why Only B9 and B12 Can Be Methylated
Because they directly participate in one-carbon metabolism and methyl group transfer reactions:

- 5-MTHF donates methyl groups
- Methylcobalamin transfers methyl groups to homocysteine

No other vitamin functions primarily as a methyl donor in this way.

🔬 Important Clarification for Formulators
Some supplement marketers misuse the term “methylated multivitamin.”

What they usually mean is:

- Contains 5-MTHF instead of folic acid
- Contains methylcobalamin instead of cyanocobalamin

It does NOT mean all B vitamins are methylated—because chemically that is impossible.

🏆 If You Were Designing a High-End MVM (Trainer/Practitioner Grade)
The “fully activated” approach would be:

- Folate as 5-MTHF
- B12 as methylcobalamin (± adenosylcobalamin blend)
- B6 as P5P
- Riboflavin as riboflavin-5-phosphate
- No folic acid
- No cyanocobalamin

But only two are truly methylated:
✔ B9
✔ B12

Your pharmacist is technically correct.

title: Protein and creatine summary for patients
content:
Key Points

Protein = building blocks; creatine = quick energy for muscles
Safe for healthy people; strong research backing
Typical intakes: protein 1.2–1.6 g/kg/day, creatine 3–5 g/day
Best for people lifting weights, older adults, low appetite
Exercise does most of the work; supplements are “extras”

This article explains what protein powders and creatine do, how much people usually take, who they’re most useful for, and why exercise still matters more than any supplement.

## What protein and creatine do

Protein powder (whey or plant-based) is basically a convenient food: it helps you reach your daily protein target to support muscle repair, growth, and healthy aging, especially if you can’t get enough from meals.1

Creatine is an energy helper stored in muscles; it fuels short, hard efforts like sprinting or heavy lifting and can improve strength, power, training capacity, and muscle size.1

## Are they safe and effective?

Higher-protein diets have not been shown to damage healthy kidneys, despite old myths.1 Creatine monohydrate is one of the most studied sports supplements and has a very favorable safety and benefit profile in healthy people.1

## Typical amounts and best types

- Protein: For most adults who care about muscle or healthy aging, a common target is 1.2–1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight per day (more for older adults, people losing weight, or heavy lifters).1
- Creatine: 3–5 grams per day is enough for almost everyone.1

Good choices are whey isolate for omnivores and plant-based blends with added leucine for vegans; for creatine, stick with plain creatine monohydrate from a reputable brand.1

## Who may benefit most and key message

People who tend to benefit most include those doing resistance training, older adults, people on appetite-suppressing weight-loss medications, and anyone who struggles to eat enough protein.1

The core takeaway: strength training builds the “cake,” protein is a thin layer of icing, and creatine is just the sprinkles—exercise is the main driver of results; supplements just give a modest boost.1

title: Fat burning zone myth
content:
“A colleague once told me, ‘I’m only walking at two miles an hour because I’m burning more fat that way,’” recalls [NAME], professor of exercise and sport science at the University of Wisconsin−La Crosse.

Why? She wanted to be in the “fat-burning zone.”

It’s true that when you’re strolling or sitting on the sofa, you do burn more calories from fat than from carbs.

“Your body doesn’t burn fat very efficiently,” notes [NAME]. “But it doesn’t need to be efficient when you’re not working hard.”

“But as we progress to a higher heart rate—that is, higher-intensity exercise—our ability to rely on fat for energy decreases and carbohydrate becomes our preferred fuel,” explains [NAME], assistant professor of kinesiology and physical education at the University of Toronto.

That's no reason to slow down

“You may be burning a greater percentage of fat during low-intensity exercise,” says [NAME], “but that doesn’t mean you’re burning a larger amount of fat. Unless you exercise for a long time, you’re not burning many calories.”

In one study, 27 women with obesity who were on a low-calorie diet were randomly assigned to cycle at either high or low intensity three times a week. The “high” group cycled for 25 minutes; the “low” group cycled for 50 minutes.

“They burned the same calories, and after eight weeks, both groups had lost the same amount of weight and body fat,” says [NAME].

The bottom line

Ignore the fat-burning zone. [NAME]’s advice: “Focus on burning more calories rather than the ratio of fat-to-carbohydrate burn.”

title: Why are the serving counts different between the chocolate and vanilla BULK products if both bags weigh 25 pounds?
content:
Summary:
The serving counts differ because chocolate and vanilla have slightly different serving weights, and the manufacturer rounds fill weights to ensure customers receive at least the labeled amount. As a result, serving counts are approximate, and both products typically contain as much or more product than advertised.

Option 2:
Although both bulk bags are sold as 25 lb products, the published serving counts are estimates based on flavor-specific serving sizes and manufacturing fill tolerances. Because chocolate has a slightly larger serving size (42 g vs. 41 g for vanilla) and the actual fill weights are rounded to ensure customers receive at least the stated amount, serving counts can differ between flavors—and in practice, customers often receive slightly more product than the labeled minimum.

Original data

From me:
The general answer is that chocolate protein will often weigh slightly more than vanilla with equal servings because of the chocolate added co-factors, but not always, and certainly not that big a difference, even if it is 25 lbs versus a single tub—but let’s check with the manufacturer.

From the manufacturer:
Chocolate typically has a high serving size due to cocoa powder, but the bulk weight might be the same due to bulk density. Additionally, there might be a serving that rounds up or down due to the bulk fill weight.

From me:
We need something clearer than that because I tried that, and the math doesn’t pan out with a flat 25 lbs, which is 11,339.8 grams. The chocolate serving is only 1 g bigger than the vanilla, meaning the discrepancy in 25 lbs would be no more than a few servings, not 18 servings. If you do the math on 25 lbs of chocolate with 284 servings and 42 g per serving, it comes to 11,928 grams, which is approximately 26.2 lbs. The vanilla 25 lb bulk with 302 servings at 41 g per serving would then weigh approximately 27.2 lbs (12,382 g). So basically, we can tell everyone that the manufacturer rounds up the bulk to cover all bases in the 25 lb containers, and sometimes one is heavier, but all are in range. In both cases, there are more servings than in a true 25 lb quantity of either product, which is why it says “about 302 servings.” In other words, you are getting more than what you paid for in either scenario.

Ask [NAME] if it is okay to say all this (also summary below). Our customers are very smart, so I have to know we are correct with this explanation.

Moral of the story—you are getting more in each because they round up and the servings are then published.

284 servings of chocolate at 42 g per serving = 11,928 g or 26.29 lbs.
302 servings of vanilla at 41 g per serving = 12,382 g or 27.2 lbs.

Going off a pure 25 lbs (no rounding), below would be the equation. Therefore, the rounding up favors the customer since there are more servings in both (284 and 302 in the current batch)—it also explains why chocolate will have fewer servings.

11,339.8 ÷ 42 g per serving = 269 servings of chocolate; 11,339.8 ÷ 41 g per serving = 276 servings of vanilla.

From the manufacturer/[NAME]:
Yes, we are aligned with [NAME]’s answer.

title: How can I prevent sharp abdominal muscle cramps during CrossFit workouts in hot, humid conditions, and could nutrition, hydration, or electrolytes be contributing?
content:
Hi [NAME],

Current scientific consensus is that most muscle cramps during exercise are primarily a neuromuscular fatigue problem, with dehydration and electrolyte losses acting as contributing factors in susceptible individuals rather than the sole cause. Therefore, your cramping may be nutrition/fluid/electrolyte related. If you are following proper hydration and diet guidelines for your activity, including supplementing with electrolytes as needed, and still cramping, it may be something else, such as simply neuromuscular fatigue. Keep in mind that low-carb diets are often associated with cramping because of low hydration and electrolytes. See below for proper fluid/electrolyte guidelines for specific situations, along with a couple of slides from our Practitioner lectures that may be helpful.

All said, the bottom line:

Based on the best available evidence, exercise-induced muscle cramps are best viewed as a problem of fatigued muscle and altered neuromuscular control, with again, dehydration and electrolyte loss serving as important contributors rather than the sole cause. For athletes and highly active individuals, the most effective long-term prevention strategy is to reduce muscle fatigue through appropriate conditioning, strength training, adequate carbohydrate and protein intake, recovery, and individualized fluid and sodium replacement. Hydration and electrolytes matter, but they work best as part of a comprehensive fatigue-management strategy rather than as stand-alone solutions.

Basic Fluid Recommendations*

- 16 oz 2 hours before activity (extra 8–16 oz 1 hour before on hot days)
- 4–8 oz every 20 minutes during activity
- 20 oz for every pound of weight loss post-activity

*If necessary (extended training sessions), use electrolyte formula and water as directed; may mix with AminoFormula.

The Current Understanding

1. Neuromuscular Fatigue (Primary Cause)

This is now considered the leading explanation for most exercise-induced cramps.

When a muscle becomes fatigued:

- Muscle spindle activity, which stimulates contraction, increases.
- Golgi tendon organ activity, which normally inhibits excessive contraction, decreases.
- The balance shifts toward excessive excitation of the motor neuron.
- The motor neuron begins firing repeatedly, producing a sustained involuntary contraction (cramp).

This explains why cramps:

- Almost always occur in muscles working hardest.
- Frequently happen late in exercise.
- Resolve when the muscle is stretched (stretching restores inhibitory signaling).

Examples:

- Calves during running
- Hamstrings during sprinting
- Quadriceps during cycling
- Forearms during gripping sports

2. Electrolyte Losses (Important in Some People)

Sweat contains:

- Sodium (largest loss)
- Chloride
- Small amounts of potassium
- Very small amounts of magnesium
- Trace calcium

Heavy "salty sweaters" may lose:

- 2–6 grams sodium/hour
- Occasionally much more

If sodium losses are not replaced during prolonged exercise (>2 hours), nerve excitability may increase, making fatigue-induced cramps more likely.

Electrolytes are therefore a risk modifier, not necessarily the root cause.

3. Dehydration

Loss of body water:

- Decreases blood volume
- Increases body temperature
- Accelerates fatigue

Again, dehydration mainly increases fatigue, which then predisposes to cramping.

Mild dehydration alone usually does not directly cause cramps.

Other Factors That Increase Risk

- Poor conditioning
- Sudden increase in training volume
- Exercise at higher intensity than usual
- Hot environments
- Previous history of cramps
- Older age
- Inadequate recovery
- Muscle damage

Beyond Hydration and Electrolytes: What Actually Helps?

1. Improve Muscular Endurance (Probably the Most Effective Prevention)

Condition the muscles to tolerate the workload.

Research consistently shows that athletes who cramp often are frequently:

- Under-conditioned for the event
- Racing harder than trained for

2. Progressive Overload

Avoid sudden jumps in:

- Mileage
- Weight
- Intensity
- Duration

3. Strength Training

Stronger muscles fatigue later.

This delays the neuromuscular changes that lead to cramping.

4. Stretching Susceptible Muscles

Regular stretching of the following appears helpful for athletes who repeatedly cramp:

- Calves
- Hamstrings
- Quadriceps
- Hip flexors

Stretching during a cramp remains one of the fastest ways to stop it.

5. Maintain Carbohydrate Availability

Low muscle glycogen:

- Increases fatigue
- Alters motor neuron firing
- Increases cramp risk

During prolonged activity (>90–120 minutes), 30–60 g carbohydrate/hour, up to 90 g/hour for endurance athletes, can reduce fatigue-related cramping.

6. Adequate Protein Intake

Protein doesn't directly prevent cramps, but it supports:

- Muscle repair
- Recovery
- Resistance to fatigue

For active individuals:

- ~1.2–2.0 g/kg/day depending on training goals

7. Heat Acclimatization

As athletes adapt to heat:

- Sweat becomes more efficient
- Sodium losses decline
- Fatigue decreases

Cramp frequency often decreases after 1–2 weeks of acclimatization.

8. Pickle Juice (Interesting Evidence)

Studies show pickle juice works too quickly, often within 1–2 minutes, for its sodium to reach the bloodstream.

Current theory:

- The strong acidic/sour stimulus activates receptors in the mouth and throat.
- These receptors send signals to the central nervous system that reduce overactive motor neuron firing.

Small amounts (about 1–2 oz or 30–60 mL) can shorten an active cramp.

Similar effects have been observed with:

- Mustard
- Spicy compounds (capsaicin)
- Specially formulated TRP (transient receptor potential) agonist products

These help stop cramps but are less well established for preventing them.

9. Magnesium

Despite its popularity, evidence in healthy athletes is generally poor.

Magnesium supplementation appears beneficial mainly when there is an actual deficiency or in certain groups, such as some older adults or during pregnancy.

Routine magnesium supplementation has not consistently prevented exercise-associated cramps.

10. Sleep and Recovery

Insufficient sleep:

- Increases fatigue
- Reduces neuromuscular control
- May increase cramp susceptibility

Recovery remains an often overlooked component of prevention.

Practical Prevention Strategy

For most active people, the following combination offers the best evidence-based approach:

- Begin exercise well hydrated.
- Replace sodium during prolonged or heavy sweating, especially if you're a salty sweater.
- Match training to the demands of the activity with progressive conditioning.
- Build muscular strength and endurance.
- Consume adequate carbohydrate during long-duration exercise to delay fatigue.
- Eat sufficient daily protein to support recovery.
- Stretch muscle groups that are prone to cramping.
- Allow adequate recovery and sleep.
- For recurrent cramps despite the above, consider carrying a small amount of pickle juice or a TRP-agonist product for rapid relief during activity.

Bottom line

Based on the best available evidence, exercise-induced muscle cramps are best viewed as a problem of fatigued muscle and altered neuromuscular control, with dehydration and electrolyte loss serving as important contributors rather than the sole cause. For athletes and highly active individuals, the most effective long-term prevention strategy is to reduce muscle fatigue through appropriate conditioning, strength training, adequate carbohydrate and protein intake, recovery, and individualized fluid and sodium replacement. Hydration and electrolytes matter, but they work best as part of a comprehensive fatigue-management strategy rather than as stand-alone solutions.

title: In defence of artificial sweeteners - artcle
content:
In Defense of Artificial Sweeteners (medscape.com)

More than 140 million Americans use artificial sweeteners, a habit driven by the irrefutable fact that excess sugar is harmful. But I'm continually amazed by alarmist headlines on the topic.

In May, the World Health Organization (WHO) released a report to support its "conditional recommendation" against the use of non-sugar sweeteners (NSS) for weight control. Despite its goal "to provide evidence-informed guidance," the WHO report includes the disclaimer that "The recommendation is based on evidence of low certainty."

Low certainty is an accurate descriptor for the findings of many of the 280-plus studies in the report. That the guidance does not apply to patients with diabetes was easily lost in the repeated mentions of the perceived dangers of these sugar alternatives.

The review included various tabletop and beverage sweeteners, including acesulfame K, aspartame, saccharin, sucralose, stevia, and stevia derivatives. Low-calorie sugars and sugar alcohols such as erythritol were excluded.

WHO looked at long- and short-term trials, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), prospective studies, and case-control studies measuring a wide range of endpoints, from dental caries to cancer. The report highlighted that some findings cannot be attributed directly to NSS use but may simply be due to their substitution for sugar. Differences in outcomes due to sex, ethnicity, and body weight status could not be assessed either. And WHO conceded the possibility of reverse causation in observational studies wherein higher-risk individuals may consume more NSS.

Nonnutritive sweeteners are given little credit for weight loss. "A significant difference in body weight and BMI was only observed in trials that reported a reduction in energy intake… rather than primarily by an inherent property of NSS that can modulate body weight (independently of energy intake)," the report reads. But isn't the desired effect of using an artificial sweetener instead of table sugar that you lower your calorie intake?

WHO noted that weight loss was not sustained — a finding in nearly every weight loss trial in history and something more attributable to human nature than the sweetener one chooses.

The document outlines that meta-analyses of prospective cohort studies show that higher intakes of NSS were associated with an increased risk for type 2 diabetes and elevated fasting glucose, while meta-analyses of randomized trials suggest no significant effect on "biomarkers used in the assessment and diagnosis of diabetes and insulin resistance, including fasting glucose, fasting insulin and hemoglobin A1c."

Similar disparities are noted with cardiovascular risk. Prospective trials suggest an increased risk for CVD, including stroke and its precursor, hypertension; but again, the RCT data found no evidence to suggest a significant effect "on biomarkers used in the assessment and diagnosis of CVDs, including blood pressure, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and other blood lipids."

Splenda and Stevia Under Fire

Predictably, some in the nonnutritive sweetener industry are incensed.

[NAME], CEO of Heartland Food Products Group, maker of Splenda, responded in a press release, "Every few years now it seems I have to come to you and clarify misleading headlines…Suggesting that sweeteners like Splenda cannot have long-term benefits is a disservice to healthcare providers, their patients, and all consumers."

Splenda has been on the US market since 1999, and [NAME] reportedly uses three to eight packets daily in his coffee and tea.

I reached out to Heartland and they sent me an eight-page document consisting of over 50 statements, summaries, and clinical trials supporting the safety of artificial sweeteners, including sucralose, an ingredient in Splenda. In 2016, [NAME] rebutted claims that sucralose was linked to cancer in Swiss male mice. These "dramatized headlines are based on one flawed study by an isolated Italian research laboratory, the Ramazzini Institute," [NAME] wrote.

Another recent headline was about the DNA-damaging effects of sucralose-6-acetate (S6A) seen in an in vitro study published in the Journal of Toxicology and Environmental Health. According to the authors, commercial sucralose samples contain up to 0.67% S6A, a manufacturing impurity.

Despite many reports linking this study to Splenda, Heartland wrote that "Splenda and its ingredients were never studied or tested in this research. We, and our suppliers, rigorously and routinely test and monitor for any impurities in our products. We can confirm that S6A is not present in Splenda Brand sucralose down to the lowest detection limit possible, which is .001% sensitivity level."

[NAME], MD, director of Clinical and Translational Research Accelerator at Yale and a regular Medscape contributor, took to Twitter to put this study in context: "The human exposure equivalent to sucralose would be 60 packets per day," he pointed out. And the blood levels of S6A with normal consumption would not "come close to the DNA damage threshold noted in the article."

When I asked about these findings, Heartland stated, "The study was primarily conducted on patients who were at an elevated risk of cardiovascular events due to their advanced age, elevated body mass and presence of pre-existing health conditions…the stated findings were only an association and cannot imply causation."

The main conclusion I've drawn on the topic of artificial sweeteners is that a lot of resources were wasted in performing underpowered, poorly designed trials on compounds that are already generally regarded as safe (GRAS) by the FDA. The WHO "conditional guideline" is, by its own description, based on a plethora of "low certainty" to "very low certainty" evidence.

The monies to produce the WHO report and many of these trials would have been better spent educating the public on the difference between simple and complex carbohydrates; the inflammatory and disease-producing effects of excess sugars; and how to prevent, diagnose, and treat diabetes.

If more trials on artificial sweeteners are planned, they should be performed on people doing human things — which does not include ingesting 60 packets of any sweetener in a single day.

In my personal N-of-1 trial, consuming sugar makes me crave more, feel sluggish, and gain weight. I don't believe that NSS alone will control my weight. But I'll continue to drink two cups of stevia-laced coffee every morning, take walks, avoid alcohol, eat my vegetables, and hope for the best.

[NAME], MD is a native Kentuckian who retired from full-time invasive cardiology. She enjoys locums work in Montana and is a champion of physician rights and patient safety. In addition to opinion writing, she enjoys spending time with her husband and daughters, and sidelines as a backing vocalist for local rock bands. Her Heartfelt column was the 2022 regional gold and national silver Azbee award winner.

title: Summary of FH document
content:
This document reviews familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), its diagnosis, genetic aspects, and management strategies to reduce cardiovascular risk.

Overview of Familial Hypercholesterolemia

Genetic disorder impairing LDL clearance, leading to lifelong elevated LDL cholesterol.

Heterozygous FH affects 1 in 250–350; homozygous FH is rarer, about 1 in 160,000–500,000.

Untreated heterozygous FH causes high risk of coronary events by age 50–60.

Assessment and Diagnosis

Clinical diagnosis relies on LDL-C ≥190 mg/dL and family history of premature ASCVD.

Physical signs include tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus, and xanthelasma.

Evaluation includes family history, physical exam, and lipid testing; genetic testing confirms diagnosis.

Cascade screening of relatives is recommended, especially in families with known FH.

Genetic testing targets LDLR, APOB, and PCSK9 genes; it confirms diagnosis and aids cascade screening.

Many with high LDL-C do not have identifiable variants but remain at risk.

Management of Heterozygous FH

Early treatment in childhood offers significant lifetime benefit.

LDL-C goals: less than 70 mg/dL without ASCVD; less than 55 mg/dL with ASCVD.

First-line therapy: high-intensity statins (e.g., rosuvastatin, atorvastatin).

Additional therapies include ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, bempedoic acid, or inclisiran if goals are unmet.

Lifestyle modifications: reduce saturated fats, increase activity, and manage weight.

Homozygous FH

Usually diagnosed around age 12 with LDL-C 400–1000 mg/dL.

Statins are less effective; LDL apheresis and novel agents like evinacumab and lomitapide are used.

These treatments lower LDL independently of LDL receptor function.

Conclusions

Diagnosis is based on LDL-C levels and family history, not solely genetics.

Early pharmacologic intervention is crucial for reducing lifetime cardiovascular risk.

Combination therapy is often necessary to meet LDL-C targets.

Genetic testing supports cascade screening and treatment decisions, especially in high-risk cases.

title: Methylene Blue
content:
Methylene blue (MB)

Takeaway:
Our PTs deliver science-supported baseline dietary support programs, including longevity stacks, which far outperform MB for improving cellular health without the side effects.

More Info
Because it’s shown promise in protecting mitochondria (energy-producing powerhouses of our cells that weaken in aging), people have started to promote methylene blue as a way to slow cellular aging, including in the brain.

MB is legal and FDA-approved as a prescription medication (e.g., for methemoglobinemia—a rare, life-threatening blood disorder where the iron in hemoglobin is oxidized, preventing it from releasing oxygen to body tissues) and as a diagnostic stain, but it is not approved for use as an over-the-counter dietary supplement. While sold online, non-pharmaceutical, unregulated methylene blue carries risks, including unknown contaminants and dangerous interactions with serotonergic drugs, which many people use daily (e.g., antidepressants). Therefore, do not use oral methylene blue products unless prescribed.

The short-term use of a pharmaceutical-grade product in a controlled medical setting is different than buying an illegal supplement off the internet and taking it every day because you’ve heard that it will give you loads of energy by “enhancing mitochondrial efficiency.”

Be aware of serious risks, including serotonin syndrome, birth defects, and haemolysis.

Your business solution: longevity stacks/bundles with proven safe and effective benefits. Moreover, any benefit of MB would be washed out with just the minimal evidence-based longevity program (MVM, omegas, proper protein) or Alln1 SuperBlend™ because of optimal cellular health with all necessary micronutrients.

Key Legal and Safety Facts
Approved Usage: FDA-approved to treat methemoglobinemia—a rare, life-threatening blood disorder where the iron in hemoglobin is oxidized, preventing it from releasing oxygen to body tissues—and used in hospitals for conditions like cyanide poisoning.

Unregulated Supplements: Many methylene blue products sold online as “supplements” for energy or brain health are not evaluated or approved by the FDA for safety or purity.

Legal Status: It is legal for medical, laboratory, and industrial use. However, using unregulated, non-pharmaceutical-grade forms for self-treatment is risky.

Risks: It can cause serious side effects, including serotonin syndrome, particularly if taken with antidepressants (SSRIs/SNRIs).

Contraindications: It should not be used by individuals with a Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.

Always consult a healthcare provider, as unregulated products may contain dangerous impurities.

Methylene blue: a controversial diagnostic acid and medication?
The toxic effects of the application of MB are dose-dependent and include serious symptoms such as hemolysis, methemoglobinemia, nausea and vomitus, chest pain, dyspnoea, and hypertension. Some countries regard MB as harmful because of the resulting skin irritation and triggering of an adverse inflammatory response. MB-induced serotoninergic toxicity clinically manifests as neuromuscular hyperactivity.

Is Methylene Blue A True Brain Booster? A Pharmacologist Explains
Methylene blue is a synthetic dye that exists as a dark green powder and takes on a deep blue color when dissolved in water. My work and that of others suggest that many synthetic dyes widely used in foods and medicines can trigger potentially harmful immune system reactions in the body. But unlike commonly used food dyes—one of which was recently banned by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration—methylene blue is not derived from petroleum, also known as crude oil. Instead, it comes from a different family of dyes, which isn’t thought to have these health concerns.

Methylene blue was first synthesized in 1876 as a dye for textiles and was valued for its intense color and ability to bind well to fabrics. Soon after, German physician [NAME] discovered its ability to stain biological tissues and to kill the parasite that causes malaria—making it one of the first synthetic drugs used in medicine.

The chemical didn’t gain widespread use as a malaria treatment because it was no more effective than quinine, the standard therapy at the time. But in the 1930s, the dye found a new use in testing the safety of raw or unpasteurized milk. If its blue color faded quickly, the milk was contaminated with bacteria, but if it remained blue, the milk was considered relatively clean.

This safety test now is largely obsolete. But it works thanks to methylene blue’s chemical superpower, which is that its molecules can swap electrons with other molecules, like a tiny battery charger.

How Do Doctors Use It Today?
That same chemical superpower enables some of methylene blue’s medical uses. Most significantly, doctors use it to treat a rare blood disorder called methemoglobinemia, in which hemoglobin, an iron-rich protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, takes on a different form that can’t do the job. Methylene blue restores hemoglobin’s function by transferring an electron.

Doctors also sometimes use methylene blue to treat the effects of carbon monoxide poisoning, septic shock, or toxicities from drugs such as chemotherapy. It is also used as a surgical dye to highlight specific tissues such as lymph nodes, or to identify where tissue is leaky and therefore may be damaged.

How Does Methylene Blue Affect The Brain?
Methylene blue can enter the brain by crossing the protective tissue barrier that surrounds it. Researchers have also found that the chemical can protect and support mitochondria, cell structures that are often described as the powerhouses of the cell. Methylene blue may help mitochondria generate energy for cells to use. For these reasons, researchers are studying methylene blue’s effect on the brain.

So far, most of what’s known about the substance’s effects on the brain comes from studies in rats and in cells grown in a lab dish—not in people. For example, researchers have found that methylene blue may improve learning, boost memory, and protect brain cells in rats with a condition that mimics Alzheimer’s disease.

Is Methylene Blue Safe?
Methylene blue is generally safe when used under medical supervision. However, the chemical has some serious risks.

For one thing, it can interact with widely used medications. Methylene blue inhibits a molecule called monoamine oxidase, whose job is to break down an important brain chemical, serotonin. Many commonly used medications for treating anxiety and depression target serotonin. Taking the supplement along with these medicines can cause a condition called serotonin syndrome, which can lead to agitation, confusion, high fever, rapid heart rate, muscle stiffness, and, in severe cases, seizures or even death.

In people with a rare genetic deficiency of an enzyme called G6PD, methylene blue can cause a dangerous condition in which red blood cells break down too quickly. At high doses, the chemical can also raise blood pressure or cause heart problems. Also, it’s considered unsafe for pregnant or breastfeeding women because it may harm the fetus or baby.

Overall, while scientists have found hints of some fascinating properties of methylene blue, much larger, longer trials are needed to know if it truly works, what the right dose is, and how safe it is over time.
